I.Verbal Aspect — the Aorist Tense

Ingressive Aorist

Romans 1:27 — "and the men likewise gave up natural relations with women." The aorist active participle of ἀφίημι ("gave up, abandoned") is ingressive, marking entrance into a state — homosexuality is entered into, not born into, and since entered volitionally it can be exited volitionally.

Romans 13:7 — "Pay to all what is owed to them." ἀποδίδωμι (to render, to discharge an obligation). ἀποδίδωμι (apo + didōmi, to give back what is owed) is in the aorist active imperative, commanding entrance into the state of discharging civil obligations.

Romans 13:12 — "let us cast off the works of darkness." ἀποτίθημι (let us lay aside). The aorist middle subjunctive of ἀποτίθημι is an ingressive aorist, contemplating the action at its initiation: entrance into a new state or condition of priorities. It is not a command to abandon everything outside doctrine but to establish doctrine as the governing first priority.

Romans 14:9 — "that he might be Lord." κυριεύω (to be Lord over). The verb of the purpose clause is the aorist active subjunctive of κυριεύω, to be Lord over, derived from κύριος. It is an ingressive aorist, contemplating the action at its inception: Christ’s entrance into the state of Lordship over each believer at the moment of faith.

Constative Aorist

Gathers an entire action — whether momentary or extended — into a single, undivided whole, viewed from the outside as one entirety.

Romans 1:3 — "concerning his Son, who was descended from David according to the flesh." ἐγένετο ("was born," from γίνομαι) is a constative aorist: it gathers the entire incarnation process — conception, gestation, birth, the giving of the spark of life by the Father — into one completed historical event. Active voice: Christ himself produces the action of becoming.

Romans 1:28 — "since they did not see fit to acknowledge God." ἐδοκίμασαν (negated, "did not see fit," from δοκιμάζω, "to test and approve") is a constative aorist: they rejected God after careful examination — the same root produces ἀδόκιμος ("disqualified") later in the verse, forming a deliberate paranomasia: you tested God and said no; God tests you and gives you a disqualified mind.

Romans 3:3 — "What if some were unfaithful?" ἠπίστησαν ("were unfaithful," from ἀπιστέω) is a constative aorist gathering all Jewish unbelief into a single entirety — an informed, deliberate rejection of the gospel, not mere ignorance.

Romans 3:23 — "for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God." ἥμαρτον ("have sinned," from ἁμαρτάνω) is a constative/gnomic aorist gathering every sin of the entire human race, from Adam's fall to the end of history, into a single axiomatic statement admitting no exception but Christ.

Romans 3:15 — "Their feet are swift to shed blood." The aorist active infinitive of ἐκχέω ("to pour out," with αἷμα, "blood") forms the standing idiom for murder — a momentary act, drawn from Isaiah 59:7.

Romans 1:4 — "and was declared to be the Son of God in power... by his resurrection from the dead." ὁρισθέντος ("having been declared/marked out," from ὁρίζω) is a constative aorist passive participle gathering the entire first-advent package — incarnation, cross, resurrection, ascension, session — into a single decreed whole made in eternity past. (Also treatable under Voice: the passive means Christ received the appointment rather than claiming it.)

Romans 4:2 — "For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about, but not before God." ἐδικαιώθη ("was justified") gathers the hypothetical act of being justified by works into one entirety, implying an entire system of self-righteousness rather than a single deed.

Romans 4:3 — "Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness." Ἐπίστευσεν ("believed") gathers Abraham's act of believing into a single point — instantaneous, non-meritorious faith.

Romans 4:17 — "before the God in whom he believed." ἐπίστευσεν here gathers into one entirety every instance of Abraham's faith-rest across his whole life, not one isolated act.

Romans 4:19 — "he considered his own body, which was as good as dead." κατενόησεν ("considered") gathers Abraham's thirteen-year comprehension of his own condition into a single point of total cognizance.

Romans 4:20 — "No unbelief made him waver concerning the promise of God." διεκρίθη ("waver") gathers the entire thirteen-year period of testing into one point of evaluation: he did not waver, not once, across the whole span.

Romans 4:25 — "who was delivered up for our trespasses." παρεδόθη ("was delivered up") gathers the entire ~three-hour judicial event of the cross into one completed whole.

Romans 5:1 — "since we have been justified by faith." δικαιωθέντες ("having been justified") gathers the whole of salvation adjustment — imputation followed immediately by justification — into one momentary action.

Romans 5:6 — "Christ died for the ungodly." ἀπέθανεν ("died") gathers the approximately three hours of the cross, during which all human sin was imputed to Christ and judged, into a single historical event.

Romans 5:8 — "Christ died for us." The same verb, ἀπέθανεν, again constative — the whole substitutionary event as one completed act.

Romans 5:9 — "Since, therefore, we have now been justified by his blood." δικαιωθέντες here is again constative, gathering the entirety of salvation adjustment into a single completed action.

Romans 5:12 — "so death spread to all men because all sinned." ἥμαρτον ("sinned") gathers the whole human race into Adam's one act: when Adam sinned, the entire race sinned — not personally, but seminally and federally, as all were present in Adam as the federal head.

Romans 5:14 — "even over those whose sinning was not like the transgression of Adam." ἁμαρτήσαντας ("had sinned," a participle) is constative: those living between Adam and Moses did commit personal sins, but those sins are not the issue in view — the reign of death did not depend on them.

Romans 5:16 — "the judgment following one trespass." ἁμαρτήσαντος (a participle behind "trespass") gathers Adam's single act of disobedience into one moment.

Romans 6:2 — "we who died to sin." ἀπεθάνομεν ("died") is a constative aorist referring to a momentary action completed at salvation: the baptism of the Holy Spirit and its result, retroactive positional truth.

Romans 6:3 — "all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death." ἐβαπτίσθημεν ("were baptized") is constative, portraying the whole event as a momentary whole — the instant of salvation adjustment.

Romans 6:4 — "we were buried therefore with him by baptism into death." συνετάφημεν ("were buried with") is constative, referring to a momentary action at salvation, not a process.

Romans 6:6 — "our old self was crucified with him." συνεσταυρώθη ("was crucified with") is constantive, referring to a single completed action at salvation — the co-crucifixion of the old sin nature with Christ.

Romans 6:9 — "Christ, being raised from the dead." ἐγερθείς is constative, gathering the resurrection event as a whole into a single past fact.

Romans 6:10 — "the death he died he died to sin, once for all." The first of two aorist active indicatives of ἀποθνῄσκω here is constative, gathering the entire judicial imputation and judgment of all personal sins into a single whole — the approximately three hours on the cross, viewed in its entirety.

Romans 6:13 (positive command) — "present yourselves to God." The aorist active imperative of παρίστημι spans the entire Christian life as a constative aorist: the action encompasses the period from salvation to physical death or resurrection, with no season during which the command is suspended.

Romans 6:19 — "just as you presented your members as slaves to impurity." παρεστήσατε gathers the entire pre-salvation period — from physical birth to the new birth — into a single unified reality.

Romans 7:2 (protasis) — "if her husband dies she is released from the law." The aorist active subjunctive of ἀποθνῄσκω is constative: it gathers three distinct phases of retroactive positional truth — rejection, separation, and divorce from the first husband — into one unified action.

Romans 7:4 — "you also have died to the law through the body of Christ." Same constative use of ἀποθνῄσκω, gathering identification with Christ in his death, burial, and resurrection into a single completed event.

Romans 7:6 — "we are released from the law, having died to that which held us captive." The aorist participle of ἀποθνῄσκω is constative, viewing the entirety of the baptism of the Holy Spirit — retroactive and current positional truth together — as a single completed event.

Romans 7:7 — "I would not have known sin." The aorist of γινώσκω, negated, gathers Paul's entire prior period of ignorance of the sin nature into a single statement.

Romans 7:11 — "sin... deceived me and through it killed me." The main verbs are constative, gathering the sin nature's entire pattern of deception and killing into a single unified statement of reality.

Romans 8:2 — "the law of the Spirit of life has set you free in Christ Jesus." ἠλευθέρωσεν ("has set free") is constative, gathering the entire action of liberation — the baptism of the Spirit, regeneration, and positional union with Christ — into one unified whole at the instant of salvation.

Romans 8:3 — "he condemned sin in the flesh." κατέκρινεν ("judged/condemned") is constative, gathering the entirety of the judicial imputation of all personal sins in human history to Christ into a single act at the cross — the approximately three hours of his spiritual death.

Romans 8:15 — "you did not receive the spirit of slavery to fall back into fear." ἐλάβετε (negated) gathers into one entirety the negative reality: the believer has not, taken as a whole, received this thing.

Romans 8:29 — "conformed to the image of his Son" (the larger sentence continues with the golden chain). προέγνω ("foreknew") is a constative aorist, gathering into one entirety the eternal foreknowledge of God — not a process but a single, timeless divine act viewed as a whole.

Romans 8:30 — "those whom he justified." ἐδικαίωσεν is constative, gathering the momentary act of imputing divine righteousness at the moment of faith into a single entirety — the second judicial imputation.

Romans 8:32 — "he did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all." παρέδωκεν ("gave him up," from παραδίδωμι) is constative, contemplating the judicial imputation of all personal sins in its entirety — every sin in human history imputed to Christ and judged at one time on the cross.

Romans 9:12 (Genesis 25:23) — "she was told." ἐρρέθη (it was said). errethē is the aorist passive indicative; its root became obsolete and was functionally replaced by the aorist passive of legō. The aorist is constative, viewing the action in its entirety: the single, momentous announcement God made to a pregnant woman before her children were born. The passive voice indicates that Rebecca receives the content of the divine communication; the indicative introduces the citation of Genesis 25:23.

Romans 9:13 (Malachi 1:2–3) — "Jacob I loved." ἀγαπάω (I loved). The aorist active indicative of agapaō is a constative aorist, contemplating the action in its entirety and referring to a condition that has obtained over an extended span of time, from the moment Jacob believed and received the imputation of divine righteousness. The love of God, which always loved His own righteousness, now loves Jacob as the possessor of that righteousness. This is technically an anthropopathism: love here communicates divine approbation, which includes propitiation.

Romans 9:13 (Malachi 1:2–3) — "but Esau I hated." μισέω (I hated). The aorist active indicative of miseō, a mental-attitude term denoting hatred, is again a constative aorist contemplating the action in its entirety. It is an anthropopathism communicating the divine policy of disapprobation toward the unbeliever, not emotional malice but a just outworking of divine holiness against persistent rejection of salvation.

Romans 9:17 (Exodus 9:16) — "and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth." διαγγέλλω (might be proclaimed throughout). The aorist passive subjunctive of diaggellō, dia (through, throughout) plus aggellō (to announce), to proclaim far and wide, is a constative aorist contemplating the action of worldwide proclamation in its entirety. The passive voice indicates that the person of Christ, revealed as Jehovah Elohim in the exodus narrative, receives the action of proclamation; the subjunctive again forms the purpose clause.

Romans 9:20 — "Why have you made me like this?" ποιέω (to make, to manufacture). The verb is the aorist active indicative of ποιέω. The constative aorist contemplates the entire action of creation in its totality. The active voice places the subject (by analogy, the arrogant, unbelieving Jew) as the one producing the interrogation, demanding from God a justification for His creative and redemptive design. οὕτως refers back to what precedes: like this.

Romans 9:22 (Exodus 6–12) — "has endured with much patience." φέρω (to carry, to bear, to endure under pressure). The main verb of the protasis is the aorist active indicative of φέρω: to carry a heavy load, to press against resistance, to endure under pressure. The constative aorist gathers Exodus 6–12 into a single whole; the active voice affirms that God's patient endurance of Pharaoh's successive refusals was His own purposeful act, the active restraint of omnipotence in the service of grace, not passive resignation or impotence.

Romans 9:31 — "did not succeed in reaching that law." φθάνω (to attain, to arrive at, to accomplish). The main verb is the aorist active indicative of φθάνω with οὐ. In classical Attic φθάνω meant to do something first, to arrive before another, to overtake (Homer used it of floodwater overtaking a man digging a ditch); by the Hellenistic period it meant simply to attain, arrive at, accomplish. The constative aorist views Israel's entire sustained attempt to obtain salvation through law-keeping as a single completed whole; the declarative indicative with οὐ emphasizes the non-attainment as an objective historical fact.

Romans 10:5 (Leviticus 18:5) — "the person who does the commandments." ὁ ποιήσας (the man who does, from ποιέω). Ho poiēsas, the articular aorist active participle of poieō, is the precise Greek equivalent of the Hebrew asher ya'aseh of Leviticus 18:5; the article functions as a relative pronoun. The constative aorist contemplates the action in its entirety, a unified whole extended across a period of time: keeping the establishment law. The active voice shows the agent, believer or unbeliever in the client nation, producing the action.

Romans 10:9 — "and believe in your heart." πιστεύω (believe). The second member of the protasis is pisteuō in the aorist active subjunctive. The constative aorist contemplates the act of faith in its entirety, the instantaneous moment anyone believes in Christ; the active voice shows the person producing the action through his own volition; the subjunctive confirms the clause is still the protasis, dependent on free will.

Romans 10:9 — "God raised him from the dead." ἤγειρεν (raised, from ἐγείρω). Ēgeiren, aorist active indicative of egeirō, is a constative aorist contemplating the resurrection in its entirety. The declarative indicative asserts the historical reality of the resurrection of Messiah as objective fact. Egeirō here denotes permanent bodily resurrection, not resuscitation.

Romans 10:14 — "in whom they have not believed." πιστεύω (they have not believed). The subordinate clause uses the constative aorist indicative of pisteuō with ouk. The constative aorist views the entirety of saving faith but regards it from the standpoint of existing results, best captured by the English perfect: in whom they have not believed. The failure is traced to malfunction within the client nation, the failure of believers to advance to maturity and be sent out as qualified proclaimers.

Romans 10:15 — "And how are they to preach." κηρύσσω (to proclaim as a herald). Kēryssō is used for the missionary proclamation of the gospel; the constative aorist gathers the entire missionary activity into one unified action.

Romans 10:16 — "they have not all obeyed the gospel." ὑπακούω (obeyed). Hupakouō is aorist active indicative. The constative aorist gathers the entire period of Israel's client-nation existence, from the Exodus in 1440 B.C. to the fall of Jerusalem in A.D. 70, into a single statement of historical fact.

Romans 10:16 (Isaiah 53:1) — "who has believed." πιστεύω. The aorist active indicative of pisteuō refers to the momentary act of believing or of rejecting. The constative aorist surveys the entire span of Israel's client-nation history and returns the same verdict: not all believed.

Romans 10:18 — "have they not heard?" ἀκούω (heard). The aorist active indicative of akouō is constative, gathering the entire period of Israel's operation as a client nation, from its inception to Paul's writing, into a single whole and asking whether across all that time the Gentiles failed to hear. The interrogative indicative assumes an actual fact that may be stated in answer.

Romans 10:19 — "did Israel not understand?" γινώσκω (to know). Israēl is the nominative subject; the verb is the constative aorist active indicative of ginōskō with ou. The constative aorist gathers into a single statement an action extended over the entire period of Israel's Old Testament history, from the Exodus through A.D. 70. The question, governed by mē, denies the denial: Israel did know, through the ritual system of the Mosaic Law; its unbelief is informed rejection, not ignorance.

Romans 11:4 (1 Kings 19:18) — "I have kept for myself." καταλείπω (I have reserved for myself). The aorist active indicative of καταλείπω, compound of κατά (down, intensive) and λείπω (to leave), is called a constative aorist, viewing the entire act of preservation as a completed whole and regarding the remnant or pivot in its entirety from the standpoint of the existing results.

Romans 11:4 (1 Kings 19:18) — "who have not bowed the knee to Baal." κάμπτω (have not bowed). κάμπτω with the negative οὐκ is an aorist active indicative. The constative aorist views the entire period of sustained pressure as a single fact: the mature believers of the pivot never compromised their maturity through the whole span of the apostasy.

Romans 11:7 — "Israel failed to obtain what it was seeking." ἐπιτυγχάνω (this it did not obtain). Against the continuous seeking stands the negated aorist active indicative of ἐπιτυγχάνω with the emphatic demonstrative οὗτος: this it did not obtain. The constative aorist sums up the whole history of Israel pursuing salvation through works, from Sinai to AD 70, in a single verdict. The active voice makes the unbelieving majority the agent of its own non-attainment through sustained negative volition.

Romans 11:10 (Psalm 69:23) — "let their eyes be darkened." σκοτίζω (let their eyes be darkened). The aorist passive imperative of σκοτίζω is a constative aorist, contemplating the action in its entirety as a fact extended over a period of time. In the passive the eyes of Jewish unbelievers and reversionistic Jewish believers receive the darkening as a consequence of their own reversionism; the eyes are objective perceptive ability, not the physical organs.

Romans 11:11 — "did they stumble." ἔπταισαν (they did stumble, from πταίω). The aorist active indicative ἔπταισαν, to stumble, is a constative aorist contemplating the comprehensive historical reality of Israel stumbling in unbelief and doctrinal rejection. It is distinguished from πίπτω in the purpose clause: Israel stumbled, but did not stumble so as to fall.

Romans 11:14 — "and thus save some of them." σῴζω (to save). The aorist active subjunctive of σῴζω is a constative aorist, gathering into a single perspective the entire scope of Jewish evangelism from AD 70 to the Rapture. The active voice identifies Paul as agent.

Romans 11:17 — "But if some of the branches were broken off." ἐκκλάω (were broken off). The indefinite pronoun with the descriptive genitive of κλάδος (some of the branches) represents a category — Jewish unbelievers in every generation. This is a constative aorist reaching from the Exodus (1440 BC), when Israel became a client nation to God, through the rapture of the church; two dispensations are in view.

Romans 11:19 — "Branches were broken off." ἐκκλάω (were broken off). The aorist passive indicative of ἐκκλάω is constative: it takes the entire period of Israel's client-nation history — from the Exodus to A.D. 70 — and treats it as a single complete event. The passive voice indicates that the unbelieving Jewish branches receive the action through temporal and eternal divine judgment.

Romans 11:22 — "those who have fallen." πίπτω (to fall). The aorist circumstantial participle of πίπτω is constative in force, gathering the entire historical period of Jewish negative volition into a single action without regard to extent or duration. The referent extends across three administrations of the fifth cycle of discipline: the Northern Kingdom (722 BC), the Southern Kingdom (586 BC), and Judea in AD 70.

Romans 11:24 — "For if you were cut from what is by nature a wild olive tree." ἐκκόπτω (you were cut off). The first main verb is the constative aorist passive indicative of ἐκκόπτω (to cut off). The constative aorist contemplates the action in its entirety; the passive voice indicates that Gentile believers receive the action; the declarative indicative asserts a dogmatic reality.

Romans 11:30 — "you were at one time disobedient to God." ἀπειθέω (had not believed). The aorist active indicative of ἀπειθέω (to disbelieve, refuse to believe, disobey through unbelief) is constative, viewing Gentile unbelief in its entirety during the Age of Israel; correctly translated had not believed. The enclitic ποτέ (at one time) anchors it in the past dispensation. The articular dative τῷ θεῷ, in the God, points to the specific, well-known God — the Lord Jesus Christ.

Romans 11:31 — "so they too have now been disobedient." ἀπειθέω (have not believed). The main verb of the apodosis is the aorist active indicative of ἀπειθέω, the same verb used in the protasis. The constative aorist contemplates Jewish unbelief in the church age in its entirety, viewed as a whole: so also now these Jews have not believed.

Romans 11:34 (Isaiah 40:13) — "For who has known the mind of the Lord." γινώσκω (has known). The aorist active indicative of γινώσκω is constative, viewing the action in its entirety, but the emphasis falls on existing results: no one has ever known — no creature in eternity past, and in time only the mature believer who has cracked the maturity barrier. The mood is an interrogative indicative used for the rhetorical question.

Romans 12:1 — "to present your bodies." παρίστημι (place your bodies under orders). The aorist of paristēmi is constative: it gathers every act of rebound and filling of the Spirit across the believer’s life into one operational whole.

Romans 12:3 — "that God has assigned." μερίζω (has assigned). Aorist active indicative of merizō. The standard translation deal is inaccurate; merizō means to divide, to distribute, to assign. It is a constative aorist covering a fact of doctrine extended over the entire course of human history: God the Father has made assignments. The declarative indicative presents it as divine reality.

Romans 12:19 — "but leave it to the wrath of God." δίδωμι (give place). After the adversative alla, the aorist active imperative of didōmi with topon (place) is a constative aorist, contemplating the action in its entirety. Paul’s imperative here carries the force of urgent entreaty rather than bare command, engaging the believer’s volition: deliberately defer to the justice of God.

Romans 13:11 — "for you to wake from sleep." ἐγείρω (to wake up). The aorist passive infinitive of ἐγείρω is a constative aorist, gathering into a single whole all that is involved in orienting to the reality of the Church Age. The passive shows that the believer receives the action: wakefulness comes through the perception and application of doctrine.

Romans 13:11 — "than when we first believed." πιστεύω (we believed). After ὅτε, the aorist indicative of πιστεύω is constative, capturing the single, instantaneous act of saving faith, the moment the believer trusted in Christ alone. From that moment every interval of time has reduced the distance to the rapture by exactly that interval.

Romans 13:12 — "The night is far gone." προκόπτω (has far advanced). προκόπτω means to cut a passage forward, to advance; used of time, that time has moved forward a significant distance. The aorist active indicative is constative, gathering into one entirety the whole of the individual believer's accumulated time on earth. The declarative indicative makes it a dogmatic statement of eschatological imminence.

Romans 13:12 — "and put on the armor of light." ἐνδύω (let us put on). The aorist middle subjunctive of the verb to put on, to clothe oneself with armor is a constative aorist, gathering into one entirety the complete act of perception by which the believer dresses his mentality for the exigencies of life. The direct middle shows direct participation in the results: maturity, capacity for life, and occupation with the person of Christ.

Romans 14:2 — "he may eat anything." ἐσθίω (to eat). The object of the strong believer’s conviction is an aorist active infinitive of ἐσθίω with the direct object πάντα, all things. The constative aorist contemplates the action of eating in its entirety, from the point of doctrinal sufficiency forward through supergrace A, supergrace B and ultra-supergrace.

Romans 14:3 — "for God has welcomed him." προσλαμβάνω (to receive, to admit into friendship). προσλαμβάνω (πρός, toward, into + λαμβάνω, to take, to receive) carries the sense of admitting someone into one’s circle, receiving into friendship or fellowship. The aorist middle indicative is constative: it gathers the entire action into a single whole and refers to the fact that the mature believer has crossed the maturity barrier and entered the status of friend of God.

Romans 14:9 — "Christ died." ἀποθνῄσκω (to die). The aorist active indicative of ἀποθνῄσκω is a constative aorist, gathering the entirety of Christ’s two deaths and burial into a single, unified action: His spiritual death (the imputation and judgment of our sins) together with His physical death and burial. The declarative indicative is an unqualified dogmatic statement of fact.

Romans 14:13 — "but rather decide." κρίνω (determine this). κρίνω reappears as an aorist active imperative with its primary lexical force restored: to separate, distinguish, determine, prefer. The aorist calls for a punctiliar decision, but the context extends that decision over time through the constative aorist. The imperative is a direct command, and with μᾶλλον (rather) and τοῦτο it reads but rather, determine this.

Romans 14:15 — "for whom Christ died." ἀποθνῄσκω (Christ died). The constative aorist active indicative of ἀποθνῄσκω gathers into one entirety Christ's substitutionary death: the judicial imputation of all personal sins to Him on the cross and their judgment by the justice of God the Father. It gathers every sin in human history, past, present at the cross, and future through the close of the Gog and Magog revolution. The indicative is declarative, an unqualified, dogmatic statement of doctrine.

Romans 14:23 — "if he eats." ἐσθίω (if he eats). The verb is the aorist active subjunctive of ἐσθίω, here covering both forbidden foods and forbidden beverages. The constative aorist gathers into a single entirety a succession of acts, each instance in which the weak believer violates his own taboos by emulating the strong believer, without regard to duration or frequency. The aorist simply presents the action as a unified fact.

Romans 15:3 — "For Christ did not please himself." ἀρέσκω (to please, to accommodate). The verb is the constative aorist active indicative of areskō (ἀρέσκω), to please, to accommodate. The reflexive dative heautou (ἑαυτοῦ) specifies that self-accommodation — living to please self — is what Christ refused. The constative aorist gathers the entire thirty-three years of the incarnation into a single fact. The active voice indicates Christ Himself produced this action.

Romans 15:3 — "fell on me." ἐπιπίπτω (to fall upon). The final verb of the quotation is the constative aorist active indicative of the compound epipiptō (ἐπιπίπτω), composed of the preposition epi (ἐπί, on, upon) plus piptō (πίπτω, to fall), meaning fell upon. The constative aorist gathers into one entirety the judicial imputation of all personal sins of the entire human race to Christ at the cross.

Romans 15:4 — "For whatever was written in former days." προγράφω (to write before, to write beforehand). The main verb is the constative aorist passive indicative of prographō (προγράφω), a compound of pro (before) and graphō (to write): to write before, to write beforehand. The constative aorist gathers into one entirety the formation of the Old Testament canon — all of its books written across approximately one millennium, from Moses circa 1441 BC to the completion of Malachi circa 432 BC under the reign of Artaxerxes I Longimanus. The passive voice indicates the canon receives the action of writing — the human authors wrote under the direction of God the Holy Spirit.

Romans 15:5 — "grant you to live in such harmony with one another." δῴη (may give). The main verb is the aorist active optative of didōmi (δίδωμι), 'to give,' rendered here 'may give.' The aorist is constative — it contemplates the action of the verb in its entirety, referring to action extended over a period of time.

Romans 15:7 — "as Christ has welcomed you." προσελάβετο (has received). The verb proslambanō appears again, this time as an aorist middle indicative. The constative aorist contemplates the action of the verb in its entirety, referring to the single momentary act of salvation in which every Church Age believer received all thirty-six divine assets simultaneously. The middle voice is an indirect middle emphasizing Christ as the agent who personally produces the action.

Romans 15:8 — "in order to confirm the promises given to the patriarchs." βεβαιῶσαι (to confirm, to establish). The final infinitive in verse 8 is the aorist active infinitive of the Greek verb bebaioō (βεβαιόω), correctly rendered to confirm or to establish. The aorist tense here functions as a constative aorist, gathering into one unified whole the second advent of Christ, His millennial reign, and the conclusion of the millennium at the Gog revolution — contemplating all of these in their entirety from Paul's present vantage point.

Romans 15:15 — "the grace given me by God." δοθεῖσαν (which has been given). The aorist tense here functions as a constative aorist, viewing the entire span of Paul's reception of grace — from his salvation through the moment of writing — as a single complete act. The passive voice identifies Paul as the recipient: the action originates with God and is directed toward Paul.

Romans 15:21 — "Those who have never been told of him." ἀνηγγέλη (it was reported). With this comes the aorist passive indicative (with negative) of anangellō (ἀναγγέλλω), meaning to report, to announce, to proclaim, to teach. The constative aorist encompasses the entire period of non-proclamation extended through the Tribulation.

Romans 15:24 — "once I have enjoyed your company." ἐμπλησθῶ (I am satisfied). The verb is the aorist passive subjunctive of empiplēmi (ἐμπίπλημι), meaning to be satiated, to be filled with, to be satisfied. The aorist contemplates the action in its entirety: the full course of Paul's teaching and fellowship with the Roman believers.

Romans 15:26 — "have been pleased." εὐδόκησαν (have decided with pleasure). The constative aorist gathers the entire act of deciding and giving into a single unified action, viewed as a whole.

Romans 15:27 — "have come to share in their spiritual blessings." ἐκοινώνησαν (have shared). The verb is the aorist active indicative of koinōneō (κοινωνέω), to share, to participate in. The constative aorist gathers the entire church-age reality into one axiomatic fact: Gentile believers have shared in spiritual things.

Romans 16:17 — "the doctrine that you have been taught." ἣν ὑμεῖς ἐμάθετε (which you have learned). The emphatic nominative plural hymeis (ὑμεῖς) underscores individual responsibility: each believer who has learned doctrine under the ministry of the Holy Spirit. The aorist active indicative of manthanō (μανθάνω) — 'to learn through teaching or instruction, to learn from someone as a teacher' — is a constative aorist, gathering up the entirety of doctrinal instruction received over an extended period into a single fact.

Culminating (Culminative) Aorist

Emphasis falls on the result of the action rather than the action itself; the transaction is gathered into one whole with stress on what flows from it — permanent, existing consequences.

Romans 1:21 — "For although they knew God, they did not honor him as God." ἐγνόντες (from γινώσκω, "knew") is a culminative aorist: it emphasizes the result of accumulated gospel-hearing — the unbeliever came to full cognizance of the issue of Christ, and that cognizance is the basis of his accountability.

Romans 4:3 — "it was counted to him as righteousness." ἐλογίσθη ("was counted/credited") is a culminative aorist: the crediting of righteousness to Abraham's account, a completed transaction with permanent, existing results. Contrast this with the constative aorist of "believed" in the same verse: the act of faith (constative) versus the permanent result of that act (culminative).

Romans 4:9 — "we say that faith was counted to Abraham as righteousness." ἐλογίσθη again, culminative: the same permanent-result force.

Romans 4:10 — "How then was it counted to him?" ἐλογίσθη, culminative — the crediting itself, viewed from its result.

Romans 4:18 — "In hope he believed against hope, that he should become the father of many nations." ἐπίστευσεν here is also called consummative: not a single momentary act but Abraham's entire trajectory of faith through decades of spiritual growth, presented as an existing result.

Romans 4:22 — "That is why his faith was counted to him as righteousness." ἐλογίσθη, culminative, closing the inclusio begun at verse 3 with the identical verb and result.

Romans 5:10 — "we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son." κατηλλάγημεν ("were reconciled") views the entire event of salvation adjustment in its completeness, with emphasis on the existing result: reconciliation, received by the believer at the moment of faith, not produced by him.

Romans 5:20 — "Now the law came in to increase the trespass, but where sin increased, grace abounded all the more." ἐπλεόνασεν ("increased") and ὑπερεπερίσσευσεν ("abounded all the more") are both culminating aorists in sequence: the first views the imputation of Adam's sin in its entirety with the existing result being the multiplication of personal sins across history; the second views the superabundant supply of grace in its entirety with the existing result being that all those sins have been imputed to Christ at the cross.

Romans 5:21 — "so that, as sin reigned in death, grace also might reign through righteousness leading to eternal life." ἐβασίλευσεν ("reigned") is culminative: it views the imputation of Adam's sin to its genetic home at birth in its entirety, then shifts to the existing result — the sovereignty of the sin nature over human life from birth onward.

Romans 6:6 — "so that the body of sin might be brought to nothing." καταργηθῇ ("might be rendered inoperative," a subjunctive) is a culminative aorist, viewing retroactive positional truth in its entirety but emphasizing the existing result: the ruling power of the sin nature has been broken.

Romans 6:10 — "he died to sin, once for all" (second half of the verse's argument). The second aorist of ἀποθνῄσκω in this verse is culminative, viewing the same judicial imputation with emphasis on the existing result: eternal salvation now available to anyone who believes.

Romans 6:18 — "you became slaves of righteousness." ἐδουλώθητε ("you became enslaved") is a culminative aorist viewing the result of the entire process: the mature believer, having exploited imputed righteousness through a system of doctrine, stands as a slave to the righteousness of God.

Romans 7:9 — "when the commandment came, sin came alive and I died." ἀπέθανον ("I died") is culminative — it does not describe a new event of death but the realization of a condition already existing from birth: spiritual death under the imputation of Adam's original sin. Paul was spiritually dead all along; the tenth commandment brought him to awareness of that condition.

Romans 8:4 — "the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us." πληρωθῇ is a culminative aorist (subjunctive): it gathers into one whole every rebound, every filling of the Spirit, every day of doctrinal perception required to crack the maturity barrier, while emphasizing the result — maturity adjustment and the consequent real imputation of blessing.

Romans 8:29 — "those whom he foreknew he also predestined." προώρισεν ("predestined") is culminative, viewing the decrees of God for the church-age believer in their entirety while regarding the result — the last three steps of the five steps to glory.

Romans 8:30 — "those whom he called." ἐκάλεσεν, used in its technical theological sense for election, can also be described as culminative in that it regards the doctrine of election in its entirety from the standpoint of existing result: every Church Age believer is, in fact, elect.

Romans 8:30 — "those whom he justified he also glorified." ἐδόξασεν is constative-culminative, gathering into one entirety both the real imputation of blessing in time at maturity and the real imputation of eternal blessing at the judgment seat of Christ.

Romans 8:32 — "he did not spare his own Son." οὐκ ἐφείσατο (see also Dramatic Aorist below) also functions culminatively, viewing the judicial imputation of all personal sins in its entirety and emphasizing the existing results — the entire complex of Church Age blessing that flows from that completed act.

Romans 9:11 — "had done nothing either good or bad." πράσσω (though they had not accomplished anything). The aorist active participle of prassō is a culminative aorist, viewing the action in its entirety from the standpoint of existing results: absolutely nothing had been accomplished. The participle is again concessive.

Romans 9:17 (Exodus 9:16) — "I have raised you up." ἐξεγείρω (I have caused you to continue in history). The aorist active indicative of exegeirō is culminative: it views the entire historical existence of Amenhotep II as a completed whole, regarded from the standpoint of its existing results, the glorification of God accomplished through and despite Pharaoh's deceitfulness, arrogance and sustained refusal. The active voice indicates Jesus Christ produces the action: the sovereign preservation of God kept Pharaoh in power. The direct object se addresses Pharaoh personally.

Romans 9:17 (Exodus 9:16) — "that I might show my power in you." ἐνδείκνυμι (that I might demonstrate). The aorist middle subjunctive of endeiknymi, en plus deiknymi, to show, to manifest, to demonstrate, is a culminative aorist: it views the demonstration of God's power across all ten confrontations in their entirety, regarded from the standpoint of their existing results, worldwide evangelism. The subjunctive expresses the potential future reference inherent in the purpose clause.

Romans 9:22 — "desiring to show his wrath." ἐνδείκνυμι (to demonstrate). The culminative aorist of the infinitive of ἐνδείκνυμι views the entire sequence of the ten plagues as a completed whole, regarded from the standpoint of the resulting demonstration.

Romans 9:23 — "in order to make known the riches of his glory." γνωρίζω (to make known, to reveal, to inculcate). The principal verb is the aorist active subjunctive of γνωρίζω, which belongs to the stronger Greek vocabulary for genuine cognitive appropriation: reception of information into the soul so that words are formed into concepts and concepts into principles. The aorist is culminative: it views the entire process of making known as a single event but regards it from the standpoint of the existing result, that the audience receives another opportunity to believe in Christ. The active voice identifies God as the producer of the action.

Romans 9:29 (Isaiah 1:9) — "we would have been like Sodom and become like Gomorrah." ἐγενήθημεν; ὡμοιώθημεν (we would have become; we would have been made like unto, from γίνομαι; ὁμοιόω). ἐγενήθημεν, aorist passive indicative of γίνομαι, is a culminative aorist: it views the preservation of Israel in its entirety from the standpoint of its existing results, a pivot of the spiritual seed of Abraham; the passive indicates the racial Jew receives the action. The parallel ὡμοιώθημεν, aorist passive of ὁμοιόω (to make like, cause to resemble), with ἄν views the unreality in its entirety from the standpoint of existing results.

Romans 9:30 — "have attained it." καταλαμβάνω (to seize, to attain, to overtake without effort). The main verb is the aorist active indicative of καταλαμβάνω, kata (down, upon, completely) + lambanō (to take, receive): seizing, winning, attaining, overtaking. In context the force is to overtake without effort, to attain through grace. The culminative aorist views the entire event of Gentile salvation in its completeness while emphasizing the existing result, the imputation of divine righteousness. The active voice makes the Gentile believer the agent, not by striving but by the non-meritorious act of faith.

Romans 9:32 — "They have stumbled over the stumbling stone." προσκόπτω (to stumble against, to trip over). προσκόπτω, pros (against, toward) + koptō (to strike), means to strike against an obstacle, to trip over something in one's path. The aorist active indicative (culminative aorist) views the entire history of Jewish rejection of Christ as a completed action with existing results, the big blot-out; the active voice indicates Israel produced it. The word implies visibility: one stumbles over what one actually sees, so stumbling does not imply ignorance but maximum information and maximum negative volition.

Romans 10:3 — "they did not submit to God's righteousness." ὑποτάσσω (to be subordinate). The main verb is the aorist passive indicative of hupotassō with ou. The passive voice denotes the result of an act of will: they were not caused to be subordinate, that is, they actively refused submission. The culminative aorist views the entire history of the Jewish rejection of the gospel as a completed whole from the standpoint of its existing result.

Romans 10:14 — "they have never heard." ἀκούω (they have not heard). The aorist active indicative of akouō is negated by ouk, the standard negative with the indicative. The culminative aorist views the entire period of common grace, the hearing of the gospel through missionary activity, in its entirety, but from the standpoint of its existing result: the Gentiles have not heard, and the existing condition is ignorance of Christ.

Romans 10:15 — "unless they are sent." ἀποστέλλω (to send out). The verb is apostellō, from which apostolos derives. The culminative aorist emphasizes the existing results: missionaries who have been properly sent produce the existing reality of evangelized populations.

Romans 10:18 (Psalm 19:4) — "Their voice has gone out." ἐξέρχομαι (has gone out). The aorist active indicative of exerchomai is culminative, viewing the totality of God consciousness across all generations and emphasizing the existing result: the voice of nature has gone out and the result stands; there is no generation in which God consciousness has been absent. The same aorist gathers all positive volition across history and presents the existing result: no one positive at God consciousness has lacked gospel information.

Romans 11:1 — "has God rejected his people?" ἀπωθέω (to push away, to refuse, to reject, to repudiate). ἀπωθέω, attested from Homer through the Koine period, is best rendered repudiate. The aorist middle indicative is a culminative aorist, viewing the act of repudiation in its entirety from the standpoint of existing results. The question asks whether God has definitively cast off Israel as His people.

Romans 11:2 — "whom he foreknew." προγινώσκω (whom He has foreknown). The relative pronoun οὕς is followed by the aorist active indicative of προγινώσκω. The culminative aorist views foreknowledge from the standpoint of its existing results; divine foreknowledge encompasses all the history of Israel, including failures and apostasies, and is the basis of the elective commitment of God to His people.

Romans 11:3 (1 Kings 19:10, 14) — "they have killed your prophets." ἀποκτείνω (they have killed). ἀποκτείνω is a compound of ἀπό (away, thoroughly) and κτείνω (to kill); the compound intensifies the action to killing with extreme violence and deliberate brutality. The aorist active indicative is culminative, viewing the whole sequence of deaths from the standpoint of the completed result: the prophets are dead. The active voice assigns the action to the reversionistic northern-kingdom Jews of about 850 BC.

Romans 11:3 (1 Kings 19:10, 14) — "they have demolished your altars." κατασκάπτω (to tear down, to demolish). κατασκάπτω is a compound of κατά (down) and σκάπτω (to dig or tear). The aorist indicative active is culminative: the speaker views the destruction in its totality, regarding the existing results, the altars gone.

Romans 11:7 — "The elect obtained it." ἐπιτυγχάνω (the elected to privilege have obtained it). Of the elect, the aorist active indicative of ἐπιτυγχάνω is called culminative: it views salvation in its entirety but accents the existing results, so that the consequence, privilege, is a present ongoing reality. The active voice indicates that Jewish believers in Christ produce the action.

Romans 11:8 (Isaiah 29:10) — "God gave them a spirit of stupor." δίδωμι (has given). The aorist active indicative of δίδωμι is culminative, viewing the whole process of the spiritual blindness of Israel, the big blot out, as a completed action seen from its result. The giving is an accomplished historical fact with visible present consequences; God gives the state of insensibility as a judicial consequence of sustained negative volition.

Romans 11:10 (Psalm 69:23) — "and bend their backs forever." συγκάμπτω (always cause their backs to bend). The aorist active imperative of συγκάμπτω (σύν, together or completely, plus κάμπτω, to bend) is a culminative aorist, viewing the big blot out in its entirety with emphasis on the result. Paul selects the LXX rendering of Psalm 69:23 for its image of the stooped back of the slave, a chronic posture of the intellect representing slavery of the intellect produced by scar tissue of the soul.

Romans 11:11 — "in order that they might fall." πίπτω (to fall, to fall into ruin). The aorist subjunctive of πίπτω is culminative, viewing the potential falling in its entirety with emphasis on the existing result: the fifth cycle of discipline, which removed client nation Israel in three stages (721 BC, 586 BC, AD 70). Israel stumbled, but not so as to fall.

Romans 11:17 — "were grafted in among the others." ἐγκεντρίζω (to engraft, to graft in). The culminative aorist passive indicative of ἐγκεντρίζω views the event in its entirety from the perspective of its existing results. The passive voice indicates that Gentile believers receive the action: they are grafted in by means of the baptism of the Holy Spirit. In ἐν αὐτοῖς, among them, autos refers to Jewish believers of the church age; the olive tree is a figure for the church as the body of Christ and the royal family of God.

Romans 11:24 — "and grafted, contrary to nature, into a cultivated olive tree." ἐγκεντρίζω (to be grafted in). The culminative aorist passive indicative of ἐγκεντρίζω views Gentile salvation during the entire Church Age as a single whole but emphasizes the existing results at the point of completion. Every Gentile who has believed in Christ during this dispensation is gathered up in this verb, and the emphasis falls on what is now true: membership in the royal family of God.

Romans 11:25 — "until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in." εἰσέρχομαι (has come in). The aorist active subjunctive of εἰσέρχομαι is culminative: it views the fullness of the Gentiles as a whole but regards it from its completing results, namely the resurrection of the church. The active voice: the church age in its entirety produces the action — when it has run its course, it terminates. The subjunctive indicates a potential future event: the rapture had not yet occurred at the time of writing but is certain.

Romans 11:30 — "but now have received mercy." ἐλεέω (you have received mercy). The aorist passive indicative is culminative, viewing Gentile salvation in its entirety from the viewpoint of its existing results: membership in the royal family of God, participation in a Gentile client nation, and eligibility for logistical grace and supergrace blessing. The passive voice: Gentile believers receive mercy from God. The indicative makes a dogmatic statement of Bible doctrine.

Romans 11:34 — "or who has been his counselor?" γίνομαι (has become). The aorist indicative of γίνομαι is culminative: it views the action in its entirety but from the viewpoint of existing results — or who has become. No one can produce the action. The predicate nominative σύμβουλος is one who accompanies another to the council chamber to advise. The mood is the interrogative indicative of the rhetorical question.

Romans 13:13 — "Let us walk properly as in the daytime." περιπατέω (let us walk). περιπατέω is the standard Pauline metaphor for the believer's pattern of life. The aorist subjunctive is a culminative aorist, viewing the entirety of the believer's walk under the Royal Family Honor Code while emphasizing the transition from one sphere of operation to another: from the laws of divine establishment to the higher demands of the honor code.

Romans 14:9 — "and lived again." ζάω (to live). The aorist active indicative of ζάω is a culminative aorist: it views the resurrection of Christ in its entirety but places the emphasis on the existing result, His ascension and present session at the right hand of the Father, where He carries the title κύριος, in full form King of Kings and Lord of Lords (Revelation 19).

Romans 15:9 — "the Gentiles might glorify God." δοξάσαι (to glorify). The infinitive is the aorist active of the verb doxazō (δοξάζω), to glorify. The culminative aorist captures the entirety of that advance and its result.

Romans 15:27 — "For they were pleased to do it." εὐδόκησαν (they decided with pleasure). The verb eudokeō (εὐδοκέω), which appeared in verse 26, is repeated here in the aorist active indicative. The aorist is culminative, viewing the entire process of motivation and decision from start to finish and emphasizing the existing result.

Romans 15:28 — "When therefore I have completed this." ἐπιτελέσας (when I have accomplished). The first participial phrase employs the aorist active participle of epiteleō (ἐπιτελέω), a culminative aorist denoting the attainment of the end of a process. The temporal participle carries action antecedent to the main verb: when I have accomplished this mission, the main action follows.

Romans 16:2 — "and help her in whatever she may need from you." παραστῆτε (you may stand beside, help). The second purpose clause employs the aorist active subjunctive of paristēmi (παρίστημι) — 'to stand beside, to help.' The culminative aorist views the entirety of the help rendered, emphasizing the existing results.

Combinative Aorist

Views an entire, ongoing function as a whole while placing emphasis on the existing result flowing from it — distinguished from the culminative aorist by describing a sustained process (rather than a single transaction) brought to its result.

Romans 4:20 — "he grew strong in his faith." ἐνεδυναμώθη ("grew strong / was strengthened") views the entire, years-long process of Abraham's doctrinal growth as a whole, with emphasis on the existing result: dynamic capacity.

Romans 4:20 — "as he gave glory to God." δοὺς ("having given," an aorist participle) gathers everything that produced Abraham's mature status and presents the result: giving glory to God.

Romans 5:15 — "much more have the grace of God and the free gift... abounded for many." ἐπερίσσευσεν ("abounded," transitive use) is a combinative aorist: it encompasses the entire work of Christ on the cross as a whole while regarding it from the standpoint of its existing results — potential, capacity, and reality all at once.

Romans 15:11 — "and let all the peoples extol him." ἐπαινεσάτωσαν (let them applaud, let them laud). The second verb in the quotation is from epaineō (ἐπαινέω), formed by the prefix epi- added to aineō. The prefix carries the sense of applauding — an overt, outward manifestation of an inward attitude. The combinative aorist tense views the worship in its entirety but regards it from the viewpoint of existing results — the mature believer applauds.

Dramatic Aorist

States the present reality of a past event with the rhetorical vividness and certitude the dramatic perfect ordinarily supplies — the aorist counterpart to the dramatic perfect, used to make an already-decided doctrinal reality feel immediate and settled.

Romans 7:11 — "sin... deceived me." ἠπάτησεν is a dramatic aorist, emphasizing the present reality of the sin nature's aggression: it does not passively receive the commandment but actively seizes it as a base of operations.

Romans 8:30 — "those whom he called" (twice in this verse, and echoed at 8:28's "called according to his purpose"). ἐκάλεσεν (aorist of καλέω, in its technical theological sense for election) is a dramatic aorist: it states the present reality of election with the certitude of a past event fixed in the divine decrees.

Romans 8:32 — "he did not spare his own Son." οὐκ ἐφείσατο is a dramatic aorist bringing the judicial imputation of sin at the cross into sharp, vivid focus.

Romans 10:21 (Isaiah 65:2) — "I have held out my hands." ἐκπετάννυμι (I have extended). The aorist active indicative of ekpetannymi, to extend or stretch out, an imploring gesture of invitation. The dramatic aorist states a present reality with the certainty of a past event: this has gone on since Moses and continues to the present. The active voice: the Lord Jesus Christ produces the action; as an anthropopathism the gesture captures the intensity and persistence of Christ's personal evangelism of Israel.

Romans 11:3 — "and I alone am left." ὑπολείπω (to be left, remaining). The aorist passive indicative of ὑπολείπω is a dramatic aorist, stating a present reality with the certitude of a completed event and giving the clause a feeling of finality. In the passive Elijah receives the action of remaining through logistical grace, though he does not frame it that way.

Romans 12:3 — "by the grace given to me." δίδωμι (which has been given). The participle from didōmi is a dramatic aorist, stating a present reality with the certitude of a past event; it covers a completed result and is translated as a perfect, which has been given. The passive voice makes the mature believer the recipient; membership in the human race is itself a grace provision, and from salvation onward grace multiplies through logistical support, supergrace A, supergrace B, and ultra-supergrace.

Romans 15:10 — "Rejoice, O Gentiles, with his people." εὐφράνθητε (be glad, rejoice). The verb rendered rejoice is the aorist passive imperative of euphrainō (εὐφραίνω). In the active voice euphrainō means to cheer someone up; in the passive it means to be glad, to enjoy oneself, to be merry, to experience elevated and stimulating happiness. This is not the standard Greek word for rejoice; the more common term would be a form of chairō (χαίρω). The dramatic aorist tense states a present reality with the certitude of a past event — an idiom traceable to the parent Indo-European language family and used here for emphasis.

Romans 15:20 — "not where Christ has already been named." ὠνομάσθη (has been mentioned). The negative adverbial phrase combines the negative particle οὐ with the particle of place ὅπου (hopou): not where. The verb is the aorist passive indicative of ὀνομάζω (onomazō), meaning to name or to mention; in the passive voice, to be known, to be mentioned. The dramatic aorist states Paul's policy with the certitude of an accomplished fact — a present reality expressed with the force of a past event: not where Christ has been mentioned.

Romans 15:23 — "to come to you." ἐλθεῖν (to come). The dramatic aorist presents a present reality with the certainty of a completed event — Paul is as good as already on his way.

Romans 15:26 — "to make some contribution." ποιήσασθαι (to make). The aorist middle infinitive of poieō (ποιέω) means simply to do, to make, to produce. The dramatic aorist states a present reality with the certitude of a past event — the offering is already being assembled and will be delivered.

Romans 16:19 — "For your obedience is known to all." ἀφίκετο (has become known). The verb is aorist middle indicative of the compound aphikneomai (ἀφικνέομαι), formed from apo (ἀπό) + hikneomai (ἱκνέομαι, to come, to arrive). It means to reach or to become known to. The aorist is a dramatic aorist: it states a present reality with the certitude of a completed past event, used here for emphasis as Paul, in greeting these mature believers, suddenly recognizes what they share in common.

Romans 16:26 — "but has now been disclosed." φανερωθέντος δὲ νῦν (but now revealed). The verb is the aorist passive participle of phaneroō (φανερόω) — 'to make manifest, to reveal, to disclose.' The aorist tense here is a dramatic aorist, stating a present reality with the certainty of a completed event: but now is revealed.

Gnomic Aorist

States an axiomatic, timeless truth, without reference to a specific past occurrence.

Romans 1:21 — "they became futile in their thinking." ἐματαιώθησαν ("were made futile," passive) is a gnomic aorist passive, stating an axiomatic fact as an invariable present reality: worthless and evil thoughts enter the vacuum left by rejected truth.

Romans 4:21 — "fully convinced that God was able to do what he had promised." ποιῆσαι ("to do/accomplish," an infinitive) is gnomic: an axiomatic truth about God's ability in general, not a reference to one past act.

Romans 8:37 — "through him who loved us." The articular aorist active participle of ἀγαπάω here is a gnomic aorist: a fact so fixed in its certainty as to be axiomatic — by Greek idiom this is properly rendered in the English present tense, "who loves us," not "who loved us" as a single past act. God's love for his own righteousness, which every believer possesses through imputation, is timeless, not a completed historical event.

Romans 9:14 — "By no means!" γένοιτο (emphatically no, from γίνομαι). In mē genoito the aorist of ginomai is gnomic, stating a timeless, absolute denial rather than a single past event. The active voice produces the action of strong negation.

Romans 11:9 (Psalm 69:22) — "Let their table become a snare." γίνομαι (may it become). The main verb is the aorist passive imperative of γίνομαι. The aorist is gnomic, describing a truth so axiomatic that it is treated as already occurring; in the passive the spiritual heritage of Israel receives the action of becoming a snare and trap.

Romans 12:6 — "the grace given to us." δίδωμι (given). The aorist passive participle of didōmi is a gnomic aorist, expressing not a single past event but a truth so fixed and axiomatic that the aorist captures its certainty; it is rendered by the English simple present. The passive voice: at salvation God the Holy Spirit bestows the gift.

The Aggressive Negative with the Aorist Participle

μή with the aorist participle contemplates the action at its very point of beginning; the negative denies that it even started — stronger than a negation of an ongoing or completed process.

Romans 4:19 — "He did not weaken in faith." μὴ ἀσθενήσας ("not having weakened") is not merely "he did not become weak" over time, but "he did not begin to falter" — there was no onset of doubt at all.

The Articular Aorist Infinitive — A Specific Occasion

Romans 14:21 — "not to eat meat or drink wine." τὸ μὴ φαγεῖν (not to eat meat in a specific situation, from ἐσθίω). The aorist tense of the infinitive is critical. The articular aorist infinitive used as a noun refers to a specific, punctiliar situation, a single occasion; the articular present infinitive refers to a general, continuous situation. The aorist therefore rules out any idea of permanent abstinence. The same holds for the aorist infinitive of πίνω (to drink) with οἶνος.

The Epistolary Aorist

Romans 15:15 — "I have written to you very boldly." ἔγραψα (I have written). With it comes the aorist active indicative of graphō (γράφω), to write. This is an epistolary aorist: the writer places himself in the position of his reader and describes as past what is present to himself but will be past by the time the letter is received.

II.Verbal Aspect — the Perfect Tense

Intensive Perfect

Emphasizes the present, standing reality of a completed past action — the strongest available affirmation in Greek that a given state of affairs obtains.

Romans 2:24 — "as it is written." γέγραπται ("it stands written," from γράφω) is a dramatic/intensive perfect passive indicative: a completed action whose results continue permanently — the Old Testament citation (Isaiah 52:5, LXX) carries ongoing, standing force as an expression of divine integrity.

Romans 3:13 — "their throat is an open grave." The perfect passive participle of ἀνοίγω ("opened") is an intensive perfect (perfect of existing state): the tomb has been opened and remains open, with everything that implies about the condition within.

Romans 4:1 — "What then shall we say was gained by Abraham... has found?" εὑρηκέναι ("has found," a perfect infinitive) carries abiding, present force for the argument — not merely "what did Abraham find" in the past, but what he stands as having found, with continuing relevance now.

Romans 4:14 — "faith is null and void, and the promise is void." κεκένωται ("is null and void") is an intensive perfect: faith would stand voided with the result that it is permanently invalidated — the strongest possible affirmation of a settled state.

Romans 5:2 — "we have obtained access." ἐσχήκαμεν ("we have obtained," perfect active of ἔχω) emphasizes a completed action whose results continue permanently: salvation adjustment is an accomplished fact, and as a result the believer now has — and always will have — access into the presence of God.

Romans 5:2 — "this grace in which we stand." ἑστήκαμεν ("we stand," perfect active of ἵστημι) is a dramatic use of the intensive perfect: a vivid assertion that the believer stood in the past and keeps on standing forever — the grammatical anchor of eternal security in this verse.

Romans 6:5 — "if we have been united with him in a death like his." γεγόναμεν (intensive perfect of γίνομαι) directs attention to the existing results of a completed action: the believer has become intimately united to the likeness of Christ's death, and that union permanently stands. The action is complete; the results are present and abiding.

Romans 9:19 — "For who can resist his will?" ἀνθίστημι (who has resisted?). The verb is ἀνθίστημι, perfect active indicative, a compound of anti (against) + histēmi (to stand): to stand against, oppose, resist. The perfect is the intensive perfect (the dramatic perfect), emphasizing the abiding result of a completed action. The active voice treats the human race generally as the agent; the interrogative indicative assumes a definite, factual answer, implying that no one has ultimately succeeded in thwarting the divine purpose.

Romans 9:25 (Hosea 2:23) — "and her who was not beloved." ἀγαπάω (those who have not been loved). The first participial form of ἀγαπάω is the perfect passive participle with the strong negative οὐ: those who have not been loved. The intensive perfect emphasizes completed action with existing results: the completion of the fifth cycle of discipline in A.D. 70, resulting in the ongoing condition of the Times of the Gentiles. The passive indicates the Jewish nation receives the action, the object of God's covenantal love withheld in disciplinary judgment.

Romans 9:29 (Isaiah 1:9) — "And as Isaiah predicted." προλέγω (to speak beforehand, to prophesy; has prophesied). The verb is the perfect active indicative of προλέγω, pro (before) + legō (to speak): to speak beforehand, to prophesy. The intensive perfect indicates completed action with continuous existing results: Isaiah's prophecy was completed under the ministry of the Holy Spirit, and its results, the canonical text, stand permanently and retain force in every generation to which its principle applies.

Romans 9:33 — "as it is written." γέγραπται (it stands written, from γράφω). γέγραπται is the perfect passive indicative of γράφω. The intensive perfect emphasizes the existing results of the act of writing: the Old Testament canon stands as a finished product with continuing authority. The passive voice reflects the mechanics of inspiration: God the Holy Spirit communicated to the human author so that the divine message was recorded with perfect accuracy. It is used formulaically to introduce Old Testament quotations.

Romans 11:8 — "just as it is written." γράφω (it stands written). The perfect passive indicative of γράφω is an intensive perfect, the perfect of existing state, emphasizing the permanent and abiding results of a completed action: the Old Testament canon stands written as a completed and authoritative whole. The passive voice indicates that the human writers received the action of divine inspiration.

Romans 11:20 — "but you stand fast through faith." ἵστημι (you stand). The perfect active indicative of ἵστημι is an intensive perfect, denoting a completed action with emphasis on existing results: at salvation the justice of God imputed divine righteousness to the believer, establishing a pipeline from divine justice to divine righteousness through which logistical grace flows — and, for the mature believer, supergrace blessing. The believer stands on the integrity of God, not on race, talent, or moral achievement.

Romans 12:19 (Deuteronomy 32:35) — "for it is written." γράφω (it stands written). The perfect passive indicative of graphō is an intensive perfect, a perfect of existing state, emphasizing the permanent, unaltered results of a completed action: the Old Testament canon stands as an enduring and authoritative document, and Paul here formally recognizes it as canonical. The passive voice encodes the mechanics of inspiration.

Romans 13:1 — "have been instituted by God." τάσσω (have been delegated). The final verb complex is a perfect periphrastic: present active indicative of εἰμί with the perfect passive participle of τάσσω (to put someone in charge, to delegate authority). The intensive perfect emphasizes the existing, permanent results of the laws of divine establishment throughout human history; the passive shows that delegated authority receives the action and does not generate itself.

Romans 13:8 — "has fulfilled the law." πληρόω (has fulfilled). The perfect active indicative of πληρόω (to fill up a deficiency) is a perfect of existing state: past completion drops out of the thought and the existing results are emphasized. The believer who exercises impersonal love stands in the condition of having filled up the Mosaic law, in its negative ethical commands, not its ceremonial or christological sections.

Romans 13:11 — "you know the time." οἶδα (by having known). The perfect active participle of οἶδα is an intensive perfect (also called the perfect of existing state): the completed past action recedes and the focus falls on the resulting condition. The existing state is knowledge, doctrine learned and now resident in the soul.

Romans 13:12 — "the day is at hand." ἐγγίζω (has drawn near). The perfect active indicative of ἐγγίζω is an intensive perfect, emphasizing the existing result of the approach: the day is not merely coming; it has already drawn close and stands in proximity. The Greek perfect in this emphatic use is often rendered by an English present to capture an established existing state. The theological force is imminence.

Romans 14:11 — "For it is written." γράφω (it stands written). The verb is the perfect passive indicative of γράφω. The intensive perfect emphasizes an existing result as a finished product: the Old Testament canon stands written with permanent authority. The passive voice captures the mechanics of inspiration, and the declarative indicative asserts the plenary verbal inspiration of Scripture.

Romans 14:23 — "is condemned." κατακρίνω (has already been condemned and is in a state of condemnation). The apodosis uses the perfect passive indicative of κατακρίνω, an intensive perfect directing attention to the existing state produced by a past action. It approximates the English present but with greater force: has already been condemned and is in a state of condemnation. The passive shows the weak believer receiving condemnation, not from an external verdict but from his own conscience; the indicative presents it as actual reality.

Romans 15:3 — "but as it is written." γράφω (it stands written). The comparative adverb kathōs (καθώς) introduces a comparison with Scripture, functioning as a standard formula for Old Testament documentation. The verb is the intensive perfect passive indicative of graphō (γράφω), correctly rendered as it stands written. The perfect tense emphasizes an existing fact: the Old Testament canon stands written as a permanent reality, the product of the Holy Spirit directing human authors. The passive voice indicates the canon receives the action — it was written through the ministry of the Spirit.

Romans 15:9 — "As it is written." γέγραπται (it stands written). Verb: gegraptai (γέγραπται), perfect passive indicative of graphō (γράφω): it stands written. The intensive perfect emphasizes the permanent, authoritative existence of the Old Testament scriptures as the Word of God.

Romans 15:14 — "I myself am satisfied about you." πέπεισμαι (I am convinced). The verse opens with the perfect passive indicative of the verb peithō (πείθω), meaning to persuade, to obey, to believe; in the passive voice, to be persuaded or convinced. The intensive perfect emphasizes existing results, directing attention to the present state produced by past action. It is correctly rendered I am convinced.

Romans 15:21 — "but as it is written." γέγραπται (it stands written). Following alla comes the adverb kathōs (καθώς), translated just as, which draws an explicit comparison between Paul's policy and the content of the quotation. Then comes the perfect passive indicative of graphō (γράφω), the standard New Testament formula for citing Scripture: it stands written. The intensive perfect emphasizes completed canonical action with enduring results — the Old Testament canon stands as written and its authority is permanent.

Romans 15:21 — "those who have never heard." ἀκηκόασιν (they have heard). The perfect tense of existing state focuses not on the past action of not hearing but on the present condition that results: they are in a state of not having heard.

Romans 16:7 — "they were in Christ before me." πρὸ ἐμοῦ γέγοναν (they have been before me). The final clause employs a perfect active indicative of ginomai (γίνομαι), 'to be, to become.' The intensive perfect tense presents an action completed in the past with results that perpetually remain: they have been in Christ, and always will be, prior to Paul. The preposition pro (πρό) plus the ablative singular of egō (ἐγώ), 'before me,' completes the construction.

Dramatic Perfect

Emphasizes the existing state resulting from a completed action, stated with rhetorical vividness — used especially for citation formulas and declarations of fact.

Romans 1:1 — "set apart for the gospel of God." ἀφωρισμένος ("having been set apart," from ἀφορίζω, a compound of ἀπό + ὁρίζω) is a dramatic perfect passive participle: the completed, irreversible act of divine appointment on the Damascus road, carried forward as a present, ongoing reality. Passive voice: Paul receives the appointment; God executes it.

Romans 4:17 — "As it is written." γέγραπται is better rendered "as it stands written," not merely "it was written": the canonical text stands in a permanent, present state of authority.

Romans 4:18 — "as he had been told." εἰρημένον ("that which had been spoken") stresses the promise's still-valid, undiminished force.

Romans 4:19 — "his own body, which was as good as dead." νενεκρωμένον ("as good as dead," literally "having been deadened") describes Abraham's body vividly and realistically, with the state persisting to the narrative present.

Romans 4:25 (and Romans 5:8, and John 19:30 as the source citation) — "It is finished." τετέλεσται is the rhetorical use of the intensive perfect, emphasizing that the saving work was completed in its entirety while Christ was still physically alive.

Romans 5:5 — "God's love has been poured into our hearts." ἐκκέχυται ("has been poured out," perfect passive of ἐκχέω) is a dramatic perfect: the action is completed, and the results are permanent and ongoing, saturating the right lobe of the soul through the daily function of doctrine intake.

Romans 6:7 — "one who has died has been set free from sin" (ESV) / "has been acquitted." δεδικαίωται (perfect passive of δικαιόω) is the Greek idiom for presenting the permanent, unalterable character of positional truth: no post-salvation sin, human good, or involvement in evil can revoke this judicial verdict of acquittal from the power of the sin nature.

Romans 7:2 — "a married woman is bound by law to her husband." δέδεται (perfect passive of δέω, "to bind") is a dramatic perfect: from the moment the woman marries, the binding is in effect not provisionally but as a fixed, continuing reality — strong rhetorical emphasis on permanence.

Romans 9:13 (Malachi 1:2–3) — "As it is written." γράφω (it stands written). The perfect passive indicative of graphō, it stands written, is the dramatic or resultative perfect: the action of inscription is complete and its results remain permanently in force, emphasizing the abiding authority of the inscripturated word. The passive voice identifies the human author, the prophet Malachi, as receiving the action, while the ultimate author is the Spirit of God.

Romans 9:22 — "prepared for destruction." καταρτίζω (to equip, prepare, fit out; having been equipped). The critical term is the perfect passive participle of καταρτίζω (katērtismena), KJV fitted to destruction. Its semantic range includes preparing stage machinery, equipping an army, outfitting a fleet, mending nets and setting broken bones. The perfect (dramatic perfect) emphasizes the completed state of unbelief resulting from cumulative negative volition. The passive indicates the vessel receives this equipping through its own negative volition, not through divine action: God does not prepare the vessel of wrath; it prepares itself.

Romans 9:25 (Hosea 2:23) — "I will call 'beloved.'" ἀγαπάω (as those who have been loved). The second participial form of ἀγαπάω is the dramatic perfect passive, emphasizing the results of restoration: the second advent and millennial reinstatement of Israel as a client nation.

Romans 10:15 (Isaiah 52:7) — "As it is written." γράφω (it stands written). The perfect passive indicative of graphō, it stands written, is a dramatic perfect emphasizing the abiding results of the completed action of inscription: the canon was written, stands written, and its authority perdures. The passive shows Isaiah 52:7 receiving the action; the declarative indicative affirms the reality of the quotation and of verbal plenary inspiration.

Romans 11:5 — "there is a remnant." γέγονεν (has come into existence, from γίνομαι). γέγονεν, perfect active indicative of γίνομαι, is a dramatic perfect, emphasizing the existing results of a past completed action: a pivot has come into existence and remains in existence. The implication is that no generation of history has been without mature believers; the pivot is a permanent structural feature of the divine administration of history.

Romans 11:25 — "a partial hardening has come upon Israel." γίνομαι (has happened). The perfect active indicative of γίνομαι is a dramatic perfect, describing a past fact with vivid present force and emphasizing the abiding results. The active voice indicates that the hardening — the scar tissue of the soul — produces the action: the rejection of truth is self-generated, not divinely imposed.

Romans 13:2 — "and those who resist." ἀνθίστημι (they who oppose). The perfect active participle of ἀνθίστημι is a dramatic perfect, a rhetorical use of the intensive perfect emphasizing the existing state of those described. The force is not that they once resisted but that opposition has become their settled condition; it characterizes them.

Romans 15:14 — "filled with all knowledge." πεπληρωμένοι (having been filled). The phrase 'filled with all knowledge' renders the perfect passive participle of plēroō (πληρόω), meaning to fill or to complete. The dramatic perfect emphasizes a completed action with enduring results: having been filled. Past cycles of doctrinal intake have produced a present state of fullness.

Romans 15:19 — "I have fulfilled the ministry of the gospel of Christ." πεπληρωκέναι (I have fulfilled). The accusative of general reference from the personal pronoun egō (ἐγώ) functions as the logical subject of the infinitive: I have fulfilled. The tense is the dramatic perfect — a rhetorical application of the intensive perfect — which describes an action completed in the past whose results continue into the present.

Romans 16:25 — "the mystery that was kept secret for long ages." σεσιγημένου (having been concealed). The perfect passive participle of the verb σιγάω (sigaō) — 'to conceal, to keep silent' — governs the phrase 'which has been concealed.' The perfect tense is a dramatic perfect, the rhetorical use of the intensive perfect, indicating a completed state with ongoing effect: this information was sealed and remained sealed across the whole of prior human history.

Perfect-as-Present

A perfect tense functioning grammatically like a present, describing a state of knowledge or condition established in the past that is currently, operatively true — distinct from the dramatic perfect in that the emphasis falls on ongoing present function rather than rhetorical vividness about a completed act.
