Romans 2:2 — "We know that the judgment of God rightly falls on those who practice such things." οἴδαμεν ("we know," from οἶδα) is morphologically a perfect functioning as a present in Koine Greek — a perfective present indicative: the mature believer has arrived at this knowledge through sustained doctrine intake, and it abides as a present operational reality.

Romans 3:19 — "Now we know that whatever the law says it speaks to those who are under the law." οἴδαμεν again functions as a perfective present (see Romans 2:2 above), the settled, abiding knowledge of the mature believer.

Romans 6:9 — "We know that Christ, being raised from the dead, will never die again." εἰδότες (perfect active participle of οἶδα, "to know") functions as a present: a state of knowledge already established and currently operative. The tense assumes inculcation — the apostle writes to believers who have already learned this doctrine, and assumes that learning has produced a current, operative state of cognizance.

Romans 7:18 — "For I know that nothing good dwells in me." οἶδα here is likewise perfect-as-present, and combined with the inferential particle γάρ signals that Paul's self-knowledge is settled, complete, and objective — the capacity for such objectivity is itself a product of doctrinal advance.

Romans 8:26 — "we do not know what to pray for as we ought." οἴδαμεν (negated) is perfect-as-present: the perfective present force here denotes the continuation of ignorance regarding proper prayer specifically in the context of undeserved suffering — not a moral failure, but a condition inherent to the situation itself.

Romans 8:16 — "the Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit." The historical present of συμμαρτυρεῖ carries a comparable perfective force to the perfect-as-present verbs above: continuation of existing results, the Spirit's testimony ongoing rather than a single past event, even though it is formally a present rather than a true perfect.

Romans 11:2 — "Or do you not know." οἶδα (to know). The perfect of οἶδα is used as a present and denotes settled, perceptive knowledge, knowledge acquired and remaining in a settled state of possession, distinct from γινώσκω, which emphasizes the process of coming to know. With the negative it forms a rhetorical challenge: the answer to whether God has rejected His people is already available in Scripture and has been all along, so ignorance of it is not excusable in those who have access to the Word.

Romans 14:14 — "I know." οἶδα (I know). οἶδα is a perfect active indicative functioning as a present tense of abiding confidence. It denotes intuitive or complete knowledge, fully assimilated rather than in process of being learned, and here signals the application of maximum doctrine perception: the mature believer knows with the certainty that doctrinal norms lodged in the conscience produce.

Romans 15:29 — "I know that when I come to you." οἶδα (I know). The governing verb is oida (οἶδα), a perfect form functioning as a present tense — a well-recognized pattern in Hellenistic Greek. Oida denotes knowledge that arises from perception and has been fully internalized: I know with settled certainty.

The Perfect of Settled Confidence

A perfect tense (of a verb of persuasion or conviction) denoting a state of confidence established in the past and continuing, unshaken, into the present — distinguished from ordinary perfect-as-present usage by the specifically volitional/emotional content of the settled state.

Romans 2:19 — "and if you are sure that you yourself are a guide to the blind." πέποιθας ("you are confident/persuaded," from πείθω) is perfective-present in force: a settled confidence whose results persist into the present — the self-righteous legalist has established, and persists in, a false confidence about his standing.

Romans 8:38 — "For I am sure that neither death nor life..." πέπεισμαι (perfect passive of πείθω, "to persuade") carries the connotation of settled, unshakeable confidence — a confidence entirely divorced from self and circumstance, grounded instead in the plan and provision of God through doctrine resident in the soul, not a fluctuating feeling.

Romans 14:14 — "am persuaded." πείθω (have received confidence). In the perfect tense πείθω denotes an existing state: doctrine has been perceived in the past and now resides in the conscience as operative norms. The passive voice indicates that the mature believer receives confidence from the absolutes of doctrinal norms rather than generating it from personal opinion; it is settled doctrinal conviction, not tentative opinion.

The Pluperfect Functioning as an Imperfect of Duration

Because οἶδα is already a perfect tense used with present force, its pluperfect form does not carry the usual "had done" sense; instead it functions as an imperfect of duration, describing a state of ignorance persisting up to a specific past point.

Romans 7:7 — "I would not have known what it is to covet." ᾔδειν (pluperfect of οἶδα) functions as an imperfect of duration: Paul's ignorance of the lust pattern persisted up to the specific moment he encountered and processed the tenth commandment — not a single past failure to know, but an extended state of not-knowing.

Consummated Perfect

Places equal weight on the process leading up to completion and on the existing result — distinguished from the intensive perfect (which stresses the settled state alone) and from the culminative aorist (which stresses the result of a single transaction).

Romans 4:14 — "the promise is void." κατήργηται ("is void") places equal stress on the process of cancellation and its ongoing consequence.

Romans 4:17 — "I have made you the father of many nations." τέθεικα ("I have made/appointed," quoting Genesis 17:5) has God speaking as though every son, every nation, every generation of Abraham's progeny is already complete — reviewing the entire future process and presenting it as accomplished, spoken at a moment of total biological impossibility.

Romans 9:6 — "the word of God has failed." ἐκπίπτω (has failed). ekpiptō is a perfect active indicative used of the alleged failure of the Word of God, an allegation Paul refutes. The perfect tense is consummative.

Romans 13:2 — "resists what God has appointed." ἀνθίστημι (have opposed). The perfect active indicative of ἀνθίστημι is a consummate perfect: completed action with abiding results. It is not a single act of rejection or a momentary lapse but a consummated process of opposition whose consequences are now in effect, a settled state reached by a completed trajectory.

Romans 15:8 — "Christ became a servant to the circumcised." γεγενῆσθαι (has become). The consummative perfect emphasizes a completed action whose results are in effect: Christ has become and remains a minister.

Iterative Perfect

Denotes an action or state recurring at intervals, rather than continuously.

Romans 4:21 — "what he had promised." ἐπήγγελται ("he had promised") indicates the promise was made at intervals, not constantly repeated: a mature believer does not require continuous reassurance, and the grammar itself reflects that.

III.Verbal Aspect — the Present Tense

Static Present

Represents a condition as a fixed, unqualified, timeless reality.

Romans 1:9 — "For God is my witness." A static present of εἰμί-type force underlies Paul's appeal — a present tense denoting an unqualified, timeless fact rather than a momentary state.

Romans 1:16 — "for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes." ἔστιν here is a static present of εἰμί: the gospel dogmatically and perpetually is the ability (δύναμις) of God, not merely an occasional demonstration of it.

Romans 1:18 — "For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness." The same verb ἀποκαλύπτεται recurs, now as a static present: the just anger of God perpetually exists as the standing posture of divine justice toward the maladjusted — without variation, without exception.

Romans 4:4 — "his wages are not counted as a gift but as his due." οὐ λογίζεται ("is not counted") states the wage principle as a flat, timeless fact.

Romans 4:5 — "his faith is counted as righteousness." λογίζεται ("is counted") asserts the crediting of righteousness as dogmatic reality.

Romans 4:5 — "believes in him who justifies the ungodly." δικαιοῦντα ("justifies," a participle) presents this as a perpetually existing divine activity/character, not a one-time event.

Romans 4:16 — "that the promise may rest [be secure]." εἶναι in this construction presents the promise's security as a perpetually existing condition established at the moment of faith.

Romans 4:21 — "that God was able." δυνατός ἐστιν ("he is able") states God's ability as a permanently existing condition.

Romans 5:5 — "hope does not put us to shame." οὐ καταισχύνει ("does not disappoint") is a static present: a condition perpetually existing, taken as a dogmatic, axiomatic fact — not a conditional promise but an absolute statement of what divine integrity is by nature.

Romans 6:9 — "death no longer has dominion over him." οὐκέτι κυριεύει ("no longer is master") is a static present with the negative temporal adverb οὐκέτι: a condition that perpetually exists — physical death is no longer able to touch the resurrected Christ.

Romans 6:10 — "the life he lives he lives to God." ζῇ (see the Cognate Accusative entry, section XV) denotes a condition that perpetually exists: Christ's resurrection body is permanently beyond corruption, decay, or death.

Romans 6:11 — "consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God." εἶναι (infinitive complement of λογίζομαι) is a static present describing a perpetually existing condition established at a definite past point (salvation) and continuing without interruption.

Romans 7:1 — "the law is binding on a person only as long as he lives." κυριεύει ("is binding," literally "lords it over") is a static present: a self-evident, timeless legal principle, true of the Mosaic law's authority in general, not one instance of it.

Romans 7:2 — "while he is living." ζῶντος (a participle) is a static present expressing a principle held as a permanent, self-evident fact: the binding of the wife endures as long as the husband lives — a general truth, not a report about one couple.

Romans 7:14 — "we know that the law is spiritual." ἐστίν ("is") is static: a timeless characterization of the law's nature.

Romans 8:9 — "assuming that the Spirit of God dwells in you." οἰκεῖ (present active of οἰκέω) is a static present: a condition that perpetually exists, God the Holy Spirit himself producing the action of indwelling every believer without exception.

Romans 8:9 — "the unbeliever... does not have [the Spirit of Christ]." οὐκ ἔχει is likewise static: the unbeliever's lack of the indwelling Spirit is a condition that always exists, not a variable or occasional state.

Romans 9:5 — "who is God over all." ὁ ὤν (the one who is, from εἰμί). ho ōn, the articular present active participle of eimi, is a static present representing a condition as perpetually existing, the ongoing reality of the hypostatic union. The active voice indicates that the Lord Jesus Christ himself produces the action: he who came in the flesh remains, perpetually and without diminishment, God.

Romans 9:8 — "are counted as offspring." λογίζομαι (are imputed). logizomai is a present passive indicative: the children of the promise receive the action on an ongoing basis. The static present represents a condition assumed as perpetually existing. The passive voice is critical: imputation is received, not achieved, something done to them by the justice of God. The indicative is declarative, a dogmatic statement of fact.

Romans 9:11 — "might continue." μένω (might remain in status quo). The present active subjunctive of menō, to remain, to abide, is a static present representing a perpetually existing condition: might remain in status quo. The active voice indicates that the predetermined plan of God, the divine decrees, produces this action of perpetual stability.

Romans 9:18 — "on whomever he wills." θέλω (he desires). The accusative relative hos, on whom, anchors the clause to specific individuals whose volition was already recorded in the divine decrees, not as an infringement on their freedom but as a perfect reading of what their freedom would produce. thelō is a static present, a doctrine taken for granted as an established fact: God's desire is not arbitrary impulse but the expression of His perfect integrity acting in full knowledge of what every human soul has chosen and will choose.

Romans 9:20 — "who are you." εἰμί (to be, to exist). Following τίς, Paul uses the present active indicative of εἰμί. The static present represents an ongoing existential fact, not a momentary state: the permanent condition of creaturely dependence. The active voice indicates the subject produces the action (existing as a creature), and the indicative interrogates a reality already in place.

Romans 9:28 (Isaiah 10:23) — "fully." συντελέω (to complete, to consummate; completing). The first participle is the present active of συντελέω, a complementary participle completing the idea of the main verb: the Lord will execute His word on the earth, completing it. The static present treats as settled fact the doctrine that the second advent will consummate the divine purpose for Israel; the active voice identifies the Lord Jesus Christ as the one who produces this completion.

Romans 10:8 — "the word of faith that we proclaim." κηρύσσω (we proclaim). Kēryssō, present active indicative, from the cognate noun kēryx, a herald, a public official proclaiming an authoritative announcement, denotes the proclamation of a herald, not informal speech. The static present represents a condition that perpetually exists: the message of faith has been proclaimed in every generation without historical interruption. The active voice assigns the action to Paul, Moses, and all true communicators of the gospel.

Romans 10:11 (Isaiah 28:16) — "the Scripture says." λέγω. Legō, present active indicative, introduces the quotation. The static present indicates that the verse cited stands permanently within the canon; the Scripture itself speaks with permanent, present authority. Legō with graphē as subject is among Paul's most formal citation formulas.

Romans 10:12 — "there is no distinction." εἰμί. The main verb is the present active indicative of eimi with ou; the predicate nominative is diastolē. The static present presents the absence of racial distinction as a truth taken for granted, a permanent, unconditional doctrinal reality, not a situational accommodation or dispensational novelty. The indicative makes a dogmatic, unqualified assertion.

Romans 11:1 — "For I myself am an Israelite." εἰμί (I am). With the first-person pronoun ἐγώ, the present active indicative of εἰμί is a static present, a condition which has perpetually existed or is taken for granted as a fixed fact. Paul says he is, not was, an Israelite: a permanent identity that neither conversion nor apostleship has dissolved.

Romans 11:13 — "Inasmuch then as I am an apostle to the Gentiles." εἰμί (I am). The present active indicative of εἰμί is a static present, representing a condition regarded as a settled, permanent fact: Paul's apostleship is not a temporary assignment but a defining characteristic of his identity and calling. The personal pronoun ἐγώ is emphatic (I myself), underscoring the unique scope and responsibility of Paul's commission rather than expressing personal pride.

Romans 11:18 — "but the root that supports you." βαστάζω (to carry, to bear, to sustain). The present active indicative of βαστάζω (to carry, bear, support, sustain; since carrying implies the exertion of power, it encompasses upholding) is a static present for a condition perpetually existing. Used negatively of the arrogant Gentile believer, who does not sustain the root, and positively of the root, the Lord Jesus Christ, who does sustain the believer.

Romans 11:23 — "for God has the power to graft them in again." εἰμί (is). γάρ introduces the theological ground. With ὁ θεός the present active indicative of εἰμί is a static present, representing a condition as perpetually existing — God's ability does not fluctuate. The predicate adjective δυνατός (able, capable) is a direct reference to the omnipotence of God as the executive force controlling the outcome of history.

Romans 13:1 — "For there is no authority except from God." εἰμί (there is no). The present active indicative of εἰμί negated by οὐ asserts a condition assumed to be perpetually existing. It is a static present, describing a state of affairs that is constant and permanent under the laws of divine establishment.

Romans 14:8 — "we are the Lord's." ἐσμέν (we are, from εἰμί). The verse concludes with τοῦ Κυρίου ἐσμέν, literally we are of the Lord. εἰμί is present active indicative; the static present denotes a condition that perpetually exists, not a state that requires maintenance or can be revoked.

Romans 14:11 (Isaiah 45:23) — "As I live." ζάω (I keep on living). ζάω appears in the present active indicative. The static present denotes a condition that has always existed and perpetually continues: God is eternal, and His attributes are eternal. The active voice indicates that God is the self-existent one, and the declarative indicative makes this a dogmatic statement of fact.

Romans 14:17 — "is not a matter of eating and drinking." εἰμί (is not). The present active indicative of εἰμί, negated by οὐ, is a static or durative present: a condition perpetually true from the moment of the believer's new birth and continuing without interruption. It is not a temporary ruling for a specific controversy but a permanent statement of what the royal family of God is and is not.

Romans 15:20 — "lest I build on someone else's foundation." οἰκοδομῶ (I should build). The verb is the present active subjunctive of οἰκοδομέω (oikodomeō), to build. The static present treats the policy as a standing fact.

Romans 16:11 — "Greet those in the Lord who belong to the family of Narcissus." τοὺς ὄντας ἐν κυρίῳ (those who are in the Lord). The present active participle of the verb εἰμί (eimi) — 'who are in the Lord' — is a static present representing a condition as perpetually existing: these believers have attained and now permanently inhabit the sphere of maturity in Christ.

Romans 16:25 — "Now to him who is able to strengthen you." τῷ δὲ δυναμένῳ (now to Him who is able). The subject of the doxology is introduced by the articular present active participle of dynamai (δύναμαι), to be able. The static present tense denotes a condition that perpetually exists: God always possesses omnipotence. Corrected translation: Now to Him who is able …

Tendential Present

Describes an action or state that is intended or purposed but not yet fully realized.

Romans 2:4 — "Or do you presume on the riches of his kindness... not knowing that God's kindness is meant to lead you to repentance?" ἄγει ("leads," from ἄγω) is a tendential present active indicative: it describes an action intended and tending toward reality without necessarily achieving it — the kindness of God has the intent of bringing a person to repentance while preserving genuine human volition.

Romans 5:1 — "we have peace with God" (subjunctive reading: "let us have peace/prosperity"). ἔχωμεν is a hortatory exhortation toward a state not yet fully possessed, not an assertion that the state already obtains.

Romans 7:14 — "I am of the flesh, sold under sin." εἰμί ("I am") is a tendential present: it describes what is inclined toward realization but is not actually, presently occurring. A carnal believer could not write Scripture — Paul's use of the first person here is objective and representative, articulating the universal vulnerability of every believer, not a personal confession of ongoing carnal status.

Romans 9:3 — "that I myself were accursed." εἶναι (to be, from εἰμί). The present active infinitive of eimi is a tendential present, describing an action desired but not occurring.

Romans 12:3 — "than he ought to think." φρονεῖν (to think, from φρονέω). The present infinitive of the verb to think in the phrase para ho dei phronein, without the huper prefix, is a tendential present: it denotes objective thinking as the intended standard, an action directed toward as an aim but not yet fully realized.

Romans 13:8 — "except to love each other." ἀγαπάω (to love). The present active infinitive of ἀγαπάω is a tendential present: it presents the action as the standard toward which the believer is directed, the intended result, without implying that the action is currently taking place. In Rome, it was not.

Romans 14:22 — "the one who has no reason to pass judgment on himself." κρίνω (not judging, not condemning). The present active participle of κρίνω with μή is a circumstantial participle of means. The present is tendential: an action that characteristically does not occur, or is inclined not to occur. The active voice shows the mature believer producing this condition by refraining; with the reflexive ἑαυτόν the not-condemning loops back to him, so happiness is partly defined by what he does not do to himself.

Romans 15:24 — "as I go to Spain." πορεύωμαι (I go). The verb is the present middle subjunctive of πορεύομαι (poreuomai, to go, to journey). The tendential present describes an action that is purposed though not yet occurring.

Romans 15:24 — "I hope to see you." ἐλπίζω (I expect). It is followed by the present active indicative of elpizō (ἐλπίζω), a verb denoting confident future anticipation rather than mere wishful thinking. The present tense functions as a tendential present — an action that is purposed but not yet in progress. Corrected translation: for I expect.

Progressive Present

Describes an action in process, ongoing at the time in view.

Romans 1:14 — "I am under obligation both to Greeks and to barbarians." The retroactive progressive present of εἰμί (ὀφειλέτης εἰμί, "I am a debtor") describes Paul's obligation as a permanent characteristic of his matured soul, begun at his own maturity adjustment and continuing without interruption as his way of life — not a temporary resolve but a continuous present reality.

Romans 2:1 — "for in passing judgment on another you condemn yourself, because you, the judge, practice the very same things." πράσσεις ("you practice," from πράσσω) is a retroactive progressive present: what began in the past and continues — self-righteous judgment is not an isolated act but a characteristic pattern of life.

Romans 2:5 — "But because of your hard and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself." θησαυρίζεις ("you are storing up," from θησαυρίζω) is a retroactive progressive present: begun at the point of maladjustment and continuing to the present — the self-righteous man believes he is building a defense; he is building his own indictment.

Romans 2:9 — "There will be tribulation and distress for every human being who does evil." The articular present middle participle of κατεργάζομαι ("bring about, produce") is a retroactive progressive present, begun at the moment of negative volition at gospel hearing and continuing — inner content working its way to outward behavior.

Romans 2:10 — "but glory and honor and peace for everyone who does good." The articular present middle participle of ἐργάζομαι ("accomplish") is likewise a retroactive progressive present, describing the mature believer who has cracked the maturity barrier and sustains active accomplishment of the good.

Romans 2:19 — "and if you are sure that you yourself are a guide to the blind." εἶναι (the infinitive of εἰμί, "to be") functions with a progressive present force in the accusative-plus-infinitive construction: a persistent, continuing state — the legalist claims to be, and continues to be, a guide and a light.

Romans 3:22 — "the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe." The articular present active participle πιστεύοντας ("those who believe," from πιστεύω) is a retroactive progressive present: an action begun in the past — at the fall of man — and continuing to the present, indicating the universal, unchanging scope of salvation through faith.

Romans 4:4 — "to the one who works." ἐργαζομένῳ ("who works") is a present participle describing action in process.

Romans 9:1 — "I am not lying." ψεύδομαι (to lie, to misrepresent). pseudomai, negated by ou, is a progressive present denoting sustained maintenance of academic integrity and intellectual honesty. The indirect middle emphasizes the intimate link between the subject and the action.

Romans 12:13 — "seek to show hospitality." διώκω (be pursuing). Present active participle of diōkō, a military term meaning to pursue, to press after with urgency. The progressive present indicates linear, uninterrupted action, keep on pursuing, and the imperative participle converts pursuit into a standing order. Hospitality is not a passive social habit but an active, disciplined orientation.

Romans 13:3 — "Then do what is good." ποιέω (keep on doing). The present active imperative of ποιέω is a progressive present, present linear action denoting continuous, uninterrupted activity. The rendering is therefore not simply do but keep on doing: the Christian's duty to God and country is a continuous pattern of life, not a one-time act.

Romans 13:4 — "be afraid." φοβέομαι (keep on being afraid). The present middle imperative of φοβέομαι is a progressive or customary present, denoting action that continues or is habitual: keep on fearing. It is not a one-time warning but a standing command to those who operate with criminal thinking.

Romans 13:6 — "you also pay taxes." τελέω (keep on paying). The present active imperative of τελέω is a progressive present, denoting linear, ongoing action: not to pay taxes once but to keep on paying without interruption. It is a continuous, binding obligation on every Church Age believer, not qualified by the fairness of the tax structure or the moral character of the government.

Romans 16:19 — "so that I rejoice over you." ἐφ’ ὑμῖν οὖν χαίρω (therefore, because of you, I am delighted). The verb rendered 'I am delighted' is the present active indicative of chairō (χαίρω), meaning to rejoice, to be glad, to be delighted. The progressive present tense denotes action in a continuing state — Paul is not merely expressing a momentary response but a sustained disposition of joy. Corrected translation: Therefore, because of you, I am delighted.

Perfective Present

Denotes the continuation of existing results into the present, stressing durative authority or force.

Romans 1:17 — "For in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith for faith." ἀποκαλύπτεται ("is revealed," from ἀποκαλύπτω) is a perfective present: the justice of God has been revealed in the past — at the cross, in the Mosaic covenant, in the prophetic tradition — and those results are now a present, active reality, comparable to English "I learned" functioning as "I have learned, and it stands."

Romans 1:27 — "men committing shameless acts with men and receiving in themselves the due penalty." κατεργαζόμενοι ("accomplishing," from κατεργάζομαι) functions as a progressive or perfective present participle: action begun in the past and continuing, or the continuation of existing results — the volitional, deliberate production of the act from an inwardly motivated lust.

Romans 2:1 — the same verse's κατακρίνεις ("you condemn," from κατακρίνω) is a perfective present: the self-condemnation came to be at the moment of judging, and its consequences persist.

Romans 3:31 — "Do we then overthrow the law by this faith? By no means! On the contrary, we uphold the law." ἱστάνομεν ("we establish," from ἱστάνω, an Attic verb distinct from ἵστημι though related) is a perfective present: the continuation of existing results — through faith in Christ, the believer establishes the true purpose of the law.

Romans 4:6 — "David also speaks." λέγει ("speaks") — the Psalms, composed in the past, remain permanently authoritative and quotable in the present.

Romans 4:12 — "who also walk in the footsteps." The perfective present of "walk" (see section XXI's vocabulary entry on στοιχέω) denotes continuation of existing results through daily doctrine intake: sustained, unbroken forward movement, not a single act.

Romans 5:2 — "let us rejoice" (ESV) / "let us boast." καυχώμεθα ("let us boast," present middle subjunctive of καυχάομαι) is a perfective present: the boasting came into existence in the past, as the believer grasped the integrity of God and eternal security, with the result now emphasized as ongoing.

Romans 5:3 — "we rejoice in our sufferings" (ESV) / "let us boast in our sufferings." καυχώμεθα again, perfective present: not a momentary response but a sustained disposition produced by resident doctrine.

Romans 6:3 — "Do you not know...?" ἀγνοεῖτε ("are you ignorant") is a perfective present: a condition of ignorance that came to exist in the past and continues as a present reality.

Romans 6:6 — "We know that our old self was crucified with him." γινώσκοντες ("knowing," a present active participle) is a perfective present, denoting the continuation of existing results — specifically the results of having perceived retroactive and current positional truth.

Romans 7:16 — "I agree with the law, that it is good." σύμφημι ("I agree") is a perfective present indicating a settled, ongoing agreement — the believer concurs with the law's excellence, not as a return to it as a standard of justification, but as a recognition of its defining function.

Romans 7:19 — "I do the very thing I hate" (the parallel clause). πράσσω ("I keep on practicing") is a perfective present denoting the continuation of existing results: an ongoing pattern of practicing evil that follows from sincerity-driven decision-making without doctrinal policy.

Romans 9:1 — "I am speaking the truth in Christ." λέγω (I communicate). legō is a present active indicative, a perfective present denoting the continuation of existing results, a past act emphasized as a present reality. The reference is to the existence and formation of the New Testament scriptures. The active voice indicates Paul produces the action as part of his triple oath; the indicative is declarative, representing reality.

Romans 9:16 (Exodus 33:19) — "but on God, who has mercy." ἐλεέω (who has mercy). The perfective present of eleeō denotes the continuation of existing results: God's mercy is not a situational response but a settled reality grounded in His eternal character and the completed decree system of eternity past.

Romans 9:18 — "So then he has mercy on whomever he wills." ἐλεέω (he shows mercy). The present active indicative of eleeō is a perfective present, a fact which has come to be in the past and is now emphasized as a continuing present reality. The mercy of God toward positive volition is not a fresh or reactive decision; it has been established since eternity past, when divine omniscience fed the actuality of human history into the computer of the divine decrees. The declarative indicative marks an absolute, dogmatic statement of doctrine.

Romans 9:18 — "and he hardens whomever he wills." σκληρύνω (he hardens). The present active indicative of sklērunō, to harden, to calcify, to make rigid, is again a perfective present: a fact established in the past, now presented as a continuing present reality. The hardening of Pharaoh refers not to divine coercion of human volition but to God's act of sustaining Pharaoh's life and authority so that his own negative volition could continue to express itself, producing increasing scar tissue and serving the purpose of worldwide evangelism.

Romans 9:33 (Isaiah 28:16) — "Behold, I am laying in Zion a stone of stumbling." τίθημι (to lay, to place, to establish). The present active indicative of τίθημι is a perfective present: it denotes what was accomplished in the past, the laying of the foundation in Zion, but emphasizes that past event as a present reality. It is used of God the Father under the title Adonai-Jehovah establishing the Lord Jesus Christ as the sole foundation for time and eternity.

Romans 10:15 (Isaiah 52:7) — "those who preach the good news." εὐαγγελίζω (those who proclaim the good news). The articular present middle participle of euaggelizō carries a perfective present, denoting a fact that came to be in the past and continues as a present reality. The middle voice is dynamic, emphasizing the active personal participation of the missionary in the proclamation.

Romans 10:16 (Isaiah 53:1) — "For Isaiah says." λέγω (communicates). Gar introduces the Isaiah 53:1 citation as biblical warrant. Legō, present active indicative, here to communicate or proclaim, is a perfective present: Isaiah's ministry belongs to the past, but his words, as part of the God-breathed canon, remain a living present reality.

Romans 11:3 — "and they seek my life." ζητέω (they seek). The present active indicative of ζητέω is a perfective present, denoting the continuation of existing results: a fact that came to be in the past, emphasized as a present reality. The apostate population produces the action; the object ψυχή here means life in the sense of physical existence.

Romans 11:17 — "although a wild olive shoot." εἰμί (being). With the predicate nominative ἀγριέλαιος (wild olive tree, a figure for Gentile unbelief prior to salvation), the present active participle of εἰμί is a perfective present: the state of being a wild olive tree came about in the past — through the fall and Gentile spiritual alienation — but its present reality is what is in view.

Romans 11:18 — "If you are." κατακαυχάομαι (you are arrogant). The perfective present refers to a fact which came to be in the past but is emphasized as a current reality. In Romans 11:18 the arrogance of Gentile believers in Rome is treated as an existing condition, not a hypothetical one, even though a first-class conditional particle introduces it.

Romans 12:3 — "but to think with sober judgment." φρονέω (but think). The second present active infinitive of the verb to think denotes objective, considered, sober engagement with reality. It is a perfective present, denoting the continuation of results already established, the ongoing habit of mind that maximum doctrine resident in the soul produces. It is an imperative infinitive: a command.

Romans 12:5 — "are one body in Christ." εἰμί (we are). The verb eimi is a perfective present: it refers to a fact that came into existence at the beginning of the Church Age and continues as a present reality, we the many are one body in Christ.

Romans 12:8 — "the one who leads." προΐστημι (he who manages administration). The articular present middle participle of proistēmi, to stand at the front, to direct, to manage, is a perfective present denoting the continuation of existing results: at salvation certain believers were given this gift, now operative as a present reality.

Romans 12:8 — "the one who does acts of mercy." ἐλεέω (he who performs acts of mercy). The articular present active participle of eleeō, to perform an active mercy, to show compassion in practical action. The perfective present again denotes the continuation of a gift bestowed at salvation and operative throughout the Church Age.

Romans 12:13 — "Contribute to the needs of the saints." κοινωνέω (contribute to). Present active participle of koinōneō, to share, to contribute. The present is a perfective present, the continuation of existing results in the mature believer’s ongoing contribution. The participle functions as an imperative participle, found consistently in Koine papyri Greek, with the force of a direct command; its primary fulfillment is doctrine intake to maturity, its secondary the sharing of material resources.

Romans 13:3 — "Would you have no fear." φοβέω (not to fear). The present middle infinitive of φοβέω is a perfective present, denoting the continuation of existing results: a state of not fearing that has been achieved and persists.

Romans 14:4 — "for the Lord is able to make him stand." δυνατέω (to be powerful, to have ability). δυνατέω is a Hellenistic verb from the classical adjective δυνατός (able, powerful), carrying the nuance of demonstrated capacity rather than abstract attribute. In Romans 14:4 it is a perfective present, emphasizing the Lord’s sustained, ongoing omnipotence as the basis for the strong believer’s stability.

Romans 14:5 — "Each one should be fully convinced." πληροφορέω (to be fully convinced, to be completely persuaded). The verb is the present passive imperative of πληροφορέω. The perfective present denotes the continuation of existing results: the doctrine has been learned in the past and now abides in the soul as a settled possession, producing confidence in application. It describes not someone operating on minimal information but a soul fully stocked with doctrine already received, so the command is to pursue full doctrinal inculcation.

Romans 14:8 — "if we die." ἀποθνῄσκω (to die). ἀποθνῄσκω appears twice in the dying clause. The first, in the subjunctive, is a perfective present (potential), emphasizing the continuation of results already established through the mature life. The grammar underscores that dying grace is not aspirational but the inevitable terminal blessing of the believer who has lived to the Lord.

Romans 14:18 — "Whoever thus serves Christ is acceptable to God and approved by men." δουλεύω (he who serves). γάρ is followed by the articular present active participle of δουλεύω (to serve as a slave, to render service); the article functions as a personal pronoun. The perfective present denotes the continuation of existing results, a state that came into being in the past and is now emphasized as a present reality. The active voice shows the mature believer producing the action, and the participle is circumstantial.

Romans 15:4 — "we might have hope." ἔχω (to have and to hold). The final verb of verse 4 is echōmen (ἔχωμεν), present active subjunctive of echō (ἔχω), meaning to have or to have and to hold. The present tense here is a perfective present, noting the continuation of existing results: when the believer is positive toward doctrine and perseveres in its perception, he arrives at a state of possessing something that abides with him. The subjunctive mood is governed by the conjunction hina (ἵνα), marking this as a purpose clause.

Romans 15:6 — "with one voice glorify." δοξάζητε (may keep on glorifying). The main verb of the purpose clause is the present active subjunctive of δοξάζω (doxazō, to glorify). The present tense is a perfective present, denoting the continuation of existing results.

Romans 15:7 — "Therefore welcome one another." προσλαμβάνεσθε (be receiving). The main verb is the present middle imperative of proslambanō (προσλαμβάνω), meaning to accept into one's society or circle of association. The same verb appeared in Romans 14:1 for the strong believer's reception of the weak. The present tense is a perfective present: it denotes the continuation of results already established by the daily function of the Grace Apparatus for Perception.

Romans 15:13 — "in believing." πιστεύειν (believing). The Greek construction is ἐν (en) plus the instrumental singular of the definite article with the present active infinitive of πιστεύω (pisteuō). The perfective present tense denotes the continuation of existing results — specifically, the ongoing use of faith to transfer Bible doctrine from the left lobe of the soul to the right lobe.

Romans 15:27 — "they ought also to be of service to them." ὀφείλουσιν (they are obligated). The obligation verb is the perfective present active indicative of opheilō (ὀφείλω), denoting the continuation of existing results: they are obligated. The adjunctive conjunction kai (καί) introduces the additional dimension: also — they are obligated also in the material realm, not only in the spiritual.

Romans 16:17 — "avoid them." ἐκκλίνετε ἀπ’ αὐτῶν (keep turning away from them). The present active imperative of ekklinō (ἐκκλίνω) — to shun, to avoid, to turn away from — is the command. The perfective present denotes the continuation of results: as doctrinal perception increases, the capacity and the determination to maintain this avoidance is sustained. The corrected translation of the full command: 'In fact, keep turning away from them.'

Customary Present

Denotes what habitually or characteristically occurs, without reference to a single instance.

Romans 1:18 — "who by their unrighteousness suppress the truth." κατεχόντων ("suppress," from κατέχω, a compound of κατά + ἔχω) is a customary present participle: the characteristic, habitual activity of the person in maladjustment, not a single act of rejection — each act deepens the pattern and accelerates the darkening described in verses 21–22.

Romans 1:20 — "For his invisible attributes... have been clearly perceived." καθορᾶται ("are clearly perceived," from καθοράω) is a customary present passive indicative: what habitually, invariably occurs when a normal human mind engages the created order at the point of God-consciousness.

Romans 2:7 — "to those who by patience in well-doing seek for glory and honor and immortality." ζητοῦσιν ("seek," from ζητέω) is a customary present participle: what habitually characterizes those positive at God-consciousness — a two-stage sequence of seeking and finding.

Romans 2:23 — "You who boast in the law dishonor God by breaking the law." καυχᾶσαι ("you boast," a deponent from καυχάομαι) is a customary present: the habitual, ongoing boast of the legalist who turns the law into self-promotion.

Romans 3:26 — "so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus." The customary present tense of δικαιόω in this verse indicates invariable repetition: God performs the identical judicial act of justification for every person who believes, without exception, without degrees.

Romans 2:1 — "you who judge practice the very same things." The articular present active participle of κρίνω ("judge") is temporal with a customary-present force: habitual action, every time you judge.

Romans 3:21 — "But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the law, although the Law and the Prophets bear witness to it." The circumstantial participle of μαρτυρέω ("bear witness") is a present tense indicating the perpetual validity of the Old Testament's canonical witness to divine integrity.

Romans 5:3 — "suffering produces endurance." κατεργάζεται ("produces") is a customary present: it denotes what habitually occurs in a mature believer under pressure, not a single event.

Romans 5:11 — "we also rejoice in God." καυχώμενοι ("rejoicing/boasting," a participle) is a customary present, denoting what habitually characterizes mature believers.

Romans 7:16 — "I do what I do not want." ποιῶ — descriptive present active indicative, confirming that the described action is a real, ongoing pattern of experience, not a hypothetical.

Romans 7:21 — "when I want to do right, evil lies close at hand." θέλω ("I wish/desire") is used as a customary present in the dative absolute construction describing a recurring resolve (see the Dative Absolute entry, section XIV).

Romans 8:28 — "all things work together for good." συνεργεῖ is a customary present: what habitually occurs in the life of the mature believer specifically — this is not a universal promise applicable to every believer in every condition, but the exclusive, habitual experience of the one who has cracked the maturity barrier.

Romans 8:37 — "we are more than conquerors." ὑπερνικῶμεν is a customary present, indicating what habitually occurs when the justice of God imputes dying blessing to the mature believer through undeserved suffering or martyrdom.

Romans 9:1 — "my conscience bears me witness." συμμαρτυρέω (to bear joint testimony, to testify together with). summartureo, a compound of sum (with) and martyreo (to testify), is a genitive singular present active participle in the genitive absolute. It is a customary present: what habitually occurs when the human writer is under the ministry of the Holy Spirit in the production of Scripture.

Romans 9:10 — "when Rebekah had conceived children." ἔχω (when she had conceived). The present active participle of echō is used with a customary present, denoting what eventually occurs, and functions as a historical present, drawing a past event into the vividness of present experience. The active voice indicates Rebecca as the agent. The participle is temporal: when she had. The direct object koitēn literally denotes sexual intercourse; the standard rendering when she became pregnant is an acceptable condensation.

Romans 9:15 (Exodus 33:19) — "on whom I have mercy." ἐλεέω (I show mercy). The present active subjunctive of eleeō after hos an is a customary present, describing what habitually occurs when a believer reaches maturity.

Romans 9:21 — "Has the potter no right over the clay." ἔχω (to have, to possess). The main verb is the present active indicative of ἔχω. The customary present indicates what habitually or reasonably occurs, a standing condition, not a momentary act. The active voice makes the potter the subject, and the indicative functions as an interrogative indicative asserting a fact the audience is expected to recognize and affirm.

Romans 11:11 — "So I ask." λέγω (I say). The inference of verse 11 is introduced by οὖν with the present active indicative of λέγω. The customary present indicates what habitually occurs after a doctrinal dissertation: Paul draws a logical conclusion by means of the rhetorical question.

Romans 12:2 — "but be transformed." μεταμορφόω (be transformed). Present passive imperative of metamorphoō, to undergo transformation, to be transfigured; here the inner transformation of thinking. The present tense is customary: it describes what habitually occurs when the believer is consistently positive toward Bible doctrine. The imperative makes it a direct command.

Romans 12:4 — "the members do not all have the same function." ἔχω (do not have). The present active indicative of echō, negated by ou, is customary, noting what habitually occurs in the function of the royal family on earth under its honor code; the declarative indicative states a dogmatic reality.

Romans 12:11 — "be fervent in spirit." ζέω (be zealous). Present active participle of zeō, to boil, to be zealous, used imperativally. In the New Testament the verb is used twice for the filling of the Holy Spirit, of Apollos in Acts 18:25 and here. The present tense is customary, the habitual pattern of the believer who maintains rebound.

Romans 12:18 — "live peaceably with all." εἰρηνεύω (live in harmony). A present active participle of eirēneuō functioning as an imperative. The customary present denotes what habitually occurs in the believer consistently positive toward doctrine and operating under the honor code; the active voice makes the mature believer the producer of the harmony. Meta pantōn anthrōpōn: with all mankind.

Romans 12:21 — "but overcome evil with good." νικάω (conquer). After the sharp adversative alla, the second imperative is the present active of nikaō: conquer. The customary present denotes what habitually occurs when the believer is positive toward doctrine. The same verb governs both commands, setting conquest by evil against conquest of evil.

Romans 13:3 — "Would you have no fear." θέλω (do you desire). The present active indicative of θέλω is customary, depicting the normal mental attitude of a believer toward governing authority.

Romans 13:4 — "for he is God's servant for your good." εἰμί (he is). The present active indicative of εἰμί is a customary present, indicating what habitually occurs under the laws of divine establishment: civil rulers habitually function as God's deputies, whether or not they are aware of that commission.

Romans 13:4 — "for he does not bear the sword in vain." φορέω (he does not wear). After γάρ, the present active indicative of φορέω (to wear, to bear, by right of authority to execute) is a customary present, denoting what habitually occurs when the laws of divine establishment function in every legitimate form of government.

Romans 13:10 — "Love does no wrong to a neighbor." ἐργάζομαι (does not produce). The present middle indicative of ἐργάζομαι negated by οὐ is a customary present, denoting what habitually occurs when the believer under the royal family honor code has doctrinal standards in place. The declarative indicative presents it as objective reality.

Romans 14:1 — "welcome him." προσλαμβάνω (to take to oneself, to receive or accept into one’s society). Paul addresses the strong believer with a present middle imperative of προσλαμβάνω. The customary present denotes what is reasonably expected to occur when the Royal Family Honor Code is operational. The imperative mood is a command: now receive that one who is weak in the doctrine.

Romans 14:2 — "One person believes." πιστεύω (to believe, to be convinced of, to hold a settled opinion). The present active indicative of πιστεύω is a customary present, denoting what habitually characterizes the mature believer: not a momentary judgment but a stable conviction formed through sustained doctrine intake. The declarative indicative affirms it as historical reality.

Romans 14:3 — "the one who eats." ἐσθίω (to eat, to consume). The verse opens with the articular present active participle of ἐσθίω, covering food and beverage alike. The customary present denotes habitual action: the strong believer characteristically operates under the law of liberty, neither constrained by legalist taboos nor swung into antinomianism.

Romans 14:5 — "One person esteems one day as better than another." κρίνω (to judge, to reach a decision). κρίνω is present active indicative in both clauses. The customary present captures what habitually occurs with the believer whose norms and standards have not been transformed by doctrine, whose conscience still runs on categories from a pre-salvation background, whether Judaism’s calendar or Gentile paganism’s ritual cycle. In the second clause the same customary present denotes the habitual posture of the doctrinally inculcated believer.

Romans 14:6 — "and gives thanks to God." εὐχαριστέω (to give thanks, to be thankful). The clause ends with καί plus the present active indicative of εὐχαριστέω, a customary present denoting what habitually characterizes the immature believer who is positive toward doctrine. This shared thanksgiving, by weak and strong believer alike, is the criterion of positive volition in the verse and the basis for mutual toleration.

Romans 14:8 — "whether we die." ἀποθνῄσκω (to die). The second conditional clause uses the present active subjunctive of ἀποθνῄσκω. The present is customary, denoting what habitually occurs when a believer’s life is completed; the active voice indicates that the mature believer’s death is itself an expression of his ongoing orientation to the Lord, not merely something that happens to him.

Romans 14:10 — "why do you despise your brother?" ἐξουθενέω (to despise, to treat with contempt). The present active indicative of ἐξουθενέω is a customary present, denoting the habitual attitude of the strong believer toward the weak, his characteristic occupational hazard.

Romans 14:15 — "your brother is grieved." λυπέω (is distressed or distracted). λυπέω is a present passive indicative: in the active, to cause pain; in the passive, to receive pain, to be distressed or distracted. The customary present denotes what habitually occurs when the weak believer, in arrogant hypersensitivity, observes the mature believer rejecting his food taboo. The injury in view is not primarily emotional hurt but the diversion of the weak believer's attention from Bible doctrine.

Romans 14:19 — "let us pursue." διώκω (we run after). The present of διώκω is the customary present of habitual momentum, not the action of a single inspired moment: the consistent exploitation of the breakthrough that logistical grace makes possible. It is the grammar of perseverance; positive volition must be exercised daily, regardless of circumstance, emotion or outward condition.

Romans 14:23 — "whoever has doubts." διακρίνω (who doubts). The customary present of διακρίνω indicates what habitually occurs whenever the weak believer violates his own personal taboos, in the Roman context food laws and beverage restrictions derived from his pre-salvation religious or ethnic background.

Romans 15:1 — "have an obligation to bear with the failings of the weak." ὀφείλω (to be obligated). The main verb is the present active indicative of opheilō (ὀφείλω), to owe, to be indebted, to be under obligation. With a following infinitive, as here, the meaning is specifically to be obligated to do something. The customary present tense denotes what habitually characterizes the mature believer under the Royal Family Honor Code. The indicative mood, rather than the imperative, is deliberate. Because the command is addressed to a specialized and numerically limited group — mature believers in a generation — the present active indicative with a following infinitive carries the force of obligation without requiring the broader imperative form.

Romans 15:2 — "Let each of us please his neighbor." ἀρέσκω (to please, to accommodate). The main verb is the present active imperative of ἀρέσκω (areskō), standardly translated 'to please.' The imperative makes this a command, not a suggestion. The customary present tense describes what habitually characterizes the mature believer: a settled disposition of thoughtful accommodation toward others. The active voice specifies that the strong believer — the subject of verse 1 — produces this action.

Romans 15:5 — "to live in such harmony with one another." φρονεῖν (to think, to set the mind on). The verb phroneō means to think, to form a thought, to hold an opinion, to set the mind on specific content, to sculpt one's mental life around particular categories. The present tense is a customary present, denoting what habitually occurs among believers who persevere in the perception of Bible doctrine.

Romans 15:11 — "Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles." αἰνεῖτε (keep on praising). The imperative in the quotation derives from the present active imperative of aineō (αἰνέω), meaning to praise or to celebrate. The customary present tense indicates habitual action: the mature believer regularly and characteristically engages in this worship.

Romans 15:14 — "that you yourselves are full of goodness." μεστοί ἐστε (you are full). The predicate nominative plural from mestos (μεστός) means full. It is paired with the present active indicative of eimi (εἰμί) — you are — in a customary present, denoting what consistently characterizes believers who have been motivated to take in doctrine persistently and now carry structurized doctrine in the soul.

Romans 15:30 — "I appeal to you, brothers." παρακαλῶ (I encourage). The main verb is the present active indicative of parakaleō (παρακαλέω), meaning to summon to one's aid, to appeal, to encourage. The customary present tense denotes what may reasonably be expected when believers recognize a communicator of Paul's stature: without any formal command, they should be supporting him in prayer.

Romans 16:1 — "I commend to you our sister Phoebe." συνίστημι (I recommend). The verb opening verse 1 is synistēmi (συνίστημι), present active indicative. The verb means to present, to introduce, to recommend someone to another party. The customary present tense denotes what habitually occurs when Paul, functioning under the honor code, certifies a mature believer to a receiving congregation.

Romans 16:18 — "they deceive the hearts of the naive." ἐξαπατῶσι (they deceive). The verb is the present active indicative of exapataō (ἐξαπατάω), a compound of ex (from) and apataō (to seduce or deceive). The present tense is a customary present, describing what habitually occurs when a believer is either uninstructed in doctrine or negative toward it.

Descriptive Present

A present tense that simply reports an action as an actual, ongoing occurrence, without the additional nuances (durative force, habitual pattern) carried by the perfective or customary present.

Romans 2:3 — "Do you suppose, O man... that you will escape the judgment of God?" λογίζῃ ("you suppose," from λογίζομαι) is a descriptive present depicting an ongoing, characteristic mental activity — shallow self-serving presumption, not careful reasoning.

Romans 1:16 — "For I am not ashamed of the gospel." ἐπαισχύνομαι (negated, "I am ashamed," a compound of ἐπί + αἰσχύνομαι) is present middle indicative describing the ongoing mental attitude of the mature believer: not merely absence of shame but positive elevation above it, since shame is the signature of reversionism.

Romans 3:4 — "By no means! Let God be true though every one were a liar." γινέσθω ("let it be," a present middle imperative of γίνομαι) stands in place of εἰμί precisely because God does not "become" anything in himself but is apprehended as reliable as doctrine reshapes the believer's thinking. Indirect middle voice: God is the agent producing the action of self-demonstration.

Romans 3:24 — "and are justified by his grace as a gift." The present passive participle of δικαιόω ("justify") emphasizes that justification is bestowed upon the believing sinner, not achieved — the passive voice itself carries the doctrine.

Romans 7:16 — "I do what I do not want." ποιῶ confirms that doing what one does not desire is an ongoing, real experience — the plainest, most direct reporting use of the present tense in this passage.

Romans 7:20 — "if I do what I do not want." Same verb, same plain-descriptive force.

Romans 8:6 — "to set the mind on the flesh is death." The two present-tense verbal nouns describing the mind's orientation function descriptively, reporting the actual, ongoing mental activity of each category of person without additional durative or habitual emphasis beyond the plain report.

Romans 11:13 — "I magnify my ministry." δοξάζω (I am magnifying). The main verb is the present active indicative of δοξάζω (to glorify, honor, praise, magnify). The descriptive present indicates ongoing action: I am magnifying. The word does not carry the connotation of boasting; it describes the proper honoring of an office whose dignity derives entirely from the one who conferred it. Paul magnifies his ministry because the Gentile mission is the mechanism of Jewish blessing.

Romans 12:16 — "Do not be haughty." ὑψηλά (do not think in terms of arrogance, from ὑψηλός). Mē governs the present active participle of phroneō with the neuter plural object ta hypsēla, lofty things, describing arrogant ambition. The descriptive present with the negative indicates an ongoing condition that must not be permitted to persist; the active voice places responsibility for compliance on the royal family believer.

Romans 13:14 — "and make no provision for the flesh." ποιέω (stop making). The present tense of ποιεῖσθε is descriptive, indicating an ongoing activity that is to cease.

Romans 14:2 — "the weak person eats only vegetables." ἐσθίω (to eat). For the weak believer the main verb is ἐσθίω in the present active indicative, a descriptive or pictorial present, bringing before the mind the ongoing scene of what the weak believer does.

Romans 14:4 — "Who are you to pass judgment." κρίνω (to judge). The participial phrase is built on the articular present active participle of κρίνω. The definite article functions as a reality pronoun, identifying the participle with the known activity of the weak believer. The present is descriptive, linear and ongoing: the one who keeps judging.

Romans 14:22 — "keep between yourself and God." ἔχω (be having it). ἔχω is repeated as a present active imperative. The descriptive present describes what is now to be going on as a continuous practice: be having it. The mature believer is commanded to keep actively maintaining the doctrine he has accumulated, not letting pressure from the weak believer or social convention erode it; where doctrine is the essential, he is to remain absolutely inflexible.

Romans 15:14 — "able to instruct one another." νουθετεῖν (to instruct). The descriptive present tense describes what is now occurring in the life of the mature believer.

Romans 16:16 — "All the churches of Christ greet you." Ἀσπάζονται ὑμᾶς αἱ ἐκκλησίαι πᾶσαι τοῦ Χριστοῦ (all the churches of Christ greet you). The verb is aspazomai (ἀσπάζομαι) in the present active indicative — a descriptive present for what is currently taking place as Paul conveys these greetings.

Aoristic Present

A present tense used to describe a punctiliar, decisive act occurring now, rather than a process or ongoing state — the present-tense counterpart to the aorist's momentary aspect.

Romans 6:11 — "consider yourselves dead to sin." λογίζεσθε ("consider," present middle imperative of λογίζομαι) is an aoristic present: a decisive act of concluding, reached now, not a process spread over time.

Romans 9:33 (Isaiah 28:16) — "and whoever believes in him." πιστεύω (to believe, to trust). The articular present active participle of πιστεύω is the aoristic present, expressing punctiliar action in present time without reference to its progress. Belief is available now, as when Isaiah wrote and when Paul wrote, in any generation: one moment taken out of time becomes the present moment of decision, one moment of non-meritorious faith in Christ constituting salvation adjustment to the justice of God.

Romans 10:4 — "to everyone who believes." πιστεύω (because he believes). The closing clause uses the articular present active participle of pisteuō, the article functioning as a personal pronoun. The present is aoristic, punctiliar action at the moment of gospel hearing; the active voice shows the individual producing the action; the participle is causal: because he believes.

Romans 10:11 (Isaiah 28:16) — "Everyone who believes in him." πιστεύω (when anyone believes). Paul renders Isaiah's Hiphil participle with pas used as a substantive by the article plus the articular present active participle of pisteuō. The aoristic present denotes punctiliar action in present time: belief in Christ takes only a moment. As a temporal participle it is correctly when anyone believes. The construction is universal in scope, Jew and Gentile without distinction, anticipating verse 12.

Romans 11:1 — "I ask, then." λέγω (I say). The present active indicative of λέγω is identified as a historical present, or more precisely an aoristic present, conveying punctiliar action in present time. With the active voice (Paul himself producing the action), the construction indicates the assertion is as immediately relevant as when first written, circa AD 58. The indicative is declarative, viewing the action from the standpoint of reality.

Romans 11:6 — "grace would no longer be grace." γίνομαι (grace is no longer grace). The present middle indicative of γίνομαι is labelled an aoristic present, denoting punctiliar action in present time, a decisive, instantaneous result. The declarative indicative represents the verbal idea from the viewpoint of reality.

Romans 11:25 — "Lest you be wise in your own sight." εἰμί (be). In the negative purpose clause the present active subjunctive of εἰμί is an aoristic present, indicating punctiliar action in present time: the perception of doctrine is the means of arresting ongoing arrogance.

Romans 12:3 — "I say to everyone among you." λέγω (I say). Present active indicative of legō, an aoristic present: punctiliar action in present time. Paul addressed the Roman believers at a specific moment, yet what he communicated carries permanent authority as part of the completed canon. The declarative indicative establishes the reality and divine authority of what follows.

Romans 12:12 — "be patient in tribulation." ὑπομένω (stand fast). Hupomenō, hupo (under) + menō (to remain), carries a military connotation documented in Herodotus: to remain under sustained attack rather than flee. The aoristic present calls for an immediate, punctiliar response when undeserved suffering arrives, and the participial imperative is a distinctive Koine idiom.

Romans 12:20 — "feed him." ψωμίζω (feed him). The present active imperative of psōmizō, to feed, whether by sitting the enemy at table or by sending food. The present is aoristic, for punctiliar action: a single, definite act of grace, produced by the believer under the empowering of doctrine, not any morality system.

Romans 13:8 — "Owe no one anything." ὀφείλω (owe). The present active imperative of ὀφείλω is labeled an aoristic present, denoting punctiliar action in present time. The imperative makes it a command: owe nothing to anyone.

Romans 13:9 — "are summed up in this word." ἀνακεφαλαιόω (is summed up). The present passive indicative of ἀνακεφαλαιόω is labeled an aoristic present, marking punctiliar action in present time: the five negative commandments are now, at this point in the argument, gathered under a single positive principle. The passive shows that the positive commandment receives the action as the instrument by which the negatives are subsumed.

Romans 14:13 — "decide never to put a stumbling block." τίθημι (not to place). The content of the strong believer's determination is the articular present active infinitive of τίθημι negated by μή. The tense calls for punctiliar instinctive action: because of the doctrinal norms resident in his conscience, the mature believer should respond correctly and immediately when a situation arises.

Romans 14:21 — "causes your brother to stumble." προσκόπτω (stumbles). προσκόπτω is a present active indicative, an aoristic (punctiliar) present: on a specific occasion the weak believer stumbles when his conscience is violated by observing the strong believer eat meat or drink wine contrary to his taboo.

Romans 16:23 — "Erastus, the city treasurer, and our brother Quartus, greet you." ἀσπάζεται ὑμᾶς Ἔραστος (Erastus greets you). The verb is the aoristic present active indicative of aspazomai (ἀσπάζομαι), to greet, to salute, to pay one's respects. The aoristic present represents a punctiliar action in present time.

Historical Present

Views a past event with the vividness of a present occurrence.

Romans 4:10 — "Was it before or after he had been circumcised?" ὄντι describes Abraham's past state with narrative vividness.

Romans 4:17 — "who gives life to the dead." ζωοποιοῦντος ("who gives life") describes God's past act of reviving Abraham and Sarah's sexual function, with the vividness of a present event.

Romans 4:17 — "and calls into existence the things that do not exist." καλοῦντος and both occurrences behind "do not exist... into existence" describe the naming of what did not exist as existing, and its restoration, both with narrative vividness.

Romans 7:21 — "So I find it to be a law." εὑρίσκω ("I discover/find") in the historical present conveys discovery with present vividness: Paul is not merely reporting a past finding but presenting the principle as immediately operative for every believer reading the text.

Romans 8:16 — "the Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit." συμμαρτυρεῖ is a historical present carrying perfective force (see Perfect-as-Present, section II).

Romans 9:4 — "They are Israelites." εἰμί (are). With hostis stands the historical present active indicative of eimi, which views a past historical reality, the past status of Israel as a client nation, with the vividness of a present occurrence. The Jews produce the action; the mood is declarative indicative for historical fact.

Romans 9:11 — "because of him who calls." ἐκ τοῦ καλοῦντος (from him who elects, from καλέω). In ek tou kalountos, from him who elects, the article tou functions as a personal pronoun referring to God the Father. The present active participle of kaleō is circumstantial. The historical present views the past function of God in omniscience, feeding facts into the computer of divine decrees, with the vividness of a present occurrence; the active voice indicates God the Father produces the action in eternity past.

Romans 9:15 (Exodus 33:19) — "For he says to Moses." λέγω (he communicates). The present active indicative of legō is the gnomic or historical present, the aoristic present, representing punctiliar action with the vividness of immediate declaration. The active voice indicates God himself speaks; the indicative affirms the historical reality of this dialogue and its quotation as doctrinal evidence. The dative Mōusei marks Moses as recipient: For he communicates to Moses.

Romans 9:17 (Exodus 9:16) — "For the Scripture says to Pharaoh." λέγω (says). legō is a historical present, treating the past event of the Exodus text with the vividness of a present occurrence, the Exodus narrative as a living, present reality. The active voice assigns the action to the Old Testament canon itself; the dative indirect object is the indeclinable Pharaō.

Romans 9:22 — "desiring to show his wrath." θέλω (willing, wishing). The present active participle of θέλω is circumstantial, expressing the attendant circumstance of God's action. The present functions as a historical present, viewing a past event with the vividness of an occurrence happening before the listener's eyes. It is not a causal or concessive participle (even though God was willing); that misreading arises from unawareness of the aposiopesis structure.

Romans 9:28 (Isaiah 10:23) — "without delay." συντέμνω (to decree). The second participle is the present active of συντέμνω. The standard rendering cut short or execute speedily reflects Attic usage that does not fit the context; the more precise meaning here is to decree. It is a historical present, viewing the divine decrees of eternity past with the vividness of a present occurrence, and a modal participle expressing the manner of the main verb: the Lord executes His word by completing what He also decreed. The adjunctive καί (also) indicates that the decree preceded creation and history absolutely.

Romans 9:30 — "who did not pursue righteousness." διώκω (to pursue, to chase after, to strive for). The articular present active participle of διώκω is a historical present: though describing Old Testament conditions, the present tense brings that period into vivid focus, as if the camera of narrative were panning across it in real time. The circumstantial participle presents the status quo of those Gentiles during Old Testament history. διώκω denotes active, sustained, effortful pursuit, a meritorious function of the human will.

Romans 9:31 — "Israel who pursued a law." διώκω (to run after, to pursue, to chase). The participle who pursued is the present active participle of διώκω. The present functions as a historical present, viewing the sustained pattern of Jewish negative volition toward Christ throughout the dispensation of Israel with the vividness of a present occurrence. The participle is circumstantial, expressing the historical circumstances of the non-attainment: Israel pursued the law through a mechanism incompatible with its own design.

Romans 10:2 — "I bear them witness." μαρτυρῶ (I testify, from μαρτυρέω). Marturō is the present active indicative of martureō, in classical Greek to testify in court. Paul uses it in its forensic sense: he presents evidence before a tribunal about Israel's spiritual condition. The historical present views a past reality with the vividness of a present occurrence; the declarative indicative presents the content as objective reality.

Romans 10:5 (Leviticus 18:5) — "Moses writes." γράφω (wrote). Graphō, to write, is a historical present that views the past act of writing Leviticus with the vividness of a present occurrence. The active voice assigns human authorship to Moses; the declarative indicative asserts the Old Testament canon as the source of the quotation.

Romans 10:8 (Deuteronomy 30:14) — "But what does it say?" λέγω. Ti, what, is followed by the present active indicative of legō. The historical present views the past message of Moses in Deuteronomy 30 with the vividness of a present occurrence; faith-righteousness is the subject; the declarative indicative makes an unqualified, dogmatic doctrinal statement.

Romans 10:20 (Isaiah 65:1) — "those who did not seek me." ζητέω (seeking). The dative plural present active participle of zēteō, to seek, is a historical present, viewing the past positive volition of Gentile believers at God-consciousness with the vividness of a present event. The author takes them as seekers in a condition of ignorance: positive but without direction, not looking for Christ by name because they lacked Israel's heritage and needed gospel content.

Romans 10:20 (Isaiah 65:1) — "those who did not ask for me." ἐπερωτάω (to ask about). The dative plural present active participle of eperōtaō, to ask or request, used attributively, with the accusative of the personal pronoun: those who did not ask about me. The historical present views the past event with the vividness of a present occurrence: Gentiles with no prior knowledge of the gospel received gospel revelation through divine initiative.

Romans 11:4 — "But what is God's reply to him?" λέγω (what says the divine answer). With χρηματισμός as subject, the present active indicative of λέγω is a historical present, reviewing the past exchange between God and Elijah with the vividness of a present occurrence and drawing the reader into the moment of divine speech.

Romans 11:9 (Psalm 69:22–23) — "And David says." λέγω (David says). The present active indicative of λέγω is a historical present: the past composition of the Psalm by David is viewed with the vividness of a present occurrence. The active voice presents David as human author under the ministry of the Holy Spirit.

Romans 11:25 — "I do not want you to be unaware of this mystery." θέλω (I do not wish). Verse 25 opens with the explanatory γάρ. The main verb is a present active indicative of θέλω with οὐ: I do not wish, I do not desire. The tense is a historical present, viewing Paul's statement with the vividness of a present occurrence. The active voice indicates Paul as the human author, while the Holy Spirit is the actual author.

Romans 13:1 — "and those that exist." εἰμί (those which do exist). The articular present active participle of εἰμί (its article functioning as an immediate demonstrative pointing back to the ἐξουσίαις) is a historical present: the past function of divine establishment is viewed as a present, ongoing occurrence. The rendering is those which do exist, not the vague powers that be of the Authorized Version.

Romans 14:8 — "if we live, we live to the Lord." ζάω (to live). ζάω appears in the present active subjunctive and then the present active indicative. The customary present of the subjunctive describes what habitually occurs after salvation: the believer continues to live. The historical present of the indicative views that life from the vantage point of its ongoing reality with the vividness of present occurrence.

Romans 15:10 — "And again it is said." λέγει (it says). The present active indicative of legō (λέγω) — it says — treats the Old Testament as a living, present word. The historical present tense of this verb views Moses' past act of writing with the vividness of a present occurrence — a standard Greek idiom for emphasis.

Romans 15:12 — "And again Isaiah says." λέγει (says). Paul's introduction uses the present active indicative of legō (λέγω), meaning to communicate or to say. The present tense is a historical present: it views the past event of Isaiah writing under divine inspiration with the vividness of a present occurrence.

Romans 16:5 — "who was the first convert to Christ in Asia." ὅς ἐστιν ἀπαρχή (who is the first fruits). The relative clause that follows employs the nominative singular relative pronoun hos (ὅς), whose antecedent is Epaenetus. With this is the present active indicative of eimi (εἰμί), the verb of being, functioning here as a historical present — a past event described with the vividness of a present occurrence. The predicate nominative is aparchē (ἀπαρχή), meaning first fruits or first convert.

Futuristic Present

Describes a future event as though already certain and therefore already in view.

Romans 2:16 — "on that day when, according to my gospel, God judges the secrets of men." κρίνει ("judges," from κρίνω) is a futuristic present: an event not yet occurred but expressed as present because of its absolute certainty.

Romans 2:27 — "Then he who is physically uncircumcised but keeps the law will condemn you." The present active participle of τελέω ("to complete, accomplish") functioning as a conditional protasis is a futuristic present: an event regarded as so certain that the present tense treats it as already occurring.

Romans 4:24 — "It will be counted to us." μέλλει (behind "it will be") treats the imputation of righteousness to future believers — not yet occurred at the time of writing — as certain and therefore already in view.

Romans 9:27 (Isaiah 10:22) — "Though the number of the sons of Israel be as the sand of the sea." εἰμί (to be). The verb in the protasis is the present active subjunctive of εἰμί. The tense is a futuristic present: a fact not yet accomplished at the moment of writing but regarded as so certain in the divine plan that it is contemplated as already in process. Paul projects a line from his own time through the Church Age, Rapture, Tribulation, Second Advent and Millennium: there will never be a day in human history without Jews on the earth.

Romans 11:26 — "The Deliverer will come from Zion." ῥύομαι (he who delivers). The deliverer is the articular present middle participle of ῥύομαι; the article ὁ functions as a personal pronoun, he who delivers, the Lord Jesus Christ. The present is futuristic: the second advent has not occurred but is so certain in prophetic thought that it is contemplated as already coming to pass — the equivalent of the prophetic perfect in Hebrew. The indirect middle emphasizes Christ as the agent.

Romans 12:19 (Deuteronomy 32:35) — "says the Lord." λέγει κύριος (says the Lord, from λέγω). The present active indicative of legō in legei Kyrios is a futuristic present: an event not yet actualized but so certain in its future occurrence that it is stated as present reality. Kyrios renders the Hebrew divine name, so the Greek Kyrios and the Hebrew YHWH refer to the same deity.

Romans 14:7 — "none of us dies to himself." ἀποθνῄσκω (to die). The present active indicative of ἀποθνῄσκω is a futuristic present: it denotes an event not yet occurred but regarded as so certain that it is contemplated as already occurring. Physical death is future for every living believer, but so real and inevitable that the text treats it as present reality.

Romans 14:8 — "we die to the Lord." ἀποθνῄσκω (to die). The second occurrence of ἀποθνῄσκω in the dying clause is a futuristic present indicative: certain in contemplation and declarative of reality. Dying grace is the inevitable terminal blessing of the believer who has lived to the Lord.

Romans 15:12 — "he who arises to rule the Gentiles." ἄρχειν (to rule). The purpose of the resurrection is stated by the present active infinitive of archō (ἄρχω), to rule. The futuristic present tense denotes an event not yet occurred but regarded as so certain that it is mentally already in existence — the equivalent of the prophetic perfect in Hebrew.
