The infinitive expresses actual result.

Romans 15:24 — "I hope to see you in passing." διαπορευόμενος (when passing through). Next is the present middle participle of diaporeuomai (διαπορεύομαι), meaning to pass through. The present tense functions here as a futuristic present — an action anticipated as imminent. The participle is temporal. Corrected translation: when passing through.

Romans 15:25 — "bringing aid to the saints." διακονῶν (ministering). The phrase 'to minister to the saints' employs the present active participle of diakoneō (διακονέω), meaning to serve, to administer, to minister. The futuristic present notes Paul's anticipated administration of the offering alongside his hope for doctrinal teaching.

Romans 15:29 — "when I come to you." ἐρχόμενος (when I come). The present tense here is a futuristic present — an event not yet occurred but so certain in Paul's thinking that it is already contemplated as in progress. Corrected translation: when I come face-to-face with you.

Retroactive Progressive Present

Describes a condition that began in the past and continues, unbroken, into the present moment.

Romans 4:17 — "the things that do not exist." μὴ ὄντα describes Abraham's sexual death as begun years before and continuing unbroken into the moment of the promise.

Romans 6:8 — "we believe that we will also live with him." πιστεύομεν ("we believe") is retroactive progressive: doctrine perceived in the past continues to be operative in the present because notional knowledge (γνῶσις) has been converted to full, exact knowledge (ἐπίγνωσις) through the non-meritorious perception link of faith. This is the daily function of GAP, not initial saving faith.

Romans 7:17 — "sin that dwells within me." οἰκοῦσα (present participle of οἰκέω) is a retroactive progressive present confirming the sin nature's permanent indwelling: the action began at birth and continues uninterrupted through the entire course of physical life, including life after salvation.

Romans 7:20 — same construction, same force: οἰκοῦσα ἁμαρτία, "sin that dwells within me" — the sin nature is not eradicated, suppressed, or diminished at the new birth.

Romans 7:21 — "evil lies close at hand." παράκειμαι ("to be present, to reside") in the retroactive progressive present indicates that evil has resided in the believer since the moment Adam's sin was imputed at birth, continuing to the present.

Romans 8:5 — "those who live according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh." φρονοῦσιν (present active indicative of φρονέω) is a retroactive progressive present: what has been occurring in the past and continues into the present — the carnal or reversionistic believer keeps thinking the things of the old sin nature, a settled and continuing orientation, not an occasional lapse.

Romans 8:9 — "you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit." ἐστέ (negated) is a retroactive progressive present: a condition begun at the moment of salvation and continuing without interruption — indeed permanently — into the present.

Romans 10:2 — "they have a zeal for God." ἔχω (to have, to possess). Echō, to have, is a retroactive progressive present: it denotes what has occurred in the past and continues into the present. The possession of zeal began in the past and is an ongoing characteristic of the Jewish unbeliever; the active voice assigns the action to him and the declarative indicative asserts it as historical reality.

Romans 10:6 (Deuteronomy 30:11–14) — "says." λέγω (communicates). Legei, present active indicative of legō, here to give expression, to communicate; faith-righteousness is personified as a communicating agent. The retroactive progressive present means that what Moses wrote in Deuteronomy 30 in the past continues to communicate its truth into the present and every subsequent generation.

Romans 12:4 — "we have many members." ἔχομεν (we have, from ἔχω). Echomen is a retroactive progressive present: the royal family has had this structure since the Church began at Pentecost and continues to have it as the Church Age moves toward the rapture. The declarative indicative expresses a dogmatic doctrinal principle.

Romans 12:8 — "the one who contributes." μεταδίδωμι (he who gives). The articular present active participle of metadidōmi; the prefix meta intensifies the simple verb didōmi, yielding imparting or giving a share with intensity of purpose. The retroactive progressive present denotes action begun at salvation and continuing into the present under the function of the gift. The participle is circumstantial.

Romans 13:4 — "on the wrongdoer." πράσσω (the one who practices). The present active participle of πράσσω is a retroactive progressive present: the action began in the past and continues into the present. The one in view is not the person who commits a single impulsive act but the habitual criminal, who has organized his life around conduct that violates the rights of others; the criminal mind precedes and generates the criminal act.

Romans 13:5 — "one must be in subjection." ὑποτάσσω (to be subordinate). The present middle infinitive of ὑποτάσσω is a retroactive progressive present: continuous subordination, regardless of who holds office.

Romans 14:1 — "As for the one who is weak in faith." ἀσθενέω (to be weak, to be deficient, to be powerless). The verse opens with a present active participle of ἀσθενέω. The present tense is a retroactive progressive present: the condition of weakness began in the past, through sustained negative volition toward Bible doctrine, and continues into the present. The active voice indicates that the weak believer himself produces this condition.

Romans 14:2 — "the weak person." ἀσθενέω (to be weak, to be without strength). The present active participle of ἀσθενέω is a causal participle, making weakness the ground for the main verb: on the other hand, that one, because of weakness. The retroactive progressive present denotes a condition that began in the past (no doctrine, or insufficient doctrine) and continues into the present.

Romans 14:6 — "observes it in honor of the Lord." φρονέω (to observe, to consider, to regard). The present active indicative of φρονέω is a retroactive progressive present: the action began at the point of reaching spiritual maturity and continues through the believer’s advance into the supergrace and ultra-supergrace stages. The declarative indicative presents the action as absolute reality.

Romans 14:10 — "Why do you pass judgment on your brother?" κρίνω (to judge, to evaluate adversely, to condemn). κρίνω is a retroactive progressive present, an action begun in the past and continuing into the present. It functions also as a present of duration: given the opportunity, this is what the weak believer characteristically and repeatedly does; it is his occupational hazard and besetting sin.

Romans 14:22 — "The faith that you have." ἔχω (which you have). The present active indicative of ἔχω (to have and to hold) is a retroactive progressive present: what began in the past continues into the present through the ongoing function of the grace apparatus for perception. It indicates sustained doctrine intake, and the declarative indicative states that believers who remain with doctrine do possess it as the basis for norms and standards in the conscience.

Romans 14:22 — "for what he approves." δοκιμάζω (he approves). After ἐν with the locative of the relative ὅς (in what), the verb is the present active indicative of δοκιμάζω: to test for the purpose of approval, to examine and accept as approved, to decide after examination. The present is retroactive progressive, an action begun in the past (the intake of doctrine) and continuing into the present, with doctrine now forming the norms and standards of the soul.

Romans 15:1 — "to bear with the failings of the weak." βαστάζω (to take up, to carry, to bear). The clause opens with the present active infinitive of bastazō (βαστάζω), meaning to take up, to carry, to bear. The retroactive progressive present tense denotes an action that began in the past and continues into the present. The active voice assigns the action to the mature believer.

Romans 15:8 — "For I tell you." λέγω (I report). The main verb is the present active indicative of legō (λέγω), used here as a communication verb meaning to report. The retroactive progressive present denotes a report originated by Paul in the past that continues valid into the present.

Romans 15:31 — "the unbelievers in Judea." ἀπειθούντων (who are disobedient). With this comes the present active participle of apeitheō (ἀπειθέω), a verb meaning to disobey, to be disobedient, or to be an unbeliever. The present tense is durative, denoting a condition that has begun in the past and continues to the present.

Romans 16:1 — "a servant of the church at Cenchreae." οὖσαν (who is). A circumstantial participle from eimi (εἰμί) introduces Phoebe's description: 'who is.' The retroactive progressive present tense denotes something begun in the past and continuing into the present, indicating stability of character — a long-established pattern of faithful ministry.

Romans 16:17 — "those who cause divisions and create obstacles." τοὺς … ποιοῦντας (those who are causing). The articular present active participle of poieō (ποιέω) — 'those who are causing' — governs two accusative plural direct objects. The retroactive progressive present indicates action begun in the past and continuing into the present.

Pictorial Present

Presents a scene as a mental photograph of an ongoing condition.

Romans 4:19 — "since he was about a hundred years old." ὑπάρχων presents Abraham's persisting condition as a single mental image.

Romans 6:16 — the present tense of παρίστημι ("present/place yourselves," discussed fully at 6:13) is pictorial: it brings before the mind the ongoing, daily process of self-placement under orders — a repeated volitional act, not a single decision. Salvation is once-for-all; the authority decision is renewed daily.

Romans 9:16 — "it depends not on human will." θέλω (from him who desires blessing). thelo appears as an articular present active participle; the article functions as a personal pronoun in the ablative of source, from him, emphasizing the negative identification of the source of divine blessing. The pictorial present presents to the mind a continuous picture of human beings desiring blessing from God. The subject can be believer or unbeliever; in context the primary referent is Esau, who kept desiring the blessing (Hebrews 12:17).

Romans 9:19 — "Why does he still find fault?" μέμφομαι (why does he still find fault). The neuter interrogative tis is rendered why; the adverb eti, yet, still, carries the force of after all that has been presented. The present middle indicative of memphomai, to find fault, to blame, is a pictorial present rendering fault-finding as ongoing and vivid. The indicative is interrogative; God is the implied subject: the objector asks how God can legitimately find fault with a person whose heart He has Himself hardened.

Romans 9:27 (Isaiah 10:22) — "And Isaiah cries out concerning Israel." κράζει (to cry out, to speak urgently, from κράζω). The main verb is κράζει, present active indicative of κράζω, whose range extends from screaming and shrieking to urgent, impassioned public speech. Cries out may give a misleading impression of raw emotion detached from content; the precise sense is urgent, emergency proclamation under conditions of extreme national crisis and doctrinal necessity. The pictorial present transports the reader into the crisis context of Isaiah's original proclamation, making its doctrinal content vivid and contemporaneous.

Romans 10:3 — "seeking to establish their own." ζητοῦντες (to seek diligently, from ζητέω). Zēteō here means to seek diligently, and what is sought, self-righteousness, has no standing before God. The present tense is pictorial, presenting the action as a scene in process: enormous energy is expended in pursuit of a category God has already nullified.

Romans 11:2 — "how he appeals to God against Israel." ἐντυγχάνω (he pleaded). The present tense of ἐντυγχάνω is a pictorial present, placing the scene vividly before the mind. The active voice makes Elijah the subject producing the action; τῷ θεῷ is the indirect object.

Romans 11:7 — "what it was seeking." ἐπιζητέω (is constantly seeking). In the compound ἐπιζητέω the prefix ἐπί intensifies ζητέω: to seek earnestly, to press toward, to pursue with concentrated effort. The pictorial present presents the action as ongoing and continuous: Israel is constantly seeking, and what it seeks is a righteousness obtained through works.

Romans 11:13 — "Now I am speaking to you Gentiles." λέγω (I speak, I say). The present active indicative of λέγω (derived from λόγος, the expression of thought) is pictorial and progressive: it presents Paul's communication as actively in progress. The active voice identifies Paul as the human author producing the action. The indicative is declarative, representing the verbal idea as reality — specifically, the reality of verbal plenary inspiration.

Romans 12:16 — "Never be wise in your own sight." γίνομαι (stop being). Mē with the present imperative of ginomai. The use of mē rather than ou confirms the imperative mood. The present is a pictorial present for events in the process of occurrence, a condition already developing among the Roman believers; the imperative of prohibition is rendered stop becoming, or in context, stop being.

Romans 14:4 — "It is before his own master that he stands or falls." πίπτω (to fall, to become a casualty). The alternative, or becomes a casualty, is the present active indicative of πίπτω, which from Homer onward carried a consistent military connotation: to fall in battle. In Romans 14:4 it is a pictorial present for reversionism in process, the believer becoming a spiritual casualty through rejection of doctrine.

Romans 14:7 — "none of us lives to himself." ζάω (to live). The present active indicative of ζάω is a pictorial present, painting the ongoing process of phase two, the believer’s life in time. The active voice indicates that he lives, not merely passively existing, but functioning within God’s plan.

Romans 14:13 — "let us not pass judgment on one another any longer." κρίνω (let us no longer judge). The pictorial present of κρίνω denotes an action currently in progress that must be discontinued. The active voice indicates that the weak believers in the Roman church are themselves producing this action.

Romans 14:20 — "by what he eats." ἐσθίω (who by eating). The participle of ἐσθίω is instrumental, indicating the means by which the evil is accomplished: by eating. The pictorial present presents the strong believer in the act of eating in circumstances where the weak believer is distracted.

Romans 15:3 — "The reproaches of those who reproached you." ὀνειδίζω (to insult, to reproach). The verb is the articular present active participle of oneidizō (ὀνειδίζω), to insult, to reproach. The pictorial present tense presents to the mind a vivid picture of the events of the cross across the six hours of the crucifixion, during which unbelieving reversionistic Jews maintained a sustained barrage of blasphemy and insult.

Romans 15:25 — "I am going to Jerusalem." πορεύομαι (I am going). The verb is the present middle indicative of poreuomai (πορεύομαι), meaning to go, to travel, to make a journey. The pictorial present tense presents the action as in process in the mind — Paul is not yet moving, but he describes the journey as if already underway.

Romans 16:22 — "I Tertius, who wrote this letter, greet you in the Lord." ἀσπάζομαι ὑμᾶς ἐγὼ Τέρτιος (I Tertius greet you). The verb in verse 22 is again the present active indicative of aspazomai (ἀσπάζομαι). Here it is a pictorial present — presenting to the mind a picture of the greeting in the process of occurring at the moment of writing.

Present of Duration

Denotes a condition that began in the past and continues, without break, up to the present moment.

Romans 1:28 — "God gave them up to a debased mind to do what ought not to be done." The articular present active participle τὰ μὴ καθήκοντα ("those things not proper," from καθήκω negated) denotes duration: what was begun in the past and continues into the present — the worthless mind keeps on doing what is improper.

Romans 6:16 — "you are slaves of the one whom you obey." ἐστε (present active of εἰμί) is a present of duration: the believer has been exercising a daily option since the moment of salvation, and that pattern of exercise is the reality being described.

Romans 9:2 — "that I have great sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart." εἰμί (there is). The present active indicative of eimi is a present of duration: a state begun in the past and continuing unbroken into the present. Paul's burden for Israel is not a recent development provoked by a single crisis but the constant companion of his apostolic ministry.

Romans 9:7 — "because they are his offspring." εἰμί (they are). The present active indicative of eimi is durative, denoting a state that began in the past and continues into the present: the existence of the Jewish race, which began with Abraham's circumcision and has continued through Isaac, Jacob, the twelve patriarchs and all subsequent generations. The active voice assigns the action to the racial Jew; the indicative is declarative.

Romans 10:3 — "being ignorant of the righteousness of God." ἀγνοοῦντες (not knowing, from ἀγνοέω). Agnoountes is the present active participle of agnoeō, to be ignorant, to not know. The present of duration (the present of unity of time) gathers up past and present action into one ongoing condition: these individuals have been and continue to be ignorant of the righteousness of God, a condition maintained across multiple points of volitional decision. The active voice shows the Jewish unbelievers themselves producing the condition.

Romans 11:2 (1 Kings 19:10, 14) — "what the Scripture says." λέγω (says, continues to say). With the singular γραφή (the specific passage in 1 Kings 19) as subject, the present active indicative of λέγω is a durative present: the Scripture continues to speak. What was written stands and continues to communicate; its declarative force is permanent and ongoing.

Romans 13:3 — "For rulers are not a terror." εἰμί (are not). The present active indicative of εἰμί with οὐ is a present of duration: the principle of establishment begun in the past continues into the present. Legitimate governmental authority does not function as a source of terror.

Romans 15:17 — "I have reason to be proud." ἔχω (I keep on having). The main verb is the present active indicative of echō (ἔχω), to have, to hold. The present tense here is the present of duration — a retroactive progressive denoting that perception of doctrine in the past, continuing into the present, has permanent implication. The translation is therefore: Therefore I keep on having.

Romans 16:4 — "to whom not only I give thanks." εὐχαριστῶ (I give thanks). The main verb is the present active indicative of eucharisteō (εὐχαριστέω), meaning to give thanks, to express genuine gratitude. The present tense is durative — it denotes gratitude that began at a specific point and continues into the present.

Romans 16:18 — "do not serve our Lord Christ." οὐ δουλεύουσιν (they do not serve as slaves). The governing verb is the present active indicative of douleuō (δουλεύω), from doulos (δοῦλος), meaning slave. The present tense is the present of duration: an action begun in the past that continues into the present.

Iterative Present

Describes an action recurring at successive instances, not a single occurrence covering all cases at once.

Romans 2:15 — "They show that the work of the law is written on their hearts." ἐνδείκνυνται ("show, demonstrate," from ἐνδείκνυμι) is an iterative present, indirect middle: what recurs at successive intervals of history — across every generation, Gentiles without the law have repeatedly, observably demonstrated this fact.

Romans 4:24 — "to whom it will be counted." λογίζεσθαι describes the imputation recurring at each instance of a person believing, not once for the whole race collectively.

Romans 7:25 — "with my mind I myself serve the law of God." δουλεύω ("I serve") is iterative — describing what occurs at successive intervals, the alternative resulting from an ongoing, repeated option, not a single decision.

Romans 13:4 — "But if you do wrong." ποιέω (if you do). The present active subjunctive of ποιέω is an iterative present, describing what is conceived of in successive periods: potential repeated action. The warning is addressed to believers, who can produce the evil when they are negative toward doctrine and moving in reversionism.

Nomic Future

A future-tense form used not to predict a single event but to state what may rightly be expected under stated conditions — an academic, classificatory statement rather than a prophecy. (Treated fully in section V.)

Romans 7:3 — "she will be called an adulteress" (ESV). χρηματίσει ("she shall be classified as") is a nomic future: a purely objective, legal-classificatory statement, not a moral denunciation.

Romans 8:32 — "he... will he not also graciously give us all things?" χαρίσεται functions simultaneously as a nomic future and a deliberative future (see section V) depending on the hearer's spiritual condition — a genuinely dual-purpose use of a single future-tense form.

Romans 11:19 — "Then you will say." λέγω (you will say). The form ἐρῶ serves as the future active indicative of λέγω, since legō does not form its own future (chapter 733). The future is a nomic future — it anticipates an action expected under the conditions stated: Gentile-believer arrogance operating within the interlocking systems of arrogance. The inferential οὖν marks what follows as the conclusion drawn by the arrogant mind from the historical fact of Israel's setting aside.

Romans 11:35 (Job 41:11) — "that he might be repaid." ἀνταποδίδωμι (it shall be repaid to him). The verse quotes Job 41:11. καί links the clause to the future passive indicative of the double compound ἀνταποδίδωμι (anti + apo + didōmi: to pay back, repay, recompense). The nomic future states a condition that can be rightly expected under normal conditions: it shall be repaid to him. God is never indebted to the creature for gifts presented.

Romans 12:20 — "you will heap burning coals on his head." σωρεύω (you will pile up). The future active indicative of sōreuō, to pile up, to heap. The future is nomic: it states a fact that may be expected under the conditions specified. The believer produces the action indirectly: his grace gesture sets in motion the justice of God.

Romans 13:2 — "will incur judgment." λαμβάνω (shall receive). The future middle indicative of λαμβάνω is a nomic future: it states a fact of judgment from God that can be expected under the specified circumstances, a fact that invariably follows anti-establishment activity.

Romans 15:12 — "in him will the Gentiles hope." ἐλπιοῦσιν (will hope). The verb is the future active indicative of elpizō (ἐλπίζω). Unusually, Paul employs the Attic Greek future form rather than the Koine form. The Attic future is also nomic here — a statement of fact or expected performance.

Romans 15:21 — "those who have never heard will understand." συνήσουσιν (they will understand). The final verb is the future active indicative of syniēmi (συνίημι), meaning to comprehend, to understand the underlying laws and meaning of a subject — in this context, technical comprehension of the gospel. The nomic future tense states a fact that may rightly be expected: those Gentiles previously ignorant of Christ will, at the second advent, arrive at full comprehension of who He is — through the startling event of His appearing.

The Aoristic Present

Romans 10:18 — "But I ask." λέγω (I say). After the adversative alla (contrasting Israel's failure as a client nation with the unimpeded advance of God's plan), legō is an aoristic present: punctiliar action in present time marking a slight change of subject to add rational emphasis to the argument. Paul himself speaks as debater; the same aoristic present opens verse 19, and verses 18–21 are the apex of his debater's technique.

Gnomic Present

Romans 12:20 — "give him something to drink." ποτίζω (give him drink). The apodosis has the present active imperative of potizō, to give drink. The present tense is gnomic: it states a perpetual standard. Whenever an antagonistic person is in a situation where you can save his life, you save his life, regardless of his attitude toward you.

IV.Verbal Aspect — the Imperfect Tense

Imperfect of Duration

Contemplates an action or state as having been continuously in progress over a period of past time, without asserting that the process is now complete.

Romans 5:13 — "sin indeed was in the world before the law was given." ἦν ("was," imperfect active of εἰμί) is an imperfect of duration: sin was in continuous existence throughout the period from Adam to Moses. Paul's point is that this ongoing state did not depend on the Mosaic law's existence — the law did not introduce sin, it only defined and declared it.

Romans 7:6 — "having died to that which held us captive." κατειχόμεθα (imperfect passive of κατέχω, "to hold down, suppress, bind") emphasizes that the tyranny of the sin nature as first husband was continuous from physical birth to the new birth. The passive voice establishes that this bondage was received, not chosen.

Romans 7:9 — "I was once alive apart from the law." ἔζων (imperfect of ζάω) is an imperfect of duration: the condition of living apart from the law was an ongoing state in past time — for Paul writing the letter it belongs to the past, but for a reader not yet instructed it may still describe a present condition, so the tense marks both the historical character of the experience and its continuing applicability to anyone not yet exposed to the law's diagnosis.

Romans 8:3 — "the law, weakened by the flesh." ἠσθένει (imperfect active of ἀσθενέω, "to be weak") is a progressive imperfect describing an ongoing condition in past time: the law was continually weak — not a single failure but a sustained state of powerlessness, owing entirely to the flesh (the sin nature) it had to contend with, not to any defect in the law itself.

Inceptive Imperfect

Denotes linear, ongoing past action viewed from its starting point, without a stated point of completion.

Romans 6:17 — "you who were once slaves of sin." ἦτε ("you kept on being," imperfect active of εἰμί) is an inceptive imperfect representing linear, ongoing past action without a stated endpoint. The positional termination of slavery to the sin nature is salvation; the experiential termination depends entirely on the believer's volitional engagement with doctrine.

Qualitative Imperfect (Quasi-Optative)

Romans 9:3 — "For I could wish that I myself were accursed." εὔχομαι (I could wish). The main verb is the imperfect middle indicative of euchomai, to pray or to wish. The imperfect functions as a qualitative imperfect, sometimes called a quasi-optative, expressing a wish that cannot be realized because of an intervening obstacle, specifically the permanent union of the believer with Christ. The force is: I would like to pray this, but I cannot.

Romans 15:22 — "I have so often been hindered." ἐνεκοπτόμην (I was being hindered). The main verb is the imperfect passive indicative of egkoptō, ἐγκόπτω, meaning to impede, to hinder, to prevent, to detain. The imperfect tense here is the qualitative imperfect: it denotes the lack of attainment of a desired goal — in this case Paul's repeated desire to come to Rome — over the entire period of his eastern ministry.

V.Verbal Aspect — the Future Tense

Romans 2:6 — "He will render to each one according to his works." ἀποδώσει ("will render," from ἀποδίδωμι) is a predictive future active indicative: Christ as presiding judge (John 5:22) produces this proportional rendering — commensurate reward or punishment, quoted from Psalm 62:12 and Proverbs 24:12.

Romans 2:12 — "All who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law, and all who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law." κριθήσονται ("will be judged," from κρίνω) is a future passive, gnomic in force: a fact rightly expected under the conditions of Jewish maladjustment — the passive voice shows the judgment coming from an external standard (the law), contrasted with the middle-voice ἀπολοῦνται ("will perish") for the Gentile, whose perishing reflects his own condition.

Romans 2:26 — "So, if a man who is uncircumcised keeps the precepts of the law, will not his uncircumcision be regarded as circumcision?" λογισθήσεται ("will be regarded/credited," from λογίζομαι) is a future passive indicative in a rhetorical question introduced by the negative οὐκ, requiring the answer "yes" — a key lexeme carried forward into Romans 4:3–5.

Romans 3:3 — "Does their faithlessness nullify the faithfulness of God?" καταργήσει ("will nullify," from καταργέω) is a deliberative future: shall their lack of faith cancel the integrity of God? The expected answer is a categorical no.

Romans 3:6 — "For then how could God judge the world?" A deliberative future underlies this rhetorical question, posed from within a debater's technique that Paul immediately overturns.

Predictive Future

Anticipates an event as certain to occur in future time.

Romans 5:7 — "one will scarcely die for a righteous person." ἀποθανεῖται (future middle of ἀποθνῄσκω) anticipates the event; the middle voice here is permissive — the agent voluntarily yields himself to the result of the action, as a soldier might fall on a grenade or a person might die from a sense of duty.

Romans 5:9 — "we shall be saved by him from the wrath of God." σωθησόμεθα (future passive of σῴζω) prophesies ultimate sanctification — the resurrection body — as a future certainty. The passive voice indicates the believer receives this: it is given, not earned.

Romans 5:10 — "we shall be saved by his life." The same verb, σωθησόμεθα, describing the believer's future deliverance in Christ's resurrection life.

Romans 5:17 — "those who receive... will reign in life." βασιλεύσουσιν (future active of βασιλεύω) is predictive: it indicates what is expected in future time, specifically eternity — the reward of rulership reserved for the mature believer, not a present condition.

Romans 5:19 — "the many will be made righteous." κατασταθήσονται (future passive of καθίστημι) is a predictive future, anticipating the imputation of divine righteousness to every future believer.

Romans 6:14 — "sin will have no dominion over you." κυριεύσει (future active of κυριεύω) combines with the negative to state a predictive future functioning as an obligation: the sin nature will not lord it over the believer — provided the believer consistently uses the grace provisions available.

Romans 7:24 — "Who will deliver me from this body of death?" ῥύσεται (future of ῥύομαι) is predictive of an ongoing rescue rather than a single dramatic event (see the Progressive Future entry immediately below).

Romans 8:11 — "he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies." A straightforward predictive future describing the resurrection of the believer's body as a future certainty, guaranteed by the same Spirit who raised Christ.

Romans 8:30 — the entire "golden chain" of verbs (foreknew, predestined, called, justified, glorified) is stated in the aorist, not the future, even though glorification is not yet experientially complete for any living believer — a deliberate grammatical choice (see the Gnomic Aorist entry, section I): in the divine decrees, all five steps are already, in effect, accomplished fact.

Romans 9:9 (Genesis 18:10) — "I will return." ἐλεύσομαι (I will come to impute blessing, from ἔρχομαι). eleusomai, future active indicative of erchomai, is a predictive future, an event expected to occur in future time. The active voice: the Lord Jesus Christ, who appeared to Abraham as the angel of the Lord, promises to fulfill the action. The indicative expresses the certainty of the imputation of divine blessing to the mature Abraham; the force is purposive, coming for the express purpose of imputing blessing.

Romans 9:15 (Exodus 33:19) — "I will have mercy on whom I have mercy." ἐλεέω (I will have mercy). Paul uses the future active indicative of eleeō, a predictive future. Because Moses used the qal imperfect, the historical printout, Paul picks up from that printout and shows the principle continues: what God did in mercy for Moses and the faithful remnant of the Exodus generation he will do for believers in Paul's day. The predictive future declares the reality of the imputation of divine blessing to the mature believer.

Romans 9:19 — "You will say to me then." εἴρω (you will say). Paul introduces the anticipated objection with a future active indicative of the obsolete Attic verb eirō, treated in Koine as the future of legō. The future is predictive: Paul predicts the thought and anticipated speech of the opposition, the debater's technique of quoting the opponent's thoughts before they are spoken. The dative of indirect object from egō, to me, situates Paul as the direct target; the post-positive inferential oun marks the question as an inference from what Paul has argued.

Romans 9:26 (Hosea 1:10) — "And in the very place." εἰμί (it shall be). The verse opens with a connective καί followed by the future active indicative of εἰμί. The future is predictive, pointing to the second advent of Christ as the moment of fulfillment; the active voice indicates that the second advent produces the action; the indicative is declarative, expressing the certainty of the fulfillment of prophecy.

Romans 9:27 (Isaiah 10:22) — "only a remnant of them will be saved." σῴζω (to save, to deliver; shall be delivered). The verb is the future passive indicative of σῴζω (sōthēsetai). The predictive future announces an event expected in future time; the passive indicates that the remnant receives deliverance, it does not deliver itself; the declarative indicative presents it as prophetic reality, the agent being the Lord Jesus Christ at His Second Advent. Paul's use of σῴζω rather than a term corresponding to the Hebrew shub (to return) adds the soteriological qualification that the returning remnant is the believing remnant.

Romans 9:28 (Isaiah 10:23) — "will carry out his sentence upon the earth." ποιέω (to execute). The main verb is the future active indicative of ποιέω, correctly rendered to execute, not to finish. The predictive future refers to the second advent, when the Lord Jesus Christ will terminate the conditions produced by Israel's negative volition toward the first advent and restore the believing remnant. ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς anchors this execution to a concrete, historical act on the earth, not a spiritual or invisible fulfillment.

Romans 9:33 (Isaiah 28:16) — "will not be put to shame." καταισχύνω (to be disgraced, humiliated, disappointed). The future passive indicative of καταισχύνω (kata + aischynō, to shame) is negated by οὐ. The predictive future states that no believer will ever be humiliated at the last judgment; the passive with the negative means the believing Jew will never face condemnation at the great white throne. Faith in Christ eliminates not only condemnation in time but disappointment in eternity (compare Romans 8:1).

Romans 10:11 (Isaiah 28:16) — "will not be put to shame." καταισχύνω (shall not be disappointed). Paul's interpretive rendering of the Hiphil of ḥûsh (to be disturbed, to panic) is the future passive indicative of kataischynō with the negative. The future is predictive, looking to the last judgment; the passive with the negative indicates that the believer will not receive the action of the verb: he will not be disappointed. The indicative is declarative for the reality of this guarantee.

Romans 10:13 (Joel 2:32) — "will be saved." σωθήσεται (will be saved, from σῴζω). The result clause uses the future passive indicative of sōzō. The shift from subjunctive in the protasis to indicative in the apodosis is significant: the subjunctive governs the condition (maybe you will call, maybe not); the indicative governs the result (if you call, you will certainly be saved). The future is predictive, a dogmatic statement of fact; the passive shows salvation received from God, not produced by the believer.

Romans 10:19 (Deuteronomy 32:21) — "I will make you jealous." παραζηλόω (I will make you jealous). Parazēloō, future active indicative, to provoke to jealousy. The predictive future prophesies a divine judgment resulting from the great inversion: the justice of God blessing Gentiles in such a way that disciplined Jews are provoked to jealousy. The direct object is the plural of sy used collectively for the nation of Israel. The second verb, parorgizō, is likewise future active indicative.

Romans 11:26 — "all Israel will be saved." σωθήσεται (shall be delivered, from σῴζω). σωθήσεται is the future passive indicative of σῴζω, which carries three meanings in the New Testament: deliverance from any danger; individual or collective physical rescue; regeneration. Context decides. Here the future is predictive, pointing to the second advent; the passive shows that Jewish tribulation believers receive divine deliverance from the greatest anti-Semitic assault in history. Regeneration is presupposed but is not the primary referent.

Romans 11:26 — "The Deliverer will come from Zion." ἥκω (will come). The main verb is the future active indicative of ἥκω, to come, to arrive: a predictive future for the second advent of the Lord Jesus Christ, affirming its historical reality. ἐκ Σιών establishes the Davidic reference: Zion, captured by David as his royal headquarters, expands in the prophets to the whole concept of a client nation to God.

Romans 11:26 — "he will banish ungodliness from Jacob." ἀποστρέφω (to remove completely). ἀποστρέφω, future active indicative, means to remove completely: a predictive future referring to the baptism of fire, one of the seven baptisms of Scripture and a defining event of the second advent. The object ἀσέβεια is used collectively for the godless ones, the unbelieving Jews, removed from the national entity through the baptism of fire.

Romans 12:19 (Deuteronomy 32:35) — "I will repay." ἀνταποδίδωμι (I will repay). The future active indicative of the triple compound antapodidōmi, anti + apo + didōmi: to discharge an obligation, to pay back, to compensate. The future is predictive: the justice of God will execute punitive action at its own appointed time.

Romans 13:3 — "and you will receive his approval." ἔχω (you will have). The future active indicative of ἔχω is predictive, denoting an idea in progress in future time. The declarative indicative views the action from the standpoint of reality: receiving recognition is a statement of fact, not merely a possibility.

Romans 14:10 — "we will all stand before the judgment seat of God." παρίστημι (to stand by, to present oneself). The future of παρίστημι is a predictive future referring to the post-rapture judgment event; the declarative indicative is a dogmatic, unqualified assertion of fact. The subject πᾶς, all, covers all believers without exception.

Romans 14:11 — "every knee shall bow to me." κάμπτω (shall genuflex). κάμπτω (to bend the knee, to genuflex) is a future active indicative. The predictive future designates an event that has not yet occurred but will occur with absolute certainty immediately following the rapture of the Church, and the declarative indicative states it as a fixed point in the divine plan.

Romans 14:12 — "will give an account." δίδωμι (shall give). δίδωμι is a predictive future active indicative: the accounting lies ahead and will certainly occur. The active voice indicates that every believer produces this action personally, and the indicative presents it as actual reality, not possibility.

Romans 15:18 — "I will not venture to speak." τολμήσω (I will presume). The main verb is a future active indicative of τολμάω (tolmaō), meaning to dare or to presume. In this context, where Paul is speaking of apostolic humility, the correct rendering is "to presume." The predictive future describes Paul's ongoing practice.

Romans 15:21 — "Those who have never been told of him will see." ὄψονται (they shall see). The predictive future anticipates the second advent when every eye shall see Him, including those Gentiles who had no prior knowledge of Him.

Romans 15:28 — "I will leave for Spain by way of you." ἀπελεύσομαι (I will go). The main verb of verse 28 is the future middle indicative of aperchomai (ἀπέρχομαι), a deponent verb middle in form but active in meaning: I will go. The future tense is a predictive future for an event expected to occur in future time.

Romans 15:29 — "I will come in the fullness of the blessing of Christ." ἐλεύσομαι (I shall come). Paul opens with the future middle indicative of erchomai (ἔρχομαι), meaning to come. The predictive future tense expresses Paul's certainty that it is God's will for him to reach Rome.

Romans 16:20 — "The God of peace will soon crush Satan." συντρίψει (will crush). The verb is the future active indicative of syntribō (συντρίβω), which means to crush, to break in pieces, to smash. The future tense is a predictive future, pointing to an eschatological event. Corrected translation: will crush, will break in pieces.

Progressive Future

A future tense describing an action that will unfold gradually, day by day, rather than occurring as a single completed event.

Romans 7:24 — "Who will deliver me from this body of death?" ῥύσεται (future of ῥύομαι, "to rescue," specifically a rescue by dragging someone out of danger when they cannot move under their own power) is a progressive future: the rescue proceeds day by day through consistent doctrinal intake, not through a single dramatic experience. The reversionistic believer cannot self-rescue — the verb itself establishes complete helplessness.

Deliberative Future

A future-tense verb used in a rhetorical question, standing in for a direct assertion — the question admits only one correct answer.

Romans 6:1 — "What shall we say then?" The opening formula employs a deliberative future of λέγω, framing the rhetorical question that opens the chapter.

Romans 6:2 — "How can we who died to sin still live in it?" ζήσομεν is a deliberative future: the rhetorical question functions as an assertion by means of a question that admits only one answer — we cannot.

Romans 8:32 — see the Nomic Future entry above: χαρίσεται functions as a deliberative future for the believer who has already cracked the maturity barrier, for whom the blessing described is already a present reality rather than a future hope.

Romans 8:33 — "Who shall bring any charge against God's elect?" ἐγκαλέσει (future active of ἐγκαλέω, "to bring charges, to accuse, to institute judicial proceedings") is a deliberative future: a rhetorical question stated in the future indicative to make a doctrinal assertion without direct declaration — no creature, whether Satan or a fellow believer, has any authorization to bring such an accusation.

Romans 8:35 — "Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?" The future of χωρίζω here functions identically: a rhetorical question expecting the answer "no one," not a genuine inquiry about a future event.

Romans 9:14 — "What shall we say then?" λέγω (shall we say). The future of legō is a deliberative future: questions of uncertainty or challenge follow this pattern, the speaker anticipating an objection and framing the response. The active voice represents Paul using the rhetorical debater's idiom to force a correct conclusion. The interrogative indicative assumes that an actual fact can be stated in answer to the question.

Romans 9:20 — "Will what is molded say to its molder." μὴ λέγω (say, from λέγω). The verbal complex is μὴ λέγω in the future active indicative. The future is a deliberative future, expressing a question of uncertainty or logical inquiry. The active voice makes the molded object the one speaking, and the interrogative indicative assumes an actual state of affairs the question brings to light. Because μή governs it, the question is rhetorical and its answer is predetermined: no.

Romans 9:30 — "What shall we say, then?" τί οὖν ἐροῦμεν (Therefore, to what conclusion are we forced?, from λέγω). Paul opens the final paragraph of Romans 9 with τί οὖν ἐροῦμεν: τί (what?), the inferential post-positive οὖν (therefore) and the future active indicative of λέγω. The future is a deliberative future used for a rhetorical question that takes the place of a deliberate assertion: rather than stating a dogmatic conclusion that would antagonize the audience, Paul converts it into a humble question. This is debater's finesse. The idiom announces a verdict rather than soliciting opinion.

Romans 10:6 (Deuteronomy 30:12) — "Who will ascend into heaven?" ἀναβαίνω (who shall ascend). The interrogative pronoun tis is followed by the future middle indicative of anabainō with eis ton ouranon. The future is deliberative rather than strictly temporal: it expresses uncertainty about the agent of an action rather than simple futurity; the question is a rationalization, not a prediction. Paul adds the gloss that this would mean bringing Christ down from above, exposing the rationalization as a denial of the incarnation: Christ has already descended.

Romans 10:7 — "Who will descend into the abyss?" καταβαίνω (who shall descend). The future middle indicative of katabainō, to go down: the deliberative future frames a question of uncertainty. The middle is an indirect middle, emphasizing that the agent produces the action upon himself; the indicative functions as an interrogative indicative. Corrected translation: or who shall descend?

Imperative Future

A future-tense verb used to express a command involving futurity — well attested in classical Greek, and paralleling (though not derived from) the Hebrew idiom of the negative plus imperfect as a prohibition.

Romans 7:7, quoting Exodus 20:17 — "You shall not covet" (ESV) / "You will not lust." οὐκ ἐπιθυμήσεις (future active of ἐπιθυμέω with the negative οὐκ) is an imperative future: the tenth commandment issued as a future-tense prohibition rather than a present-tense one, a construction with genuine classical precedent, not merely a Hebraism.

Romans 13:9 — "You shall not commit adultery." μοιχεύω (thou shalt not commit adultery). μοιχεύω is a future active indicative with οὐ. The future functions as an imperative (the imperative future), a construction found throughout classical Greek and not a Hebraism. Because a command necessarily involves futurity, the future indicative with the negative expresses the prohibition directly and forcefully. The same construction governs φονεύω, κλέπτω, and ἐπιθυμέω in the verse.

Romans 13:9 (Leviticus 19:18) — "You shall love your neighbor as yourself." ἀγαπάω (thou shalt love). ἀγαπήσεις is an imperative future, expressing a command that involves ongoing future conduct. It is also a cohortative indicative: the future indicative conveys the force of a binding command, thou shalt love. The believer as a member of the Royal Family, functioning within the Honor Code, produces the action.

Gnomic Future

Romans 9:7 (Genesis 21:12) — "Through Isaac shall your offspring be named." καλέω (shall be elected, designated). The future passive indicative of kaleō is a gnomic future, a statement of absolute doctrinal fact. The passive voice indicates that Abraham's racial descendants receive the action: they are designated or elected through Isaac. The indicative declares historical reality.

Romans 10:5 (Leviticus 18:5) — "shall live by them." ζάω (shall live). Zēsetai, the future middle indicative of zaō, is a gnomic future: it states a factor of performance that may be expected under the conditions of keeping establishment in a client nation. It refers to quality of life in a client nation, not to salvation or eternal life as a direct gift.

Romans 11:14 — "to make my fellow Jews jealous." παραζηλόω (I shall stimulate to emulation). The future active indicative of παραζηλόω (para, alongside + ζηλόω, to be zealous, to emulate) means to stimulate to emulation, to provoke to jealousy in the positive sense of motivating imitation. The future is gnomic — not prophetic but stating what may be rightfully expected under normal conditions throughout the Church Age: Gentile belief in Christ, visibly blessed by God, motivates Jewish positive volition toward the gospel.

Romans 11:21 — "neither will he spare you." φείδομαι (will spare). The future middle indicative of φείδομαι is gnomic — a statement of what may rightly be expected as a matter of settled divine policy. The same standard applied to the Jewish unbeliever and to the Jewish client nation in apostasy is applied without modification to the Gentile believer who enters the same categories of failure, including anti-Semitism.

Romans 11:22 — "Otherwise you too will be cut off." ἐκκόπτω (you also will be cut off). The future passive indicative of ἐκκόπτω (to cut off, remove, sever) is gnomic-futuristic: it states what may be judicially expected when a believer enters reversionism or the interlocking systems of arrogance. The passive voice: the Gentile believer receives the action; the indicative: the reality of divine discipline is unqualified. It refers to removal from blessing by divine discipline, not to any loss of eternal salvation.

Romans 15:9 — "I will praise you among the Gentiles." ἐξομολογήσομαί (I will acknowledge openly, I will praise). The principal verb is the future middle indicative of exomologeomai (ἐξομολογέομαι). The compound with ex- intensifies the meaning: to acknowledge openly, to praise, to celebrate. The tense is the gnomic future — a statement of performance rightfully expected under the normal conditions of receiving divine blessing. The middle voice is the indirect middle, emphasizing the agent — David himself — as the one who produces the action of praise.

Romans 15:9 — "and sing to your name." ψαλῶ (I will sing with instruments). The second verb is the future active indicative of psallō (ψάλλω), meaning to sing to the accompaniment of musical instruments. The tense is again gnomic: such praise is the normal response to divine blessing.

VI.Mood

Indicative — Declarative vs. Potential Use

The indicative is the mood of reality, but within a debater's argument it can present a premise potentially — exploring what follows from an assumption without asserting the assumption itself.

Romans 4:2 — "For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about, but not before God." The indicative ἐδικαιώθη here is used potentially, within a debater's-technique first-class condition (see section IX): the premise is assumed for the sake of argument, then shown to lead to an impossible conclusion (boasting before God), and therefore rejected.

Romans 4:14 — "For if it is the adherents of the law who are to be heirs, faith is null and void." Same potential-indicative-within-debater's-technique structure.

Romans 4:17 — "who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist." Here the indicative participles are declarative, not potential: they state, as settled fact, the character of God's action.

Romans 7:24 — "Who will deliver me?" The interrogative indicative mood here signals that an answer exists even as the question is being asked — the answer, developed fully in Romans 8, is the Holy Spirit plus Bible doctrine resident in the soul.

The Subjunctive of Emphatic Negation — οὐ μή

The double negative οὐ μή with the subjunctive is the strongest possible negation available in Greek.

Romans 4:8 — "blessed is the man against whom the Lord will not count his sin." οὐ μὴ λογίσηται — the double negation with the aorist subjunctive states categorically and permanently that the Lord will never, under any circumstance, hold this sin against the believer's account.

Hortatory Subjunctive

Includes the speaker with the audience in a course of action not yet undertaken.

Romans 5:1 — "we have peace with God" (subjunctive reading, "let us have prosperity"). ἔχωμεν — the omega ending marks this as subjunctive, not indicative (a critical textual and grammatical distinction: the omicron form ἔχομεν would be declarative "we have," but the best manuscript evidence and internal logic favor the hortatory ἔχωμεν) — Paul exhorts believers, himself included, toward exploitation of the peace already established.

Romans 5:2 — "let us rejoice" (ESV, "we rejoice"). καυχώμεθα is likewise hortatory: an exhortation, not a flat assertion of present fact.

Romans 5:3 — "let us rejoice in our sufferings" (ESV, "we also rejoice"). Same hortatory force, extending the exhortation into the realm of undeserved suffering.

Romans 13:12 — "So then let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light." ἀποτίθημι (let us lay aside). The hortatory subjunctive is tantamount to a command but differs from the imperative in that it takes cognizance of human volition: the exhortation is addressed to the will, not merely to behavior. A second hortatory subjunctive (put on) follows in the same verse.

Romans 13:13 — "Let us walk properly." περιπατέω (let us walk). The aorist subjunctive of περιπατέω is hortatory, commanding the royal family to walk honorably as the subject of the action who also shares in its results.

Romans 14:13 — "let us not pass judgment on one another any longer." κρίνω (let us no longer judge). κρίνω is a present active subjunctive. The subjunctive is hortatory, a first-person command in which the speaker includes himself. With a negative adverb it functions as the equivalent of an imperative while explicitly recognizing that volition is the operative factor: Paul cannot compel obedience, and each believer must be motivated from what is resident in his own soul.

Potential Subjunctive

A subjunctive expressing an action or result qualified by contingency — the outcome depends on a condition being met, not stated as an unconditional certainty.

Romans 6:4 — "in order that... we too might walk in newness of life." περιπατήσωμεν (potential subjunctive) establishes newness of life as a potential, not an automatic reality — converted into actuality only through the capacity factor of doctrine resident in the soul.

Romans 6:6 — "so that the body of sin might be brought to nothing." καταργηθῇ (potential subjunctive with ἵνα) is likewise qualified by contingency, pointing toward the believer's future perception and application of retroactive positional truth.

Romans 7:2 (protasis of the third-class condition) — the subjunctive mood of the protasis "if her husband dies" is potential, appropriate to a condition of probability (see Conditional Sentences, section IX).

Romans 8:4 — "in order that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us." πληρωθῇ is a potential subjunctive: not all believers necessarily advance to the maturity this verse describes; the potential depends on two consistent functions — rebound as needed, and the daily function of GAP.

Romans 9:15 (Exodus 33:19) — "on whom I have mercy." ἐλεέω (whomever I show mercy). The subjunctive mood with hos an is potential, implying a future reference qualified by the element of contingency, namely the believer's consistent positive volition toward doctrine. The potential is genuine and open in every generation.

Romans 9:23 — "in order to make known the riches of his glory." γνωρίζω (that He might make known). In the ἵνα clause the aorist active subjunctive of γνωρίζω is a potential subjunctive implying future reference within the final clause.

Romans 10:9 — "if you confess with your mouth." ὁμολογέω (if you will make a statement to God). Homologeō is aorist active subjunctive. The aorist contemplates the action in its entirety, a momentary, punctiliar event at the point of salvation; the active voice shows the believer producing the action. The subjunctive is the potential subjunctive, used with ean to introduce the protasis of the third-class condition, encoding the function of free will in salvation.

Romans 10:14 — "How then will they call on him." ἐπικαλέω (shall they call). The main verb is the aorist middle subjunctive of epikaleō, established in verse 13 as a synonym for saving faith. The constative aorist views the momentary act of faith as a single whole; the middle is the intensive middle, giving the verb an individualistic application (each person must personally exercise this act); the subjunctive is potential, implying future reference qualified by contingency.

Romans 11:14 — "and thus save some of them." σῴζω (might save). The subjunctive mood of σῴζω is potential — the outcome depends on the individual volition of every Jew who hears the gospel. This preserves the integrity of human free will within the plan of God. Salvation is not coerced; Paul's ministry creates the conditions and the stimulus, and each individual Jew must respond by non-meritorious faith in the Lord Jesus Christ.

Romans 13:4 — "But if you do wrong." ποιέω (if you do). The potential subjunctive indicates that the production of evil is contingent on the believer's doctrinal status: positive volition toward doctrine prevents it; reversionism enables it.

Romans 14:8 — "whether we live or whether we die." ζάω (to live). ζάω is in the present active subjunctive, the required mood for the protasis of a third-class condition; it is a potential subjunctive, acknowledging the sovereignty of God over the continuation of physical life. The subjunctive of ἀποθνῄσκω carries the same potential force: the rapture remains an open alternative, so not every Church Age believer will experience physical death.

Romans 14:23 — "if he eats." ἐσθίω (if he eats). The subjunctive of ἐσθίω is potential, indicating that the believer may or may not eat; the choice remains with him.

Potential Indicative

Conveys obligation, impulse, or possibility rather than flat assertion, often with an indefinite subject.

Romans 5:7 — "for one will scarcely die for a righteous person." The construction with τις and the future middle conveys a soldier's instinctive impulse or duty — an indefinite subject acting from impulse rather than a specific, named agent acting from calculated obligation.

Romans 6:14 — "sin will have no dominion over you" — functions as a potential indicative of obligation: what the believer is obligated to experience given the design of grace, provided the grace provisions are used.

Romans 7:20 — "if I do what I do not want." θέλω with the negative here is a potential indicative establishing that the desire not to follow the sin nature's trends is realizable only through doctrine.

Romans 7:25 — the two options of the closing correlative (see section X) are respectively cast as a potential indicative of obligation (serving God's law with the mind) and a potential indicative of impulse (serving sin's law with the flesh) — the same grammatical category, obligation versus impulse, distinguishing principled choice from reactive drift.

Romans 9:3 — "For I could wish." εὔχομαι (I could wish). The indicative mood of euchomai is potential: the potential indicative of impulse, expressing an inner compulsion that reason immediately recognizes as impossible to execute.

Romans 9:6 — "the word of God has failed." ἐκπίπτω (has failed). With ekpiptō the indicative mood is potential, indicating an allegation without foundation: the Word of God has not failed.

Romans 9:29 (Isaiah 1:9) — "we would have been like Sodom." γίνομαι (we would have become). The apodosis uses the aorist passive indicative of γίνομαι with ἄν, a potential indicative of condition. The contingent element resides in ἄν, not in the indicative mood, which retains its force as the mood of certainty; the construction introduces no genuine doubt but states that an outcome would have become reality had the condition been met, a condition that never will be met. ἄν is largely untranslatable but locates the contingency in the condition rather than the verb.

Romans 11:23 — "will be grafted in." ἐγκεντρίζω (they shall be grafted in). The apodosis uses the future passive indicative of ἐγκεντρίζω. The future is gnomic — what will be the case under the conditions described. The passive voice: at the moment of faith the Jewish unbeliever receives the grafting in — the baptism of the Holy Spirit, entering him into the royal family of God. The indicative is a potential indicative: the result is certain if the condition is met, but personal volition must act.

Romans 11:25 — "I do not want you to be unaware." θέλω (I do not wish). The mood of οὐ θέλω is a potential indicative of obligation.

Romans 11:35 (Job 41:11) — "Or who has given a gift to him." προδίδωμι (to give first). The aorist active indicative of προδίδωμι (pro, before + didōmi, to give: to give first, in advance) is constative. The indicative is a potential indicative of obligation — the indicative used to face the reality of giving as an obligation belonging to worship and to the understanding of true wealth. No creature can place God in debt by giving first.

Romans 13:9 — "are summed up in this word." ἀνακεφαλαιόω (is summed up). The indicative mood of ἀνακεφαλαιοῦται is potential, signaling an obligation that the believer may or may not be meeting.

Romans 14:7 — "none of us lives to himself." ζάω (to live). The indicative mood of ζάω is a potential indicative of obligation: it presents the principle of how life is designed to be lived, what should be the case, rather than necessarily describing current practice. God has a plan for the life of every believer, so the believer has meaning, purpose and definition beyond self-interest.

Romans 15:28 — "I will leave for Spain by way of you." ἀπελεύσομαι (I will go). The indicative mood here is potential — a potential indicative of obligation — declaring Paul's duty.

The Optative of Wishing — μὴ γένοιτο

The optative mood expresses a wish; combined with the strong negative μή, this fixed idiom is the strongest negative denial available in Koine Greek.

Romans 6:2 — "By no means!" μὴ γένοιτο rejects the hypothetical premise (that grace could license continued sin) with total, categorical force.

Romans 6:15 — "By no means!" Same fixed idiom, rejecting the same category of hypothetical at a later point in the argument.

Romans 7:7 — "By no means!" μὴ γένοιτο again, categorically repudiating the hypothetical conclusion that the law itself is sin — the aorist optative of γίνομαι combined with μή constitutes the strongest available refutation available in the language, a total rejection of the premise, not a qualified disagreement.

Romans 7:13 — "By no means!" A third occurrence, rejecting the suggestion that the good law itself became the cause of spiritual death to the believer.

Romans 9:14 — "By no means!" μὴ γένοιτο (emphatically no, from γίνομαι). Paul's answer is mē genoito, mē with the aorist active optative of ginomai, the strongest negative formula in New Testament Greek. The optative is a deliberative optative, the debater's optative: it assumes doubt on the part of the hearers in order to answer it definitively; the writer does not share the doubt. The divine name does not appear in the Greek; it is correctly rendered emphatically no. It is a categorical refusal of the premise, characterizing the suggestion of divine partiality as a form of blasphemy against the character of God.

Romans 11:1 — "By no means!" μὴ γένοιτο (let it not be so; Definitely not; Emphatically not, from γίνομαι). μὴ γένοιτο, the aorist optative of γίνομαι with the negative μή, reinforces the negative already implied by the grammar of the question. Literally let it not be so, the idiom functions as an emphatic repudiation and is among the strongest negatives available in Greek; Paul uses it as his standard formula for denying a false inference from a rhetorical question.

Romans 11:11 — "By no means!" μὴ γένοιτο (of course not, definitely not, from γίνομαι). Paul appends his standard refutation formula, μὴ γένοιτο, the optative of γίνομαι: literally may it not be so, idiomatically of course not. It is his sharpest expression of categorical denial.

The Imperatival Participle

A participle that functions as a command while retaining its participial form.

Romans 6:6 — "We know that our old self was crucified with him." γινώσκοντες functions imperativally: the participle carries the force of a command to recognize and apply this fact, not merely to note it in passing.

Romans 12:9 — "Abhor what is evil." ἀποστυγέω (detest). Present active participle of apostygeō, a compound of apo (from, away from the original source) + stygeō (to hate): to hate from the original source, to detest, to loathe. The participle functions as an imperative, a Koine characteristic: detest the evil.

Romans 12:10 — "Outdo one another in showing honor." προηγέομαι (esteem others more highly than yourself). Present middle participle (imperative use) of proēgeomai, compound of pro (before) and hēgeomai (to lead, to be chief): to esteem, to give precedence to. The imperative participle is idiomatic to Koine Greek and carries the force of a command. The idiom signifies: make it a matter of honor to give precedence to others, the antithesis of inordinate competition.

Romans 12:12 — "Rejoice in hope." χαίροντες (be rejoicing, from χαίρω). Present active participle of chairō used as an imperative, a construction peculiar to Koine Greek and absent from classical Attic, which uses the infinitive for imperatival force. The present tense denotes linear, progressive action, ongoing rejoicing: be rejoicing, continuously, with reference to the hope.

Romans 12:16 — "Live in harmony with one another." φρονέω (be thinking). The present active participle of phroneō is used as an imperative, a construction peculiar to Koine Greek in which the participle functions as a command. The word means to think, to hold a mental attitude, to exercise the cognitive faculty with directional intent: sustained, purposeful thinking oriented by an objective standard.

Romans 12:17 — "Repay no one evil for evil." ἀποδίδωμι (pay back). A present active participle of apodidōmi (apo, back, + didōmi, to give) used in the imperative sense, a construction characteristic of Koine Greek attested extensively in the papyri. In context the verb denotes repayment in the sense of revenge or retaliation. The customary present denotes what habitually characterizes the mature believer under the royal family honor code.

Direct Middle Voice (Reflexive)

The middle voice where the action returns directly to the subject.

Romans 6:11 — "consider yourselves dead to sin." λογίζεσθε (present middle imperative) is a direct middle: the believer performs the action of reckoning upon himself, the subject and object of the action being one and the same.

Romans 9:3 — "that I myself." αὐτός (I myself). The middle voice of euchomai is reflexive and redundant, reinforced by the intensive pronoun autos, yielding the idiom I myself. It emphasizes that Paul speaks of his own person as the proposed substitute, not a hypothetical third party.

Romans 11:1 — "has God rejected his people?" ἀπωθέω (to repudiate). The middle voice of ἀπωθέω is a direct middle: the subject acts with a view toward participating in the results of the action. The question is whether God Himself, acting on His own behalf and from His own volition, has definitively cast off Israel as His people; the action would be self-generated.

Romans 11:6 — "grace would no longer be grace." γίνομαι (grace is no longer grace in itself). The middle voice of γίνομαι is a direct middle: the subject, grace, acts with reflexive force and the results refer back to grace itself. Mixing grace with works destroys the category reflexively: grace is no longer grace in itself, or grace as such.

Romans 11:17 — "and now share in the nourishing root of the olive tree." γίνομαι (to become). The final clause of verse 17 is introduced by the culminative aorist middle indicative of γίνομαι. The direct middle voice indicates that the agent — the Gentile believer — acts with a view toward participating in the results of the action. The predicate nominative is συγκοινωνός, joint partaker, a term used in secular Greek for business partners.

Romans 13:2 — "will incur judgment." λαμβάνω (shall receive). The middle voice of λαμβάνω is a direct middle, referring the results of the action back to the agent with reflexive force: they bring this upon themselves. The punishment is self-incurred.

Romans 13:5 — "one must be in subjection." ὑποτάσσω (to be subordinate). The middle of ὑποτάσσω is direct: the subject is the beneficiary of his own subordination, participating in and benefiting from the outcome.

Romans 13:12 — "let us cast off the works of darkness." ἀποτίθημι (let us lay aside). The middle of ἀποτίθημι (and of the following verb, put on) is the direct middle: the subject participates directly in the results of the action.

Romans 14:10 — "For we will all stand before the judgment seat of God." παρίστημι (to present oneself, to stand by). The future middle indicative of παρίστημι carries a military nuance in the direct middle voice: to place oneself under orders to an authority, to present oneself before a superior officer. The direct middle indicates the believer acts with a view toward participating in the outcome, reward or loss of reward.

Romans 14:14 — "for anyone who thinks it unclean." λογίζομαι (who presumes). The governing participle of the exception clause is the articular present middle participle of λογίζομαι (to impute, account, presume, infer, conclude). It employs the direct middle to expose the presumption of the weak believer: he acts with a view toward participating in the anticipated outcome of his taboo observance, expecting divine blessing as a result.

Romans 14:23 — "whoever has doubts." διακρίνω (who doubts). The main participle is the present middle of διακρίνω. In the active it means to separate, differentiate, make a distinction; in the middle, as here, it takes on a reflexive force: to take issue with oneself, to doubt, to waver. The compound with διά intensifies the reflexive and internal character of the doubt.

Romans 15:12 — "he who arises to rule the Gentiles." ἀνιστάμενος (he who rises). The direct middle voice indicates that the subject, the Lord Jesus Christ, participates in the results of His own resurrection.

Romans 15:28 — "and have delivered to them what has been collected." σφραγισάμενος (having myself certified). The second participial phrase uses the aorist middle participle of sphragizō (σφραγίζω), meaning to seal or to certify. The middle voice — a direct reflexive middle — refers the results of the action directly back to Paul himself: and have myself certified.

Indirect Middle Voice

The middle voice used to indicate the action's spontaneous production by the subject, without necessarily returning the action directly to the subject as its own object (contrast the direct middle above).

Romans 7:9's ἀνέζησεν ("sin came alive," aorist indicative of ἀναζάω) functions with an indirect-middle-like force even though formally active: the sin nature itself is presented as the spontaneous producer of its own activation, not merely a passive recipient of the commandment's arrival.

Participles — Circumstantial and Articular

A circumstantial participle describes the attending condition of an action without itself being the main verb; an articular participle takes the definite article and functions substantivally.

Romans 4:4 — "to the one who works" — ἐργαζομένῳ is an articular participle functioning substantivally, "the one working."

Romans 4:5 — "believes in him who justifies the ungodly" — δικαιοῦντα, an articular participle naming God by his characteristic action.

Romans 4:12 — "who also walk in the footsteps" — a circumstantial participle describing the attending condition of genuine faith.

Romans 4:20–21 — "he grew strong... being fully convinced" — πληροφορηθείς is a circumstantial participle describing the condition under which Abraham's growth occurred.

Romans 5:1 — "since we have been justified" — δικαιωθέντες, a circumstantial participle giving the ground for the exhortation that follows.

Romans 5:10 — "while we were enemies" — ὄντες, a circumstantial participle describing the condition of the human race at the moment reconciliation occurred.

Romans 5:11 — "through whom we have now received reconciliation" — a circumstantial construction describing the means by which believers now stand.

Romans 6:9 — "We know that Christ, being raised from the dead" — ἐγερθείς, a circumstantial aorist participle.

Romans 7:21 — "when I want to do right." The articular present active participle of θέλω functions substantivally within a dative absolute construction (see section XIV): "to me, the one wishing to do the honorable."

Romans 8:37 — "him who loved us." The articular aorist active participle of ἀγαπάω functions substantivally, "the one who loves us" (see the Gnomic Aorist entry, section I).

Romans 9:20 — "to its molder." τῷ πλάσαντι (to the one who molded it, to its molder, from πλάσσω). The indirect object is the articular aorist participle of πλάσσω, dative singular, used substantively. The articular participle in the ascriptive use functions as a noun, denoting the potter as the one whose defining activity is the act of forming. The definite article in the dative serves as a possessive pronoun: to its molder.

Romans 10:3 — "and seeking to establish their own." ζητοῦντες (by seeking, from ζητέω). Two participles stand side by side. Agnoountes is circumstantial, expressing the attendant circumstances under which the main verb takes place. Zētountes, the present active participle of zēteō, is instrumental: it expresses the means by which the main verb is accomplished, and by seeking.

Romans 10:14 — "without someone preaching." κηρύσσω (the one who proclaims, a missionary). The word the King James renders preacher is not a noun but a present active participle of kēryssō, to herald, to proclaim publicly, used substantively as a noun: the one who proclaims, in context a missionary, a believer who crosses a national boundary from a client nation to present the gospel abroad. This is a missionary passage by interpretation, not a personal witnessing passage.

Romans 12:3 — "I say to everyone among you." εἰμί (who is among you). The articular present active participle of eimi, who is, combined with en hymin, among you, makes the address universal and personal simultaneously; pas, used as a substantive in the dative, means each one, every one. Paul addresses all Church Age believers, each of whom stands individually before the justice of God.

Romans 12:7 — "he who teaches." διδάσκω (if teaching). The gift of teaching is introduced by eite followed by a present active participle of didaskō functioning as a noun, a substantive participle denoting the person possessing and exercising the gift. The infinitive again functions as the imperative in the apodosis.

Romans 12:11 — "serve the Lord." δουλεύω (when serving). The participle of douleuō is a temporal present active participle, when serving. Its temporal force limits ambassadorial service to specific occasions rather than every moment of the believer’s existence, preserving balance and sanity in the Christian way of life. The dative kyriō with the generic article designates the Lord Jesus Christ as the God-man, in whose interest all service is conducted.

Romans 12:20 — "for by so doing." ποιέω (for by doing this). The result clause is introduced by an explanatory gar with the present active participle of poieō. The customary present denotes habitual action; the participial phrase is instrumental, for by doing this, with the near demonstrative houtos as object: the specific act of providing food and water to an enemy.

Romans 13:8 — "for the one who loves another." (when he loves, from ἀγαπάω). In the ground clause introduced by γάρ, the articular present active participle of ἀγαπάω is temporal: for when he loves.

Romans 13:11 — "you know the time." οἶδα (by having known). The participle of οἶδα is instrumental, indicating the means by which the command (this do also) is carried out: this do also by having known.

The Interrogative Indicative

Romans 10:14 — "in whom they have not believed." πιστεύω. In the first rhetorical question the indicative is the interrogative indicative, assuming that an actual answer to the question exists and is forthcoming. The same label is used for the questions of Romans 10:7, 10:18, and 10:19.

Romans 13:3 — "Would you have no fear of the one who is in authority?" θέλω (really, do you desire?). θέλω is an interrogative indicative, assuming that a factual answer exists: of course every person desires to live free from fear of government.

Romans 14:10 — "why do you despise your brother?" ἐξουθενέω (to despise). The interrogative indicative signals that an actual fact may be stated in answer to the question: here the fact is the attitude of contempt. In the parallel question to the weak believer, the interrogative indicative of κρίνω assumes an actual fact that can be answered: apostasy, reversionism, ignorance of doctrine, legalism and violation of the honor code.

The Deliberative Subjunctive

Romans 10:14 — "And how are they to believe in him." πιστεύω (shall they believe). Pisteuō in the aorist active subjunctive: the constative aorist gathers the entire act of believing into a single event; the active voice shows the Gentiles producing the volitional act of faith on the principle of efficacious grace. The subjunctive is deliberative, a standard feature of the rhetorical question series: in a sequence of rhetorical questions it sets up a logical progression used to prove a point by successive demonstration.

The Attributive (Adjectival) Participle

Romans 10:21 (Isaiah 65:2) — "a disobedient and contrary people." ἀπειθέω (disobedient; obstinate). Two present active participles in the accusative singular function as attributive (ascriptive) participles confirming two stages of spiritual collapse. Apeitheō (alpha-privative negating peithō) is disobedient, the initial rejection of Christ that begins the big blackout. Antilegō (anti, against + legō), to speak against, is obstinate, the accumulated scar tissue of the soul, the full development of the big blackout after sustained rejection.

Romans 12:1 — "as a living sacrifice, holy." ζῶσαν (living, from ζάω). The sacrifice is described by two adjectives: zōsan, the adjectival use of the present active participle of zaō, living, and hagian, from hagios, set apart, consecrated, the term denoting royal status in the sacrificial context. The sacrifice is living because the believer continues to live after offering it, and holy because the believer belongs to the royal family of God.

The Imperative of Entreaty

Romans 11:9 (Psalm 69:22) — "Let their table become a snare." γίνομαι (may it become, let it be). The imperative of γίνομαι is not a command but an imperative of entreaty, corresponding to the Hebrew jussive: may it become, let it be.
