Romans 11:10 (Psalm 69:23) — "let their eyes be darkened." σκοτίζω (let their eyes be darkened). The imperative of σκοτίζω is not a command in the strict sense but an imprecatory entreaty, the imperative of urgency, expressing the force of a request within the imprecatory prayer of the Psalm.

Romans 16:3 — "Greet Prisca and Aquila." Ἀσπάσασθε (greet). The verb is the aorist active imperative of aspazomai (ἀσπάζομαι), meaning to greet, to pay respects to. The imperative mood is the imperative of entreaty, not command — it carries the force of a warm personal request rather than a formal directive.

The Aorist Imperative ἴδε as an Interjection

Romans 11:22 — "Note then." ἴδε (behold, from ὁράω). ἴδε is the aorist active imperative of ὁράω used as an interjection: a command to focus attention — a dramatic pause in the oral delivery that forces every listener to look up and re-engage. The form is imperative: not an invitation but a command to attend. With the post-positive inferential οὖν, which draws its force from the first word, ide oun means: focus now on what follows as the direct result of everything that has preceded.

The Voluntative Optative

Romans 15:5 — "May the God of endurance and encouragement grant you." δῴη (may give). The optative mood is the voluntative optative, expressing Paul's wish or strong desire for the future. The optative contains no guarantee of realization; it presents the action as conceivable and desired, not certain.

Romans 15:13 — "May the God of hope fill you." πληρώσαι (may fill). The main verb is the aorist active optative of plēroō (πληρόω), meaning to fill up, to fulfill, to implement where there is emptiness. Third, the optative mood is rare in the New Testament. This is the voluntative optative, expressing a wish for a future time — specifically, the attainment of spiritual maturity and the full function of the honor code as a system of integrity.

The Imperative of Permission

Romans 15:11 — "Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles." αἰνεῖτε (praise). The imperative mood functions here as an imperative of permission — the command is in compliance with an expressed desire on the part of the one who is its object.

VII.Voice

The Divine Passive

The passive voice used where the agent is God, left grammatically implicit but doctrinally unmistakable.

Romans 2:25 — Circumcision material throughout uses the divine passive pattern consistently seen across Romans (see the Divine Passive entries in Romans 4–8): the believer receives; he does not produce.

Romans 1:1 — "set apart for the gospel of God." The perfect passive participle ἀφωρισμένος is passive: Paul receives the appointment; God executes it (see also Perfect Tense).

Romans 1:4 — "and was declared to be the Son of God in power... by his resurrection from the dead." The passive voice of ὁρισθέντος ("having been declared") shows Christ receiving the appointment made in eternity past, not claiming it for himself.

Romans 4:2 — "if Abraham was justified by works" — ἐδικαιώθη, passive, with God as the implicit agent (hypothetically, in this debater's-technique case).

Romans 4:3 — "it was counted to him" — ἐλογίσθη, passive, God the implicit crediting agent.

Romans 4:7 — "blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven" — ἀφέθησαν, passive, God the forgiving agent.

Romans 4:9 — "we say that faith was counted to Abraham" — ἐλογίσθη, passive.

Romans 4:10 — "How then was it counted to him?" — ἐλογίσθη, passive.

Romans 4:14 — "faith is null and void" — κεκένωται, passive.

Romans 4:20 — implicit throughout the account of Abraham's strengthening — the passive constructions consistently locate God, not Abraham, as the producer of the spiritual growth described.

Romans 4:21 — "fully convinced" — πληροφορηθείς, passive, the conviction produced in Abraham by an external, divine agent.

Romans 4:22 — "his faith was counted to him as righteousness" — ἐλογίσθη, passive.

Romans 4:25 — "who was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification" — παρεδόθη and ἠγέρθη, both passive, God the Father the implicit agent throughout.

Romans 5:1 — "we have been justified" — δικαιωθέντες, passive.

Romans 5:5 — "God's love has been poured into our hearts" — ἐκκέχυται, passive, though here the agent (God) is explicit rather than merely implicit, reinforcing the same theological pattern.

Romans 5:9 — "we have now been justified" — δικαιωθέντες, passive.

Romans 5:10 — "we were reconciled to God" — κατηλλάγημεν, passive.

Romans 5:19 — "the many will be made righteous" — κατασταθήσονται, passive.

Romans 6:3 — "all of us who have been baptized" — ἐβαπτίσθημεν, passive.

Romans 6:4 — "we were buried therefore with him" — συνετάφημεν, passive.

Romans 6:6 — "our old self was crucified with him" — συνεσταυρώθη, passive.

Romans 6:7 — "one who has died has been set free" — δεδικαίωται, passive.

Romans 7:6 — "we are released from the law" — κατηργήθημεν, passive.

Romans 7:14 — the law's spiritual origin is framed throughout by implicit passive constructions consistent with this same pattern: the human subject consistently receives; he does not produce.

Romans 9:26 (Hosea 1:10) — "there they will be called 'sons of the living God.'" καλέω (to call, to name, to designate). ἐκεῖ (there) specifies that the reversal occurs at the identical geographical point of the original renunciation, the land of Israel. The future passive indicative of καλέω points to the second advent; the passive indicates that Israel receives the designation from God; the indicative is declarative for a dogmatic statement of doctrine.

Romans 11:7 — "but the rest were hardened." ἐπωρώθησαν (were hardened, from πωρόω). In οἱ δὲ λοιποὶ ἐπωρώθησαν the aorist passive indicative of πωρόω presents the hardening as something that happened to the rest. The passive reflects a judicial act: God confirmed them in the condition they had chosen by sustained negative volition. It is not arbitrary imposition from without but divine ratification of a direction the will had already established.

Middle Voice

Distinct semantic category, not collapsed into the passive.

Romans 2:17 — "But if you call yourself a Jew and rely on the law." ἐπαναπαύῃ ("rely upon," from ἐπαναπαύω, a compound of ἐπί + ἀναπαύω) is present middle indicative — a dynamic middle emphasizing the subject's own active reliance, his complete dependence on the law as an instrument of salvation.

Romans 3:25 — "whom God put forward as a propitiation." προέθετο (middle voice of προτίθημι) is a middle-indirect voice construction stressing God the Father as the agent producing the public display of Christ as the mercy seat.

Romans 4:8 — "will not count." λογίσηται (aorist middle subjunctive) — the middle voice here carries a nuance of personal interest or involvement distinct from a bare passive rendering.

Romans 7:11 — "sin... deceived me." Note that the main verbs of this verse are active, not middle, which is itself significant: the sin nature is presented as an aggressive external agent acting upon Paul, not merely a force he inadvertently cooperates with.

Romans 10:13 (Joel 2:32) — "everyone who calls on the name of the Lord." ἐπικαλέω (will call upon). Epikalesētai is the aorist middle subjunctive of epikaleō, a synonym for faith. The constative aorist captures the moment of faith as a single point; the middle is the dynamic middle, emphasizing that the subject participates in the outcome, calling upon the Lord with a view toward receiving salvation; the subjunctive indicates potentiality, the opportunity existing until the final breath while volition determines whether it is exercised.

Romans 12:9 — "hold fast to what is good." κολλάω (adhere to). Present middle participle of kollaō, to glue, to weld, to cling to, to adhere; it functions as an imperative. In the New Testament the verb does not appear in the active voice, only the middle and passive. With a person as object it refers to intimate personal union; with a principle, as here, it means to adhere to, to be bonded to.

Romans 13:1 — "Let every person be subject to the governing authorities." ὑποτάσσω (be subordinating yourselves). ὑποτάσσω is a present middle imperative. The middle voice emphasizes voluntary, self-disciplined subordination to duly constituted authority.

Romans 13:4 — "be afraid." φοβέομαι (keep on being afraid). The middle of φοβέομαι is a dynamic middle, emphasizing that the fear is the self-produced consequence of the agent's own criminal orientation.

Romans 13:14 — "But put on the Lord Jesus Christ." ἐνδύω (put on). ἐνδύω (to clothe oneself, to put on a garment) is an aorist middle imperative, used figuratively for the believer's advance to maturity through sustained doctrine intake. The middle form emphasizes volitional participation in the result of the action.

Romans 14:11 — "every tongue shall confess to God." ἐξομολογέω (shall confess). ἐξομολογέω is a future middle indicative. With the prefix in the active voice it means to promise or to consent; in the middle voice, as here, it means to confess, to acknowledge, to declare openly. The confession of the royal family is directed to God the Father regarding the person and work of the Son.

Romans 15:26 — "to make some contribution." ποιήσασθαι (to make). The middle voice is the dynamic middle, emphasizing the active, volitional participation of the subject.

Deponent Verbs

A deponent verb lacks an active-voice form in Greek but carries active meaning.

Romans 3:9 — "Are we Jews any better off? Not at all." προῃτιασάμεθα is a deponent verb — middle in form, active in meaning — "we have already filed the indictment," pointing back to the case built across Romans 1:18–2:29.

Romans 5:2 — "let us rejoice" (ESV, "we rejoice"). καυχώμεθα is deponent: middle in form, active in meaning — the believer himself is the one boasting.

Romans 5:3 — "let us rejoice in our sufferings." Same deponent verb, καυχώμεθα.

Romans 5:7 — "one will scarcely die" — τολμᾷ (behind the fuller construction) is a deponent verb meaning "to dare," middle in form but active in meaning.

Romans 5:11 — "we also rejoice in God" — καυχώμενοι, the same deponent verb in participial form.

Romans 8:19 — "the creation waits with eager longing." ἀπεκδέχεται (present middle of the deponent ἀπεκδέχομαι) is middle in form but active in meaning: the material universe itself is presented as the one producing the action of waiting.

Romans 8:32 — "he did not spare." ἐφείσατο (middle in form) is likewise deponent: God the Father, not a passive recipient, produces the action of the verb.

Romans 9:19 — "Why does he still find fault?" μέμφομαι (to find fault, to blame). memphomai is a classical Attic word appearing in Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides before entering Paul's Koine vocabulary; in Greek tragedy it was associated with the concept of the tragic flaw (hamartia). As a deponent verb it carries active meaning in the middle voice.

Romans 11:21 — "God did not spare the natural branches." φείδομαι (did not spare). The aorist middle indicative of φείδομαι is a deponent verb — middle in form, active in meaning — and carries the negative οὐ appropriate to the indicative mood. The aorist summarizes a series of acts extended over time into a single historical fact (a constative aorist). The objective genitive of κλάδος refers to the Jewish unbelievers of verses 17–19.

Romans 12:10 — "Outdo one another in showing honor." προηγέομαι (to esteem). Proēgeomai is a deponent verb, middle in form and active in meaning.

Romans 13:10 — "Love does no wrong to a neighbor." ἐργάζομαι (to work, to produce). ἐργάζομαι is deponent, middle in form and active in meaning, indicating that the advancing or mature believer himself produces the action.

Romans 15:18 — "what Christ has accomplished through me." κατειργάσατο (has accomplished). The verb κατειργάσατο (katērgasato) is the aorist middle indicative of κατεργάζομαι (katergazomai), meaning to achieve, to accomplish, to work out, to bring about. It is a deponent verb — middle in form but active in meaning. The constative aorist contemplates the entirety of Paul's missionary activity up to the point of writing — approximately half of his total service — as a unified whole.

Romans 16:2 — "that you may welcome her in the Lord." προσδέξησθε (you may welcome). The first clause contains the aorist middle subjunctive of prosdechomai (προσδέχομαι), 'to welcome, to receive.' The constative aorist gathers into one entirety the whole of Phoebe's stay in Rome. The middle voice is deponent — active in meaning — with the Roman believers as the agents.

Indirect Middle

Emphasizes the agent as the one producing the action for his own interest or from his own capacity.

Romans 1:2 — "which he promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures." προεπηγγείλατο ("promised beforehand," from προεπαγγέλλομαι) is an aorist middle indicative — specifically a direct middle: it establishes that every writer of an Old Testament book personally participated in the results of the action, meaning each writer was himself saved and adjusted to the justice of God, and so communicated the gospel not as external information but as personal knowledge. The indirect middle would only show personal interest; the direct middle shows personal participation in the result.

Romans 1:16 — "For I am not ashamed of the gospel." ἐπαισχύνομαι is present middle, an indirect middle: Paul as agent produces the state of unashamedness rather than merely participating in its results.

Romans 3:4 — "Let God be true though every one were a liar." γινέσθω (present middle imperative of γίνομαι) is an indirect middle: God himself is the agent producing the action of self-demonstration through the doctrines that vindicate him — not merely interested in but the active author of that demonstration.

Romans 1:15 — "so I am eager to preach the gospel." The aorist middle infinitive εὐαγγελίσασθαι (from εὐαγγελίζομαι) carries indirect-middle force, emphasizing Paul himself as the agent personally producing the action of proclamation.

Romans 5:2 — "let us rejoice." καυχώμεθα — beyond its deponent classification, the form also carries indirect-middle force: the believer boasts from his own perceived interest in the object of the boast (the hope of the glory of God).

Romans 5:3 — "let us rejoice in our sufferings." Same indirect-middle nuance applied to the more difficult object of boasting.

Romans 9:17 (Exodus 9:16) — "that I might show my power in you." ἐνδείκνυμι (that I might demonstrate). The middle voice of endeiknymi is the indirect middle, emphasizing God as the agent producing the action in a uniquely personal way.

Romans 9:22 — "desiring to show his wrath." ἐνδείκνυμι (to demonstrate, to show forth, to exhibit publicly). The aorist middle infinitive of ἐνδείκνυμι expresses the purpose of the participle: God, willing to demonstrate. The middle voice is an indirect or intensive middle, emphasizing God as the agent whose own character is directly expressed in the action: not an external display only, but a revelation of who He intrinsically is.

Romans 10:5 (Leviticus 18:5) — "shall live by them." ζάω (shall live). In zēsetai the middle voice is the indirect middle, emphasizing the agent as producing the action of living rather than merely participating in its results.

Romans 10:20 (Isaiah 65:1) — "I have shown myself." γίνομαι (I became). The verb rendered became manifest is the aorist middle indicative of ginomai, correctly I became, not simply I was. The constative aorist views the action as extended over the entire dispensation of Israel, from the Exodus to AD 70. The middle is the indirect middle: Christ as agent produces the action of self-revelation in behalf of Gentiles who were positive at God consciousness.

Romans 11:27 — "when I take away their sins." ἀφαιρέω (to remove). The middle voice of ἀφαιρέω is the indirect middle, emphasizing the Lord Jesus Christ as the agent fulfilling the new covenant to Israel.

Romans 12:8 — "the one who leads." προΐστημι (he who manages). The middle voice of proistēmi is the indirect middle, emphasizing the agent as the one who produces the action in his own interest and sphere. The circumstantial participle implies that God distributes this gift in sufficient quantity to supply every legitimately functioning local church.

Romans 12:16 — "but associate with the lowly." συναπάγω (associate with). The present middle participle of synapagō, syn (with) + apagō (to lead away), carries in the middle the sense of associating with. It is an indirect middle: the agent produces the action rather than merely participating in its results. It is an imperatival participle with linear force: sustain this association as consistent practice.

Romans 12:17 — "give thought to do what is honorable." προνοέω (respect). Present middle participle of pronoeō, pro (before) + noeō (to think): to think beforehand, to have regard for, to respect. The customary present denotes habitual conduct; the indirect middle indicates that the mature believer produces the action rather than merely participating in its results; the participle functions as an imperative.

Romans 13:3 — "Would you have no fear." φοβέω (not to fear). The middle voice of φοβέω is the indirect middle: the believer as agent produces the action rather than merely participating in its results.

Romans 14:1 — "welcome him." προσλαμβάνω (to receive, to accept into one’s society). The middle voice of προσλαμβάνω in the command is an indirect middle: it emphasizes that the agent, the strong believer, is himself the one producing the action of reception.

Romans 15:20 — "to preach the gospel." εὐαγγελίζεσθαι (to proclaim the gospel). The present middle infinitive of εὐαγγελίζω (euangelizō) means to proclaim the gospel. The middle voice focuses attention on the subject as the agent producing the action — Paul, the missionary — as a matter of personal policy rather than as a participant in the results. The retroactive progressive present indicates an action begun in the past and continuing into the present throughout Paul's missionary career.

Romans 16:19 — "For your obedience is known to all." ἀφίκετο (has become known). The middle voice is an indirect middle, highlighting the believers themselves — as agents of authority orientation — as producing the action.

Permissive Middle

A middle-voice form in which the subject voluntarily yields himself to the result of the verb's action.

Romans 5:7 — "one will scarcely die for a righteous person." ἀποθανεῖται (future middle) — the subject voluntarily yields himself to death; the action is not imposed on him from outside, but consented to and permitted.

Romans 10:12 — "all who call on him." ἐπικαλέω. Tous epikaloumenous auton is the articular present middle participle of epikaleō, used in the permissive middle voice as a synonym for saving faith, the voluntary, non-meritorious act of believing in the Lord Jesus Christ.

The Impersonal Passive

Romans 10:10 — "one believes." πιστεύω (mankind believes). The verb is the present passive indicative of pisteuō in the impersonal construction: the subject is absent and the verb implies a subject as a category of the human race (mankind believes) rather than a specific individual. The impersonal passive conveys principle, how salvation has always functioned, not a personal appeal; direct appeals use the second-person active. The same impersonal passive appears with homologeō in the second clause (it is confessed).

The Passive Voice — The Subject Receives the Action

Romans 12:2 — "but be transformed." μεταμορφόω (be transformed). The passive voice indicates that the transformation is effected upon the believer, not by the believer. It is not self-generated; the agent is the Holy Spirit working through the mechanics of GAP as Bible doctrine moves into the believer’s soul and renovates the pattern of thought.

The Reciprocal Middle

Romans 15:7 — "welcome one another." προσλαμβάνεσθε (be receiving one another). The middle voice is a reciprocal middle — both the weak and the strong believer are the acting agents, each receiving the other.

VIII.Negation

οὐ — Negation of Objective Fact

Used with the indicative to negate a fact as an absolute reality.

Romans 4:4 — "his wages are not counted as a gift." οὐ λογίζεται.

Romans 4:2 — implicit in the negative conclusion of the debater's-technique argument ("but not before God").

Romans 4:10 — "not after, but before he was circumcised" — the negation establishes the historical fact.

Romans 4:20 — "No unbelief made him waver." οὐ διεκρίθη, negating the objective fact of doubt across Abraham's entire test.

Romans 5:5 — "hope does not put us to shame." οὐ καταισχύνει.

Romans 7:7 — "You shall not covet." οὐκ ἐπιθυμήσεις with the imperative future (see section V) denies the reality of the alleged action as an absolute prohibition.

Romans 7:15 — "I do not understand my own actions." οὐ γινώσκω — a plain factual negation of comprehension.

Romans 8:9 — "the unbeliever... does not have [the Spirit of Christ]." οὐκ ἔχει.

Romans 9:1 — "I am not lying." οὐ ψεύδομαι (I am not lying, from ψεύδομαι). The second leg of the oath is the negative affirmation ou pseudomai, a present middle indicative of pseudomai, to lie, to misrepresent, with the negative particle ou used with the indicative mood.

Romans 9:6 — "For not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel." οὐ (not). The objective negative adverb ou denies the reality of an alleged fact. The alleged fact is that possession of the genes of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob constitutes automatic membership in the true Israel and automatic claim on the promises of God.

Romans 9:8 — "it is not the children of the flesh who are the children of God." οὐ (these are not). houtoi refers back to the racial Jews. The negative ou denies the reality of an alleged fact, the objective negative used when the speaker contradicts a claim that is being or might be made; with eimi supplied by ellipsis: these are not. The predicate nominative tekna theou uses the generic article to indicate God as unique. Racial descent from Abraham does not produce heirship of the covenant promises or automatic salvation.

Romans 9:21 — "Has the potter no right over the clay." οὐ. The question is introduced by ἤ and reinforced by οὐ placed within it. In Greek, οὐ within an interrogative does not mean the answer is negative; it signals that the expected answer is affirmative: Is it not the case that the potter possesses authority? Of course it is. The force is entirely different from μή, which expects a negative answer. Paul's choice of οὐ leads the audience to affirm what they already know to be obviously true, so the affirmation can be turned back upon their objection.

Romans 9:24 — "not from the Jews only." οὐ (not). The final clause of verse 24 opens with the objective negative οὐ. οὐ is used with the indicative mood and, when a verb is omitted by ellipsis, its presence signals the mood of the implied verb. μή governs the subjunctive, optative, imperative and certain infinitival constructions. In questions, μή anticipates a negative answer, οὐ a positive one.

Romans 10:2 — "but not according to knowledge." οὐ. After alla comes the strong negative adverb ou, which with the indicative mood denies the reality of an alleged fact.

Romans 10:3 — "they did not submit." οὐ. Ou with the indicative mood makes a declarative denial of fact: they did not submit.

Romans 10:16 — "But they have not all obeyed the gospel." οὐ (not all). After alla (contrasting universal outreach with Israel's rejection), the subject is the negative ou combined with the substantive adjective pas: not all. The construction does not imply that only a few heard; it asserts that not all who heard responded with obedient faith.

Romans 11:2 — "God has not rejected his people." οὐκ (has not, from οὐ). In verse 2 the aorist middle indicative of ἀπωθέω stands with the negative οὐκ. The construction is an emphatic denial that God has rejected Israel.

Romans 11:18 — "it is not you who support the root." οὐ (you, and only you, do not). Paul places the negative οὐ before the emphatic pronoun σύ: ou su — you, and only you, do not. The construction isolates and emphasizes the subject to heighten the irony of the arrogant believer's self-inflation. Corrected translation: you alone do not sustain the root.

Romans 13:1 — "For there is no authority except from God." οὐ (not). οὐ is used rather than μή because the indicative mood is in view: this is a declarative, objective, dogmatic statement of doctrine, not a condition or subjunctive possibility.

Romans 14:6 — "the one who abstains, abstains in honor of the Lord." οὐ (not). In the same clause the participle of ἐσθίω takes μή (he who does not eat), while the indicative of ἐσθίω takes οὐ (he does not eat). οὐ is used because the mood is indicative; μή is reserved for the imperative, subjunctive, participle and infinitive. The declarative indicative with οὐ presents objective reality, and the retroactive progressive present denotes an ascetic standard absorbed in the past and actively applied in the present.

Romans 14:17 — "is not a matter of eating and drinking." οὐ (not). οὐ is the standard negative for indicative mood statements. Negating the static present of εἰμί, it produces an absolute denial: the kingdom of God is not eating and drinking.

μή — Negation of Potential or Volitional Action

Used with participles, subjunctives, and infinitives.

Romans 4:5 — implicit throughout the discussion of one who does not work but believes.

Romans 4:17 — "the things that do not exist" — μὴ ὄντα, negating potential/hypothetical existence rather than a flat historical fact.

Romans 4:19 — "He did not weaken in faith." μὴ ἀσθενήσας (see the Aggressive Negative entry, section I).

Romans 5:14 — the negation implicit in describing those "whose sinning was not like the transgression of Adam" involves a μή-type qualification of the manner of sinning, not its bare fact.

Romans 9:14 — "Is there injustice on God's part?" μή (there is no injustice with God, is there?). The predicate nominative adikia requires a verb, which is supplied. The negative mē carries the expectation of a negative answer: There is no injustice with God, is there?

Romans 9:20 — "Will what is molded say to its molder, 'Why have you made me like this?'" μή. Paul introduces the second half of verse 20 with μή. οὐ denies the fact; μή denies the idea or thought behind the fact. When μή introduces a question it signals that a negative answer is expected and the question is rhetorical: posed not to solicit information but to compel the listener to acknowledge a conclusion already implicit in his own premises. Paul has already determined the answer: no, of course not.

Romans 9:30 — "who did not pursue righteousness." μή (not). The articular present active participle of διώκω is accompanied by μή, the standard negation used with participles in Greek. The active voice with μή indicates that these Gentiles, as free agents exercising self-determination from the common lump of clay, did not choose the path of self-righteousness.

Romans 10:19 — "did Israel not understand?" μή. Mē governs the interrogative. When mē introduces a question it signals that the expected answer is negative: the question is rhetorical. It means Israel did not fail to know, did they? and the answer is no, they did not fail to know; they knew. Israel's failure was not a failure of comprehension but of volition.

Romans 11:8 — "eyes that would not see." μή (not). The articular infinitives take μή rather than οὐ because the infinitive requires the subjective negative; μή negates with subjective or purposive force, making the negative purpose clause precise, while οὐ accompanies the indicative as an objective denial.

Romans 12:3 — "not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think." μή (stop thinking). Mē combined with an infinitive sets up an imperative of prohibition. Unlike ou, which negates indicative verbs, mē governs subjunctive, optative, infinitive, and participial constructions. Here mē plus the present active infinitive constitutes a direct imperative: stop doing this.

Romans 12:14 — "bless and do not curse them." καταράομαι (do not curse). Kai with mē and the present middle (deponent) imperative of kataraomai, to curse, to call down evil upon, to imprecate: an antagonistic mental attitude toward the persecutor, the opposite of objectivity. The prohibition targets the instantaneous reactive impulse to curse, which is incompatible with doctrine-informed, objective thinking.

Romans 13:3 — "Would you have no fear." μή (not). The infinitive φοβεῖσθαι is negated by μή, because μή accompanies infinitives in Greek. μή negates volitional and modal constructions (infinitives, subjunctives, imperatives), whereas οὐ negates indicative statements of fact.

Romans 13:13 — "not in carousing and drunkenness." μή (let us not). With the subjunctive mood, the negative μή produces a hortatory prohibition: let us not.

Romans 14:1 — "but not to quarrel over opinions." μή (not). The command is limited by μή with the phrase εἰς διακρίσεις διαλογισμῶν. μή, as distinct from οὐ which denies fact, denies the idea: not for the purpose of getting into quarrels about opinions. The strong believer is to receive the weak believer without making an issue out of his erroneous views.

Romans 15:1 — "and not to please ourselves." μή (not). Following the connective conjunction kai (καί), the text introduces a negative sub-final purpose clause: the present active infinitive of areskō (ἀρέσκω) with the negative mē (μή). Areskō means to please, to strive to please, or to accommodate. The negative purpose clause indicates intended result: and not to accommodate ourselves.

Romans 15:20 — "lest I build on someone else's foundation." ἵνα μή (lest). A negative purpose clause follows, introduced by ἵνα μή (hina mē). The conjunction ἵνα (hina) introduces a purpose clause, which always takes the subjunctive mood; accordingly, the negative is μή (mē) rather than οὐ, which is reserved for indicative constructions.

μηδέ — Compound Negative Prohibition

A stronger form of μή used to prohibit an ongoing action while adding a further negated element.

Romans 6:13 — "Do not present your members to sin." μηδέ compounds the prohibition, adding a further negated clause to the preceding one within the same command.

Romans 14:21 — "or do anything that causes your brother to stumble." μηδέ (nor do anything else). μηδέ (nor) introduces the infinitive of πίνω, and a second μηδέ follows. In classical Greek a repeated μηδέ after a list of specifics creates formula ellipsis: the second occurrence functions as a general classifier, nor do anything else. Meat and wine are representative examples; the second μηδέ extends the principle to any behavior that produces the same result.

mē with the Present Imperative — Prohibition of an Ongoing Action

Romans 6:12 — "Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body." μὴ βασιλευέτω — a present imperative negated by μή, prohibiting an action already in some sense underway, rather than one not yet begun.

Romans 11:18 — "do not be arrogant toward the branches." κατακαυχάομαι (stop assuming arrogant superiority). Verse 18 delivers the apodosis of the first-class condition begun in verse 17. μή with the present middle imperative of κατακαυχάομαι (kata, over, against + kauchaomai, to boast) forms an imperative of prohibition: Stop assuming arrogant superiority over the branches. The progressive present indicates an ongoing tendency among Gentile believers in Paul's day; the indirect middle shows the Gentile believer producing the action in a way that damages himself. The compound expresses boasting that asserts imagined superiority — the verbal form of contempt — and the prohibition is directed against anti-Semitism.

Romans 11:20 — "So do not become proud." φρονέω (stop thinking). μή with the present active imperative of φρονέω is a prohibition against the continuation of an action already in progress: Stop thinking. A prohibition in the aorist subjunctive forbids the inception of an act not yet begun; one in the present imperative demands cessation of an act already underway. With the accusative neuter plural of ὑψηλός the phrase means to think within the framework of arrogance — inside the interlocking systems of arrogance.

Romans 12:2 — "Do not be conformed to this world." συσχηματίζω (stop being conformed). Present passive imperative of suschēmatizō, to be molded after something, shaped by an external pattern. Mē with the present imperative produces the imperative of prohibition, stop being conformed: the action is already in progress and must cease. The passive voice shows the reversionistic believers receiving the action, shaped by an external force; the present tense is descriptive of what was occurring in the congregation.

Romans 12:19 — "never avenge yourselves." ἐκδικέω (stop avenging yourselves). Mē with the present active participle of ekdikeō (ek + dikē), to punish, to take vengeance, functioning imperativally. The negative with the present imperative signals the cessation of an ongoing action: the descriptive present confirms that the Roman believers were actually taking vengeance into their own hands. The direct object is the reflexive heautous.

Romans 12:21 — "Do not be overcome by evil." νικάω (stop being conquered). Mē with the present passive imperative of nikaō: stop being conquered. The present tense is descriptive of what was already in process among the Roman believers. The passive voice: the believer is being conquered, not because evil is irresistible, but because he has opened himself to it through neglect of doctrine. Hupo plus the ablative of kakos: by evil.

Romans 13:14 — "and make no provision for the flesh." ποιέω (stop making). The present middle imperative of ποιέω is negated by μή. An imperative of prohibition with the present tense carries the force stop doing what you are currently doing.

Romans 14:3 — "Let not the one who eats despise the one who abstains." ἐξουθενέω (to treat with contempt, to reject with disdain). The verb is the third person singular present active imperative of ἐξουθενέω. μή with the present imperative prohibits ongoing action: stop doing what you are already doing. The strong believer in Rome had already fallen into this pattern, and Paul commands him to discontinue it.

Romans 14:3 — "let not the one who abstains pass judgment on the one who eats." κρίνω (to judge, to evaluate adversely, to pass sentence). The second imperative governs the weak believer. Again μή with the present imperative of κρίνω means stop judging: the action is already in progress and must be discontinued. The object is that one, the mature believer who eats without restriction.

Romans 14:15 — "do not destroy with your food the one for whom Christ died." ἀπόλλυμι (stop destroying). The clause opens with a present active imperative of ἀπόλλυμι (to kill, destroy, void, deprive of, ruin) with μή. μή is the only negative used with the imperative mood; οὐ is restricted to the indicative. The pictorial present describes the mature believer's carelessness as an ongoing process, and the negative command demands that it cease: stop destroying.

Romans 14:16 — "do not let what you regard as good be spoken of as evil." βλασφημέω (let not ... be slandered). The main verb is a present passive imperative of βλασφημέω with μή, an imperative of prohibition. The descriptive present describes what is currently occurring in Rome. The passive voice identifies the mature believer's good as receiving the action: his advance to maturity is what is slandered when he fails to use the law of love in lieu of the law of liberty on the appropriate occasions.

Romans 14:20 — "Do not, for the sake of food, destroy the work of God." καταλύω (do not demolish). καταλύω is a present active imperative with μή: a prohibition against the ongoing demolition of the work of God.

οὐ μή + Subjunctive — Emphatic Negation

See section VI above for the full treatment of Romans 4:8's οὐ μὴ λογίσηται.

The Idiom οὐ μόνον δέ... ἀλλὰ καί

"And not only this, but also."

Romans 5:3 — "More than that" (ESV) / "And not only this." οὐ μόνον δέ introduces the idiom, extending the argument beyond the immediately preceding point.

Romans 5:11 — "More than that" (ESV) recurs, extending the argument of reconciliation into the further reality of present rejoicing in God.

Romans 9:10 — "And not only so, but also." μόνον (and not only this). The opening of verse 10 uses the post-positive particle de combined with the negative ou and the adverb monon (from monos, alone, only), used as an accusative of respect functioning adverbially: and not only this. The phrase signals a transition from the first case history, Ishmael and Isaac, to the second, and that a stronger or more definitive illustration follows.

Romans 9:10 — "but also when Rebekah had conceived children." ἀλλὰ (but). alla is used here in its ascensive function to introduce an additional case history that intensifies the argument. The earlier case histories, Abraham's sons by three different mothers, established that the mother is not the determining factor; now Paul adds a case that eliminates even the variable of different mothers, and the conjunction signals that further cases are coming, the hardening of Pharaoh and the contrast between Pharaoh and Moses.

Romans 9:10 — "but also when Rebekah had conceived children." καί (also). Alongside alla appears the ascensive use of kai, functioning adverbially: also, even. In its ascensive use kai marks a point that heightens what precedes it and prepares for something still more definitive to follow later in the chapter.

Romans 9:24 — "not from the Jews only but also from the Gentiles." οὐ μόνον … ἀλλά (not only … but also). The neuter μόνον functions as a limiting adverb (only); paired with οὐ it forms not only, limiting the scope before the adversative ἀλλά (but also) introduces the contrasting element. The construction establishes the universality of the calling: not only from among the Jews but also from among the Gentiles.

Romans 13:5 — "not only to avoid God's wrath but also for the sake of conscience." οὐ μόνον (not only ... but also). The construction οὐ μόνον ... ἀλλὰ καί signals that fear of punishment is one ground for subordination, with a second ground, conscience, to follow.

οὔτε... οὔτε — The Correlative Negative List

A repeated negative conjunction pairing off items in a catalogue, each pair (or single item) exhaustively denying the possibility of the stated thing accomplishing the action in view.

Romans 8:38–39 — "For I am sure that neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us..." The list is structured as four οὔτε... οὔτε couplets followed by two singles, organized into six categories of challenge (human events in history; angelic powers; time itself; supernatural powers; the spatial extremes of the universe; and, finally, a catch-all covering any remaining created thing). The whole series is introduced by an epexegetical ὅτι ("that"), marking the content of Paul's settled conviction (see the Perfect of Settled Confidence entry, section II) and functioning as the grammatical and rhetorical capstone of the entire chapter.

οὐδέ — Not Even, Neither

Romans 9:7 — "and not all are children of Abraham because they are his offspring." οὐδέ (neither, not even). The verse opens with the negative conjunction oude, compounded from ou and de, not even or neither. It is a strong negation reinforcing the denial of the preceding verse: not only has the word of God not failed, but not even descent from Abraham constitutes the criterion for true Jewish identity.

Romans 9:16 — "it depends not on human will or exertion." οὐδέ (nor). The second negative clause is joined by oude, ou plus de, and not, nor, connecting from him who runs to from him who desires and forming a comprehensive two-part negation of human initiative as the source of divine blessing. Again the articular present active participle with the ablative of source functions as a personal pronoun.

Romans 11:21 — "neither will he spare you." οὐδέ (neither, nor). The apodosis opens with οὐδέ, neither, nor. The King James omits this word entirely, losing the tight logical correlation with the protasis: for if God spared not … neither will he spare you. The neither is the hinge of the argument and makes the consistency of divine justice explicit.

μήπω... μηδέ — Double Negation in the Concessive Genitive Absolutes

Romans 9:11 — "though they were not yet born and had done nothing either good or bad." μηδέ (and not, nor). The second genitive absolute is introduced by the negative disjunctive particle mēde, and not, nor. It coordinates with mēpō to establish a double negation: neither had the twins been born, nor had they accomplished anything.

μή + Aorist Subjunctive — The Subjunctive of Prohibition

Romans 10:6 — "Do not say in your heart." μή (think not, from λέγω). The clause opens with the aorist active subjunctive of legō plus mē. Legō here functions idiomatically for the formation of words in thought, the activity of the right lobe prior to verbal expression, so the corrected translation is think not rather than say not. The aorist contemplates the action in its totality and forbids it by means of mē: the subjunctive of prohibition. The prohibition is comprehensive: the rationalization that salvation is unattainable is forbidden at its source, in the right lobe, before it can be verbalized.

μὴ οὐκ — The Double Negative in Rhetorical Questions

Romans 10:18 — "have they not heard?" μὴ οὐκ. The question carries a double negative, mē ouk. In questions formed with mē a negative answer is expected; with ouk, an affirmative answer. When both are combined, the negative particle governs the verb and the result is a strong expectation of an affirmative answer, setting up the most emphatic possible affirmation in the reply (menounge). It is one of the strongest affirmative constructions in Greek.

μή in a Question Expecting a Negative Answer

Romans 11:1 — "has God rejected his people?" μή (God has not repudiated His people, has He?). The question of Romans 11:1 is introduced by the negative particle μή, which in an interrogative context always demands a negative answer. The grammar already signals the answer before Paul gives it: He has not.

Romans 11:11 — "did they stumble in order that they might fall?" μή (they did not stumble so as to fall into ruin, did they?). The question is introduced by μή, which in a direct question signals that a negative answer is expected, in contrast with οὐ, which in a question expects a positive answer. Paul frames the question so that the only honest answer is no.

οὐκέτι — Logical, Not Temporal

Romans 11:6 — "it is no longer on the basis of works." οὐκέτι (then not, logically not). οὐκέτι, ordinarily the temporal no longer, functions here logically: then not, a necessary and exclusive consequence with no temporal implication. Paul is not saying grace once operated and has ceased; if grace is operative, works is categorically eliminated as a principle, and grace and works are antithetical systems.

μηδείς — Never, Nothing, No One

Romans 12:17 — "Repay no one evil for evil." μηδείς (never). The negative mēdeis, a strong negative pronoun used as adverbial negation, means never or in no way; paired with the participle of apodidōmi it forms an absolute prohibition against retaliatory conduct.

Romans 13:8 — "Owe no one anything." μηδείς (nothing; anyone). The direct object is the accusative neuter singular of μηδείς, nothing; the indirect object is the dative masculine singular of the same adjective, anyone. The full command is: owe nothing to anyone, aimed at the believer who incurs obligation without intending to fulfill it.

μηκέτι / οὐκέτι — No Longer, the Cessation of a Practice in Progress

Romans 14:13 — "let us not pass judgment on one another any longer." μηκέτι (no longer). The adverb μηκέτι means no longer, not from now on. It presupposes that the original recipients were already guilty of the honor code violations catalogued throughout chapters 12–14. It is not a hypothetical warning but a command to cease an ongoing practice; combined with the hortatory subjunctive it commands the immediate and permanent discontinuation of judging.

Romans 14:15 — "you are no longer walking in love." οὐκέτι (no longer). The temporal adverb οὐκέτι means no longer, not now but no longer. It indicates that the strong believer's walk according to love has been abandoned: not that it never existed, but that it has ceased in the present situation through retaliation or contempt toward the weak believer.

ὅς + οὐ — The Idiom of Exception

Romans 15:18 — "except what Christ has accomplished through me." ὧν οὐ (except what). The clause contains a second negative, οὐ (ou), combined with the relative pronoun ὧν (hōn). The literal rendering "which Christ has not accomplished" produces the opposite of the intended meaning. But ὅς (hos) plus οὐ (ou) is a recognized Greek idiom meaning "except what." This is not a double negative in the English sense. The correct translation is therefore: "except what Christ has accomplished."

Romans 15:23 — "since I no longer have any room for work in these regions." μηκέτι τόπον ἔχων (no longer having a region). Paul uses the present active participle of ἔχω (echō, to have), coupled with the negative adverb μηκέτι (mēketi), meaning no longer rather than a simple negation. The accusative singular direct object is τόπος (topos), a region or geographical sphere of ministry.

IX.Conditional Sentences

Greek conditional sentences fall into four classes, each summarized by a single governing concept.

First Class — Reality

Assumes the protasis as true (whether for genuine assertion or, in debater's technique, for the sake of argument).

Romans 2:17–23 — "But if you call yourself a Jew and rely on the law and boast in God... you then who teach others, do you not teach yourself?" This entire span is structured as a single first-class condition: the protasis (vv. 17–20) grants all the legalist's premises as true, and the apodosis (vv. 21–23) then draws from those premises the devastating conclusion that the legalist is guilty of the very things he condemns in others.

Romans 3:3 — "What if some were unfaithful? Does their faithlessness nullify the faithfulness of God?" εἰ with the indicative forms a first-class condition: the protasis, "if some did not believe," treats Jewish unbelief as a historical reality assumed true for the argument, with the apodosis then asking — and definitively answering in verse 4 — whether such maladjustment can nullify God's own integrity.

Romans 3:30 — "since God is one." εἴπερ (a compound of εἰ intensified by περ) introduces a first-class condition presenting the unity of the Godhead as established fact, not hypothesis: since the Godhead is one in essence, the justice of God justifies circumcised and uncircumcised alike, by the same faith.

Romans 4:2 — "For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about, but not before God." A first-class condition used in debater's technique: the premise is assumed true for the sake of the argument, then shown to lead to an impossible result and therefore rejected.

Romans 4:14 — "For if it is the adherents of the law who are to be heirs, faith is null and void." Same debater's-technique use.

Romans 5:10 — "For if while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son, much more, now that we are reconciled, shall we be saved by his life." The established-premise use: the protasis is genuinely true and serves as the basis for an a fortiori inference (see section XI) to the apodosis.

Romans 5:17 — "For if, because of one man's trespass, death reigned through that one man, much more will those who receive the abundance of grace... reign in life." Same established-premise structure supporting a fortiori reasoning.

Romans 6:5 — "For if we have been united with him in a death like his, we shall certainly be united with him in a resurrection like his." εἰ with the indicative treats the protasis as reality: since union with Christ in his death is an established fact, the apodosis follows with certainty.

Romans 7:20 — "Now if I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells within me." The first-class condition here assumes the reality of the inner conflict — this is a real, ongoing experience, not hypothetical.

Romans 8:9 — "assuming that the Spirit of God dwells in you." εἴπερ (a compound of εἰ intensified by περ, "if indeed," "if after all," or "since") introduces a first-class condition affirming, as a settled fact, that the Holy Spirit indwells every Church Age believer — the condition is not introducing genuine doubt.

Romans 8:9 (second clause) — "if in fact anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ" (ESV: "does not belong to him"). A second first-class condition, using the simple εἰ with the indefinite pronoun τις functioning not as a genuine unknown but as a category-specifier — here, the category of the unbeliever.

Romans 8:17 — "if children, then heirs... provided we suffer with him." A first-class condition assumed as reality, grounding the believer's heirship and, conditionally, participation in Christ's sufferings and glory.

Romans 8:31 — "If God is for us, who can be against us?" A first-class condition presenting an established truth (God is, in fact, for us) as the premise for the rhetorical question that follows.

Romans 9:22 — "What if God." εἰ δέ (Moreover if, as is the case). The sentence opens not with what but with the conditional particle εἰ followed by the indicative, the standard first-class condition: a supposition presented from the viewpoint of reality, if, and it is assumed to be true. It concedes the reality of the protasis for the argument. Here the conceded reality is the entire preceding demonstration: God did harden Pharaoh's heart, did execute judgment through ten plagues, did act with sovereign freedom in the Exodus.

Romans 11:6 — "But if it is by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works." εἰ (if, and it is). εἰ introduces a first-class condition, a supposition from the standpoint of reality: grace is in fact the operative principle. It is not a hypothetical but a declaration of fact framed as a logical argument, logical in form but dogmatic in content.

Romans 11:12 — "Now if their trespass means riches for the world, and if their failure means riches for the Gentiles." εἰ (if, and it is true). After the transitional δέ, rendered now, εἰ introduces a first-class condition, continued into the second protasis by καί. Paul treats both protases as established facts: the apostasy of Israel has already produced Gentile blessing, and the argument proceeds on that basis.

Romans 11:14 — "in order somehow to make my fellow Jews jealous." εἰ (if somehow). The verse opens with εἰ, introducing the protasis of a first-class condition — the supposition is assumed to be true from the author's viewpoint. The enclitic πῶς adds somehow, in some way; the combined force is if somehow, a realistic, not merely hypothetical, expectation. The first-class condition assumes as true that Paul's Gentile ministry will in fact stimulate racial Israel to emulation, and it requires the declarative indicative of παραζηλόω.

Romans 11:15 — "For if their rejection means the reconciliation of the world." εἰ (for if). Verse 15 opens again with εἰ, a first-class condition assuming the protasis to be true. The post-positive explanatory γάρ may be rendered for if or now if, connecting the verse to the argument of verse 12. The corrected translation adds the affirmation: for if their rejection has become the reconciliation of the world, and it has.

Romans 11:16 (Isaiah 11:1) — "and if the root is holy, so are the branches." εἰ (if … and He is). εἰ introduces a first-class condition — supposition from the viewpoint of historical reality; what is supposed is already true. The root (ῥίζα, with the generic article indicating a unique category) is the Lord Jesus Christ in His first advent, drawn from Isaiah 11:1. The first-class condition affirms the reality: the root is holy — a reference to the incarnation, the hypostatic union, and the impeccability of Christ in His humanity.

Romans 11:17 — "But if some of the branches were broken off." εἰ (if … and they were). Verse 17 opens with the transitional δέ (moreover), turning to the other side of the picture. εἰ again introduces a first-class condition, supposition from the viewpoint of historical reality. The long first-class condition that begins in verse 17 has its apodosis in the command of verse 18.

Romans 11:18 — "If you are, remember it is not you who support the root." εἰ (and since you are arrogant). εἰ with the indicative introduces a first-class condition — a supposition from the viewpoint of reality: the arrogant distortion of grace was actually occurring among the Gentile believers in Rome. δέ is transitional with no adversative force. The present middle indicative of κατακαυχάομαι is a perfective present — a state of arrogance that has developed over time and now exists. Corrected translation: and since you are arrogant.

Romans 11:21 — "For if God did not spare the natural branches." εἰ (if, since). εἰ introduces a first-class condition — a supposition from the standpoint of reality — which may be translated since as well as if, since both convey a true premise. The articular ὁ θεός does not emphasize the quality of the divine person but identifies God as one well known to the reader — a reminder rather than a definition. Corrected translation: For if God spared not the natural branches, and He did not spare them.

Romans 11:24 — "For if you were cut from what is by nature a wild olive tree." εἰ (since). εἰ introduces the protasis of a first-class condition — supposition from the viewpoint of reality. The argument treats the salvation of the Gentiles as an established, verifiable fact, hence the corrected translation for since you Gentiles were cut off. With it stands the proleptic use of σύ, referring to Gentile believers at Rome.

Romans 12:18 — "If possible." εἰ (if it is possible — and it is). Ei introduces a first-class condition: when ei governs an indicative or an implied indicative, it signals if, and it is true. The predicate nominative is the neuter plural of dunatos, functioning without an expressed verb; the verb to be is supplied: if it is possible, and it is. Possible here is a synonym for capacity: all things are possible to the believer who has doctrine resident in the soul.

Romans 13:9 — "and any other commandment." καί (and if there is any other commandment). εἰ introduces a first-class conditional clause (if, and it is true), affirming that a positive commandment exists to cover the five negatives. Chapter 408's corrected translation renders it and if there is any other commandment, and there is.

Romans 14:15 — "For if your brother is grieved by what you eat." εἰ (if). εἰ with the indicative introduces the protasis of a first-class condition, supposition from the viewpoint of reality. The condition is assumed to be true for the purposes of the argument: for if because of food your brother is distressed or distracted.

Romans 15:27 — "For if the Gentiles have come to share in their spiritual blessings." εἰ (if, and it is true). This introduces a first-class conditional clause, εἰ (ei), a supposition from the viewpoint of reality — the condition is assumed to be true.

Second Class — Unreality (Contrary to Fact)

Assumes the protasis as false, used to explore what would follow if a known-untrue premise were true.

Romans 9:29 (Isaiah 1:9) — "If the Lord of hosts had not left us offspring, we would have been like Sodom and become like Gomorrah." εἰ μή … ἄν (except … would have). Paul's quotation of Isaiah 1:9 is a second-class conditional sentence, the contrary-to-fact condition in past time. εἰ with μή forms the idiom εἰ μή, literally if not, idiomatically except or unless; the apodosis contains ἄν, marking the unfulfilled result of an unfulfilled condition. The second-class condition supposes a circumstance contrary to fact, thereby affirming the opposite with maximum logical force: the grammar asserts that the complete absence of a Jewish remnant is a historical impossibility. The second-class condition is theology expressed in syntax.

Third Class — Probability

Uses ἐάν ("if") plus the subjunctive mood, expressing a real element of uncertainty combined with a real element of likelihood — genuinely open, pending some further condition.

Romans 2:25 — "For circumcision indeed is of value if you obey the law, but if you break the law, your circumcision becomes uncircumcision." ἐάν with the subjunctive introduces a third-class condition — future possibility with a genuine element of contingency. The verse's apodosis is placed before its protasis, an inversion reflecting the historical fact that circumcision preceded the Mosaic law.

Romans 7:2–3 — "if her husband dies she is released from the law of her husband... if she lives with another man while her husband is alive, she will be called an adulteress." ἐάν with the subjunctive of ἀποθνῄσκω (v.2) and of γίνομαι (v.3) both introduce third-class protases: the outcome is genuinely contingent on which of two possibilities obtains. Applied to the spiritual analogy in the surrounding chapters, the third-class condition makes the believer's divorce from the sin nature strictly contingent on faith in Christ: if the individual believes, the divorce is accomplished; if not, the first marriage remains in force.

Romans 8:13 — "For if you live according to the flesh you will die, but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live." Both halves of this verse present the believer's two live, genuinely open outcomes as contingencies dependent on which pattern of life is actually chosen.

Romans 9:27 (Isaiah 10:22) — "Though the number of the sons of Israel be as the sand of the sea." ἐάν (if). ἐάν with the subjunctive is the formal grammatical marker of the third-class condition, technically the more probable future condition; the fourth-class condition, by contrast, is the less probable future condition. Both the supposition and its consequence refer to future events.

Romans 10:9 — "if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead." ἐάν (if). Ean with the subjunctive introduces a third-class condition, the condition of probability: if, maybe yes or maybe no. It encodes genuine probability in either direction; the outcome depends on the function of free will. The protasis has two members (homologeō and pisteuō, both aorist active subjunctive); the indicative of sōzō then states the result. No coercion, psychological pressure, or manufactured emotion enters; the decision belongs entirely to the individual.

Romans 10:9 — "you will be saved." σῴζω (you will be saved). The clause ends with the future passive indicative of sōzō, the first indicative in the conditional construction. The subjunctive throughout the protasis signaled contingency; the indicative now signals certainty: once the condition of faith is met, salvation is declared as dogmatic fact. It is a futuristic indicative; the passive voice shows the believer receiving salvation, not producing it.

Romans 10:13 (Joel 2:32) — "everyone who calls on the name of the Lord." ὅς ἂν. Pas, whoever, is the antecedent of the relative pronoun hos; the particle an following it denotes that the action of the verb depends on a condition. Together hos an form the equivalent of the protasis of a third-class conditional sentence, indicating contingency: some will and some will not, but the offer stands without qualification. The subjunctive governs the condition; the future passive indicative sōthēsetai governs the result.

Romans 10:15 — "unless they are sent." ἐάν (unless). Ean with the negative mē produces a third-class condition: unless they are sent out. The condition acknowledges genuine contingency: the client nation may or may not fulfill the sending function. It indicates contingency rather than impossibility; where a client nation has failed to send, God retains the capacity to provide a messenger through extraordinary means, and the necessity of such provision is itself the measure of that nation's malfunction.

Romans 11:22 — "provided you continue in his kindness." ἐάν (if you persist). ἐάν plus the subjunctive is a third-class condition, a more probable future probability with an element of contingency: maybe you will, maybe you will not. The present active subjunctive of ἐπιμένω (to continue, persist, remain in) is perfective — the continuation of results already established. The dative of sphere ἐν τῇ χρηστότητι yields: if you persist in the sphere of the integrity of God.

Romans 11:23 — "if they do not continue in their unbelief." ἐάν (if they do not persist). ἐάν introduces the third-class condition, expressing what is possible but undetermined: if, and it may or may not be true. The present active subjunctive of ἐπιμένω is a progressive present denoting an ongoing state of persistence; the Jewish unbelievers themselves produce the action. The subjunctive is the potential subjunctive of a third-class protasis. The condition preserves genuine volition: God does not override human will.

Romans 12:20 — "if your enemy is hungry, feed him." πεινάω (if the one hostile to you is hungry). The conditional clause takes the present active subjunctive of peinaō. The third-class condition expresses contingency: the offender may or may not still be alive to receive the meal, since the justice of God may already have removed him. The sarcasm of the passage inheres here. The present is pictorial and the subjunctive potential.

Romans 12:20 — "if he is thirsty, give him something to drink." ἐάν (if he is thirsty). Ean introduces a third-class condition, a condition of probability or possibility projecting a real contingency. The protasis has the present active subjunctive of dipsaō, thirst in the sense of life-threatening dehydration; the scenario is a life-or-death emergency. The believer may or may not encounter this test, but when he does, the command governs.

Romans 13:4 — "But if you do wrong, be afraid." ἐὰν δὲ τὸ κακὸν ποιῇς (but if you do the evil). ἐάν with the subjunctive forms a third-class condition, a more probable future condition implying genuine uncertainty: the believer may or may not produce evil, depending on his relationship to Bible doctrine. The apodosis is φοβοῦ, keep on being afraid.

Romans 14:8 — "For if we live, we live to the Lord, and if we die, we die to the Lord." ἐάν τε (just as when, from ἐάν). Standard translations treat ἐάν here as a simple third class conditional, if we live. ἐάν with the subjunctive alone would indicate a third class, more probable future condition. But the combination of the enclitic τε with ἐάν is a rare idiom that converts ἐάν into the functional equivalent of ὅταν, when rather than if: just as when we live, we live to the Lord. This turns the clause from a hypothetical condition into a description of the believer’s actual, habitual state after salvation.

Romans 14:8 — "whether we live or whether we die." ἐάν (if). In the second half of verse 8, ἐάν is the standard marker of a third-class condition, a more-probable-future condition: it does not assert that the event will occur but treats it as genuinely possible. Both conditions are genuine possibilities within the plan of God: the believer may continue to live or may die, and in either case the conclusion stands, we are the Lord’s.

Romans 14:23 — "if he eats." ἐάν (if). The protasis is introduced by ἐάν, presenting a third class condition: possibility without prejudice as to fulfillment. The weak believer does not have to eat or drink; if the action would violate his norms and standards he is entirely free to decline. The third class condition does not compel the action but establishes it as a possibility.

Romans 15:24 — "once I have enjoyed your company for a while." ἐάν (if). The final clause of verse 24 is governed by a third-class conditional introduced by ean (ἐάν) plus the subjunctive mood, identifying the condition as more probable future — possible but not certain of fulfillment. The condition reads: if first I am satisfied with you in part.

Fourth Class — Possibility (Remote)

Expresses a merely conceivable outcome, with the least degree of expectation of the four classes. No verse in Romans 1–16 is labeled by the source as a fourth-class condition.

X.Comparative Sentences

Distinct from conditional sentences: these draw an analogy between two clauses rather than an inference from a premise.

hōsper... houtōs — "Just as... so also"

Romans 5:21 — "so that, as sin reigned in death, grace also might reign through righteousness leading to eternal life." ὥσπερ... οὕτως draws the formal parallel between the reign of sin and the reign of grace.

Romans 11:30 — "For just as you were at one time disobedient to God." ὥσπερ (just as). The protasis is introduced by ὥσπερ, signalling a comparative clause; its apodosis in verse 31 is introduced by οὕτως: just as … so. A comparative clause introduces an analogous thought to elucidate or emphasize the principal clause; the two clauses are related not as cause to effect or hypothesis to conclusion but as analogy to principle. γάρ precedes ὥσπερ, introducing the unit as explanation of verse 29.

Romans 11:31 — "so they too have now been disobedient." οὕτως (so also). οὕτως opens the apodosis of the comparative clause begun with ὥσπερ in verse 30, followed by the adjunctive καί (so also) and the demonstrative οὗτοι, these, the Jews of the church age. The adverb houtōs and the pronoun houtoi are morphologically distinct forms with distinct functions, a distinction obscured in English because omega and omicron are rendered by the same letter.

houtōs kai — "So also"

Romans 5:19 — "For as by the one man's disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one man's obedience the many will be made righteous." οὕτως καί completes the Adam/Christ comparison begun in the first half of the verse.

Romans 11:5 — "So too at the present time." οὕτως οὖν καί (therefore in the same manner also, from οὕτως). Verse 5 opens with οὕτως οὖν καί, the hinge of the Elijah analogy. οὕτως is an adverb of manner, rendered in the same manner rather than even so; οὖν is inferential; καί is adjunctive, also. The adjunctive καί brings the present generation alongside the generation of Elijah as a genuine parallel, not a distant illustration.

The Elliptical Comparative — Verbs Supplied from Context

Romans 5:18 — "Therefore, as one trespass led to condemnation for all men, so one act of righteousness leads to justification and life for all men." The second half of the comparison omits its own verb, expecting the reader to supply it from the first half — a deliberate compression that mirrors the tight parallelism Paul is drawing between Adam and Christ.

men... de — "On the One Hand... But on the Other Hand"

The classical formal-contrast construction.

Romans 5:16 — "And the free gift is not like the result of that one man's sin. For the judgment following one trespass brought condemnation, but the free gift following many trespasses brought justification." μέν... δέ structures the contrast between the singular origin of condemnation and the multiple-trespass origin of justification.

Romans 7:12 — "So the law is holy" — the emphatic use of μέν alone (without an immediately paired δέ in this instance) functions as "as a matter of fact, in fact," a strong inferential affirmation rather than the full two-sided contrast.

Romans 7:25 — "So then, I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh I serve the law of sin." A full, deliberately symmetrical μέν... δέ construction — pure classical Attic style — presenting the believer's two live options with equal grammatical weight, leaving the choice to volition: serving God's law with the mind (an iterative present, an obligation) against serving sin's law with the flesh (the verb elided and understood from context, an impulse).

Romans 9:21 — "one vessel for honorable use and another for dishonorable use." ὁ μέν … ὁ δέ (on the one hand … on the other hand). The verse concludes with the correlative ὁ μέν … ὁ δέ, the definite article plus the affirmative particle μέν and the contrastive particle δέ. It divides the produced objects into two categories without suggesting that the distinction is arbitrary or that either category is inherently defective in its material.

Romans 11:22 — "severity toward those who have fallen, but God's kindness to you." μέν … δέ (on the one hand … but on the other hand). Paul opens the second half of verse 22 with μέν, a classical particle always used correlatively with δέ, producing a concessive clause followed by an adversative clause. This classical Attic style is the register Paul adopts whenever the theological contrast is at its sharpest. The men clause covers divine severity toward the unbelieving Jew; the de clause the integrity of God toward the Gentile believer.

Romans 11:28 — "As regards the gospel, they are enemies for your sake. But as regards election, they are beloved." μέν … δέ (on the one hand … on the other hand). Verse 28 opens with an Attic correlative: μέν, followed later by δέ. The classical pairing introduces a formal contrast that governs the entire verse: two parallel but contrasting statements about Israel — Jewish unbelievers as enemies and Jewish believers as beloved.

Romans 14:2 — "One person believes he may eat anything, while the weak person eats only vegetables." μέν … δέ (on the one hand … on the other hand). Paul opens verse 2 with the classical Attic correlative particles μέν and δέ: μέν introduces the strong believer, δέ (with its adversative connotation) the weak believer. This is not the common Koine idiom but the formal rhetoric of classical Attic prose; Paul, when theologically excited or doctrinally precise, reverts to classical constructions, as already observed in Romans 5.

Romans 14:5 — "One person esteems one day as better than another, while another esteems all days alike." μέν … δέ (on the one hand … on the other hand). Verse 5 opens with explanatory γάρ introducing a two-sided explanation, confirmed by the classical correlating particles μέν and δέ, which structure the verse as a genuine antithesis between two types of believers: the weak believer who judges one day above another, and the strong believer who considers every day alike as from the Lord.

ὡς — Comparative Particle

Romans 9:25 (Hosea 2:23) — "and her who was not beloved I will call 'beloved.'" ὡς (as, in the manner that). The modal participle is introduced by the comparative particle ὡς, signifying the manner of transition: those who have not been loved will be constituted as those who have been loved, not by any change in their racial identity but by their volition toward the first advent of Christ at the second advent.

Romans 9:27 (Isaiah 10:22; Genesis 22:17; 26:4; 28:14) — "as the sand of the sea." ὡς (as). The comparative particle ὡς introduces the simile as the sand of the sea. The predicate nominative is ἄμμος (sand), modified by the descriptive genitive of θάλασσα (sea), echoing the Abrahamic covenant promises.

Romans 9:29 (Isaiah 1:9) — "we would have been like Sodom and become like Gomorrah." ὡς (like, as). In the apodosis of the second-class condition ὡς introduces the predicate nominative Σόδομα, which stands collectively for the five cities of the Canaanite Pentapolis; in the parallel clause καὶ ὡς Γόμορρα ὡμοιώθημεν, ὡς governs the nominative Gomorra. Except for the Lord's preservation of a remnant, Israel would have been completely and permanently destroyed with no continuation in history.

Romans 9:32 — "but as if it were based on works." ὡς (as, as if). Following the adversative is the comparative ὡς, characterizing the quality of Israel's pursuit: they pursued as if by works, ὡς capturing the self-deceived confidence with which they treated law-observance as though it were a legitimate path to righteousness.

Romans 12:3 — "each according to the measure of faith that God has assigned." ὡς (as, inasmuch as). The conjunction hōs introduces a correlative of comparison, correctly translated as or inasmuch as. The subject ho theos carries the definite article specifying the God previously identified and well known in context.

καὶ οὕτως — Modal, Not Temporal

Romans 11:26 — "And in this way all Israel will be saved." καὶ οὕτως (and in this manner). καί introduces a result drawn from the preceding argument; οὕτως refers anaphorically to what precedes, in this manner. The phrase is not temporal (and then) but modal (and in this manner): it draws together the olive-tree analogy of verses 17–25 and declares its eschatological conclusion. Paul is not asserting that all ethnic Jews will be saved automatically, but that the process he has described will issue in the deliverance of Israel as a regenerate community.

kathaper... houtōs — Just As... So

Romans 12:5 — "so we, though many, are one body in Christ." οὕτως (so). The transitional adverb houtōs draws the conclusion from the comparative, and kathaper links this clause explicitly to the preceding one. The nominative plural of polus with the definite article is rendered the many, the totality of believers in the body of Christ: so we, the many, are one body in Christ.

τε … τε — Correlative Just As … So Also

Romans 14:8 — "if we live, we live to the Lord, and if we die, we die to the Lord." τέ (just as … so also). Verse 8 opens with explanatory γάρ plus the enclitic particle τε appearing twice in correlation, τε … τε. The construction establishes a correlative relationship, just as … so also, introducing the paired clauses governing both life and death.

men... alla — The Attic Correlative To Be Sure... But

Romans 14:20 — "Everything is indeed clean, but." μέν (to be sure ... but). The second clause begins with the Attic affirmative particle μέν used correlatively with the adversative ἀλλά that follows. This classical construction sets up a direct contrast, on the one hand ... but on the other hand: between the correct doctrinal principle (all foods are clean) and its wrong application.

XI.A Fortiori Arguments

If the greater has been accomplished, the lesser follows with stronger reason. The fixed idiom is πολλῷ μᾶλλον ("much more"), though the underlying logic recurs even without the fixed phrase.

Romans 5:9 — "Since, therefore, we have now been justified by his blood, much more shall we be saved by him from the wrath of God." πολλῷ μᾶλλον — if the greater (justification, accomplished at the cost of Christ's blood) has been secured, the lesser (final deliverance from wrath) follows with much greater certainty.

Romans 5:10 — "For if while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son, much more, now that we are reconciled, shall we be saved by his life." Same fixed idiom, same structure: reconciliation while enemies (the harder case) guarantees final salvation now that friendship is established (the easier case).

Romans 5:15 — "much more have the grace of God and the free gift by the grace of that one man Jesus Christ abounded for many." The a fortiori argument applied to the disproportion between Adam's single sin and Christ's superabounding grace.

Romans 5:17 — "much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and the free gift of righteousness reign in life through the one man Jesus Christ." The greatest of the four a fortiori statements in Romans 5, applying the principle to future reigning in resurrection life.

Romans 8:32 — "He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also graciously give us all things?" This is the a fortiori argument in its purest form across all the material processed: the greater gift (the Son, given up to judgment) makes the lesser gift (everything else) certain — stated here as a rhetorical question rather than the fixed πολλῷ μᾶλλον idiom, but identical in logical structure.

Romans 8:4's πληρωθῇ (see section I) is grounded in the same a fortiori logic carried over from Romans 5: the imbalance between the greater (imputed righteousness, already given) and the less (blessing in time, not yet realized) demands resolution, and a fortiori reasoning guarantees that resolution will come.

Romans 8:30's five-step chain is itself a chain of a fortiori inferences: foreknowledge guarantees predestination, which guarantees calling, which guarantees justification, which guarantees glorification — each step following from the prior with the same "how could it be otherwise" force.

Romans 11:12 — "how much more will their full inclusion mean!" πόσος / μᾶλλον (how much more, from πόσος). The apodosis introduces the a fortiori principle through two elements: the dative of the interrogative correlative pronoun πόσος, taken not as an instrumental (by how much) but as a dative of advantage, and the comparative adverb μᾶλλον. Together they yield how much more, the logical pivot on which the verse turns.

Romans 11:12 — "how much more will their full inclusion mean!" πόσῳ μᾶλλον (much more). Whenever this formula (πολλῷ μᾶλλον, here πόσῳ μᾶλλον) appears in the argument of Romans, an a fortiori inference is drawn from the immediately preceding doctrinal fact. At Romans 11:12 it introduces the inescapable conclusion that follows from the stated premise: if Jewish discipline produced Gentile blessing, Israel's fullness will produce even greater Gentile blessing. The glossary lists the phrase at Romans 5:9, 10, 15, 17; 8:32; 11:12.

Romans 11:24 — "how much more will these, the natural branches, be grafted back into their own olive tree." πόσῳ μᾶλλον (how much more). The concluding clause is introduced by πόσῳ μᾶλλον, how much more — the Greek equivalent of the Latin a fortiori, with greater reason. The construction has appeared repeatedly in Romans, always governing an argument from the greater to the lesser or from the more difficult to the less difficult: if God saves the Gentile, He will save the Jew who believes in Christ.

XII.Ellipsis, Aposiopesis, and Brachylogy

Ellipsis is the grammatical omission of words the reader is expected to supply from context. Aposiopesis is the specific case where the omitted material must be drawn from the immediately preceding context. Brachylogy is deliberate grammatical compression more broadly.

Romans 5:18 — "Therefore, as one trespass led to condemnation for all men, so one act of righteousness leads to justification and life for all men." The second clause omits its own verb by ellipsis, supplying it from the first clause (see the Elliptical Comparative entry, section X).

Romans 6:5 — "For if we have been united with him in a death like his, we shall certainly be united with him in a resurrection like his." The second half compresses what could be a full parallel clause into a brief echo, trusting the reader to supply the fuller sense from the first half.

Romans 7:2 — "For a married woman is bound by law to her husband while he lives."
