There is no verb at all in the Greek of this clause (see the Predicate Nominative without a Copula entry, section XIV) — the King James Version's supplied "hath" does not correspond to any word in the original; the predicate adjective ὕπανδρος alone completes the clause grammatically.

Romans 7:25's second clause (the μέν side) elides the verb entirely on the δέ side, understood from the μέν clause by classical convention — Greek routinely omits a verb already established by a parallel clause rather than repeating it.

Romans 8:5 — "but those who live according to the Spirit set their minds on the things of the Spirit." Paul employs ellipsis here: the verb φρονέω, stated explicitly in the first half of the verse, is left to be supplied in the second half rather than repeated.

Romans 9:5 — "To them belong the patriarchs." πατέρες (from whom are the fathers, from πατήρ). eimi is implied by Pauline ellipsis. The predicate noun pateres, fathers or ancestors, takes the generic article comprehending the category as a whole: from whom are the fathers, the regenerate patriarchal ancestry of Israel, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, each of whom attained maturity adjustment to the justice of God.

Romans 9:6 — "But it is not as though the word of God has failed." οὐχ οἷος (this is not to imply that, from οἷος). The Greek opens with ou joined to hoios, a derivative correlative pronoun used in classical Attic Greek as part of an elliptical idiom, employed this way by Euripides. The pronoun stands in the predicate nominative without a stated verb, requiring the reader to supply the present indicative of eimi; this is not an addition to the text but a grammatical necessity. The idiom means: not such as, not of that kind, not as implying. Concluded by hoti, it reads: However, this is not to imply that. Paul uses it to arrest the reader before he drops the substantive point.

Romans 9:9 — "For this is what the promise said." οὗτος (the word of the promise is this). The passage is elliptical throughout. The present active indicative of eimi is implied and must be supplied; the predicate nominative is the demonstrative houtos, yielding: for the word of the promise is this.

Romans 9:22 — "What if God, desiring to show his wrath and to make known his power, has endured with much patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction." ἀποσιώπησις (aposiopesis). Aposiopesis is a figure in which a speaker deliberately breaks off a conditional sentence: the protasis (the if-clause) is stated in full, but the apodosis is suppressed, compelling the listener to supply it from the force of the argument; when he supplies it he has in effect agreed with the speaker's conclusion. Paul begins a first-class conditional clause in verse 22 and carries the protasis through verses 22 and 23, then withholds the apodosis. It is the culminating technique in the sequence of debating strategies across Romans 9: the debater's question (v. 14), the rhetorical question (v. 19), the debater's analogy and finesse (vv. 20–21).

Romans 9:22 — "What if God, desiring to show his wrath and to make known his power, has endured with much patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction." ἀνακόλουθον (anacoluthon). An anacoluthon is a construction in which a sentence begins along one syntactical path and deliberately shifts to another without completing the first: a controlled digression that returns to the main argument. The deviation is not an error but a device that advances the argument. Verses 22–24 contain multiple anacoluthon sequences embedded within the governing aposiopesis (the illustrative digressions of Ishmael, Esau and Pharaoh).

Romans 9:22 — "What if God, desiring to show his wrath and to make known his power, has endured with much patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction." ὑπερβατόν; χιασμός (hyperbaton; chiasmus). Hyperbaton is the artificial displacement of words from their natural order to assign an emphasis the normal order could not convey. A specific form present in verses 22–24 is chiasmus, clauses or terms arranged in an inverted parallel scheme (A–B–B'–A'), used to reinforce the theological symmetry between the vessel of wrath and the vessel of mercy. Its appearance inside an aposiopesis that itself contains anacoluthon represents a density of literary technique without parallel in the Pauline corpus.

Romans 9:32 — "Because they did not pursue it by faith, but as if it were based on works." οὐκ (did not pursue, from διώκω). The negative is οὐκ, the strong indicative negative, used because the following verb is in the indicative. The verb to be supplied by ellipsis is the present active indicative of διώκω; the subject is Israel and the object, implied from verse 31, is the law understood in terms of its true purpose.

Romans 10:1 — "my heart's desire and prayer to God for them is that they may be saved." δέησις. No main verb appears in the clause; it is supplied by ellipsis. The nominative singular subject deēsis, the standard New Testament word for petition or prayer, stands with the definite article functioning as a possessive pronoun, yielding my prayer.

Romans 10:17 — "So faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ." δέ. The verse contains no finite verb; the ellipsis must be resolved in translation: that faith comes from a message. The continuative de introduces a second clause, again with no finite verb: moreover, that message comes through the agency of a doctrinal discourse about Christ.

Romans 11:7 — "What then?" τί οὖν (Therefore, to what conclusion are we forced? How stands the case?, from τίς). τί οὖν is an Attic debater formula question: the neuter interrogative τί (what, not who) with the post-positive inferential οὖν. The full form would include the future active indicative of λέγω, what shall we say then?, but the verb is omitted in Attic elliptical style; it introduces a verdict compelled by the preceding argument, not a genuine question.

Romans 11:11 — "salvation has come to the Gentiles." ἡ σωτηρία (this salvation belongs to the Gentiles, from σωτηρία). The middle clause of verse 11 is a deliberate ellipsis: ἡ σωτηρία with the dative plural of ἔθνος and no finite verb. The compression is emotionally significant: Paul expresses the tragedy of the transfer of client-nation responsibility from Israel to Gentile nations not through lamentation but through grammatical compression.

Romans 11:12 — "Now if their trespass means riches for the world." πλοῦτος (riches). Verse 12 contains no finite verb, an ellipsis reflecting the strong emotional undercurrent of Paul as human author. The predicate nominative πλοῦτος requires a supplied linking verb: present γίνομαι in the first protasis (becomes the riches of the world, with descriptive genitive κόσμου), aorist γίνομαι in the second (became, the completed event of AD 70), and future εἰμί in the apodosis (will be).

Romans 11:15 — "what will their acceptance mean but life from the dead?" τίς (what will be). The interrogative τίς is distinguished from the indefinite pronoun by its accent. Because the clause is elliptical, the future active indicative of εἰμί must be supplied: what will be. The predicate nominative is formed from the definite article functioning as a possessive pronoun followed by πρόσλημψις, a technical term for Israel's restoration: What will their acceptance be?

Romans 11:16 — "and if the root is holy, so are the branches." εἰμί (is). As throughout this passage, Paul employs ellipsis — the deliberate omission of the verb — reflecting his emotional engagement with his subject. The present active indicative of εἰμί is supplied, with ἁγία as predicate: If the root, the Lord Jesus Christ, is holy — and He is. The apodosis is introduced by the adjunctive καί (so also): the branches (κλάδοι, believing Jews of the church age) are also holy, a positional holiness derived from union with the holy root.

Romans 11:22 — "but God's kindness to you." χρηστότης (the integrity of God). The adversative δέ introduces the contrasting subject χρηστότης with the possessive genitive of θεός. The absence of a verb in the second clause is deliberate: no predicate is needed. The integrity of God stands as its own complete reality toward the Gentile believer, giving a clean antithesis — severity to those who rejected Christ; the integrity of God toward those who believed.

Romans 11:27 — "and this will be my covenant with them." οὗτος (also this is). The verse opens with καί used adverbially (also or therefore). The subject is the nominative feminine singular of the immediate demonstrative οὗτος, this. Paul employs ellipsis — a characteristic intensification device in New Testament Greek — omitting the verb; to be must be supplied: also this is.

Romans 11:36 — "For from him and through him and to him are all things." . Three prepositional phrases follow in rapid succession, each with αὐτός as object referring to the Lord Jesus Christ. No verb is expressed — this is ellipsis. The subject is the neuter plural of πᾶς, all things, with the definite article functioning as a demonstrative pronoun.

Romans 12:6 — "if prophecy." προφητείαν (if prophecy, prophesy, from προφητεία). Eite (the conditional particle ei + the enclitic te) introduces the first representative gift. The accusative singular of general reference propheteian appears without an expressed infinitive; the ellipsis demands the aorist active infinitive of propheteuō, functioning as an imperative: if prophecy, prophesy. If the gift exists, use it.

Romans 12:9 — "Let love be genuine." ἀγάπη (your love). The nominative singular agapē is the subject, with the definite article functioning as a possessive pronoun. The construction is elliptical: the verb is omitted, though several verbs could supply the predicate (should be, must function). The omission itself is emphatic: if love is the subject, its necessary existence and function are self-evident.

Romans 12:16 — "Live in harmony with one another." αὐτός (the same mental attitude). The direct object is the accusative neuter singular of autos used without a governing noun; the noun must be supplied from context, the cognate phronēma, mental attitude. It means not identical thoughts on every subject but thinking that proceeds from the same doctrinal frame of reference, the royal family honor code.

Romans 14:23 — "because the eating is not from faith." ἀποσιώπησις. The concluding clause ὅτι οὐκ ἐκ πίστεως is grammatically compressed, an instance of aposiopesis: a figure in which the speaker breaks off and leaves part of the construction unstated, typically to signal heightened intensity. Paul employs it in its classical Attic form: the protasis is stated in full, but the apodosis is only partially expressed, and the reader supplies the ellipsis from context.

Romans 14:23 — "For whatever does not proceed from faith is sin." οὐκ (not). The subject is the nominative neuter singular adjective pas (πᾶς), meaning “everything.” The negative ouk (οὐκ) requires the elliptical insertion of the present active indicative of esthiō (ἐσθίω), “to eat,” giving the clause the force of “everything which is not eaten.”

Anacoluthon

Romans 9:3 — "For I could wish that I myself were accursed and cut off from Christ." ἀνακόλουθον (not following, inconsistent). Anacoluthon is a construction in which a sentence begins on one syntactical trajectory and then shifts, leaving the original structure incomplete. Paul employs it deliberately in Romans 9:3 as a rhetorical device of intensification, compounded in this passage with a chiasmus.

Romans 9:22–24 — "What if God, desiring to show his wrath and to make known his power, has endured with much patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction." ἀνακόλουθον (grammatical discontinuity). A sentence that begins with a protasis but does not complete the expected apodosis is a recognized classical Greek construction signalling great emotional intensity in the speaker. Romans 9:22–24 contains the most discussed anacoluthon in the Greek New Testament, reflecting Paul's intense emotional involvement in his argument for the election of Israel.

XIII.Genitive Absolute

Romans 2:15 — "their conscience also bears witness, and their conflicting thoughts accuse or even excuse them." The genitive absolute construction with συνειδήσεως ("conscience") as its subject stands grammatically independent of the main clause — the Gentile conscience functions as an independent witness alongside, not dependent on, the Mosaic law the Gentile does not possess.

A participial construction grammatically independent of the main clause.

Romans 5:6 — "For while we were still weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly." The temporal clause functions with genitive-absolute-like independence from the main clause that follows.

Romans 5:8 — "but God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us." Same construction, independently describing the condition of the human race at the time of Christ's death.

Romans 7:3 — "if she lives with another man while her husband is alive." ζῶντος τοῦ ἀνδρός ("the husband living") is a genitive absolute: the genitive singular of ἀνήρ serves as the subject of a genitive participle of ζάω, and the whole construction stands grammatically detached from the main clause — mirroring, in its very detachment, the logical detachment of the hypothetical scenario Paul is describing (a scenario he immediately goes on to rule out) from the actual illustration he intends.

Romans 9:1 — "my conscience bears me witness in the Holy Spirit." συμμαρτυρέω (my conscience bearing joint testimony with me). The genitive absolute contains three genitive elements: syneidēsis (conscience) as the subject of the participle; the instrumental of association from egō, with me; and the genitive singular present active participle of the compound summartureo, to bear joint testimony. Translation: my conscience bearing joint testimony with me.

Romans 9:11 — "though they were not yet born." μήπω (though they had not yet been born, from γεννάω). The first genitive absolute is mēpō, not yet, with an aorist passive participle of gennaō, to be born. The twins are the implied subject, supplied here from context rather than in the genitive. The aorist passive represents a momentary action, the point-in-time event of birth, which had not yet occurred; the passive indicates birth is something done to them. The participle is concessive: though not yet having been born.

The Ablative Absolute

Romans 9:16 — "but on God, who has mercy." ἐλεῶντος (from God who has mercy, from ἐλεέω). After alla comes an ablative absolute, a construction that places a noun-plus-participle unit grammatically independent from the main clause, throwing it into emphatic relief. Its subject is theos in the ablative of source, from God, with the present active participle of eleeō: from God who has mercy. It places the true source of blessing in emphatic grammatical isolation.

XIV.The Dative Absolute, the Uncopulated Predicate Nominative, and the Nominative Absolute

Dative Absolute

A participial construction using the dative case, functioning much like the genitive absolute but marking the person to or for whom the described condition holds, with temporal force.

Romans 7:21 — "when I want to do right, evil lies close at hand." The phrase behind "when I want" is, more literally, "to me, the one wishing to do the honorable" — a dative absolute: dative singular of ἐγώ ("to me") plus the articular present participle of θέλω. The construction functions temporally: "when I desire." The present active participle here is customary, describing what is expected of a believer as a member of the royal family of God — and the active voice represents Paul as the reversionistic believer for the purpose of personalizing the illustration, not as a description of Paul's own condition at the time of writing.

The Predicate Nominative Without a Copula (Ellipsis of "To Be")

Greek does not require an explicit verb "to be" when a predicate nominative or adjective stands in direct relationship to its subject; the clause is grammatically complete without it.

Romans 7:2 — "a married woman is bound..." — more precisely, the underlying clause "the married woman [is] under the authority of a husband" supplies no verb at all in the Greek; the predicate adjective ὕπανδρος ("under the authority of a husband") alone completes the clause. The King James Version's inserted "hath an husband" supplies a verb (ἔχω) that is not present in the original.

Romans 9:26 (Hosea 1:10) — "'You are not my people,'" λαός (you are not my people). The proleptic personal pronoun (you) identifies the recipients: the Jews of the northern kingdom in Hosea's day, expanded by Paul's citation to all Jews in every generation. The predicate nominative of λαός with οὐ and the possessive genitive of the first-person pronoun yields you are not my people; the verb of being is supplied, as required by the predicate nominative construction.

Romans 10:4 — "Christ is the end of the law." εἰμί. The verb is supplied by legitimate ellipsis: the present active indicative of eimi governs two nominative-case nouns and so takes no expressed form. The predicate nominative is telos. The ellipsis is grammatically legitimate and standard in Greek prose.

Romans 10:8 — "The word is near you." ἐγγύς (near). The adverb of space engys, near, appears with the enclitic dative of su, to you as an individual. There is no verb, and the ellipsis is natural: the message of salvation by faith is near to you, nearer than the law on stone tablets or a scroll, nearer than heaven or Sheol.

Romans 12:1 — "holy and acceptable to God." εὐάρεστος (well-pleasing). The predicate adjective euarestos is a predicate nominative with an implied present active indicative of eimi: this is well-pleasing. The dative tō theō is a dative of indirect object, with the definite article functioning as a possessive pronoun to underscore the believer’s relationship to God the Father: to our God.

Romans 12:10 — "Love one another with brotherly affection." φιλόστοργος (be devoted). Philostorgos, compound of philos and storgē (natural family affection), is a predicate nominative plural meaning devoted in the sense of familial attachment. There is no finite verb; the present active imperative of the verb to be is supplied: be devoted. Eis plus allēlous: to each other.

Romans 14:14 — "it is unclean for anyone who thinks it unclean." κοινός (to that one, the weak believer, it is unclean, from εἰμί). The closing clause is elliptical: εἰμί is supplied to complete the predicate, with κοινός as the predicate. The rendering is to that one, the weak believer, it is unclean.

Romans 14:18 — "Whoever thus serves Christ is acceptable to God and approved by men." εὐάρεστος (pleasing to the God). Because of ellipsis the present active indicative of εἰμί is understood, its presence signalled by the predicate nominative εὐάρεστος (pleasing, acceptable, well-pleasing). With τῷ θεῷ it reads pleasing to the God. Pleasing God is the function of the royal priesthood, related to maximum doctrine resident in the soul and maturity adjustment to the justice of God.

Romans 14:21 — "It is good." καλός (it is honorable). Because καλός stands as a predicate nominative, the verb to be is implied: it is honorable.

Romans 16:20 — "The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you." ἡ χάρις … μεθ’ ὑμῶν (the grace … with you). The verb eimi (εἰμί) must be supplied: 'The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ is with you.'

Romans 16:27 — "to the only wise God be glory forevermore." ᾧ ἡ δόξα (to whom is the glory). The relative pronoun hō (ᾧ), dative singular, with the antecedent theos, introduces the elliptical clause: 'to whom is the glory.' The copula 'is' is supplied from context.

The Nominative Absolute

An adjective or substantive standing alone in the nominative case with no finite verb governing it — an independent, verbless construction that throws grammatical weight onto what follows, more abrupt even than the uncopulated predicate nominative.

Romans 8:3 — "For God has done what the law... could not do." The underlying Greek opens with τὸ ἀδύνατον ("the impossible," or "what was impossible") standing alone in the nominative, neuter, with no finite verb — a rare construction in which an idea is expressed independent of any verbal relationship, its only further specification being a descriptive genitive ("of the law"). The sentence is structurally abrupt, and deliberately so: the suspended opening throws the entire weight of the verse onto the divine action that follows.

Romans 13:11 — "Besides this you know the time." τοῦτο (this do also, from οὗτος). After adjunctive καί, the demonstrative τοῦτο stands as an independent nominative neuter singular. When an idea is conceived independently of any verbal relationship it may stand alone in the nominative (the independent, parenthetic, or absolute nominative); the construction yields the idiomatic this do also.

The Predicate Nominative with Verbs of Becoming or Being Appointed

Certain verbs (εἰμί, γίνομαι, καθίστημι) take a predicate nominative describing the resulting state.

Romans 5:19 — "the many will be made righteous." δίκαιοι stands as a predicate nominative completing κατασταθήσονται.

Romans 6:16 — "you are slaves of the one whom you obey." δοῦλοι ("slaves") stands as a predicate nominative completing ἐστε.

Romans 7:3 — "she will be called an adulteress." μοιχαλίς stands as a predicate nominative completing χρηματίσει (see the Nomic Future entry, section III), the classificatory verb naming the legal category into which she falls.

Romans 10:20 (Isaiah 65:1) — "I have shown myself." ἐμφανής (manifest). With ginomai the predicate nominative is emphanēs, manifest, known, comprehended: Christ became emphanēs, the full, comprehensible revelation of the object of faith, to Gentiles who did not ask about him by name.

Romans 11:6 — "grace would no longer be grace." χάρις (grace itself). In the conclusion the predicate nominative, grace itself, stresses that grace is not merely a method but a principle with inherent integrity; it cannot be diluted or blended. Once works are introduced, the category of grace ceases to function as grace.

Proleptic Word Order

A pronoun or other element placed earlier in the sentence than its normal grammatical position would require, for the sake of emphasis — the element is "anticipated" ahead of where it would otherwise fall.

Romans 8:9 — "You, however, are not in the flesh but in the Spirit." The second-person pronoun σύ stands in the emphatic, proleptic position — placed first in the Greek sentence for stress — immediately followed by an intensified δέ ("in fact," "indeed"). The combined effect announces a decisive distinction: you — and precisely you as a believer — are categorically different from the unbeliever just described.

Romans 9:20 — "who are you." σύ (you). The personal pronoun σύ appears in the proleptic position, placed ahead of the verb for emphasis, functioning almost as a second vocative: you, specifically you, who are you? The question forces the creature to reckon with his own ontological status before God.

Romans 11:17 — "and you, although a wild olive shoot." σύ (you). Having addressed the broken branches, Paul pivots by means of the proleptic use of the second-person pronoun σύ — referring to all Gentile believers, in the dispensation of Israel (as in Romans 9:30–33) as well as all born-again believers in the church age.

Romans 14:4 — "Who are you to pass judgment on the servant of another?" σύ (you there). Verse 4 opens with the personal pronoun σύ in the proleptical position, before the main verb and its object, for maximum rhetorical emphasis. It interrupts the argument to confront the weak believer personally, You there, forcing him to attention before the indictment is delivered.

Romans 14:10 — "Why do you pass judgment on your brother?" σύ (but you). The verse opens with δέ, contrasting the Lordship of Christ in verse 9 with the assault on that Lordship by the judging believer. The pronoun σύ is used proleptically, placed first in the clause for emphasis, best rendered But you, addressed to the weak believer, the one guilty of judging.

Romans 14:22 — "The faith that you have." σύ (you there). The verse opens with the proleptic use of the second person singular pronoun σύ, you there, which gives the pronoun emphatic weight before the main clause arrives. It is addressed primarily to the mature (strong) believer, with secondary application to every advancing believer positive toward doctrine.

The Appositional (Parenthetical) Nominative

Romans 10:12 — "the same Lord is Lord of all." Κύριος. Kyrios occurs twice in the verse. The appositional nominative is technically a solecism by standard classical rules, though it may also be regarded as the Attic parenthetical nominative; either way the translation is unaffected: the same Jesus is Lord of all.

Romans 16:21 — "Timothy, my fellow worker, greets you." Τιμόθεος ὁ συνεργός μου (Timothy, my co-worker). Paul designates Timothy with the appositional nominative synergos (συνεργός), co-worker or fellow laborer. The term does not imply equality. It implies that they occupy the same field and serve the same Lord.

The Independent Nominative

Romans 11:4 (1 Kings 19:18) — "bowed the knee." γόνυ (knee). γόνυ is identified as standing in the nominative rather than the accusative expected after a transitive verb. As an independent nominative it names the concept, the bowing of the knee, rather than the physical act: what matters is not posture but mental assent to idolatry.

The Accusative Absolute (Anacoluthon)

Romans 12:1 — "which is your spiritual worship." λογικήν (your rational and spiritual worship, from λογικός). The phrase is an accusative absolute functioning as an anacoluthon. Logikos carries a dual semantic range, rational and spiritual, because all spiritual function is rational by definition; emotionally driven religious experience falls outside its scope. Latreia is worship or service rendered to God, encompassing the five tenets of worship, each requiring the filling of the Holy Spirit and Bible doctrine resident in the soul.

XV.The Cognate Accusative

A construction in which the direct object of a verb is drawn from the same root as the verb itself.

Romans 6:10 — "the life he lives he lives to God." ζῇ... ζῇ — the verb "lives" is repeated with a cognate object built from the same root, intensifying the assertion: Christ's life is defined by, and consists entirely of, the very act of living itself in relationship to God, with no remainder given to any other reference point.

XVI.Case Usage

Genitive of Relationship

Romans 1:6 — "you also are among those who are called to belong to Jesus Christ." κλητοί stands as a nominative plural verbal adjective — the key word of the verse — with Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ functioning as a genitive of relationship: election grounded entirely in the person of the Lord.

Romans 9:10 — "our forefather Isaac." πατρός (our father). Isaac is identified with the genitive of relationship patros and the possessive genitive of egō: our father. The first-person plural encompasses both racial Jews and regenerate Jews; Paul includes himself and all Jewish readers in a shared heritage so that the distinction he is about to draw will carry its full force.

Romans 9:21 — "over the clay." πηλοῦ (wet clay, mud, from πηλός). The genitive of relationship following ἐξουσία is πηλοῦ, genitive singular of πηλός (wet clay or mud). The potter possesses authority over raw, unformed, wet material that has no inherent shape of its own until the potter acts upon it; in the analogy the clay represents the body, the container for the soul.

Romans 9:27 (Isaiah 10:22) — "the sons of Israel." υἱός (son). Modifying ἀριθμός is the genitive of relationship, plural of υἱός, followed by the indeclinable Israel. Sons of Israel designates ethnic, racial Israel, the physical descendants of the patriarchs, distinguished from the spiritual seed of Abraham, the category of the remnant defined in the apodosis.

Romans 11:17 — "share in the nourishing root of the olive tree." συγκοινωνός (joint partaker, partner). Two genitives of relationship follow συγκοινωνός: the genitive of ῥίζα — the root, the Lord Jesus Christ — and the possessive genitive of πιότης, fatness, richness, prosperity. Gentile believers have become partners of both the root and the prosperity of the olive tree, encompassing logistical grace blessing and supergrace blessing.

Romans 13:4 — "for he is God's servant." θεοῦ (of God, from θεός). θεοῦ with διάκονος is a genitive of relationship: the ruler stands in a specific relation to God as the one from whom his commission derives. It establishes both the derivation of the ruler's authority (from God) and his accountability (to God).

Romans 14:10 — "your brother." ἀδελφός (brother). The direct object is ἀδελφός with the genitive of relationship from the personal pronoun, your brother, a fellow member of the royal family of God. The accusative singular emphasizes that the judging is directed at specific individuals in one’s immediate periphery.

Romans 14:19 — "what makes for peace." εἰρήνη (those things related to the prosperity). The first direct object is the accusative neuter plural article used as a demonstrative, those things, establishing a categorical concept. It is followed by the genitive singular of relationship from εἰρήνη, used in its foundational sense of prosperity, wholeness, well-being. The generic article comprehends spiritual maturity as a single whole, distinguished from all other categories of spiritual status.

Romans 14:19 — "for mutual upbuilding." οἰκοδομή (those things related to the edification complex). καί introduces a second direct object, again an accusative neuter plural article (those things), with the genitive singular of relationship from οἰκοδομή, the edification complex of the believer: the inner structure of Bible doctrine built up in the soul through consistent function of the grace apparatus for perception.

Romans 15:14 — "my brothers." ἀδελφοί μου (my brethren). Paul addresses this commendation to the vocative plural of adelphos (ἀδελφός), translated brethren or brothers. With the genitive of relationship from the first-person singular personal pronoun egō, the phrase is rendered my brethren.

Ablative of Source

Indicates the origin from which something proceeds.

Romans 1:1 — "set apart for the gospel of God." θεοῦ ("of God") is an ablative of source in the phrase εἰς εὐαγγέλιον θεοῦ: God is the origin from which both the gospel and Paul's appointment proceed.

Romans 2:18 — "and know his will." ἐκ τοῦ νόμου ("from the law") is an ablative of source: the Mosaic law is the fountainhead of the legalist's instruction — Paul disputes not the law's legitimacy but the hermeneutic applied to it.

Romans 2:26 — "the righteous requirements of the law." δικαιώματα stands with an ablative of source from νόμος: "the righteous requirements from the law" — referring to the three adjustments to the justice of God that the law depicts.

Romans 3:25 — "whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood, to be received by faith." ἀνοχῇ ("forbearance/clemency," from ἀνοχή) appears with an ablative of source from θεός: the suspension of judgment on pre-cross sins originated in God's deliberate clemency, not in any deficiency of his justice.

Romans 2:29 — "whose praise is not from man but from God." ἐκ θεοῦ ("from God," an ablative/genitive of source) identifies the true Jew's approval as originating in the justice of God rather than human community — the fourth and eternal adjustment, dispensed at the judgment seat of Christ.

Romans 3:2 — "they were entrusted with the oracles of God." λόγια ("oracles," accusative plural, distinct from λόγος) designates the entire Old Testament canon entrusted to Israel, its source specified by an ablative of absolute source from θεός.

Romans 4:2 — the ground of Abraham's (hypothetical) boasting would derive from works as its source.

Romans 4:12 — "the father of the circumcised who are not merely circumcised but who also walk in the footsteps of the faith that our father Abraham had" — the faith in view has Abraham's own faith as its historical source and pattern.

Romans 5:1 — "we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ" — peace, in this construction, proceeds from Christ as its source.

Romans 6:23 — "the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord." Eternal life proceeds from God as its source, in Christ Jesus as its channel.

Romans 8:2 — "the law of the Spirit of life." The phrase "of life" is an ablative singular of source from ζωή, not a genitive: not "the Spirit of life" in a simple possessive sense, but "the Spirit who is the source of eternal life."

Romans 8:9 — "the Spirit of Christ." Likewise an ablative of source (not a genitive of possession): the Holy Spirit does not belong to Christ as property, but proceeds from him — the doctrine of Procession.

Romans 9:5 — "and from their race, according to the flesh, is the Christ." ὁ Χριστός (from whom). Paul repeats the ablative of source construction, from whom, with the verb again implied by ellipsis, followed by the predicate nominative ho Christos: in fact, from whom is the Christ.

Romans 9:30 — "a righteousness that is by faith." ἐκ πίστεως (from the source of faith, from πίστις). ἐκ πίστεως employs ἐκ with the ablative of source from πίστις. The ablative of source is used when the origin of the thing is in view; here it underscores that the origin, the generating point of divine righteousness as received by the believer, is faith, non-meritorious volition directed toward the Lord Jesus Christ. Faith is the origin-point through which divine righteousness is received, not the meritorious cause of it.

Romans 11:27 — "my covenant." παρ’ ἐμοῦ (from me). The prepositional phrase παρά plus the ablative of source of ἐγώ is correctly translated from me, referring to God: Also, this is the covenant to them from me.

Romans 11:29 — "the gifts and the calling of God." θεοῦ (from God). The ablative singular θεοῦ, from God, governs both nouns: the grace benefits and the election are both sourced in God.

Romans 12:1 — "by the mercies of God." θεοῦ (from the justice of God). The ablative of theou functions as an ablative of source: the origin of the mercies is God, specifically the justice of God. The definite article does not mark God as unique but points to the particular attribute that is the source of these blessings, the justice of God as the channel through which all grace flows to the believer.

Romans 12:3 — "the measure of faith." πίστις (from doctrine). Pistis carries three meanings: a non-meritorious system of perception (faith), an attribute (faithfulness), and a body of content, that which is believed, doctrine itself. The third is operative here. The ablative of source indicates origin: the standard of thinking originates from doctrine.

Romans 13:1 — "For there is no authority except from God." ὑπό (except delegated by God). ὑπό with the ablative of θεός indicates source or origin. When ὑπό governs the ablative it specifies the ultimate source from which something proceeds: God is the origin of the entire system of authority that operates under the laws of divine establishment.

Romans 15:29 — "the blessing of Christ." Χριστοῦ (from Christ). The ablative singular of Christos (Χριστός) marks Christ as the source from which all blessing flows. The corrected translation therefore reads: I shall come in full measure of blessing from Christ.

Romans 15:30 — "by the love of the Spirit." διὰ τῆς ἀγάπης τοῦ πνεύματος (through love from the Spirit). The construction is dia plus the genitive of agapē (ἀγάπη), meaning through love, followed by the ablative of source from pneuma (πνεῦμα), identifying the Holy Spirit as the source. The correct rendering is: through love from the Spirit — love generated by the Spirit, of which the Spirit is the source.

Romans 16:5 — "the first convert to Christ in Asia." τῆς Ἀσίας (from Asia). The ablative of source governs the proper noun Asia (Ἀσία). The King James renders this 'Achaia,' but the best manuscripts read Asia — the Roman proconsular province of Asia, located in western Asia Minor (modern western Turkey).

Romans 16:26 — "to bring about the obedience of faith." εἰς ὑπακοὴν πίστεως (for the purpose of obedience from doctrine). The English versions render this 'the obedience of faith,' but the ablative of source requires a different reading. Pistis carries three semantic ranges: faith, confidence, and the content of that in which one has confidence — doctrine itself. In this context the ablative of source governs the translation: 'for the purpose of obedience from doctrine.'

Ablative of Means

Romans 4:14 — "if it is the adherents of the law who are to be heirs" — the means by which heirship would be secured, in this rejected hypothesis, is adherence to the law.

Romans 3:26 — the same verse's ἐκ πίστεως ("by faith") is an ablative of means, with the objective genitive Ἰησοῦ specifying Christ as the object: faith's effectiveness derives entirely from its object, not from any quality in the one exercising it.

Romans 1:5 — "through whom we have received grace and apostleship." The relative pronoun following διά is a genitive of means/agency: grace and apostleship were received through the agency of the resurrected Christ named in verse 4.

Romans 5:15 — "much more have the grace of God and the free gift by the grace of that one man Jesus Christ abounded for many." The means by which the free gift abounds is specifically the grace of Christ.

Romans 5:16 — "the free gift following many trespasses brought justification." The trespasses function, in this construction, as the occasion rather than the means proper, but the underlying ablative-of-means logic governs how the "gift" reaches "many."

Romans 6:17 — "you... have become obedient from the heart to the standard of teaching to which you were committed." The means by which obedience was produced is doctrine received into the heart.

Romans 9:31 — "a law that would lead to righteousness." δικαιοσύνη (by means of human self-righteousness). The genitive of means is expressed by the ablative singular of δικαιοσύνη. When means is expressed with the concept of origin, the ablative case is used in place of the instrumental. The origin here is human self-righteousness, the attempt to produce a righteousness acceptable to God by keeping the law, in direct antithesis to the divine righteousness of verse 30 (corrected translation: Israel, who ran after the law by means of human self-righteousness).

Romans 9:32 — "Because they did not pursue it by faith, but as if it were based on works." ἐκ πίστεως; ἐξ ἔργων (by means of faith; by means of works, from πίστις; ἔργον). ἐκ πίστεως is ἐκ plus the ablative of means from πίστις. The ablative of means, rather than the instrumental, is used because the means carries the implication of source or origin: faith as the divinely appointed channel through which righteousness flows. πίστεως is singular: one act of faith in Christ, one time, produces eternal salvation. ἐξ ἔργων is ἐκ plus the ablative plural of ἔργον: many works accumulated over a lifetime, none sufficient. The contrast of singular πίστεως and plural ἔργων encapsulates the argument of Romans on adjustment to the justice of God through faith.

Romans 10:5 — "based on the law." ἐκ νόμου (by means of the law). Ek with the ablative of means from nomos: by means of the law. Corrected translation of the framing clause: You see, Moses wrote about the righteousness which is by means of the law.

Romans 10:6 — "based on faith." ἐκ πίστεως (by means of faith). Ek with the ablative of means from pistis. The ablative of means, rather than the ordinary instrumental case, is used because the expression of means carries the added implication of origin or source: the righteousness originates from faith and is received by means of faith. It stands in direct opposition to the works-righteousness of law-keeping.

Romans 13:1 — "have been instituted by God." ὑπὸ θεοῦ (by God). The closing phrase ὑπὸ θεοῦ employs the ablative of means with ὑπό, here carrying the nuance of origin: God is the ultimate source from which all legitimate civil authority is derived.

Romans 14:14 — "in itself." δι' ἑαυτοῦ (by means of itself, from ἑαυτοῦ). δι' ἑαυτοῦ uses διά with the ablative of the reflexive pronoun. The ablative is selected rather than the simple instrumental because the means expressed also indicates origin: the food itself, by its own constitution, is not the source of uncleanness. Contamination, where it exists, is always introduced from outside and is never inherent in the substance.

Romans 14:16 — "what you regard as good." σύ (attained by you). The article carries the ablative of means from the plural of σύ: by you, attained by you. The ablative is used rather than the standard instrumental when means is accompanied by the idea of origin or source. The source and means of attaining spiritual maturity is the perception of Bible doctrine, the daily function of GAP; the mature believer is the one from whom this good originates and by whom it is attained.

Romans 14:23 — "For whatever does not proceed from faith is sin." ἐκ πίστεως (by means of doctrine). This is followed by the prepositional phrase ek pisteōs (ἐκ πίστεως), the ablative of means: “by means of doctrine.” The word pistis (πίστις) in this context carries its extended sense of the content of that which is believed — Bible doctrine — rather than the simple act of believing.

Instrumental Case

Expresses impersonal means.

Romans 1:29 — "They were filled with all manner of unrighteousness." πάσῃ ἀδικίᾳ is an instrumental of means — by/with all anti-justice — describing the maladjusted soul's total saturation.

Romans 3:24 — "and are justified by his grace as a gift." χάριτι ("by grace") is an instrumental case identifying grace as the means — the standard operating procedure — by which the justice of God administers justification; it is not an emotion or attitude in God.

Romans 5:2 — "through whom we have also obtained access by faith into this grace in which we stand." τῇ πίστει — faith is the instrumental means by which access is obtained, not itself the meritorious cause.

Romans 5:9 — "we have now been justified by his blood." τῷ αἵματι — instrumental of means: the blood of Christ is the specific instrument by which justification is secured.

Romans 5:15 — "by the grace of that one man Jesus Christ" — τῇ χάριτι, instrumental of means.

Romans 7:2 — "stands bound to her husband by law." νόμῳ — instrumental of means (Mosaic law as the instrument of the binding).

Romans 7:25 — "with my mind... with my flesh." νοΐ and σαρκί are both instrumental datives of means, naming the two competing instruments through which the believer's daily choice of allegiance is exercised.

Romans 9:17 (Exodus 9:16) — "that I might show my power in you." σύ (by means of you). The phrase rendered by means of you uses en plus the instrumental dative of the personal pronoun sy. The direct object dynamis, power, divine omnipotence demonstrated through the ten plagues, is modified by the possessive genitive of egō: in order that I might demonstrate my power by means of you.

Romans 10:5 (Leviticus 18:5) — "shall live by them." ἐν αὐτοῖς (by them). En with the instrumental of autos, third person plural, rendered by them: by the statutes, the establishment ordinances.

Romans 10:10 — "with the heart one believes." καρδία (by means of the right lobe). Kardia is in the instrumental singular, the instrumental of means: by means of the right lobe. The second clause likewise has the instrumental of stoma, by means of the mouth. The right lobe is the organ of thought, volition, and perception where saving faith originates; the mouth is the enunciator of thought formed in the right lobe and contributes no merit to the transaction.

Romans 11:6 — "if it is by grace." χάριτι (by means of grace, from χάρις). The dative singular χάριτι is an instrumental of means: by means of grace. Grace here is not sentiment but the policy of divine integrity, the mechanism by which the justice of God imputes blessing to the righteousness of God resident in the believer.

Romans 11:20 — "They were broken off because of their unbelief." ἀπιστία (because of unbelief). The instrumental singular ἀπιστία (alpha-privative + πίστις) expresses intermediate means: because of unbelief. The unbelief is comprehensive — rejection of Christ as Savior, of establishment principles, of freedom through military victory, of just jurisprudence, and of Bible doctrine by those already believing. The result is the fifth cycle of discipline culminating in A.D. 70.

Romans 11:20 — "but you stand fast through faith." πίστις (because of faith). The instrumental singular πίστις functions as an instrumental of cause: because of faith. Three senses converge: saving faith, the faith-rest drill in its three stages, and doctrine itself resident in the soul. The Gentile believer stands because of what faith appropriates, not because of what faith is in itself; faith is the non-meritorious instrument, the integrity of God is the source.

Romans 11:30 — "because of their disobedience." ἀπείθεια (because of their unbelief). The protasis closes with the instrumental of cause from ἀπείθεια (unbelief, disobedience-through-unbelief) with a possessive genitive plural of οὗτος: because of the unbelief of those, the Jews — the collective Jewish unbelief that terminated Israel's client-nation function and transferred that status to Gentile nations.

Romans 12:2 — "by the renewal of your mind." ἀνακαίνωσις (by the renovation). The means of transformation is an instrumental dative, tē anakainōsei. The nuance of anakainōsis is renovation rather than mere repetition or rededication: as a building’s interior is fundamentally rebuilt, the mind is renovated when human viewpoint is systematically displaced by divine viewpoint through maximum doctrine.

Romans 12:8 — "in generosity." ἁπλότης (with generosity). En plus the instrumental singular of haplotēs specifies manner: with generosity. This corrects older translations that rendered the term simplicity, losing the connotation of abundant, uncomplicated liberality.

Romans 12:8 — "with zeal." σπουδή (with diligence). En plus the instrumental singular of spoudē, diligence, earnestness, zeal, specifies the manner of the gift of administrative management: he who manages administration with diligence.

Romans 12:8 — "with cheerfulness." ἱλαρότης (with graciousness). En plus the instrumental singular of hilarotēs; the correct rendering is with graciousness rather than with hilarity. The explicit addition of graciousness is a safeguard against the arrogance that can corrupt any spiritual gift, since the gift does not automatically carry the mental attitude required for its proper function.

Romans 12:21 — "overcome evil with good." ἀγαθός (by means of the good). The prepositional phrase shifts: the first clause used hupo plus the ablative, conquered by evil; the second uses en plus the instrumental of agathos, conquer evil by means of the good.

Romans 14:17 — "in the Holy Spirit." ἐν πνεύματι ἁγίῳ (by means of the Holy Spirit, from πνεῦμα). The case of πνεύματι is instrumental dative: by means of the Holy Spirit. The happiness of the kingdom of God is not self-generated but sustained by the agency of the indwelling Holy Spirit, the constant supply-mechanism within the grace pipeline.

Romans 14:18 — "Whoever thus serves Christ is acceptable to God and approved by men." ἄνθρωπος (by man). δόκιμος is followed by the instrumental plural of means from ἄνθρωπος: and respected by man. The instrumental of means shows that mankind is the sphere and instrument through which this respect is expressed, the ambassadorial counterpart to the priestly function toward God.

Romans 15:13 — "by the power of the Holy Spirit." ἐν δυνάμει πνεύματος ἁγίου (by means of the power of the Holy Spirit). The final prepositional phrase qualifies the abounding in hope: it is accomplished 'by means of the power of the Holy Spirit.' The construction is ἐν plus the instrumental of δύναμις (dynamis), followed by a possessive genitive from πνεῦμα ἅγιον (pneuma hagion) — the Holy Spirit.

Romans 15:16 — "sanctified by the Holy Spirit." ἐν πνεύματι ἁγίῳ (by the Holy Spirit). The phrase is en (ἐν) plus the locative — or here best read as the instrumental — of pneuma hagion (πνεύματι ἁγίῳ), yielding the translation by the Holy Spirit.

Romans 15:18 — "by word and deed." λόγῳ καὶ ἔργῳ (by word and by deed). The instrumental singular λόγῳ (logō), from λόγος (logos), here designates doctrinal communication — the primary content of missionary work. The instrumental singular ἔργῳ (ergō), from ἔργον (ergon), means deed, action, or in this context, occupation — the professional function of the missionary.

Romans 15:19 — "by the power of signs and wonders." ἐν δυνάμει (by means of power). The verse continues the sentence begun in verse 18 with the prepositional phrase en dunamei (ἐν δυνάμει), meaning by the power or by means of power. The preposition en (ἐν) with the instrumental case of dunamis (δύναμις) denotes the enabling power through which Paul's apostolic work was accomplished.

Romans 16:16 — "Greet one another with a holy kiss." ἐν φιλήματι ἁγίῳ (with a holy kiss). The prepositional phrase that follows uses en (ἐν) with the instrumental singular of hagios (ἅγιος) and the noun philēma (φίλημα): 'with a holy kiss.'

Romans 16:20 — "will soon crush Satan." ἐν τάχει (in a short time). The clause closes with the preposition en (ἐν) plus the instrumental singular of tachos (τάχος), meaning with speed, in a short time. Corrected translation: in a short time.

Instrumental of Association

A dative form (using the intensive pronoun) denoting the party with whom a shared action or identification occurs.

Romans 6:4 — "we were buried therefore with him by baptism into death." αὐτῷ — the instrumental of association identifying Christ as the one with whom the believer's identification occurs.

Romans 7:3 — "if she lives with another man." The instrumental of association governs ἀνήρ here, though — note — in this occurrence ἀνήρ refers not to the legitimate husband but to a different man entirely (see the vocabulary note on ἀνήρ vs. ἄνθρωπος below), reinforced by the adjective ἕτερος ("another of a different kind").

Romans 15:32 — "be refreshed in your company." ὑμῖν (with you). The instrumental of association from the personal pronoun su (σύ) — 'with you' — specifies the Romans as Paul's companions in this rest.

Romans 16:14 — "and the brothers who are with them." τοὺς σὺν αὐτοῖς ἀδελφούς (the brethren associated with them). The phrase tous syn autois adelphous (τοὺς σὺν αὐτοῖς ἀδελφούς) — the brethren associated with them — identifies the broader congregation. The preposition syn with the instrumental plural of autos conveys association: the royal family meeting together with the five named individuals.

Dative of Advantage

Indicates the party for whose benefit an action occurs.

Romans 1:14 — "I am under obligation both to Greeks and to barbarians, both to the wise and to the foolish." σοφοῖς functions as a dative of advantage (it is to the mature believer's benefit to continue receiving doctrine) while ἀνοήτοις functions as a dative of disadvantage, referencing the condition of spiritual failure.

Romans 4:16 — "That is why it depends on faith, in order that the promise may rest on grace and be guaranteed to all his offspring." The promise is secured for the advantage of Abraham's spiritual offspring.

Romans 4:20 — "he grew strong in his faith as he gave glory to God" — the growth described redounds to God's advantage in the sense that it results in his glorification.

Romans 9:12 — "she was told." αὐτῇ (to her, from αὐτός). The indirect object autē is the dative singular of the intensive pronoun autos, which serves as the third-person personal pronoun. The dative is a dative of advantage: it was to Rebecca's advantage to know these things, and she acted upon this knowledge throughout her life in favor of her younger son.

Romans 10:4 — "to everyone who believes." πᾶς (to each one). Pas, used as a substantive in the dative singular, yields to each one, a dative of advantage and indirect object emphasizing individual application: imputation of divine righteousness occurs for each believer at the moment of personal faith.

Romans 11:13 — "Now I am speaking to you Gentiles." σύ (to you). The indirect object is the dative plural of σύ, used as a dative of advantage: to you, to your benefit. The object of address is the dative plural of ἔθνος, Gentiles — those who do not carry the genetic line of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The term ethnos establishes a dispensational contrast: the Jews constitute a category apart; all other members of the human race are Gentiles.

Romans 12:6 — "the grace given to us." ἡμῖν (to us, for us, from ἐγώ). The dative plural hēmin functions both as a dative of indirect object and as a dative of advantage: the gifts are given to us and for our benefit as the corporate body of Christ, not merely to the individual recipient.

Romans 13:3 — "to good conduct." ἀγαθός (moral function). The phrase rendered good works is a dative of advantage from ἀγαθός with ἔργον. ἀγαθός denotes intrinsic goodness or inner worth; here it means moral function as defined by the laws of divine establishment (protection of and respect for freedom, privacy, and property), not religious observance or general social benevolence.

Romans 13:4 — "for your good." σοί (to you, from σύ). The dative of advantage σοί connects the magistrate's divine servanthood directly to the benefit of believers and unbelievers alike: civil authority exists for the advantage of those under it.

Romans 14:7 — "For none of us lives to himself, and none of us dies to himself." ἑαυτῷ (for himself, from ἑαυτοῦ). The critical exegetical issue is the dative of the reflexive pronoun ἑαυτῷ: not a simple dative of reference but a dative of advantage or disadvantage (dativus commodi et incommodi), referring the action back to its own subject. Whether for himself is advantage or disadvantage is not fixed by the grammar but by the believer’s use of freedom. Applied to both the living and the dying clause, it generates four categories: advantage in life (advance to maturity), disadvantage in life (reversionism), advantage in death (dying grace), disadvantage in death (the sin unto death).

Romans 15:1 — "and not to please ourselves." ἑαυτοῦ (ourselves). The dative plural of advantage from the reflexive pronoun heautou (ἑαυτοῦ) places emphasis on the norms and standards of the subject — the mature believer.

Romans 15:5 — "grant you." ὑμῖν (to you). The indirect object is the dative plural of the second-person personal pronoun — 'to you,' referring to all members of the royal family of God. This is a dative of advantage where positive volition toward doctrine exists, and a dative of disadvantage where negative volition prevails.

Dative of Reference

Indicates the entity toward which or with respect to which an action is directed.

Romans 5:10 — "we were reconciled to God" — τῷ θεῷ, dative of reference: the reconciliation is with reference to God specifically as the offended party.

Romans 6:2 — "How can we who died to sin still live in it?" τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ, dative of reference: the believer's death is with reference to the sin nature's ruling authority.

Romans 6:10 — "the death he died he died to sin, once for all" — τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ, dative of reference again, marking what the death is with reference to.

Romans 6:11 — "consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God" — both τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ and τῷ θεῷ function as datives of reference, marking the two poles of the believer's reckoning.

Romans 7:4 — "you also have died to the law." τῷ νόμῳ — dative of reference: the believer's death is with reference to the law's authority specifically, not a literal physical death.

Romans 7:25 — the datives τῷ νοΐ and τῇ σαρκί could also be read partly as datives of reference (the sphere in which each service occurs) alongside their instrumental force (the means by which it occurs) — Greek often allows both nuances to sit together in a single dative form.

Romans 10:3 — "they did not submit to God's righteousness." δικαιοσύνη. With the verb stands the dative singular of reference from dikaiosynē together with the possessive genitive of theos. Dikaiosynē theou is the central subject of Romans and the organizing axis of the adjustment to the justice of God: not an attribute God admires in us, but His own perfect righteousness imputed at the moment of faith in Christ.

Romans 12:10 — "Love one another with brotherly affection." φιλαδελφία (with reference to your brotherly love). The verse opens with a dative of reference singular from philadelphia, with the definite article functioning as a personal pronoun: with reference to your brotherly love. This is a specialized category of love commanded for members of the royal family of God toward one another, distinct from the three standard categories of love.

Romans 12:10 — "Outdo one another in showing honor." τιμή (with reference to your honor). The second clause opens with a dative singular of reference from timē: with reference to your honor. Every believer possesses honor by virtue of the judicial imputation of divine righteousness at salvation; honor in the royal family is constituted by the imputation itself, not earned.

Romans 12:11 — "Do not be slothful in zeal." σπουδή (with reference to application of doctrine). The verse opens with a dative of reference singular from spoudē. In classical Attic it means haste or speed; in Koine it shifts to diligent application, that which must be accomplished with the urgency of a rapid military maneuver (Herodotus used it in this tactical sense). The dative of reference frames the command: with reference to the application of doctrine.

Romans 12:11 — "be fervent in spirit." πνεῦμα (with reference to the Holy Spirit). The dative of reference singular from pneuma with the generic article identifies God the Holy Spirit as unique and eternal: with reference to the Spirit.

Romans 12:12 — "Rejoice in hope." τῇ ἐλπίδι (with reference to the hope, from ἐλπίς). The dative singular of the definite article functions as a generic article (a usage found in Koine Greek and the papyri), and the dative of reference introduces the sphere within which the action of the participle takes place: with reference to the hope.

Romans 14:6 — "abstains in honor of the Lord." Κύριος (with reference to the Lord, from κύριος). The dative singular of κύριος functions as a dative of reference and dative of advantage simultaneously: with reference to the Lord, and to our advantage in doing so. The abstaining believer is consciously orienting his behavior toward the Lord Jesus Christ; this sincerity does not validate his conclusions, but it shows he is living in positive volition toward the Lord.

Romans 14:8 — "we live to the Lord." Κυρίῳ (to the Lord, from κύριος). The dative κυρίῳ with the generic article is a dative of reference, with reference to the Lord, rendered to the Lord. The believer in positive volition lives with reference to the Lord’s plan, honor code and glory: his life is Lord-referential, not self-referential.

Romans 16:25 — "the mystery that was kept secret for long ages." χρόνοις αἰωνίοις (with reference to long ages past). The dative plural of chronos (χρόνος) denotes elapsed time, a succession of events. Together, the idiom means with reference to long ages past, a technical expression for all dispensational history prior to the Church Age.

Dative of Indirect Object

Romans 4:3 — "Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness." αὐτῷ, dative of indirect object: the party to whom the crediting is made.

Romans 1:7 — "To all those in Rome who are loved by God and called to be saints." ὑμῖν and, earlier in the verse, πᾶσιν, both function as datives of indirect object: the Roman believers are the designated beneficiaries of a plan they did not initiate — they receive, they do not produce.

Romans 4:22 — "That is why his faith was counted to him as righteousness." Same construction, same indirect-object force.

Romans 7:21 (twice, "to me") — see the Dative Absolute entry, section XIV, for the fuller discussion of this dative's function within that construction.

Romans 9:7 — "shall your offspring be named." σοί (your seed). The nominative sperma is followed by the dative singular indirect object soi, to you. Literally a seed to you in Isaac, an idiom for your seed in Isaac.

Romans 9:20 — "to answer back to God." τῷ θεῷ (to God, from θεός). τῷ θεῷ is a dative of indirect object, used with the generic article to emphasize the uniqueness and transcendence of the God being addressed: not one deity among many, but the eternal, self-existent Creator. The creature who answers back to this God overestimates himself at the precise rate at which he underestimates God.

Romans 9:29 (Isaiah 1:9) — "had not left us offspring." ἡμῖν (to us, from ἐγώ). ἡμῖν, dative plural of the first-person pronoun, is the dative of indirect object, identifying the ones in whose interest the action is performed. The benefit of preservation extends to Gentiles: the survival of Gentile civilization is contingent on the survival of the Jewish race.

Romans 10:2 — "I bear them witness." αὐτός. The dative plural of the intensive pronoun autos functions as a dative of indirect object, referring to the Jewish people.

Romans 10:16 — "obeyed the gospel." εὐαγγέλιον (the gospel). The indirect object is the dative singular of euangelion, the good news, which is not primarily about human sinfulness but about what Christ accomplished with respect to sin: salvation requires nothing from the recipient but non-meritorious faith in Christ.

Romans 11:4 — "I have kept for myself." ἐμαυτῷ (for myself, from ἐμαυτοῦ). The dative singular reflexive pronoun ἐμαυτῷ is an indirect object of interest; the action is referred back to the subject. God has reserved the seven thousand for Himself, for His own purpose and plan, and His judgment supersedes that of Elijah: in His evaluation there are seven thousand believers superior in current spiritual status to Elijah himself.

Romans 11:25 — "has come upon Israel." Ἰσραήλ (to Israel). The dative of Ἰσραήλ is a dative of indirect object specifying the recipients of the hardening: it has happened to Israel. The basis for the fifth cycle of discipline in AD 70 has been perpetuated in every generation of the church age; individual rejection adds scar tissue to the soul, and the aggregate produces the conditions for collective discipline.

Romans 11:27 — "my covenant with them." αὐτός (to them). The indirect object is the dative of αὐτός used as a third person plural pronoun, to them, specifying those in whose interest the new covenant was given — the Jewish believers of the millennium who survive the tribulation.

Romans 12:3 — "by the grace given to me." ἐγώ (to me). The dative singular indirect object from the personal pronoun, to me, indicates the one in whose interest grace has been given. Paul writes from within the framework of mature adjustment to the justice of God, anticipating verses 4–8, where spiritual gifts function at maximum capacity only from within maturity status.

Romans 13:7 — "Pay to all what is owed to them." πᾶς (to all). The indirect object is the dative plural of πᾶς used as a substantive, to all: the dative of indirect object indicates the ones for whom the act is performed, any system of authority within the national entity. The direct object is the accusative plural of ὀφειλή, obligations: discharge your obligations to all.

Romans 14:11 — "every knee shall bow to me." ἐγώ (to me). The dative singular indirect object is the first-person pronoun, referring to the Lord Jesus Christ as the one in whose interest the genuflexion is performed.

Romans 14:12 — "to God." τῷ θεῷ (to God, from θεός). The dative singular indirect object is τῷ θεῷ, with the definite article used generically to identify the divine being in His essential character as the one to whom all accountability flows. The judge is the Lord Jesus Christ, to whom the Father has committed all judgment (John 5:22).

Romans 16:27 — "to the only wise God be glory forevermore." μόνῳ σοφῷ θεῷ (to God alone wise). The adjective sophos refers specifically to the omniscience of God as the faculty by which He knows all things — actual and contingent, past and future, individual and corporate — simultaneously and exhaustively.

Genitive of Reference

Marks the category or sphere to which a noun's action or state pertains.

Romans 6:6 — "so that the body of sin might be brought to nothing." τῆς ἁμαρτίας ("of sin") is a genitive of reference, marking the sphere to which the "body" in view pertains — the physical body considered specifically as headquarters of the sin nature.

Romans 14:1 — "quarrel over opinions." διαλογισμῶν (about opinions, from διαλογισμός). διακρίσεις means differentiation or quarrel; διαλογισμῶν is a genitive of reference plural, about opinions, that is, about non-essentials: background norms, taboos and personal convictions that do not constitute Bible doctrine.

Descriptive Genitive

Romans 4:12 — "the father of the circumcised" — τῆς περιτομῆς, describing the category of people in view by their defining mark.

Romans 1:29 — "envy, murder, strife..." Ἴριδος ("of strife," a descriptive genitive) opens the catalogue of evil-functions, naming not a single act but a habitual disposition.

Romans 3:1 — "Then what advantage has the Jew?" Ἰουδαίου stands as a descriptive genitive, encompassing both the racial and the national identity of Israel as the fourth race and priest nation — not religious practice alone.

Romans 8:2 — the descriptive genitive of πνεῦμα ("of the Spirit") identifies the Holy Spirit as author and agent of "the principle" (νόμος) named in Romans 8:2.

Romans 9:23 — "for vessels of mercy." ἔλεος (mercy). The genitive of ἔλεος is a descriptive genitive identifying the character of the vessel. Mercy here is not sentiment but grace in action: the justice of God imputing blessing to the righteousness of God resident in the mature believer.

Romans 9:26 (Hosea 1:10) — "'sons of the living God.'" ζάω (to live). The genitive modifier is the descriptive genitive singular present active participle of ζάω: of the living God. The present tense emphasizes the continuous, eternal life of God, standing in implicit contrast to the idols of the nations and to the deadness of the soul produced by the great blot out.

Romans 10:8 — "the word of faith." πίστις (the message of faith). Rhēma is followed by the descriptive genitive singular of pistis: rhēma pisteōs is correctly the message of faith, specifically salvation by faith in Christ rather than by keeping the Mosaic law.

Romans 11:8 (Isaiah 29:10) — "a spirit of stupor." πνεῦμα κατανύξεως (a state of mind of insensibility, from πνεῦμα). πνεῦμα is used not of the divine Spirit but of a state of mind, the orientation of the right lobe of the soul. The descriptive genitive κατανύξεως, from κατανύσσω (to prick, to pierce, hence to stupefy), defines that state of mind: stupefaction or insensibility.

Romans 11:33 — "the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God." καὶ … καὶ (both … and). What is inexhaustible is identified by a possessive genitive of πλοῦτος, wealth in the sense of abundance. The nature of that wealth is specified by a doubled καὶ … καὶ, both … and, a classical device for introducing two coordinate genitives of description: σοφία and γνῶσις, both governed by the possessive genitive of θεός.

Romans 12:6 — "in proportion to our faith." πίστις (the doctrine). Pistis here is a descriptive genitive singular with the generic use of the definite article. Of its three senses (trust, faithfulness, the accepted content of Christian teaching), the third applies: in agreement with the doctrine.

Romans 12:13 — "the needs of the saints." ἅγιος (of the saints). The indirect object is the dative plural of chreia, needs, and the genitive modifier is the descriptive genitive plural of hagios: all Church Age believers as royal family of God.

Romans 12:20 — "burning coals." πυρός (of fire, from πῦρ). The accusative plural anthrakas, burning coals, is made explicit by the descriptive genitive singular of pyr: burning coals of fire. The phrase refers to divine judgment, the justice of God intervening against the one who has persisted in hostility, upon his head.

Romans 13:12 — "the works of darkness." σκότους (of darkness, from σκότος). σκότους is a descriptive genitive. The phrase ἔργα τοῦ σκότους does not primarily refer to personal sin; ἔργον connotes production, structured activity, works, not the vocabulary of individual moral failure. The referent is the whole system of human good and evil that is the devil's world-policy.

Romans 13:12 — "the armor of light." φωτός (of light, from φῶς). φωτός is a descriptive genitive. Since the context places us in the night of the Church Age, this is not natural light but light in darkness: by analogy, Bible doctrine.

Romans 14:7 — "none of us." οὐδείς (not one of us). The subject is οὐδείς, an adjective functioning as a substantive, no one, not one. It is qualified by the descriptive genitive plural of ἐγώ, limiting the reference to the royal family of God, the body of Church Age believers.

Romans 14:17 — "the kingdom of God." θεοῦ (of God, from θεός). The subject βασιλεία is qualified by the descriptive genitive θεοῦ. The phrase could in principle refer to a civil kingdom, but the genitive immediately marks the referent as spiritual. In Romans, addressed to Church Age believers, kingdom of God designates the royal family of God in this dispensation, regenerate believers in union with Christ through the baptism of the Holy Spirit.

Romans 15:1 — "the failings of the weak." ἀδύνατος (impotent, powerless, impossible). The accusative plural direct object is the noun asthenēma (ἀσθένημα), weaknesses or infirmities. The genitive modifier is the adjective adynatos (ἀδύνατος), in the descriptive genitive plural. Adynatos means impotent, powerless, impossible — all nuances pointing to deficiency of doctrine. Critically, the use of this adjective implies a positive trajectory: the believer so described is one who will rectify the deficiency through continued intake of doctrine.

Romans 15:5 — "the God of endurance and encouragement." ὑπομονῆς καὶ παρακλήσεως (of perseverance and of encouragement). Modifying the subject are two descriptive genitive singular nouns. The first is hupomonē (ὑπομονή), translated 'perseverance' or 'endurance.' The second is paraklēsis (παράκλησις), 'encouragement' or 'comfort,' also carried forward from verse 4.

Romans 15:19 — "by the power of signs and wonders." σημείων καὶ τεράτων (of signs and of wonders). The power is specified through two descriptive genitives. First, sēmeiōn (σημείων), the genitive plural of sēmeion (σημεῖον), meaning remarkable events, signs, or miracles. Second, teratōn (τεράτων), the genitive plural of teras (τέρας), meaning an omen, a wonder, or a portent.

Romans 15:29 — "the fullness of the blessing of Christ." εὐλογίας (of blessing). The noun eulogia (εὐλογία), a descriptive genitive singular, designates the six categories of divine blessing imputed to the believer who has cracked the maturity barrier.

Romans 16:4 — "all the churches of the Gentiles give thanks as well." πᾶσαι αἱ ἐκκλησίαι τῶν ἐθνῶν (all the churches of the Gentiles). The phrase pasai hai ekklēsiai tōn ethnōn (πᾶσαι αἱ ἐκκλησίαι τῶν ἐθνῶν) — “all the churches of the Gentiles” — employs the nominative plural of pas (πᾶς), meaning all without exception, combined with ekklēsia (ἐκκλησία), local assembly, and the descriptive genitive plural of ethnos (ἔθνος), Gentile peoples or nations.

Romans 16:23 — "Gaius, who is host to me and to the whole church, greets you." ὁ ξένος μου καὶ ὅλης τῆς ἐκκλησίας (my host, also host of the entire church). Gaius is identified by two appositional phrases. First, the appositional nominative singular from ξένος (xenos), host or guest-friend, with the possessive genitive singular of the personal pronoun ἐγώ (egō): my host. Second, the descriptive genitive singular from ὅλος (holos, whole, entire) plus ἐκκλησία (ekklēsia): the entire church.

Romans 16:25 — "according to the revelation of the mystery." κατὰ ἀποκάλυψιν μυστηρίου (according to the revelation of the mystery). The third phrase is κατὰ ἀποκάλυψιν μυστηρίου (kata apokalypsin mystēriou). The noun ἀποκάλυψις (apokalypsis) means revelation, unveiling, or disclosure. The genitive μυστηρίου (mystēriou) is descriptive, specifying what is disclosed: the mystery — church age doctrine.

Objective Genitive

The noun in the genitive functions as the object of the verbal idea contained in the noun it modifies.

Romans 5:5 — "God's love has been poured into our hearts." ἡ ἀγάπη τοῦ θεοῦ can be read with an objective-genitive nuance in some contexts (love directed toward God), though the dominant sense here is subjective (God's own love toward the believer) — the two readings are worth distinguishing precisely because English "of" flattens them together.

Romans 6:16 — "you are slaves... leading to righteousness" — the genitive relationship between slavery and its object.

Romans 7:4 — "the law of her husband" (the underlying analogy at 7:2) uses a genitive that functions objectively with respect to the governing relationship named.

Romans 7:5 — "the passions of sins." παθήματα... ἁμαρτιῶν — the plural genitive of ἁμαρτία with the plural noun παθήματα ("impulses, trends") designates the sinful trends as, in Paul's own marriage analogy, the "children" produced by the first marriage: the trend toward sin, toward human good, and toward evil.

Romans 10:2 — "a zeal for God." θεός (for God). The accusative direct object zelos (zeal or jealousy, depending on context; here religious zeal directed toward God) is followed by the objective genitive of theos, correctly rendered for God. Israel possesses a zeal for God; the problem is what that zeal lacks.

Romans 10:14 — "of whom they have never heard." οὗ (about whom). The relative clause uses the objective genitive singular of the relative pronoun hos, correctly about whom.

Romans 10:17 — "the word of Christ." Χριστοῦ (about Christ). The genitive Christou is objective: the discourse is about Christ.

Romans 11:13 — "an apostle to the Gentiles." ἔθνος (of the Gentiles). With ἀπόστολος stands an objective genitive plural of ἔθνος, of the Gentiles, delimiting the sphere of Paul's apostolic commission. It is also an adverbial genitive of reference: Paul's apostleship is directed toward, and qualified by reference to, the Gentile world.

Romans 12:2 — "by the renewal of your mind." νοῦς (of your thought). Nous, the conscious mind, understanding, thought pattern, is an objective genitive: it is the object of renovation through maximum doctrine resident in the soul. It corresponds to the right lobe of the soul, the location of epignosis.

Romans 13:9 — "You shall love your neighbor as yourself." σου (near to you, from σύ). In τὸν πλησίον σου the genitive σου is an objective genitive: near to you. The corrected translation is you shall love the one near you.

Romans 15:8 — "a servant to the circumcised." περιτομῆς (of circumcision). The objective genitive singular peritomēs (περιτομῆς) — literally 'of circumcision' — is used here as a synonym for the Jews, the circumcised people. Corrected translation of the opening clause: For I report that Christ has become a minister to the circumcision.

Romans 15:12 — "to rule the Gentiles." ἐθνῶν (the Gentiles). With the infinitive stands the objective genitive plural of ethnos (ἔθνος), Gentiles.

Romans 15:13 — "fill you with all joy." πάσης χαρᾶς (with all happiness). The first content of the filling is expressed by the objective genitive: pasēs charās (πάσης χαρᾶς). The adjective pas (πᾶς) in the genitive singular feminine means 'all' — total, without remainder. The noun chara (χαρά) is God's happiness — the happiness that belongs to God's own nature and is imparted to the believer through the filling. The corrected translation: 'fill you with all happiness.'

Romans 15:14 — "filled with all knowledge." πάσης γνώσεως (all knowledge). The objective genitive follows: pasēs gnōseōs (πάσης γνώσεως), all knowledge or all thinking of doctrine. Here gnōsis (γνῶσις) is used not in its technical sense as the first stage in the function of GAP, but in the non-technical sense of thinking — the same sense in which the word appears in 1 Corinthians 2:16, 'the mind [thinking] of Christ.'

Romans 15:27 — "they owe it to them." αὐτῶν (to them). The object of the obligation is expressed by the objective genitive plural of the intensive pronoun autos (αὐτός), correctly translated 'to them' — referring to the Jewish believers in Jerusalem.

Romans 16:25 — "and the preaching of Jesus Christ." τὸ κήρυγμα Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ (the proclamation of Jesus Christ). The noun κήρυγμα (kērygma) is derived from κῆρυξ (kēryx), a herald, and denotes a formal public communication or proclamation. Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ is an objective genitive: the proclamation that has Jesus Christ as its content and its agent.

Appositional Genitive

Two nouns placed in a genitive relationship where the second renames or explains the first.

Romans 5:2 — "this grace in which we stand" involves, in the fuller Greek construction behind "access... into this grace," an appositional relationship clarifying exactly what the "access" secured actually consists of.

Romans 15:13 — "May the God of hope." ὁ θεὸς τῆς ἐλπίδος (the God of the hope). The phrase ho theos tēs elpidos (ὁ θεὸς τῆς ἐλπίδος) employs a genitive of apposition. The genitive of apposition designates an object in an individual and uses the genitive of another noun to designate the same thing. Here elpis (ἐλπίς), hope, stands in apposition to ho theos: Jesus Christ is the hope.

Romans 15:16 — "the offering of the Gentiles may be acceptable." ἡ προσφορὰ τῶν ἐθνῶν (the offering consisting of the Gentiles). The subject of the purpose clause is the nominative singular prosphora (προσφορά), meaning the act of bringing or presenting an offering. The offering in view is the Gentiles themselves — not an offering made by the Gentiles but an offering consisting of the Gentiles, expressed by the appositional genitive plural of ethnos (ἔθνος, nation, Gentile people).

Genitive of Time (Adverbial)

Marks a distinction of time-category rather than a specific point or duration.

Romans 5:18 — "Therefore, as one trespass led to condemnation for all men" — the temporal framing of "one trespass" situates the event within a category of time (a single, decisive past occasion) rather than specifying a duration.

Romans 11:25 — "until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in." ἄχρι οὗ (until which time). The limiting clause opens with the Attic adverb ἄχρι used as a conjunction, followed by the relative pronoun οὗ, an adverbial genitive of time. ἄχρι οὗ is an Attic idiom meaning until which time; its appearance in a Koine epistle signals a concept of exceptional theological weight. The hardening of Israel is not permanent; it is bounded by a definite terminus, the completion of the church age.

Anarthrous Constructions — Quality Over Identity
