The absence of the definite article on an otherwise-expected noun emphasizes the quality of the thing named.

Romans 2:17 — "But if you call yourself a Jew." ἐν θεῷ ("about relationship with God") is anarthrous, emphasizing the qualitative perfection of God rather than mere identity, even as Paul exposes the arrogance of invoking the divine name as backdrop for boasting.

Romans 4:5 — "believes in him who justifies the ungodly" — ἀσεβῆ is anarthrous, emphasizing the quality of ungodliness as a category rather than pointing to one specific ungodly individual.

Romans 5:1 — "we have peace with God" — εἰρήνην is anarthrous, emphasizing the quality of the peace in view (prosperity, a settled condition) rather than identifying "the peace" as a single previously-mentioned item.

Romans 6:9 — "death no longer has dominion over him" — θάνατος anarthrous, emphasizing death as a category or power rather than one specific death-event.

Romans 6:13 — "present yourselves to God as those who have been brought from death to life" — the anarthrous nouns here stress the qualitative contrast between the two states rather than identifying particular, previously-named instances of each.

Romans 6:14 — "sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace" — both νόμον and χάριν are anarthrous, stressing the qualitative categories (law as a system, grace as a system) rather than one specific law or one specific gift.

Romans 6:19 — "you presented your members as slaves to impurity and to lawlessness" — the anarthrous nouns stress the qualitative character of the former slavery.

Romans 7:6 — "newness of spirit" (ESV). The anarthrous construction of πνεῦμα ("spirit") with the noun καινότης ("newness") emphasizes the quality of the Holy Spirit — incorruptibility — as the defining characteristic of the new marriage counselor, not merely one particular occurrence of newness.

Romans 7:14 — "sold under sin" (ESV). While not itself anarthrous in every occurrence, ἁμαρτία functions across this chapter primarily as a qualitative category (the sin nature as a governing power) rather than a particular identified act — consistent with its anarthrous or generically-articled use throughout Romans 5–7.

Romans 9:1 — "speaking the truth." ἀλήθεια (doctrine). The accusative singular direct object alētheia means truth and, in this context, doctrine, the content of Christianity as absolute truth. The absence of the definite article emphasizes the high quality of the noun.

Romans 9:2 — "great sorrow." μεγάλη λύπη (great sorrow). The predicate nominative megalē lupē is anarthrous, and anarthrous predicate nominatives emphasize quality rather than identity. The sorrow is not merely large in extent but of the highest quality: legitimate, honorable sorrow that a mature man of honor is entitled and obligated to carry for those he loves.

Romans 9:8 — "are counted as offspring." εἰς σπέρμα (for seed). In eis sperma, for seed, the absence of the definite article before sperma calls attention to its qualitative aspect: the seed of Abraham in view is not physical seed but spiritual seed, not those who carry his DNA but those who carry his faith and therefore his righteousness by imputation.

Romans 9:22 — "vessels of wrath." σκεῦος (vessel, container). σκεῦος appears in the nominative plural without the article. The absence of the article does not merely indicate indefiniteness; it draws attention to the qualitative character of the noun. Here, however, the anarthrous form specifically highlights the high value God has placed upon every unbeliever: every sin of every person who would ever reject Christ was imputed to Christ on the cross and judged there (2 Peter 3:9).

Romans 9:23 — "for vessels of mercy." σκεῦος (vessel, container). The anarthrous construction, the absence of the definite article, calls attention to the qualitative excellence of the vessel rather than its identity. These are vessels of high quality, defined by the mercy that operates on them.

Romans 9:28 (Isaiah 10:23) — "for the Lord." κύριος (Lord). The subject κύριος, referring to the Lord Jesus Christ, appears without the definite article; the anarthrous construction emphasizes the qualitative uniqueness of His person. Throughout the remainder of Romans 9 and into chapter 10, Kyrios consistently designates the Lord Jesus Christ as deity, with particular reference to the second advent.

Romans 9:30 — "That Gentiles who did not pursue righteousness." ἔθνη (Gentiles, nations, from ἔθνος). The subject ἔθνη appears without the definite article. The absence of the article does not indicate indefiniteness as in English; it emphasizes the qualitative character of the noun. Here anarthrous ἔθνη highlights the high quality of certain Gentiles who in Old Testament times exercised positive volition toward the gospel and believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, rather than Gentiles as an undifferentiated class.

Romans 9:31 — "Israel who pursued a law." νόμον (law, from νόμος). The accusative singular νόμον, the Mosaic law, appears without the article. The anarthrous construction calls attention to the character and quality of the law rather than its mere identity. There is nothing wrong with the law itself; the distortion arises from the genitive of means governing Israel's relationship to it.

Romans 10:4 — "For Christ is the end." Χριστός. The subject Christos, nominative singular, is the fourth word in the Greek order. The absence of the article is qualitative, emphasizing the unique nature of the person rather than mere identification, and underscores the hypostatic union: eternal God and true humanity, the last Adam, impeccable.

Romans 11:13 — "Inasmuch then as I am an apostle to the Gentiles." ἀπόστολος (apostle). The predicate nominative is the anarthrous ἀπόστολος. The absence of the article emphasizes quality and character: Paul is not merely the apostle in a generic sense, but one who fully possesses the character and authority that the title denotes.

Romans 11:15 — "the reconciliation of the world." καταλλαγή (reconciliation). The predicate nominative καταλλαγή stands without the article, which emphasizes the quality of the noun rather than its particularity. In English the article is supplied (the reconciliation) because English and Greek operate on opposite principles: Greek uses the definite article for de-emphasis; its omission highlights the qualitative force. Reconciliation removes six barriers: sin, the penalty of sin, physical birth, human self-righteousness, divine immutability, and position in Adam.

Romans 11:22 — "Note then the kindness and the severity of God." χρηστότης (integrity). The first direct object, the accusative of χρηστότης (lexical range goodness, kindness, moral excellence), appears without the article. The absence of the article shifts emphasis from identity to quality: Paul is not pointing to the goodness of God as a named attribute among others but emphasizing the qualitative perfection of that goodness. The anarthrous form demands a translation that stresses origin and character: integrity.

Romans 11:33 — "the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God." ὦ βάθος πλούτου καὶ σοφίας καὶ γνώσεως θεοῦ. There are no articles in ὦ βάθος πλούτου καὶ σοφίας καὶ γνώσεως θεοῦ. The absence of the article emphasizes the qualitative aspect of each noun; in English the definite article is the standard device for conveying exactly that emphasis, so the articles are retained in translation. Competent translation carries the grammatical emphasis, not merely the lexical content, across the linguistic boundary.

Romans 14:6 — "in honor of the Lord." κύριος (to the Lord). The indirect object is the dative singular of κύριος without the article. The absence of the definite article emphasizes the quality of the noun: the Lord Jesus Christ in His perfection is the referent. For clarity in English, the definite article is supplied.

Romans 15:2 — "to build him up." οἰκοδομήν (edification complex). The second prepositional phrase is πρός (pros) plus the accusative of οἰκοδομή (oikodomē): to the edification complex. The noun oikodomē is anarthrous — there is no definite article — which in Greek emphasizes quality rather than identity. Paul is not simply referring to a process of building up; he is emphasizing the high quality and completeness of the edification complex as a structure.

Romans 15:12 — "in him will the Gentiles hope." ἔθνη (Gentiles). The subject is the anarthrous plural of ethnos, Gentiles — the absence of the definite article emphasizing quality: these are believing Gentiles, survivors of the Tribulation whose survival is the product of doctrine.

Accusative of General Reference

Romans 4:12 — "the father of the circumcised" involves an accusative-of-reference nuance in the fuller construction describing what category of persons the fatherhood in view concerns.

Romans 2:1 — "Therefore you have no excuse, O man, every one of you who judges. For in passing judgment on another you condemn yourself, because you, the judge, practice the very same things." σεαυτόν ("yourself") stands in emphatic position as an accusative of general reference — a reflexive pronoun foregrounding self-condemnation as the theological climax of the verse, since the judge pronounces his own verdict.

Romans 2:19 — "and if you are sure that you yourself are a guide to the blind." σεαυτόν functions again as an accusative of general reference, the subject of the infinitive εἶναι, emphasizing that the legalist's frame of reference is himself, not God.

Romans 3:22 — "the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe." πάντας ("all," from πᾶς) in the phrase εἰς πάντας indicates that salvation is universally available to every member of the human race without distinction.

Romans 9:5 — "according to the flesh, is the Christ." κατὰ σάρκα (the one coming in the flesh). With kata sarka, the accusative of general reference introduced by the article to demands the insertion of a pertinent infinitive, yielding the phrase the one coming: in fact, from whom is the Christ, the one coming in the flesh. kata sarka qualifies the mode of the Messiah's coming in history, the incarnation through the genetic line of Israel, contrasted implicitly with his eternal existence as God over all.

Romans 11:8 — "eyes that would not see and ears that would not hear." ὀφθαλμός (eyes). ὀφθαλμούς and ὦτα are accusatives plural of general reference functioning as the subjects of the articular infinitives. The eyes carry the connotation of concentrated perception (the reading of Scripture), the ears the reception of oral instruction (synagogue reading and apostolic preaching).

Romans 12:18 — "so far as it depends on you." τὸ ἐξ ὑμῶν (as much as it depends on you). The idiom to ex hymōn is composed of the accusative of general reference from the article to, the preposition ek, and the ablative plural of sy. It means as much as it depends on you, the degree to which the matter lies within your own sphere of responsibility and capacity.

Romans 13:11 — "for you to wake from sleep." ὑμᾶς (you, from σύ). ὑμᾶς is an accusative of general reference serving as the subject of the following infinitive.

Romans 14:14 — "for anyone who thinks it unclean." τι (something, from τις). The accusative neuter singular of the indefinite pronoun τις works on two levels at once: it is the direct object of λογίζομαι and the accusative of general reference serving as the subject of the following infinitive. As an indefinite pronoun it represents a category rather than a specific individual, the entire class of weak believers.

Romans 15:8 — "For I tell you that Christ became a servant." Χριστόν (Christ). The accusative with infinitive construction is standard Greek syntax for indirect discourse after a verb of reporting.

Romans 15:9 — "the Gentiles might glorify God." τὰ ἔθνη (the Gentiles). The accusative plural of general reference is drawn from the noun ethnos (ἔθνος), Gentiles, with the generic definite article representing the category as a whole. The accusative of general reference serves as the subject of the infinitive.

Romans 15:13 — "you may abound in hope." ὑμᾶς (you). The subject is in the accusative of general reference — the second person plural personal pronoun σύ (su) — indicating that the abounding in hope is the direct purpose for which the God of hope fills the believer with happiness and prosperity.

The Predicate Nominative with Verbs of Becoming or Being Appointed

See section XIV above for the fuller treatment introduced by Romans 7's uncopulated predicate nominative construction; Romans 5:19, 6:16, and 7:3 all illustrate this pattern and are treated fully there.

Dative of Possession

Romans 9:2 — "that I have great sorrow." ἐγώ (I have). The clause uses a standard Greek idiom of possession with the dative singular of egō, to me. The idiom, there is to me, is best rendered I have; it de-emphasizes mere ownership and foregrounds the experiential reality of what is carried. Paul locates the sorrow within himself as the one who must bear it.

Romans 9:9 (Genesis 18:10) — "and Sarah shall have a son." Σάρρα (Sarah will have). eimi with the dative of indirect object from the proper noun Sarra constitutes an idiom meaning to have: there will be to Sarah, or Sarah will have. Sarah is the beneficiary of the divine imputation.

Romans 12:19 (Deuteronomy 32:35) — "Vengeance is mine." ἐκδίκησις (punishment belongs to me). The nominative ekdikēsis, punishment or the administration of justice, here refers positively to punitive action by the justice of God. The dative of the personal pronoun egō is a dative of possession: literally punishment to me, translated punishment belongs to me. The administration of punitive justice is the exclusive prerogative of God.

The Vocative of Address

Romans 9:20 — "O man." ὦ (O). The interjection ὦ follows Semitic usage as employed in Koine Greek, not Attic. It precedes a vocative and carries a qualitative judgment about the person addressed: it is never used when addressing someone who is correct, but is reserved for those who are wrong. Paired with the vocative singular of ἄνθρωπος (the generic term for a human being, mankind as a category), Ō anthrōpe is an address to someone whose thinking has gone seriously astray.

Romans 11:33 — "Oh, the depth of the riches." ὦ. The verse opens with the exclamation ὦ, a classical Greek form, not a Koine construction; in classical usage it stands before a vocative for address or invocation, and introduces an exclamation. The predominantly classical register signals that Paul is operating at the highest register of Greek prose — the maximum intensity of formal worship. The exclamation excludes an abstract addressee; it is directed to the living God.

Romans 12:1 — "brothers." ἀδελφοί (brethren, from ἀδελφός). The vocative plural establishes the family context of the exhortation: the honor code is the code of the royal family of God, governing the attitude of each member toward every other member, grounded in the shared imputation of divine righteousness at salvation.

Romans 12:19 — "Beloved." ἀγαπητοί (beloved ones, from ἀγαπητός). The vocative plural agapētoi, an adjective used as a substantive, is not a sentimental flourish but a doctrinal reminder of the believer’s standing: loved by Father, Son, and Holy Spirit on the basis of the imputed righteousness each believer possesses. It is placed before the prohibition of revenge to ground the command in doctrinal security.

Romans 13:1 — "Let every person be subject to the governing authorities." ψυχή (all human beings). The verse opens with a vocative address built from the adjective πᾶς (all) and the noun ψυχή in the vocative feminine singular. ψυχή carries three related meanings (soul, life, human being), and here the third is primary: the address is to every person who has received the imputation of human life, believer and unbeliever alike.

Romans 15:10 — "Rejoice, O Gentiles." ἔθνη (O Gentiles). The vocative plural of ethnos (ἔθνη), O Gentiles, encompasses several distinct categories.

Nominative of Appellation

Romans 9:26 (Hosea 1:10) — "'sons of the living God.'" υἱός (adult son). The nominative of appellation consists of υἱός (adult son, with full standing in the household) with the possessive genitive θεοῦ. The designation is not merely people of God but sons of God, a qualitative elevation reflecting the pattern of Abraham, who became a child of God through faith: sonship is conferred through faith, not ethnic descent.

The Double Accusative of Subject and Predicate

Romans 10:9 — "that Jesus is Lord." Κύριον (Jesus as Lord). The phrase often rendered the Lord Jesus is a double accusative of subject and predicate: Iēsoun is the accusative subject and Kyrion the accusative predicate. The correct translation is Jesus as Lord, a predicate assertion about the identity of Jesus, not a title phrase.

Romans 16:10 — "Greet Apelles, who is approved in Christ." Ἀπελλῆν τὸν δόκιμον (Apelles, the tested and approved one). This is a double accusative construction: Apelles is the direct object, and dokimos (δόκιμος) is the predicate object.

Nominative of Reference

Romans 10:19 — "First Moses says." πρῶτος (first). The ordinal adjective prōtos is used as a nominative of reference to introduce Moses as the first of several witnesses called to testify regarding Israel's understanding of the gospel.

Adverbial Accusative of Time

Romans 10:21 (Isaiah 65:2) — "All day long." ὅλος (the whole day). The accusative feminine singular of holos with the accusative of hēmera, the whole day, forms an adverbial phrase: not a literal 24-hour day but day in and day out, every generation of the dispensation of Israel, the aggregate of every individual appeal across the Jewish age.

Locative of Time

Romans 11:5 — "at the present time." ἐν τῷ νῦν καιρῷ (in this present period of time, from καιρός). ἐν with the locative of time governs καιρός, a qualitatively and historically defined period rather than clock time (χρόνος); νῦν fixes the application to the moment Paul writes. The phrase points to the Church Age as the present dispensation, in which the principle operative in the time of Elijah still operates.

Romans 11:31 — "by the mercy shown to you." τῷ ὑμετέρῳ ἐλέει (in your time of mercy). With the verb stands a locative of time from the possessive ὑμέτερος and ἔλεος: τῷ ὑμετέρῳ ἐλέει, in your time of mercy, the church age — the period during which Gentile client nations function under divine blessing and Gentiles serve as the primary evangelists to the Jewish people.

Genitive of Source (Origin)

Romans 11:5 — "chosen by grace." χάριτος (of grace, by grace, from χάρις). The genitive χάριτος marks the origin of the selection: it originates in grace, not in human merit, ethnic identity, or religious performance. The remnant exists because God has acted in grace, and its existence is itself the evidence that God has not repudiated His people.

Dative of Disadvantage

Romans 11:8 — "God gave them." αὐτοῖς (to them, to their detriment, from αὐτός). The dative plural αὐτοῖς is a dative of disadvantage: the judicial giving of the state of insensibility is not a neutral transaction but a consequence working against the recipients. What God gives in judicial response to arrogance is discipline, not blessing.

Romans 11:9 (Psalm 69:22) — "a retribution for them." αὐτοῖς (to them, against them, from αὐτός). The dative plural αὐτοῖς closing the citation is a dative of disadvantage: for a retribution to them, against them.

Romans 13:2 — "resists what God has appointed." διαταγή (ordinance, divine institution). διαταγή, in the dative singular, means divine institution, ordinance. The dative functions both as indirect object and as dative of disadvantage: those who oppose the ordinance do so to their own detriment and to the detriment of the society in which they live.

Romans 13:2 — "and those who resist will incur judgment." ἑαυτοῖς (to themselves, from ἑαυτός). ἑαυτοῖς is the dative plural of disadvantage from the reflexive pronoun. Because the action is referred back to the subject, the construction is reflexive: the punishment is self-incurred. The anti-establishment believer, by his own choices, generates the conditions under which divine discipline follows.

Romans 13:3 — "but to bad." κακός (evil function). After ἀλλά the dative of disadvantage follows from κακός, which in this context denotes crime: the violation of freedom, privacy, or property. Evil function includes crime, revolution, conspiracy to overthrow government, political assassination, and any system that deprives the individual of freedom, privacy, and property under the pretext of the common good.

Romans 14:20 — "it is wrong for anyone." τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ (to that man, from ἄνθρωπος). The predicate is κακόν (evil, bad, harmful). The dative of disadvantage τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ identifies the strong believer as the one to whom the evil accrues: it becomes evil to that man, the strong believer. A right thing applied wrongly becomes κακός.

Locative of Sphere

Romans 11:23 — "if they do not continue in their unbelief." ἀπιστίᾳ (in unbelief, from ἀπιστία). The object of persistence is the locative of sphere ἀπιστίᾳ, unbelief — not mere intellectual doubt but active, volitional rejection of Christ, specifically the sustained national rejection constituting the great blot out. Corrected translation of the protasis: if they do not persist in their unbelief.

Romans 11:24 — "be grafted back into their own olive tree." ἴδιος (their own). The subject of the apodosis is οὗτοι, these — Jews who believe in Christ, the natural branches (κατὰ φύσιν). The verb is again a future passive indicative of ἐγκεντρίζω. The destination is expressed with the locative of sphere from ἴδιος: their own olive tree. The Jews are not grafted into something foreign; they are restored to what is properly theirs — the spiritual heritage their unbelief forfeited.

Romans 14:1 — "weak in faith." τῇ πίστει (in the doctrine). The phrase τῇ πίστει is a locative of sphere: the weakness is in the sphere of doctrine. The generic use of the definite article treats Bible doctrine as a category distinct from all other categories of knowledge.

Possessive Genitive

Romans 12:2 — "what is the will of God." θέλημα (the will of God). The interrogative pronoun tis introduces the indirect question, and the possessive genitive of theos modifies thelēma, the will, purpose, or plan of God: that you may prove what the will of God is.

Romans 13:2 — "resists what God has appointed." θεοῦ (of God, from θεός). The possessive genitive θεοῦ identifies the διαταγή specifically as the ordinance of God: the laws of divine establishment as God's authorized system of authority for the human race, not a human construction.

Romans 14:8 — "we are the Lord's." τοῦ Κυρίου ἐσμέν (we are of the Lord, from κύριος). In τοῦ Κυρίου ἐσμέν the genitive of κύριος with the generic article is a possessive genitive functioning as a predicate genitive, expressing possession and relationship: the absolute ownership and sovereign authority of the Lord Jesus Christ over all believers, living and dead.

Romans 15:19 — "the gospel of Christ." τοῦ Χριστοῦ (of the Christ). The possessive genitive Christou (Χριστοῦ) — 'of the Christ' — identifies its source and content. The complete clause reads: I have fulfilled the good news of the Christ.

Romans 15:27 — "their spiritual blessings." τοῖς πνευματικοῖς αὐτῶν (spiritual things belonging to them). The object is the dative plural of pneumatikos (πνευματικός), spiritual things, with the possessive genitive of the intensive pronoun autos (αὐτός), functioning as a third-person personal pronoun: spiritual things belonging to them — that is, belonging to the Jews.

Romans 15:33 — "Now the God of peace be with you all." ὁ θεὸς τῆς εἰρήνης (the God of prosperity). The nominative singular subject is ho theos (ὁ θεός), 'the God,' with the definite article specifying the God of Scripture. Joined to this is the genitive of possession from the noun eirēnē (εἰρήνη), traditionally rendered 'peace.' The primary meaning of eirēnē is prosperity, welfare, and wellbeing — the same semantic range carried by the Hebrew shalom. The genitive of possession therefore declares that God possesses an unlimited supply of prosperity.

Romans 16:18 — "they deceive the hearts of the naive." τὰς καρδίας τῶν ἀκάκων (the hearts of the innocent). The direct object is the accusative plural of kardia (καρδία), heart — the right lobe where thought exists. The possessive genitive plural of akakos (ἄκακος) describes the victims. The adjective means innocent or unsuspecting — used of newborn children who are ignorant, lacking discernment.

Romans 16:20 — "The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you." ἡ χάρις τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ (the grace belonging to our Lord Jesus Christ). The key noun is charis (χάρις), nominative singular — grace, the policy of the justice of God in blessing humanity. The genitive construction tou Kyriou hēmōn Iēsou Christou (τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ) is a possessive genitive: the grace belonging to our Lord Jesus Christ.

The Appositional Accusative

Romans 12:2 — "what is good and acceptable and perfect." ἀγαθός (the good, the well pleasing, and the complete). The will of God is described by three appositional accusatives: agathos (intrinsically good, derived from the perfect attributes of God, not human good), euarestos (always well pleasing to God), and teleios (complete, having attained the end, maturity adjustment to the justice of God). The three terms are not synonyms but sequential stages in the protocol plan of God, corresponding to the first, second and third potentials.

Romans 16:1 — "our sister Phoebe." τὴν ἀδελφὴν ἡμῶν (our sister). The appositional accusative adelphēn (ἀδελφήν), 'sister,' uses the feminine suffix to confirm that Phoebe is a woman believer; when the masculine form adelphos (ἀδελφός) is used, it includes all believers generically.

Romans 16:3 — "my fellow workers in Christ Jesus." τοὺς συνεργούς μου (my fellow workers). The phrase “my fellow workers” renders the accusative plural direct object from the noun synergos (συνεργός), meaning co-worker, fellow laborer. It stands in apposition to Prisca and Aquila, which is why it appears in the accusative case.

Romans 16:5 — "Greet my beloved Epaenetus." τὸν ἀγαπητόν μου (my beloved). Paul qualifies Epaenetus with the accusative singular adjective agapētos (ἀγαπητός), meaning beloved — one who is the object of deep personal affection. The possessive genitive singular of egō (ἐγώ) — my — specifies that this is Paul's own expression of personal love.

Romans 16:9 — "Greet Urbanus, our fellow worker in Christ." τὸν συνεργὸν ἡμῶν (our fellow worker). Paul applies to Urbanus the appositional accusative singular συνεργός (synergos), fellow worker or co-laborer. The compound joins σύν (syn, with) and ἔργον (ergon, work).

Dative of Association

Romans 12:16 — "associate with the lowly." ταπεινοῖς (with those of humble status, from ταπεινός). The dative of association governs tapeinois, those who are low, of humble station. The word describes how such people appear to the arrogant eye, people offering no social advantage; the command is to associate with them on the basis of shared imputed righteousness, not as condescension.

The Neuter Plural as Abstract

Romans 12:17 — "what is honorable." καλός (what is honorable). The accusative neuter plural of kalos, because it is neuter plural, carries the abstract meaning honorable things or what is honorable: the institutions and principles of divine establishment that the mature believer is commanded to respect.

Adverbial Accusative of Manner

Romans 13:9 — "You shall love your neighbor as yourself." σεαυτόν (as yourself). σεαυτόν (a compound of σύ and αὐτός) is, by its accusative ending, an adverbial accusative of manner. That category matters: it does not make love of self the norm or measure. Self-regard is unstable, and God does not base a divine command on an unstable quantity; the norm is the believer's own norms and standards as shaped by doctrine resident in the soul.

Locative Case

Romans 13:13 — "as in the daytime." ἡμέρα (as in the day). ὡς, used as a relative adverb of comparison, is followed by the locative of ἡμέρα. Since we are now in night, daytime is eternity; the command is to calibrate the believer's conduct by the norms of eternity rather than the shifting standards of time.

Dative of Space

Romans 14:13 — "in the way of a brother." ἀδελφός (in front of his brother). The phrase uses the dative of space from ἀδελφός, the weak believer. The spatial nuance reinforces the image of field of fire: the weak believer's range of doctrinal flexibility is narrow, so almost any action of the strong believer falls within his line of sight, and the obligation falls on the strong believer because his wider field of fire gives him greater capacity and greater responsibility.

Instrumental of Cause

Romans 14:15 — "with your food." βρῶμα (because of that food). The definite article used as a demonstrative with the instrumental singular of βρῶμα is an instrumental of cause, a development from the instrumental of means: means expresses the intermediary producing a result, cause points to the original factor. Deficiency in doctrine is the ultimate cause; the food taboos at issue in Rome are the intermediate factor.

Genitive of Possession

Romans 14:20 — "the work of God." ἔργον τοῦ θεοῦ (the work of God, from ἔργον). ἔργον (work, deed, plan) takes the genitive of possession θεοῦ. The generic article sets the plan of God apart from every human plan as a category unto itself: God's work from conception in eternity to execution in time.

Dative of Presence

Romans 15:5 — "with one another." ἐν ἀλλήλοις (in the presence of one another). The phrase is en allēlois (ἐν ἀλλήλοις) — the preposition en plus the dative plural of the reciprocal pronoun allēlōn (ἀλλήλων). The reciprocal pronoun in the plural signifies an interchange of action — what goes on between persons in contact. The dative of presence yields the translation 'in the presence of one another.'

Subjective Genitive

Romans 15:18 — "to bring the Gentiles to obedience." ἐθνῶν (of the Gentiles). The subjective genitive plural ἐθνῶν (ethnōn), from ἔθνος (ethnos), translated "Gentiles" or "nations," identifies the scope of Paul's missionary mandate.

Adverbial Accusative of Frequency

Romans 15:22 — "I have so often been hindered." τὰ πολλά (many times). The accusative neuter plural of polus, πολύς, used adverbially, modifies the verb: “many times.” The detention was not a single episode.

Ablative of Agency

Romans 15:24 — "to be helped on my journey there by you." ὑφ’ ὑμῶν (by you). The connective conjunction kai (καί) is followed by the preposition hypo (ὑπό) plus the ablative of agency from the personal pronoun su (σύ): and by you.

Ablative of Comparison

Romans 15:26 — "for the poor among the saints at Jerusalem." εἰς τοὺς πτωχοὺς τῶν ἁγίων (to the destitute ones among the saints). The prepositional phrase uses eis (εἰς) with the accusative plural of ptōchos (πτωχός), meaning destitute, impoverished — not merely poor in a relative sense but completely without resources. This is followed by the ablative of comparison plural from hagios (ἅγιος), correctly translated among the saints — not of the saints.

Adverbial Accusative of Reference

Romans 16:6 — "who has worked hard for you." πολλά (with reference to many things). The accusative plural of polys (πολύς), functioning as an adverbial accusative, indicates that her labor extended across many areas: 'with reference to many things.'

Romans 16:12 — "who has worked hard in the Lord." πολλὰ ἐκοπίασεν ἐν κυρίῳ (labored to exhaustion with reference to many things in the Lord). But her clause adds the adverbial accusative of reference from πολύς (polys), many, meaning with reference to many things. Persis does not simply work to exhaustion in a single sphere; her production is diversified across many spheres simultaneously.

XVII.Prepositions

χωρίς — Apart From

Romans 3:21 — "But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the law." χωρίς governs the genitive of νόμος as an improper preposition: divine righteousness is disclosed entirely apart from, without reference to, any system of legal works.

Romans 10:14 — "without someone preaching." χωρίς (apart from). The adverb chōris functions here as an improper preposition, apart from, without, governing the genitive. It introduces the condition of absence, apart from one who proclaims, underscoring that the absence of a messenger is a structural, not incidental, deficiency.

ἐκ — Source or Origin

Romans 2:27 — "who am uncircumcised by nature." ἐκ φύσεως (ἐκ + genitive) is used idiomatically for a natural, inborn condition — uncircumcised as a matter of birth, not merely as an unperformed ritual.

Romans 3:20 — "For by works of the law no human being will be justified in his sight." ἐξ ἔργων νόμου (ἐκ + genitive) marks the excluded source: not from works of the law — the law's true function is to produce the knowledge of sin, not justification.

Romans 3:26 — "it was to show his righteousness at the present time, so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus." ἐκ πίστεως Ἰησοῦ (ἐκ + genitive) is an ablative of means: by means of faith, with Jesus as the object specified by the objective genitive.

Romans 9:6 — "not all who are descended from Israel." ἐξ Ἰσραήλ (descended from Israel). pantes refers to racial Jews; the article hoi is used as a relative pronoun with pantes as antecedent, and the phrase ex Israel uses ek with the indeclinable proper noun Israel: descended from Israel, physical descent from Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

Romans 9:10 — "by one man." ἐξ ἑνός (from one). ex henos, ek with the genitive of the numeral heis, is theologically significant: it excludes any ambiguity about the paternity of the twins. Both children share one father. With one father and one mother, the only remaining variable is the individual volition of each son, isolating regeneration as the sole determining factor between Jacob and Esau.

Romans 9:11 — "not because of works but because of him who calls." ἐκ (not of works). ek with the genitive plural of ergon, ek ergōn: as an ablative of source, not from works; as an instrumental ablative, not by works. Either rendering communicates the same theological point: election excludes all human works, any human performance, moral achievement or religious activity, as the source or means of divine blessing. The plural is significant: it comprehends every category of human performance; with the objective negative ou the construction denies the false concept that human works of any kind are the basis of divine blessing.

Romans 9:24 — "not from the Jews only but also from the Gentiles." ἐξ Ἰουδαίων … ἐξ ἐθνῶν (from among the Jews … from among the Gentiles). The preposition used with both nouns is ἐξ, from among, indicating selection out of a larger group. ἔθνη refers to the non-Jewish nations as a collective category. In the Church Age, the dispensation of the royal family of God, the distinction between Jew and Gentile is abolished in Christ (Galatians 3:28); election therefore embraces the entire human race without racial restriction.

Romans 10:9 — "from the dead." ἐκ νεκρῶν (out from among the dead). Ek nekrōn uses the ablative of separation: Christ was raised out from among the dead. The phrase underscores the uniqueness of His resurrection; at the time of Romans 10 He alone holds a resurrection body.

Romans 10:17 — "faith comes from hearing." ἀκοή (from a message). Ek plus the ablative of akoē, a message, the content of a report or communication. The ablative of source indicates origin. The point is foundational: no one believes without first receiving information; the gospel must be heard before it can be believed.

Romans 11:6 — "on the basis of works." ἐξ ἔργων (by means of works, from ἐκ). ἐξ ἔργων, ἐκ with the ablative plural of ἔργον, expresses means with the implication of origin or source. The plural is deliberate: every category of human activity that might be offered as a basis for divine blessing is comprehended and excluded together, including legitimate and honorable human works.

Romans 11:36 — "from him." ἐξ αὐτοῦ (from the source of Him). ἐξ αὐτοῦ — ek/ex plus the ablative of autos — is the ablative of source: from the source of Him. It identifies the Lord Jesus Christ as God, the original source of both logistical grace and supergrace blessing, of salvation and every temporal and eternal blessing.

Romans 13:3 — "and you will receive his approval." ἐξ αὐτῆς (from it, from that authority). The phrase means from it, that is, from that authority, the authority of human government. The pronoun is feminine because it refers back to the feminine noun ἐξουσία; rather than repeat the noun, Paul uses a pronoun of matching gender.

Romans 13:11 — "for you to wake from sleep." ἐξ ὕπνου (out of sleep). ἐξ ὕπνου means out of sleep: ἐκ with the ablative expresses separation from the existing condition. ὕπνος is the root of English hypnotic; it is used figuratively for doctrinal indifference, apathy, and disorientation to the Church Age, generally associated with reversionism.

Romans 14:23 — "not from faith." ἐκ πίστεως (by means of doctrine, from πίστις). ἐκ πίστεως uses ἐκ with the ablative of πίστις, negated by the indicative negative οὐκ. In this doctrinal context the ablative with ἐκ denotes source or means, so the rendering is by means of doctrine. Doctrine resident in the soul through GAP is the source of legitimate norms and standards of conscience; the weak believer eating without such a norm acts without the doctrinal basis that would make the action coherent in the Christian life.

ὑπέρ — For the Sake Of

Romans 1:5 — "for the sake of his name." ὑπὲρ τοῦ ὀνόματος αὐτοῦ (ὑπέρ + genitive) marks the ultimate purpose for which grace, apostleship, and doctrinal obedience among the nations all exist.

Romans 15:9 — "glorify God for his mercy." ὑπὲρ ἐλέους (for His mercy). The prepositional phrase that follows is huper (ὑπέρ) plus the ablative of eleos (ἔλεος), mercy or grace, with a possessive pronoun: for His mercy.

Romans 15:30 — "on my behalf." ὑπὲρ ἐμοῦ (on behalf of me). Finally, hyper (ὑπέρ) plus the ablative of egō means on behalf of me, making Paul the explicit subject of intercession.

Romans 16:4 — "who risked their necks for my life." ὑπὲρ τῆς ψυχῆς μου (on behalf of my life). The prepositional phrase ὑπὲρ τῆς ψυχῆς μου (hyper tēs psychēs mou) employs ὑπέρ (hyper) with the genitive, meaning 'on behalf of' or 'for the sake of.' Here it signifies Paul's physical life.

κατά + Accusative

Means "according to" — but frequently, in Romans 6–8, carries a stronger force than the English preposition suggests.

Romans 1:3 — "concerning his Son, who was descended from David according to the flesh." κατὰ σάρκα (κατά + accusative of σάρξ) indicates standard or norm — "according to the standard of humanity" — establishing that Christ's humanity is genuine and complete, not docetic. Contrasted with κατὰ πνεῦμα in the following verse.

Romans 2:2 — "We know that the judgment of God rightly falls... according to truth." κατὰ ἀλήθειαν (κατά + accusative) expresses the norm by which the divine verdict is rendered.

Romans 4:1 — "What then shall we say was gained by Abraham, our forefather according to the flesh?" κατὰ σάρκα — according to the flesh, i.e., by natural human descent.

Romans 4:4 — "Now to the one who works, his wages are not counted as a gift but as his due." The κατά-relationship here (implicit in the surrounding argument) frames wages as strictly proportional to work performed.

Romans 5:6 — "at the right time Christ died for the ungodly." κατὰ καιρόν — according to the appointed time, a fixed point in the divine plan rather than an arbitrary moment.

Romans 8:5 — "those who live according to the flesh." κατὰ σάρκα — the corrected sense is "dominated by the flesh," not merely "in agreement with" or "corresponding to" it. κατά with the accusative here conveys domination and authority: it identifies the governing power-source of the believer's thought life at any given point, not a loose correspondence.

Romans 8:33 — "against God's elect." κατά here shifts to a hostile/adversative sense: accusation directed against a target — a different nuance of the same preposition entirely dependent on context.

Romans 9:3 — "my kinsmen according to the flesh." κατὰ σάρκα (according to earthly descent). kata sarka (kata plus the accusative of sarx) indicates the standard or mode of a relationship: earthly, physical descent. It distinguishes the racial and national Israel, the progeny of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, from the spiritual Israel of regenerate believers.

Romans 9:9 (Genesis 18:10) — "About this time next year." κατὰ τοῦτον τὸν καιρόν (at this time). kata governs the accusative of houtos plus kairos: at this time or during this time. The reference is to the appointed time of Abraham's maturity adjustment to the justice of God, not merely a calendar point but a spiritual milestone at which divine blessing is imputed.

Romans 9:11 — "God's purpose of election." κατὰ ἐκλογήν (in relationship to election). kata with the accusative here denotes relationship: in relationship to election.

Romans 10:2 — "not according to knowledge." κατά (as a result of). Kata with the accusative can denote a norm or standard, but here it also expresses the reason or basis for something, a causal nuance. The zeal of the Jewish unbeliever does not originate from, nor is it governed by, epignosis. Best rendering: but not as a result of knowledge of doctrine.

Romans 11:5 — "chosen by grace." κατ' ἐκλογὴν χάριτος (according to an election by grace, from κατά). In κατ' ἐκλογὴν χάριτος, κατά with the accusative ἐκλογήν indicates the standard or norm: according to election. The phrase specifies the standard of the existence of the pivot.

Romans 11:21 — "the natural branches." κατά (according to nature). κατά plus the accusative of φύσις means according to nature — an idiom meaning natural. The natural branches are the Jewish people, whose spiritual heritage includes the Abrahamic, Palestinian, Davidic, and New Covenants, the Mosaic law, the prophetic canon, and the entire Old Testament revelation; despite it God did not spare the Jewish unbeliever, the fifth cycle of discipline in AD 70 being the primary historical referent.

Romans 11:28 — "As regards the gospel." κατά (with reference to). κατά with the accusative of εὐαγγέλιον does not mean concerning as subject matter but with reference to — a standard or sphere of evaluation. Used twice in the verse: with reference to the gospel; as far as their election (ἐκλογή) is concerned.

Romans 12:6 — "according to the grace given to us." κατὰ χάριν (according to the grace, from κατά). Kata with the accusative denotes standard or norm: the gift conforms to, and is governed by, grace. The category of the gift, the degree of its expression, and the scope of its function are all grace provisions, undeserved and unearned.

Romans 12:6 — "in proportion to our faith." ἀναλογία (in agreement with). Kata plus the accusative of analogia, right relationship, proportion, correspondence, carries the sense of conformity or agreement: in agreement with, a right relationship rather than a numerical ratio. Every exercise of the gift of prophecy must agree with the body of doctrine.

Romans 14:15 — "you are no longer walking in love." κατά (according to the standard of love). κατά with the accusative of ἀγάπη means according to the standard of love. With περιπατέω it establishes ἀγάπη as the governing measure of the strong believer's conduct toward the weak.

Romans 14:22 — "keep between yourself and God." σεαυτόν (in relationship to yourself, from σεαυτοῦ). κατά with the accusative of the reflexive pronoun σεαυτόν denotes a relationship to self: in relationship to yourself. Doctrine forms the norms and standards of the believer's own conscience before God; it is not a club to wield over the conscience of another believer.

Romans 15:5 — "in accord with Christ Jesus." κατὰ Χριστὸν Ἰησοῦν (according to Christ Jesus). The verse closes with the prepositional phrase kata Christon Iēsoun (κατὰ Χριστὸν Ἰησοῦν), 'according to Christ Jesus.' The preposition kata with the accusative establishes the standard of conformity.

Romans 16:5 — "Greet also the church in their house." κατ’ οἶκον αὐτῶν (in their home). The genitive plural indicates that the home belongs jointly to Priska and Aquila.

Romans 16:25 — "according to my gospel." κατὰ τὸ εὐαγγέλιόν μου (according to my gospel). Each phrase employs the Greek preposition κατά (kata), here governing the accusative and establishing a norm or standard. The first phrase is κατὰ τὸ εὐαγγέλιόν μου (kata to euangelion mou) — according to my gospel / my good news.

Romans 16:26 — "according to the command of the eternal God." κατ’ ἐπιταγὴν τοῦ αἰωνίου θεοῦ (by decree of the eternal God). The disclosure of the mystery occurs 'by decree of the eternal God' — the prepositional phrase kata plus the accusative singular of epitagē (ἐπιταγή) — 'in accordance with the command' or 'by decree of.' With this is the possessive genitive of the adjective aiōnios (αἰώνιος) with theos (θεός): by decree of the eternal God.

διά — Genitive vs. Accusative

The case governs the sense: διά + genitive = means/agency; διά + accusative = cause/ground, never purpose.

Romans 1:8 — "First, I thank my God through Jesus Christ for all of you." διά + the genitive is a statement of mechanism: all access to God the Father is mediated through the completed cross-work and continuing high-priestly ministry of Christ — no relationship with God exists independently of him.

Romans 2:12 — "All who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law, and all who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law." διὰ νόμου (διά + genitive) expresses means: judgment reaches the Jew through the specific instrument of the Mosaic law.

Romans 3:22 — "the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ." διὰ πίστεως Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ (διά + genitive) specifies the channel: not law-keeping but faith, through which righteousness reaches the believer.

Romans 3:25 — "whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood, to be received by faith. This was to show God's righteousness, because in his divine forbearance he had passed over former sins." διά with the accusative (see also the Case Usage entries above on ἀνοχή) marks the ground of the forbearance shown toward pre-cross sins.

Romans 4:13 — "the promise to Abraham and his offspring that he would be heir of the world did not come through the law." διὰ νόμου, genitive, means/agency — the promise's channel of arrival was specifically not the law.

Romans 4:25 — "who was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification." διά here with the accusative in both clauses marks cause/ground: delivered up because of our trespasses (the ground necessitating the delivering-up), raised because of our justification (the ground necessitating the resurrection) — not "for the purpose of," which would require a different construction.

Romans 5:10 — "we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son." διὰ τοῦ θανάτου, genitive, means: the death itself is the instrument/channel of reconciliation.

Romans 5:19 — "For as by the one man's disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one man's obedience the many will be made righteous." διά with the genitive in both halves, means: disobedience and obedience are the respective channels through which each result comes.

Romans 6:4 — "We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life." διὰ τῆς δόξης, genitive, means: the Father's glory is the specific instrument of the resurrection.

Romans 7:4 — "you also have died to the law through the body of Christ." διὰ τοῦ σώματος — genitive, means: the physical, human body of Christ (his literal death) as the means by which the believer's death to the law's authority is accomplished.

Romans 8:3 — "through the flesh." διὰ τῆς σαρκός — genitive, means: the sin nature as the channel through which the law's weakness operated.

Romans 8:37 — "through him who loved us." διά + the genitive of the articular participle of ἀγαπάω — means: God the Father, as the one who loves, is the channel through whom supreme victory is won.

Romans 10:17 — "through the word of Christ." διὰ ῥήματος Χριστοῦ (through the agency of). Dia with the genitive rhēmatos: through the agency of a doctrinal discourse about Christ. Rhēma denotes a spoken word or discourse. The communicator (evangelist, pastor, missionary, or witnessing believer) stands between the written word and the unbeliever, conveying this content.

Romans 11:10 (Psalm 69:23) — "and bend their backs forever." διὰ παντός (always, constantly, from διά). διὰ παντός, literally through all, functions as an adverbial idiom of the Septuagint tradition meaning always or constantly. It specifies the permanent, unremitting character of the bent back: not episodic but perpetual.

Romans 11:28 — "they are enemies for your sake." δι' ὑμᾶς (because of you). δι' ὑμᾶς — dia plus the accusative plural pronoun — means because of you or for your sake, referring to Gentile believers and by extension the entire royal family of God. The final phrase διὰ τοὺς πατέρας, because of the fathers, uses the same construction for the patriarchal line Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

Romans 11:36 — "through him." δι᾽ αὐτοῦ (through the agency of Him). δι᾽ αὐτοῦ — dia plus the ablative of autos. Although dia with the genitive normally expresses means or agency, when the ablative is used the emphasis falls on the source. Rendered through the agency of Him, it emphasizes the mechanics by which all blessing flows from its source to its recipients.

Romans 12:3 — "For by the grace given to me." διὰ τῆς χάριτος (through the grace, from χάρις). Dia plus the genitive means through. The phrase governs the entire statement: grace, the policy of the justice of God in providing blessing for the believer, covers the entire arc of the divine plan, from human life itself through salvation, logistical support and blessing at maturity.

Romans 13:5 — "but also for the sake of conscience." διά (because of). In ἀλλὰ καὶ διὰ τὴν συνείδησιν, διά with the accusative expresses cause or ground: subordination is required because of the conscience, not merely because of external compulsion. With the genitive διά would mean through, by means of.

Romans 13:6 — "For because of this." διὰ τοῦτο (because of this, for this reason). διὰ τοῦτο, διά with the accusative of the near demonstrative οὗτος, means because of this or for this reason. It refers back to verse 5 and the status of government as divine servant in the administration of establishment.

Romans 14:15 — "by what you eat." βρῶμα (because of food). διά with the accusative βρῶμα indicates cause or reason: because of food. The food and beverage taboo is the non-essential around which the conflict between strong and weak believers in Rome crystallizes; no food is intrinsically unclean, and the issue is the mental attitude and doctrinal deficiency of the weak believer.

Romans 14:20 — "to make another stumble by what he eats." προσκόμματος (who by eating gives offense, from πρόσκομμα). The closing phrase is διά with the genitive of πρόσκομμα (offense, stumbling, injury, damage). διά with the genitive denotes attendant circumstances: literally eating with offense, idiomatically who by eating gives offense. The offense is given to the positive weak believer, who is distracted from the intake of doctrine.

Romans 15:4 — "through endurance." διὰ ὑπομονῆς (through perseverance). The instrumental genitive construction dia hupomonēs (διὰ ὑπομονῆς) means through perseverance. The noun hupomonē (ὑπομονή) denotes the capacity to remain under pressure, to continue steadfastly when not stimulated, not interested, not naturally engaged.

Romans 15:9 — "Therefore I will praise you." διὰ τοῦτο (because of this). The quotation begins with the preposition dia (διά) plus the accusative singular of the demonstrative pronoun houtos (οὗτος): dia touto, meaning because of this. When dia governs the genitive it means through; with the accusative it means because of or on account of.

Romans 15:15 — "because of the grace given me by God." διὰ τὴν χάριν (because of that grace). The phrase dia tēn charin (διὰ τὴν χάριν) — 'because of that grace' — is governed by dia plus the accusative singular of charis (χάρις), the standard New Testament term for grace. The construction expresses causal ground: Paul's bold, repeated teaching is grounded in and warranted by grace.

Romans 15:18 — "through me." δι’ ἐμοῦ (through me). The final prepositional phrase δι᾽ ἐμοῦ (di' emou), διά (dia) plus the genitive of ἐγώ (egō), means "through me." Paul is the instrument; Christ is the agent.

Romans 15:28 — "by way of you." δι’ ὑμῶν (by means of you). The prepositional phrase following employs dia (διά) plus the genitive plural of the second-person pronoun: by means of you.

Romans 15:30 — "by our Lord Jesus Christ." διὰ τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ (by our Lord Jesus Christ). Paul grounds his appeal in the person of the Lord Jesus Christ, using dia (διά) plus the possessive genitive of the first-person pronoun plus the ablative of means from Kyrios (Κύριος): by our Lord Jesus Christ.

Romans 15:32 — "so that by God's will I may come to you." διὰ θελήματος θεοῦ (by the will of God). The governing phrase is dia thelēmatos theou (διὰ θελήματος θεοῦ): 'by the will of God.' The preposition dia with the ablative of thelēma (θέλημα) denotes the source of the blessing; the possessive genitive of theos (θεός) identifies that sovereignty as belonging to God.

Romans 16:26 — "and through the prophetic writings has been made known to all nations." διά τε γραφῶν προφητικῶν (through the prophetic scriptures). The agency of disclosure is expressed by the prepositional phrase dia plus the genitive plural of graphē (γραφή) — 'through writings' — modified by the descriptive genitive plural of the adjective prophētikos (προφητικός). The correct translation is through the prophetic scriptures, referring to the New Testament canon, which was in the process of formation when Paul wrote Romans in approximately AD 58.

Romans 16:27 — "through Jesus Christ! Amen." διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ (through Jesus Christ). The prepositional phrase dia (διά) + the genitive of Iēsous Christos (Ἰησοῦς Χριστός) — 'through Jesus Christ' — identifies the Second Person of the Trinity as the medium through which the wisdom of God is revealed and executed in history.

παρά — Sense Shifts Entirely by Case

Romans 4:18 — "In hope he believed against hope." παρ' ἐλπίδα — the ESV and KJV render this "against hope," but the correct sense of παρά plus the accusative here is "beyond hope," not adversarial opposition to hope: Abraham believed beyond the point where ordinary hope could reach, not in defiance of some competing hope.

Romans 1:25 — "who worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator." παρά with the accusative denotes a mutually exclusive comparison — "rather than," not "more than": the creature was chosen to the complete exclusion of the Creator, not merely preferred above him.

Romans 9:14 — "Is there injustice on God's part?" παρὰ τῷ θεῷ (with God). para tō theō, with God, is literally alongside God, the dative of association, in the sphere of God. The clause asserts by rhetorical question with mē that there is no injustice in the divine sphere; the construction demands a negative answer.

Romans 11:24 — "grafted, contrary to nature." παρὰ φύσιν (contrary to nature). The destination is εἰς plus the accusative καλλιελαίαν, the good or cultivated olive tree, and the grafting is described as παρὰ φύσιν, contrary to nature — a horticultural anomaly, since branches of a wild stock are not ordinarily grafted into cultivated trees. Paul's point: the salvation of the Gentiles is itself an act of divine grace overriding natural categories.

Romans 12:3 — "than he ought to think." παρ’ ὃ δεῖ φρονεῖν (beyond what you ought to think). Para plus the accusative neuter singular of the relative pronoun: the neuter asks what rather than who, pointing to a standard rather than a person. With the impersonal dei, it is necessary, obligatory, the phrase means beyond what is obligatory for one to think.

Romans 12:16 — "Never be wise in your own sight." παρ' ἑαυτοῖς (in your own estimation). Para with the locative plural of the reflexive pronoun, literally by yourselves, functions as an idiom meaning in your own estimation. The reflexive refers the action back to its own subject: stop being wise in your own estimation.

Romans 14:5 — "one day as better than another." παρά (greater than). ἡμέρα appears twice in the first clause: once as object of the verb and once with παρά plus the accusative, which here carries the comparative sense greater than: judges one day greater than another day. This comparative use of παρά is a standard classical construction indicating superiority or preference.

ἐπί — Sense Shifts by Case

Romans 4:5 — "believes in him who justifies the ungodly" — the fuller construction elsewhere in this discussion using ἐπί with a case governs the object of belief/trust.

Romans 4:18 — "as he had been told, 'So shall your offspring be.'" The construction governing what the promise rests "upon" uses ἐπί in a locative/basis sense.

Romans 5:14 — "Yet death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those whose sinning was not like the transgression of Adam." The reign of death extending "over" a category of persons uses ἐπί in this governing/dominating sense.

Romans 9:5 — "God over all." ἐπὶ πάντων (ruler over all). The predicate nominative theos is followed by epi pantōn, over all. The elliptical force of the expression points to sovereignty: the one who is God, ruler over all.

Romans 9:33 (Isaiah 28:16) — "and whoever believes in him." ἐπί (on, over). The prepositional phrase is ἐπί plus the third-person singular pronoun: to believe on him. ἐπί carries the sense of over as well as on, a deliberate paranomasia: you have stumbled over the rock; now come back and believe on the rock. The inversion of the stumbling becomes the invitation to faith.

Romans 10:11 — "believes in him." ἐπί (on him). Epi plus the locative of autos (serving as the third-person personal pronoun, Greek having no distinct nominative third-person personal pronoun): on him, Christ as the object of saving faith.

Romans 10:19 (Deuteronomy 32:21) — "those who are not a nation." ἐπί (over a no-nation). Epi plus the locative singular of ethnos, qualified by the negative adverb: over a no-nation, a Gentile nation lacking client-nation status.

Romans 11:13 — "Inasmuch then as I am an apostle to the Gentiles." ἐπί (inasmuch as, to the degree that). The clause opens with ἐπί followed by the relative pronoun ὅσος, indicating extent or degree; with the accusative ἐπί expresses extent or degree: inasmuch as, to the degree that. The inferential οὖν is appended, so the combined force is therefore, to the degree that — a heavily inferential construction that grounds Paul's self-description in the logic of the preceding argument (verses 11–12).

Romans 11:22 — "severity toward those who have fallen." ἐπί (upon). ἐπί with the accusative regularly denotes motion toward or extension over a recipient. The article τούς functions as a demonstrative pronoun, directing attention to the unbelieving Jew as the specific recipient of divine severity — the branches broken off in verse 17.

Romans 15:12 — "in him will the Gentiles hope." ἐπ’ αὐτῷ (in Him). The preposition epi (ἐπί) governs the locative case of the intensive pronoun autos (αὐτός) used as a personal pronoun, yielding 'in him.'

Romans 15:20 — "on someone else's foundation." ἐπ’ ἀλλότριον θεμέλιον (onto a foundation belonging to another). The prepositional phrase ἐπὶ θεμέλιον (epi themelion) uses ἐπί with the accusative to express motion or direction: on, up to, over, onto a foundation.

πρός + Accusative

Directional/relational.

Romans 4:2 — "he has something to boast about, but not before God." πρὸς θεόν — directional/relational: the boasting is oriented toward, and would need to stand up in relation to, God specifically.

Romans 5:1 — "we have peace with God." πρὸς τὸν θεόν — relational: peace is not merely an internal state but a restored relational orientation toward God.

Romans 5:2 — "through whom we have also obtained access... into this grace." The relational directionality of "access" is governed by a πρός-type construction in the underlying Greek argument.

Romans 10:1 — "prayer to God." πρὸς τὸν θεόν (face to face with the God). Pros plus the accusative of theos means face to face with God or to the God. The accusative after pros regularly connotes proximity and personal address, so the phrase carries the relational force of direct approach: prayer brings the believer face to face with God the Father, the specific target and processor of prayer.

Romans 10:21 (Isaiah 65:2) — "But of Israel he says." Ἰσραήλ (face to face with). Pros plus the accusative with the indeclinable proper noun Israēl. Because Israēl takes no case endings, the article indicates the case and thereby the correct sense of the preposition. Pros plus the accusative means face to face with, not simply to: but face to face with Israel.

Romans 15:17 — "my work for God." πρὸς τὸν θεόν (pertaining to God). The closing prepositional phrase is pros (πρός) plus the accusative of theos (θεός), with the definite article — pros ton theon (πρὸς τὸν θεόν). The preposition with the accusative can indicate direction toward, relationship with, or pertaining to. Here the best translation is pertaining to God.

Romans 15:22 — "from coming to you." πρὸς ὑμᾶς (face to face with you). The phrase closes with pros hymas, πρὸς ὑμᾶς — “to you” or “face to face with you,” the preposition pros, πρός with the accusative carrying the nuance of direct, personal encounter.

εἰς + Accusative

Marks predicate result, purpose, or reference.

Romans 1:1 — "set apart for the gospel of God." εἰς εὐαγγέλιον θεοῦ uses εἰς with the accusative to express cause and purpose, not subordination: Paul was appointed because the gospel required an apostle of his specific preparation, not merely placed "under" the gospel.

Romans 4:3 — "it was counted to him as righteousness." εἰς δικαιοσύνην — marks the predicate result: crediting resulting in the status of righteousness.

Romans 4:11 — "he received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith." εἰς σφραγῖδα — marks purpose/result: circumcision given for the purpose of being a seal.

Romans 4:16 — "That is why it depends on faith, in order that the promise may rest on grace and be guaranteed to all his offspring." εἰς marks the purpose of the arrangement.

Romans 4:20 — "No unbelief made him waver concerning the promise of God." The reference-marking function of εἰς-type constructions governs what the unwavering faith concerned.

Romans 5:18 — "so one act of righteousness leads to justification and life for all men." εἰς δικαίωσιν ζωῆς — marks result: the one act of righteousness resulting in justification-of-life.

Romans 6:3 — "all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death." εἰς Χριστόν and εἰς τὸν θάνατον αὐτοῦ — both mark the sphere/result into which the baptism places the believer.

Romans 6:16 — "you are slaves of the one whom you obey, either of sin, which leads to death, or of obedience, which leads to righteousness." εἰς θάνατον and εἰς δικαιοσύνην — both mark result: each pattern of obedience leads to (results in) its respective outcome.

Romans 6:19 — "so now present your members as slaves to righteousness leading to sanctification." εἰς ἁγιασμόν — marks result: righteousness, when consistently presented, results in sanctification.

Romans 8:15 — "for the purpose of fear." εἰς φόβον, an accusative of purpose.

Romans 8:28 — "for the purpose of good." εἰς ἀγαθόν — the preposition with the accusative expressing purpose or result: not merely a favorable outcome but the entire designed result of the divine plan.

Romans 9:5 — "blessed forever." εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας (forever). The temporal phrase eis tous aiōnas, literally to the ages, is an idiom meaning forever.

Romans 9:17 (Exodus 9:16) — "For this very purpose." εἰς αὐτὸ τοῦτο (for this very purpose). Before the verb Paul includes a short prepositional purpose phrase, eis auto touto: eis with the accusative expresses a brief purpose clause. The phrase reads for this same purpose, for this very purpose, establishing that what follows is not incidental but the direct declaration of divine intentionality.

Romans 9:21 — "one vessel for honorable use and another for dishonorable use." εἰς τιμήν / εἰς ἀτιμίαν (for the purpose of honor / for the purpose of dishonor). σκεῦος is a general term for any manufactured container and carries no intrinsic moral content. What differentiates the two categories is εἰς plus the accusative, forming a purpose clause: one vessel is made εἰς τιμήν, for the purpose of honor; the other εἰς ἀτιμίαν, for the purpose of dishonor. The alpha-privative in ἀτιμία negates τιμή: dishonor is the absence or reversal of honor. The distinction is determined by the creature's volitional response to divine authority, not by arbitrary divine assignment.

Romans 9:23 — "which he has prepared beforehand for glory." εἰς δόξαν (for glory, for the purpose of glory). The purpose of the preparation is expressed by εἰς plus the accusative of δόξα: for glory, or more fully, for the purpose of glory. It stands in deliberate contrast to for destruction (εἰς ἀπώλειαν) closing verse 22; the chiastic movement destruction / glory summarizes the two trajectories diverging from a single lump of clay: negative volition produces a vessel for destruction; positive volition, as previously prepared by God on the basis of His foreknowledge, a vessel for glory.

Romans 9:31 — "did not succeed in reaching that law." εἰς νόμον (unto the law; the purpose of the law). The final prepositional phrase εἰς νόμον, into or unto the law, is rendered in the corrected translation as the purpose of the law: the goal toward which the pursuit was directed but which was never reached.

Romans 10:1 — "that they may be saved." εἰς σωτηρίαν (for salvation). The third prepositional phrase is eis plus the accusative of sōtēria, for salvation. The directional force of eis points to salvation as the goal toward which the prayer is aimed.

Romans 10:4 — "for righteousness." εἰς δικαιοσύνην (with reference to righteousness). Eis with the accusative expresses reference or respect: with reference to righteousness. Christ is the termination of the law not in every conceivable sense but specifically with respect to how a person obtains standing before God. The phrase eliminates the law as a means of producing righteousness acceptable to God.

Romans 10:10 — "and is justified." εἰς δικαιοσύνην (resulting in righteousness). Eis with the accusative of dikaiosynē expresses result: resulting in righteousness, the imputed righteousness of God. In the second clause eis with the accusative of sōtēria likewise expresses result: resulting in salvation. The mouth does not produce salvation; it expresses before God what has already been accomplished in the right lobe through faith.

Romans 10:14 — "in whom they have not believed." εἰς (in whom). The object of calling is expressed by eis plus the accusative of the relative pronoun hos, correctly in whom. In later Koine eis plus the accusative frequently absorbed the function of en plus the dative, and the usage here retains that idiomatic sense.

Romans 11:9 (Psalm 69:22) — "a snare and a trap, a stumbling block and a retribution for them." εἰς (for a snare). Four phrases of εἰς with the accusative (παγίδα, θήραν, σκάνδαλον, ἀνταπόδομα) state what the table becomes: εἰς παγίδα means for a snare, into the function of a snare. The snare is the existence of responsibility: possessing the written Word, the Levitical ritual pointing to Christ, and the prophetic testimony creates accountability.

Romans 11:32 — "consigned all to disobedience." εἰς ἀπείθειαν (with reference to disobedience). εἰς plus the accusative of ἀπείθεια (a state of disobedience, willful rejection of divine authority) expresses the sphere or condition into which the human race has been locked: the structural state of disobedience resulting from the imputation of Adam's original sin.

Romans 11:36 — "to him are all things." εἰς αὐτόν (for Him). εἰς αὐτόν — eis plus the accusative of autos — is rendered for Him with reference to time: all things exist for Him, pointing to the purposive goal of history in the person of Christ. Christ controls history as its source, its agent, and its goal.

Romans 12:16 — "Live in harmony with one another." εἰς (toward one another). Eis, the preposition of direction or purpose with the accusative, plus the reciprocal allēlous specifies the object of the commanded thinking: other believers. The preposition implies active movement of thought toward the other person, not passive awareness.

Romans 13:4 — "for your good." εἰς τὸ ἀγαθόν (for the purpose of the good). The advantage is defined by εἰς τὸ ἀγαθόν, for the purpose of the good. The generic article with ἀγαθός ties the phrase to Romans 8:28: the good here is the specific good defined by the Protocol Plan of God, the freedom necessary for evangelism, daily intake of Bible doctrine, and maturity adjustment to the justice of God.

Romans 13:4 — "an avenger who carries out God's wrath." εἰς (for the purpose of divine wrath). εἰς with the accusative of ὀργή expresses purpose or goal: for the purpose of divine wrath. The punitive function of civil authority is therefore not merely sociological but theological; it participates within its bounded sphere in the divine administration of justice.

Romans 14:9 — "For to this end." εἰς τοῦτο (for this reason, for this purpose, from εἰς). The verse opens with εἰς τοῦτο, the preposition governing the accusative neuter demonstrative: for this reason or for this purpose. It is immediately followed by explanatory γάρ (you see, for), signaling that what follows explains and integrates everything developed in the preceding verses.

Romans 15:2 — "for his good." εἰς τὸ ἀγαθόν (for the purpose of the good). The first prepositional phrase is εἰς (eis) plus the accusative singular of ἀγαθός (agathos) with the definite article: εἰς τὸ ἀγαθόν. The preposition eis plus the accusative expresses purpose: for the purpose of. The definite article before agathos denotes a distinct, identifiable category — not generic goodness, but the specific good that Paul has already defined earlier in Romans.

Romans 15:4 — "was written for our instruction." εἰς διδασκαλίαν (for our instruction). The preposition is eis (εἰς, for, unto) plus the accusative singular of didaskalian (διδασκαλίαν, instruction, teaching) with the possessive pronoun hēmeteran (ἡμετέραν, our). The sense is: for our instruction, instruction that belongs to us as Church Age believers.

Romans 15:7 — "for the glory of God." εἰς δόξαν τοῦ θεοῦ (for the purpose of the glory of God). The verse closes with the preposition eis (εἰς) plus the accusative singular of doxa (δόξα) and the possessive genitive of theos (θεός): for the purpose of the glory of God.

Romans 15:18 — "to bring the Gentiles to obedience." εἰς ὑπακοήν (resulting in obedience). A prepositional phrase follows: εἰς ὑπακοήν (eis hypakoēn). Εἰς (eis) plus the accusative introduces a result clause. ὑπακοή (hypakoē) means obedience.

Romans 15:25 — "I am going to Jerusalem." εἰς Ἰερουσαλήμ (to Jerusalem). The prepositional phrase is eis Ierousalēm (εἰς Ἱερουσαλήμ), to Jerusalem. The preposition eis with the accusative indicates directional movement toward a goal.

Romans 16:6 — "who has worked hard for you." εἰς ὑμᾶς (for you). The prepositional phrase eis hymas (εἰς ὑμᾶς) — rendered 'for you' or 'on your behalf' — directs the labor outward toward the Roman congregation. The object of her work was others.

Romans 16:19 — "For your obedience is known to all." εἰς πάντας (to all). The accusative plural eis pantas (εἰς πάντας) — preposition eis (εἰς) plus adjective pas (πᾶς) — means to all or to everyone. The corrected translation of the full clause: Certainly, the report of your obedience has become known to all.

Romans 16:19 — "wise as to what is good." σοφοὺς … εἰς τὸ ἀγαθόν (wise with reference to the good). The accusative plural of sophos (σοφός) — wise ones, learned ones, sagacious ones — governs the prepositional phrase that follows. The preposition eis (εἰς) plus the accusative singular of agathos (ἀγαθός) forms a technical expression: wise with reference to the good. In the Epistle to the Romans, agathos in this technical sense refers specifically to the plan of God.

Romans 16:26 — "has been made known to all nations." εἰς πάντα τὰ ἔθνη (to all the Gentiles). The prepositional phrase that follows is eis (εἰς) + pas (πᾶς) + ethnos (ἔθνος): literally, 'to all the Gentiles.'

ὑπέρ — Substitution

Expresses substitution: "instead of," "in place of."

Romans 5:6 — "Christ died for the ungodly." ὑπὲρ ἀσεβῶν — substitution: Christ died in the place of the ungodly, not merely on their behalf in a general sense.

Romans 5:7 — "For one will scarcely die for a righteous person." ὑπὲρ δικαίου — the same substitutionary preposition applied to the human analogy Paul introduces.

Romans 5:8 — "while we were still sinners, Christ died for us." ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν — substitution: Christ's death stands in the place of what the sinner would otherwise owe.

Romans 8:32 — "gave him up for us all." ὑπέρ plus the genitive of πᾶς and the first-person pronoun expresses substitutionary atonement: on behalf of, in place of, all of us.

Romans 8:26 — the compound ὑπερεντυγχάνει (see the vocabulary entry, section XIX) is itself built on ὑπέρ, "on behalf of," fused directly into the verb.

Romans 9:3 — "for the sake of my brothers." ὑπὲρ τῶν ἀδελφῶν μου (for the sake of my brethren). huper plus the genitive expresses substitutionary benefit: in behalf of, or for the sake of, my brethren. adelphos here designates the racial Jew, Paul's fellow members of the same genetic line from Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, not spiritual brotherhood in the body of Christ.

Romans 10:1 — "for them." ὑπέρ (on behalf of). Hyper with the ablative plural of autos (serving as a third-person personal pronoun) expresses substitutionary or representational intercession, on behalf of them, referring to unbelieving Israel. In prayer, hyper marks the intercessor as standing in the place of another before God.

Romans 14:15 — "the one for whom Christ died." ὑπέρ (in behalf of whom). ὑπέρ with the ablative singular of the relative pronoun ὅς yields in behalf of whom or instead of whom, the prepositional phrase of substitution. It emphasizes that Christ's death was a judicial substitute for both the strong and the weak believer, and brings Christ into focus as the origin and exemplar of the royal family honor code.

ἀπό — "From," Marking Separation or Source

Romans 7:9 — "I was once alive apart from the law." χωρὶς νόμου (using χωρίς rather than ἀπό, an improper preposition meaning "apart from, separate from") marks Paul's condition as one of separation from the law's diagnostic function specifically — not physical distance but conceptual/experiential separation from the law's exposing work.

Romans 9:3 — "cut off from Christ." ἀπὸ τοῦ Χριστοῦ (separated from the Christ). The prepositional phrase apo Christou is the genitive of separation: consequently separated from the Christ.

Romans 11:25 — "a partial hardening has come upon Israel." ἀπὸ μέρους (in part). With the subject πώρωσις (hardness, insensibility, obstinacy — scar tissue of the soul, the blackout of the soul) stands ἀπὸ μέρους, apo plus μέρος (a part, portion, division), correctly translated in part. The hardening is partial, not universal: in every generation there are Jews who believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, the true Israel of Romans 9:6.

Romans 15:15 — "on some points." ἀπὸ μέρους (in certain parts). The prepositional phrase apo merous (ἀπὸ μέρους) is an idiom meaning in certain parts or in some sections. It refers to specific passages within the epistle — passages of heightened urgency in which Paul has sounded a red alert, calling believers to doctrinal awareness, thoughtfulness toward others, and sensitivity to their surroundings.

Romans 15:24 — "for a while." ἀπὸ μέρους (in part). The prepositional phrase apo merous (ἀπὸ μέρους) — literally 'from a part' — is an idiom meaning partly, in some measure, in part. The phrase is significant: Paul does not expect complete satisfaction with the entire congregation, but with a portion.

ἐν — Locative of Sphere, and the Formula "In Christ"

The preposition ἐν with the locative marks either a literal location or, throughout Paul, the sphere of positional union with Christ — the standard formula for positional truth.

Romans 3:24 — "and are justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus." ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ (ἐν + locative/dative) marks the sphere in which redemption is located — positional truth language consistent with Paul's usage throughout Romans.

Romans 8:1 — "no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus." ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ is the standard positional-truth formula, marking the sphere of the believer's union with Christ established by the baptism of the Holy Spirit.

Romans 8:2 — "in Christ Jesus" recurs in the same technical sense.

Romans 8:9 — "you are... in the Spirit." ἐν πνεύματι, locative of sphere, marking the believer's realm of existence as under the Spirit's domain rather than the flesh's.

Romans 9:1 — "in Christ." Χριστός (in Christ). Christos with en: in Christ. Paul, though a Jew by physical birth, is Royal Family of God through regeneration. By this phrase he separates himself from the Old Testament writers and their gift of prophecy; he writes under the gift of apostleship, locating himself within the Church Age dispensation and its unique doctrinal content.

Romans 9:1 — "in the Holy Spirit." ἐν πνεύματι ἁγίῳ (in the Holy Spirit). The phrase en pneumati hagiō closes the genitive absolute: the conscience of the human writer bears joint testimony in conjunction with and under the authority of the Holy Spirit, the ultimate author of Scripture.

Romans 9:26 (Hosea 1:10) — "And in the very place where it was said to them." ἐν τῷ τόπῳ οὗ (in the place where, from τόπος). The prepositional phrase is ἐν plus the locative of τόπος (place, location), followed by the adverb of place οὗ (where). The combined phrase designates a specific geographical location: the land of Israel, the same territory overrun by the Assyrians in 721 BC. In that same land the second advent reversal will occur; the same land of judgment becomes the land of fulfillment.

Romans 10:8 — "in your mouth." ἐν (in your mouth). En plus the locative of stoma with the possessive genitive of su: in your mouth. The mouth is the organ of expression; the illustration demonstrates proximity, nothing external to the person being as near as his own mouth, and establishes that salvation is conveyed by no external ceremony, rite, or physical act.
