Romans 11:2 (1 Kings 19:10, 14) — "what the Scripture says about Elijah." ἐν Ἠλίᾳ (about Elijah, in the passage concerning Elijah, from ἐν). ἐν Ἠλίᾳ is a prepositional phrase of reference. ἐν with a personal noun in the dative marks the textual locus of the citation, the section of Scripture dealing with the named individual, here 1 Kings 19:10 and 14.

Romans 11:25 — "Lest you be wise in your own sight." ἑαυτοῦ (in your own estimation). The predicate adjective φρόνιμος (wise, prudent) takes its precise meaning from the phrase ἐν plus the dative of the reflexive ἑαυτοῦ: literally in yourselves, idiomatically in your own estimation. Taken alone, stop being wise would contradict the thrust of the epistle; the command is to cease self-generated, self-referential intellectual arrogance rooted in doctrinal ignorance.

Romans 12:7 — "in his teaching." διδασκαλία (in the gift of teaching). En plus the locative of didaskalia means in the sphere of the teaching, that is, within the gift: the pastor-teacher functions within this sphere rather than diverting into service or administration.

Romans 12:8 — "in his exhortation." παράκλησις (in the gift of counseling). En plus the locative singular of the cognate noun paraklēsis: in the sphere of the gift of counseling. If counseling, then counsel in the gift of counseling.

Romans 14:14 — "in the Lord Jesus." ἐν κυρίῳ Ἰησοῦ (in the Lord Jesus, from ἐν). The phrase defines the sphere within which the confidence operates: confidence grounded in union with Christ, the believer's positional truth established by the baptism of the Spirit at salvation. Within that union God has a plan for each individual that demands inflexibility in the doctrinal essentials and full flexibility in the non-essentials.

Romans 14:18 — "Whoever thus serves Christ is acceptable to God and approved by men." ἐν τούτῳ (in this, from ἐν). ἐν with the locative singular of the demonstrative οὗτος refers back to the function of the royal family honor code just described: the mature believer's flexibility in the non-essentials, superseding the law of liberty with the law of love. He serves the Christ in this.

Romans 15:9 — "I will praise you among the Gentiles." ἐν ἔθνεσι (among the Gentiles). The prepositional phrase is en (ἐν) plus the locative plural of ethnos (ἔθνος): en ethnesin, meaning among the Gentiles. The Septuagint renders the Hebrew precisely with this Greek phrase, and Paul quotes accordingly.

Romans 15:17 — "In Christ Jesus." ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ (in Christ Jesus). The prepositional phrase en Christō Iēsou (ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ) establishes the sphere within which this esprit de corps exists. En plus the locative indicates that positional union with Christ is the ground of the communicator's confidence.

Romans 16:8 — "Greet Ampliatus, my beloved in the Lord." τὸν ἀγαπητόν μου ἐν κυρίῳ (my beloved in the Lord). He is identified by a single appositional phrase: 'my beloved in the Lord,' from the accusative agapētos (ἀγαπητός) plus the prepositional phrase en kyriō (ἐν κυρίῳ), 'in the Lord' — designating positional relationship to Christ as the basis of the bond.

ὑπέρ + Genitive of Reference — Concerning

Romans 9:27 (Isaiah 10:22) — "concerning Israel." ὑπέρ (concerning, with reference to). ὑπέρ with the genitive of reference governs the indeclinable proper noun Ἰσραήλ (indeclinable, as is standard for Semitic proper nouns in Greek). The genitive of reference indicates the subject matter or concern of Isaiah's proclamation: he speaks with reference to Israel. This is distinguished from the accusative use of ὑπέρ, which conveys spatial or representational senses.

ἕως — Improper Preposition, Until

Romans 11:8 (Deuteronomy 29:4) — "down to this very day." ἕως (until this very day). ἕως, an improper preposition taking the genitive, forms with σήμερον and ἡμέρα the idiom until this very day, drawn from Deuteronomy 29:4. It is a roving expression anchored to no calendar date but advancing with the moment of reading: true in AD 58, at AD 70, and through every Church Age generation until the second advent and the restoration of Israel.

κατά — Adverbial Individually

Romans 12:5 — "and individually members one of another." κατά (individually). The preposition kata functions adverbially in Koine idiom to mean individually, followed by the predicate nominative plural of melos, parts: and individually parts one of another. The individuality of each believer within the one body provides the framework for the doctrine of spiritual gifts in verses 6–8.

μετά — With (Genitive) vs. After (Accusative)

Romans 12:15 — "Rejoice with those who rejoice." μετά (with). Meta plus the genitive plural of the present participle of chairō. With the genitive meta means with, a rapport preposition expressing participation and association; with the accusative it means after. The participle is an aoristic present: while their rejoicing lasts, the command requires sharing that joy.

Romans 15:10 — "with his people." μετὰ τοῦ λαοῦ αὐτοῦ (with His people). The prepositional phrase with His people is meta (μετά) plus the genitive singular of laos (λαός) with the possessive genitive of the intensive pronoun autos (αὐτός), used in Koine Greek as the third-person personal pronoun: his. Meta with the genitive indicates accompaniment — Gentiles rejoicing together with the Jewish people of God.

Romans 16:20 — "The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you." μεθ’ ὑμῶν (with you). The prepositional phrase meta (μετά) plus the genitive plural of sy (σύ) — meth' hymōn (μεθ’ ὑμῶν) — means 'with you,' carrying the force of accompaniment and protection.

ἀντί — Substitution, Instead Of

Romans 12:17 — "evil for evil." ἀντί (for). Anti is a substitutionary preposition meaning instead of or against. In the idiomatic kakon anti kakou it produces evil for evil, retaliation in kind.

ἐνώπιον — Improper Preposition In the Sight Of

Romans 12:17 — "in the sight of all." ἐνώπιον (in the sight of). The improper preposition enōpion, governing the genitive, plus pas anthrōpos denotes visibility before an audience: the believer’s respect for what is honorable is to be visible to all mankind, not merely to fellow believers.

περί + Genitive — The Subject Matter of the Account

Romans 14:12 — "of himself." περὶ ἑαυτοῦ (concerning himself, from περί). περί with the genitive of the reflexive pronoun denotes the subject matter of the account: the believer's own life and decisions. It categorically excludes bringing anyone else into the accounting; no deflection, no mitigating circumstances supplied by others, and no advocate.

Improper Prepositions — ἕνεκεν, ἐνώπιον

Romans 14:20 — "for the sake of food." βρῶμα (because of food). βρῶμα is used with the improper preposition ἕνεκεν to form the phrase because of food or on account of food that opens 14:20. The term covers all categories of dietary substance.

Romans 14:22 — "between yourself and God." ἐνώπιον (before God). The adverb ἐνώπιον functions as an improper preposition with the genitive of θεός: before God, in the sight of God. It establishes the vertical axis of the command: the mature believer's doctrinal norms exist in relationship to God, not to what he can persuade other believers to accept.

μέχρι — As Far As

Romans 15:19 — "all the way around to Illyricum." κύκλῳ μέχρι τοῦ Ἰλλυρικοῦ (on a circuit as far as Illyricum). The phrase kai kuklō mechri tou Illyrikou (καὶ κύκλῳ μέχρι τοῦ Ἰλλυρικοῦ) is rendered in some translations as round about unto Illyricum, but the correct translation is: on a circuit, even on a circuit, as far as Illyricum. The locative singular kuklō (κύκλῳ) means on a circuit or in a ring. The preposition mechri (μέχρι) plus the genitive of Illyrikon (Ἰλλυρικόν) means as far as Illyricum.

παρά — Three Cases, Three Meanings

Romans 16:17 — "contrary to the doctrine that you have been taught." παρὰ τὴν διδαχήν (contrary to the doctrine). The preposition para (παρά) governs three different cases with three distinct meanings: with the ablative, 'from'; with the locative, 'alongside'; with the accusative, 'against' or 'contrary to.' Here it governs the accusative of didachē (διδαχή), 'doctrine' or 'teaching.' The meaning is therefore 'contrary to the doctrine.'

ὑπό + Accusative — Under

Romans 16:20 — "crush Satan under your feet." ὑπὸ τοὺς πόδας ὑμῶν (under your feet). The phrase hypo tous podas hymōn (ὑπὸ τοὺς πόδας ὑμῶν) — hypo (ὑπό) plus the accusative plural of pous (πούς), foot, with the genitive plural of the personal pronoun sy (σύ) — is correctly translated under your feet.

XVIII.Particles and Conjunctions

Romans 2:3 — "Do you suppose... that you will escape the judgment of God?" ὅτι here is objective, introducing the content of what is presumed rather than functioning causally: "that you will escape" — the object of the self-righteous person's presumption.

Romans 3:9 — "What then? Are we Jews any better off? Not at all." The abrupt volley of short rhetorical questions is Paul's own debater's technique, immediately overturning the very premise he has voiced.

γάρ — Inferential/Explanatory "For"

Introduces the ground or explanation of a preceding statement.

Romans 1:18 — "For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven." γάρ here is illative — "therefore, for this reason" — the logical linchpin connecting the revelation of God's justice in blessing (v. 17) to its revelation in judgment (v. 18): because justice is revealed as blessing for the adjusted, it is therefore also revealed as judgment against the maladjusted.

Romans 2:1 — "For in passing judgment on another you condemn yourself." γάρ here is explanatory and causal: it introduces the reason the self-righteous judge stands without defense — in the very sphere in which he judges others, he practices the same things.

Romans 2:25 — "For circumcision indeed is of value if you obey the law." γάρ gives the apodosis its explanatory, confirmatory force: "so on the one hand, circumcision is indeed beneficial."

Romans 3:2 — "To begin with, the Jews were entrusted with the oracles of God." πρῶτον μέν does not mean "chiefly," as older translations render it, but "in the first place" — the primary item in an intended sequence of advantages, completed by γάρ and ὅτι: "for since in the first place."

Romans 3:3 — "Well then, how stands the case with regard to the two alternatives?" τί γάρ, an idiom composed of the interrogative τί and the postpositive γάρ, is the Koine equivalent of the classical τί πότερος: it introduces two mutually exclusive alternatives — here, adjustment and maladjustment to the justice of God — not a literal "for what?"

Romans 3:22–23 — "for there is no distinction: for all have sinned." γάρ in its explanatory function occurs twice in close succession, each time supplying the grounds for the preceding assertion: no distinction between Jew and Gentile, because all alike have sinned.

Romans 3:28 — "For we hold that one is justified by faith apart from works of the law." γάρ here draws the concluding inference of the entire argument developed since 3:21.

Romans 4:2 — "For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about." γάρ introduces the ground for the rhetorical question of verse 1.

Romans 4:3 — "For what does the Scripture say?" γάρ introduces the scriptural warrant.

Romans 4:13 — "For the promise to Abraham... did not come through the law." γάρ grounds the preceding assertion about the nature of Abraham's heirship.

Romans 5:6 — "For while we were still weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly." γάρ introduces the explanatory ground of the hope just described.

Romans 5:7 — "For one will scarcely die for a righteous person." γάρ introduces the illustrative human analogy.

Romans 6:7 — "For one who has died has been set free from sin." γάρ grounds the preceding exhortation.

Romans 7:1 — "Do you not know, brothers... that the law is binding on a person only as long as he lives?" γάρ (implicit in the surrounding argument's structure) introduces the illustrative principle that follows.

Romans 7:18 — "For I know that nothing good dwells in me." γάρ grounds Paul's preceding admission with a stated reason.

Romans 8:2 — "For the law of the Spirit of life has set you free." γάρ grounds the "no condemnation" declaration of verse 1 with its causal explanation.

Romans 8:3 — "For God has done what the law, weakened by the flesh, could not do." γάρ explains why the law's righteous requirement needed a different solution.

Romans 8:15 — "For you did not receive the spirit of slavery." γάρ grounds the assertion of verse 14 (that those led by the Spirit are sons of God).

Romans 8:16 — introduces the following clause's tie to what precedes: the Spirit's witness explains and confirms the sonship just asserted.

Romans 8:38 — "For I am sure that neither death nor life..." γάρ grounds Paul's confidence in the preceding rhetorical question-and-answer sequence about separation from Christ's love.

Romans 9:3 — "For I could wish." γάρ (for). Verse 3 opens with the explanatory particle gar, which connects Paul's wish to be cherem to his declaration of grief in verses 1–2, providing the content and measure of that grief.

Romans 9:6 — "For not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel." γάρ (for). The second clause begins with the explanatory use of gar, introducing the ground or explanation of the preceding denial.

Romans 9:9 (Genesis 18:10) — "For this is what the promise said." γάρ (for). Verse 9 opens with the post-positive explanatory gar, signalling that additional explanation of the claim of verse 8 is forthcoming: verse 9 supplies the scriptural grounding by citing the word of promise from Genesis 18:10.

Romans 9:11 — "though they were not yet born." γάρ (for). The verse opens with the explanatory, post-positive gar, marking a parenthesis inserted to explain the second case history of the twins; its understood subject, Esau and Jacob, is drawn from the preceding verse.

Romans 9:15 (Exodus 33:19) — "For he says to Moses." γάρ (for). The verse opens with gar in its explanatory function, introducing a clause that grounds the argument about Israel's election in the historical event of the Exodus, linking the origin of the Jewish nation to the principle governing all believers, the divine decrees of election, foreknowledge and predestination.

Romans 9:17 — "For the Scripture says to Pharaoh." γάρ (for). The explanatory postpositive gar has introduced each successive verse of this passage, linking each explanation to the one before it in a chain of logically dependent clauses, a structural pattern that displays remarkable rhetorical discipline.

Romans 9:19 — "For who can resist his will?" γάρ (then, therefore). The second debater's question opens with the inferential post-positive conjunctive particle γάρ. It is not a simple connective but an inferential particle: the second question is logically generated by the first, so in this context the inferential sense is better rendered then or therefore than for.

Romans 9:28 (Isaiah 10:23) — "for the Lord will carry out his sentence upon the earth." γάρ (for). The verse opens with the postpositive explanatory γάρ, connecting it to the statement in verse 27 that the remnant shall be saved. γάρ here explains the basis and manner of that salvation: the Lord will execute His word in fulfillment of what He decreed.

Romans 10:2 — "For I bear them witness." γάρ. The verse opens with the explanatory use of the post-positive particle gar, for. Post-positive particles never begin a Greek sentence; gar always occupies second position. Here it introduces the evidence that supports Paul's prayer and concern stated in verse 1.

Romans 10:3 — "For, being ignorant." γάρ. Gar stands second in the Greek but moves to the front of the English clause. This is the explanatory use: Paul explains the ground for his statement in verse 2 that Israel's zeal is not according to knowledge of doctrine; zeal divorced from doctrine is the functional consequence of not knowing what God's righteousness is.

Romans 10:4 — "For Christ is the end of the law." γάρ. Gar introduces the cause or reason for the preceding statement, grounding verse 4 in verses 1–3: Israel's failure to submit to God's righteousness is explained by the fact that Christ is the termination of the law with reference to righteousness.

Romans 10:5 — "For Moses writes." γάρ. Gar is explanatory here, you see: what follows explains verse 4's assertion that Christ is the termination of the law with reference to righteousness, introducing Old Testament documentation.

Romans 10:10 — "For with the heart one believes." γάρ. Gar, for you see, introduces the logical ground for verse 9: the reason mouth and mind together constitute the nearness of salvation is that faith in the right lobe is the source and the verbal acknowledgment is the result.

Romans 10:12 — "For there is no distinction." γάρ. Gar functions as in verse 11: to add explanation to explanation. Verses 11 and 12 are successive layers of inference, each drawing out a further implication of the universal availability of salvation: anyone who believes, no distinction, the same Lord over all.

Romans 10:13 (Joel 2:32) — "For 'everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved." γάρ. Gar is explanatory: Paul provides Old Testament documentation, the scriptural warrant from Joel 2:32, for the assertion of verse 12 that the same Lord is Lord of all, rich toward all who call upon Him.

Romans 11:1 — "For I myself am an Israelite." καὶ γάρ (for also, from γάρ). καὶ γάρ is a compound connective: καί (also, even) plus the post-positive explanatory conjunction γάρ. Together they introduce an amplification of the strong negative that precedes, offering the existence of Paul himself as a believing Israelite as the explanatory ground of his denial that God has repudiated Israel.

Romans 11:21 — "For if God did not spare the natural branches." γάρ (for). Verse 21 opens with γάρ in its explanatory function: it provides the doctrinal ground for the prohibition of verse 20. The reason the Gentile believer must stop thinking in arrogance is that the justice of God has a demonstrated track record of administering discipline without favoritism.

Romans 11:24 — "For if you were cut from what is by nature a wild olive tree." γάρ (for, for you see). The verse opens with the explanatory γάρ in the post-positive position, rendered for or for you see. It introduces the logical basis for the a fortiori argument that follows.

Romans 11:29 — "For the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable." γάρ (for). The verse opens with γάρ functioning explanatorily: what follows is the doctrinal ground for the entire argument of Romans 11 regarding Israel's past rejection, present remnant, and future restoration.

Romans 11:32 — "For God has consigned all to disobedience." γάρ (for). The verse opens with the post-positive inferential γάρ, signalling a logical conclusion drawn from the comparative argument of verses 30–31. It points back to the reciprocal mercy structure; verse 32 identifies the common denominator — the universal lockup of the human race under disobedience.

Romans 11:34 (Isaiah 40:13) — "For who has known the mind of the Lord." τίς (who then). The first rhetorical question opens with τίς followed by the post-positive γάρ in its explanatory use, providing a reason or documentation within an interrogative frame. The combination is correctly rendered who then.

Romans 12:3 — "For by the grace given to me." γάρ (for). An illative use of the post-positive conjunctive particle gar introduces a reason, why the renovation of thought commanded in verse 2 is not merely desirable but necessary, grounding the exhortation in grace as the divine policy for blessing the royal family of God. Such particles immediately discipline the clause to its intended meaning and eliminate false constructions.

Romans 12:4 — "For as in one body." γάρ (for). The postpositive explanatory particle signals that what follows is not a new subject but the necessary explanation of what has preceded: the demanding program of verses 1–3 is explained by the believer’s membership in an eternal royal family whose corporate integrity depends on the proper function of each differentiated part.

Romans 12:19 (Deuteronomy 32:35) — "for it is written." γάρ (for). The post-positive gar expresses cause or reason and functions as a connective link introducing Old Testament documentation (Deuteronomy 32:35) for the prohibition of revenge: the reason this command stands is that the following stands written.

Romans 13:1 — "For there is no authority except from God." γάρ (for). γάρ is used in its explanatory function. It signals that what follows is not a separate assertion but the theological ground of the preceding imperative: the command to subordinate oneself rests on a theological reality about the nature and source of all authority.

Romans 13:3 — "For rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad." γάρ (for). Explanatory γάρ introduces the ground or reason for the principle of verses 1–2: authority is not to be resisted because it serves a divinely ordained protective function.

Romans 13:6 — "For because of this you also pay taxes." γάρ (for, for this reason). γάρ is used here in its inferential sense, drawing a self-evident truth from verse 5: because establishment authority is the servant of God, participation in that authority through taxation is the obvious obligation of the believer.

Romans 13:9 — "For the commandments." γάρ (for instance). Explanatory γάρ is rendered for instance: what follows is a concrete illustration of the principle of verse 8 that love fulfills the law.

Romans 14:3 — "for God has welcomed him." γάρ (for). The explanatory clause is introduced by the post-positive particle γάρ in its explanatory function: what follows gives the ground for the double prohibition of contempt and judging. The mature believer is the friend of God, so judging him is an assault on the divine master’s household.

Romans 14:7 — "For none of us lives to himself." γάρ (for). Verse 7 opens with the explanatory, post-positive γάρ, linking it to the preceding context rather than introducing an independent maxim. It introduces the doctrinal basis for the honor code obligations of verse 6.

Romans 14:15 — "For if your brother is grieved by what you eat." γάρ (for). Verse 15 opens with a causal clause introduced by the postpositive γάρ, expressing cause or reason. It introduces the causal basis for the honor-code obligation of the strong believer.

Romans 14:17 — "For the kingdom of God." γάρ (for). In verse 17 γάρ carries a stronger inferential force than its usual explanatory sense. It signals that the time has come to draw a conclusion, a scale of priorities, from the sustained argument of Romans 14:1–16: a transition from sustained argument to doctrinal conclusion.

Romans 14:18 — "Whoever thus serves Christ is acceptable to God and approved by men." γάρ (for). The verse opens with the explanatory conjunctive particle γάρ, linking the statement to the preceding context and signalling a new unit of thought. In ancient manuscripts, with letters run together and no punctuation, such particles were primary markers of syntactical transition and have been undervalued as tools of interpretation.

Romans 15:4 — "For whatever was written in former days." γάρ (for). Verse 4 opens with the explanatory conjunction gar (γάρ), which answers the implicit question: why does Paul document his argument from the Old Testament when believers now live in the Church Age? The answer follows immediately.

Romans 15:8 — "For I tell you." γάρ (for). Verse 8 begins with the post-positive conjunctive particle gar (γάρ), used here to express inference leading to a self-evident conclusion.

Romans 15:18 — "For I will not venture to speak." οὐ γάρ (for not). The verse begins with οὐ γάρ (ou gar), the post-positive explanatory conjunction gar combined with the negative ou. The conjunction is explanatory — "for" — and the negative is the first of two negatives in the verse.

Romans 15:26 — "For Macedonia and Achaia." γάρ (for). The verse opens with the explanatory post-positive conjunctive particle gar (γάρ), which signals that Paul is now explaining the reason for his projected Jerusalem journey.

Romans 16:18 — "For such persons." γάρ (for). The verse opens with the post-positive conjunctive particle gar (γάρ), used here in its explanatory function: for. It provides the doctrinal rationale for the command to separate issued in verse 17.

οὖν — Inferential "Therefore"

Marks a logical conclusion drawn from what precedes.

Romans 2:1 — "Therefore you have no excuse, O man." διό is an inferential conjunction introducing a self-evidently drawn conclusion — distinguished from οὖν, which signals a non-obvious inference requiring deliberate reasoning: the verdict on self-righteousness follows necessarily and immediately from chapter 1.

Romans 3:1 — "Then what advantage has the Jew?" οὖν is inferential, signaling that the question arises from the demonstration in chapter 2 that divine justice is perfectly impartial toward Jew and Gentile alike.

Romans 3:31 — "Do we then overthrow the law by this faith? By no means! On the contrary, we uphold the law." ἀλλά here is the strong adversative introducing the positive counter-assertion after the categorical negation μὴ γένοιτο — "on the contrary," not the weaker "yea" of older translations. οὖν, opening the verse, draws the inference from the unity of the Godhead established in verse 30.

Romans 5:1 — "Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God." οὖν draws the conclusion of the entire argument of chapters 1–4.

Romans 6:1 — "What shall we say then? Are we to continue in sin?" οὖν ties the rhetorical question to the preceding discussion of grace abounding.

Romans 6:12 — "Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body." οὖν draws the practical imperative from the doctrinal argument just completed.

Romans 7:3 — "Accordingly, she will be called an adulteress if she lives with another man while her husband is alive." οὖν (implicit as "accordingly" in the sense-flow) draws the conclusion from the principle stated in verse 2.

Romans 7:25 — "So then, I myself serve the law of God with my mind." ἄρα οὖν, a doubled inferential construction, drawing the strongest possible logical conclusion from the entire preceding wretched-man argument.

Romans 8:1 — "There is therefore now no condemnation." ἄρα (a close cousin of οὖν, also inferential) draws the triumphant conclusion of the whole argument running from Romans 5 through 7.

Romans 8:12 — "So then, brothers, we are debtors, not to the flesh." ἄρα οὖν again, drawing the practical obligation from the doctrinal argument of the preceding verses.

Romans 8:31 — "What then shall we say to these things?" οὖν ties the triumphant rhetorical question to the entire preceding chain of doctrine.

Romans 9:14 — "What shall we say then?" οὖν (therefore). The interrogative tis, here neuter, is correctly rendered what rather than who. The post-positive inferential oun, always the second word in its clause, functions in this formula question as an idiom of conclusion: the question is designed to draw a conclusion from what has preceded. Corrected translation: Therefore to what conclusion are we forced?

Romans 9:19 — "You will say to me then." οὖν (therefore). The post-positive inferential oun indicates that the debater's questions being introduced are inferences the opposition draws from Paul's argument about the hardening of Pharaoh's heart: Therefore you will say to me.

Romans 10:14 — "How then will they call on him." πῶς (consequently, how). The interrogative particle pōs, used for a direct question about how something comes to be, is coupled with an inferential particle signaling that the clause introduces a result from what precedes. The combined force is consequently, how: what follows is the logical result of verse 13.

Romans 11:1 — "I ask, then." οὖν (therefore, then). The post-positive inferential particle οὖν draws a logical inference from what precedes, here the material of Romans 9:16–33 and 10:19–21. It introduces the debater question of Romans 11:1 as flowing directly out of those conclusions.

Romans 12:1 — "I appeal to you therefore." οὖν (therefore). The inferential conjunction denotes that what follows is an inference from what has preceded. It reaches back across the parenthesis of chapters 9–11 to the doctrinal summit of chapter 8: Romans 8 describes the mature believer and the X + Y + Z imputation plan, and Romans 12 draws the inference of how to advance toward that goal under the honor code of the royal family of God.

Romans 13:7 — "Pay to all what is owed to them." οὖν (therefore). οὖν draws an inference from the argument just concluded. The command to render dues to all generalizes the specific principle of tax payment into a comprehensive account of Christian responsibility toward all aspects of civil authority: taxes, customs, respect, and honor.

Romans 13:12 — "So then let us cast off the works of darkness." οὖν (therefore). Inferential οὖν signals that what follows is a conclusion demanded by the preceding eschatological premise.

Romans 14:8 — "So then, whether we live or whether we die." οὖν (so not only). In the second half of verse 8 the inferential οὖν is combined with the enclitic τε, which shifts the sense from therefore to so not only. The additive τε broadens the scope of the inference, linking the living clause and the dying clause as coordinate members of a single theological statement.

Romans 14:12 — "So then." ἄρα οὖν (so therefore). The illative particle ἄρα and the transitional inferential conjunction οὖν together function as a strong inferential transition (so therefore, consequently then). What follows is the inescapable logical conclusion drawn from the eschatological reality just stated: the big genuflection and the judgment seat of Christ generate immediate and binding practical consequences for how each believer lives today.

Romans 14:13 (Isaiah 45:23) — "Therefore." οὖν (therefore). The inferential conjunction οὖν draws a conclusion from the entire preceding discussion: the rapture, the great genuflection of Isaiah 45:23 and the judgment seat of Christ. All of that eschatological instruction has a single practical application: believers are accountable to the Lord, not to one another.

Romans 14:16 — "So do not let what you regard as good be spoken of as evil." οὖν (therefore). Verse 16 opens with the inferential οὖν, indicating that what follows is an inference drawn from the command of verse 15b against destroying the weak believer.

Romans 14:19 — "So then." ἄρα οὖν (consequently, so then). ἄρα is inferential, indicating a logical conclusion; οὖν is likewise inferential with an added transitional force. Together they signal movement toward a weighty and decisive conclusion, best rendered consequently or so then, with the transitional nuance slightly dominant. Verses 17 and 18 were introduced by γάρ; verse 19 shifts from explanatory grounding to conclusive exhortation.

Romans 15:17 — "In Christ Jesus, then, I have reason to be proud." οὖν (therefore). Verse 17 opens with the inferential post-positive conjunctive particle oun (οὖν), correctly rendered therefore.

διό — "Therefore, For Which Reason"

A stronger and more formal inferential particle than οὖν, typically introducing a more weighty or climactic conclusion.

Romans 4:22 — "That is why his faith was counted to him as righteousness." διό introduces the climactic conclusion of the entire Abraham illustration.

Romans 13:5 — "Therefore one must be in subjection." διό (for this reason, therefore). διό marks an inference presented as self-evident. What follows is not a conditional or tentative instruction but a logical conclusion that the argument of verses 1–4 makes inescapable.

Romans 15:7 — "Therefore welcome one another." διό (therefore). The verse opens with the inferential conjunction dio (διό), rendered in the King James as 'wherefore' and here as 'therefore.' Dio signals a self-evident inference — a conclusion so immediately derivable from the preceding context that it requires no elaborate argumentation.

Romans 15:22 — "This is the reason why." διὸ καί (for this reason also). The verse opens with dio kai, διὸ καί — a combination of dio, διό (a self-evident inference: “for this reason,” “therefore”) and the conjunctive kai, καί (“also”).

hoti — Multiple Functions: Causal, Recitative (Quotation), Substantive ("That"), Epexegetical

A single Greek word covering several distinct grammatical functions that English must render with different constructions.

Romans 4:3 — "For what does the Scripture say? 'Abraham believed God...'" ὅτι here is recitative, introducing a direct quotation (equivalent to opening quotation marks) rather than being translated as a word at all.

Romans 4:17 (introducing the Genesis 17:5 quotation) — ὅτι again functions recitatively.

Romans 5:3 — "knowing that suffering produces endurance." ὅτι here introduces a substantive clause functioning as the object of "knowing" — the "that" of indirect statement.

Romans 6:9 — "We know that Christ, being raised from the dead, will never die again." ὅτι as substantive/object clause after εἰδότες.

Romans 7:14 — "For we know that the law is spiritual." ὅτι as substantive/object clause.

Romans 8:16 — "the Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God." ὅτι as substantive clause, the content of the joint testimony.

Romans 8:38–39's closing "For I am sure that neither death nor life..." — ὅτι here is epexegetical, unpacking the specific content of Paul's settled conviction (πέπεισμαι) named at the head of the sentence — functioning almost as a colon in English, introducing the itemized list that follows rather than a simple "that"-clause.

Romans 9:2 — "that I have great sorrow." ὅτι (that). hoti follows immediately upon the triple oath of verse 1 and introduces the content that the oath was sworn to guarantee. It is the content function, translated that, connecting the sworn affirmation of Paul's integrity to the burden he expresses.

Romans 9:6 — "it is not as though the word of God has failed." ὅτι (that). The idiom ouch hoios is concluded by hoti, which resumes the discourse and introduces the content of what is being negated: However, this is not to imply that.

Romans 9:7 — "because they are his offspring." ὅτι (because). Following oude, hoti introduces a causal clause: neither because or not even because, the insufficient ground for inheritance. The full phrase: neither because they are Abraham's seed.

Romans 9:12 (Genesis 25:23) — "'The older will serve the younger.'" ὅτι. After verbs of saying or speaking, hoti functions as a recitative conjunction, the equivalent of opening quotation marks, introducing the content of the divine declaration to Rebecca, the citation of Genesis 25:23.

Romans 9:17 (Exodus 9:16) — "'For this very purpose I have raised you up." ὅτι. Paul introduces the Exodus quotation with hoti functioning as a quotation marker, the Greek equivalent of an opening quotation mark; in this usage it need not be translated, or may be rendered simply as quote.

Romans 9:30 — "That Gentiles who did not pursue righteousness have attained it." ὅτι (that). After the rhetorical question ὅτι functions not merely as that but as a marker signalling that the content of a demanded conclusion is about to be stated: the paradox that Gentiles, outside the covenant economy of the Mosaic law, have secured the righteousness Israel failed to obtain.

Romans 9:32 — "Why? Because they did not pursue it by faith." διὰ τί … ὅτι (Why? Because.). διὰ τί, διά (because, on account of) plus the interrogative pronoun, is a reinforced interrogative meaning why?, pressing the rhetorical point with maximum force; Paul is not asking because he lacks the answer but to bring the hearer to confront his own failure. ὅτι, causal, introduces the answer. The διὰ τί … ὅτι construction is a standard Greek idiom for posing and answering a diagnostic question: Why? Because.

Romans 10:2 — "that they have a zeal for God." ὅτι. After verbs of statement hoti introduces the content of the testimony and is translated that; here it follows martureō to introduce the substance of Paul's testimony about Israel.

Romans 10:5 (Leviticus 18:5) — "that the person who does the commandments shall live by them." ὅτι. After graphō, hoti functions as the hoti recitativum, the Greek device for introducing direct quotation, equivalent to modern quotation marks. Used this way it is not translated; it simply marks the opening of the cited text from Leviticus 18:5.

Romans 10:9 — "because, if you confess." ὅτι (namely). Verse 9 opens with hoti as a content marker after a verb of proclamation: verse 8 said the message is near, and verse 9 specifies its content. The rendering is namely rather than the weaker that: what follows is not a new proposition but the precise content of what has been said to be near.

Romans 11:25 — "a partial hardening has come upon Israel." ὅτι (that). ὅτι, after a verb of perception, introduces the content of that perception as a declarative statement. Here it introduces the specific content of the mystery of which Paul does not wish the Gentile believer to be ignorant.

Romans 11:36 — "For from him and through him and to him are all things." ὅτι (because). The verse opens with causal ὅτι, because, providing the ground for the three rhetorical questions: no one can be God's counselor, advisor, or creditor because all things originate from Him, flow through Him, and exist for Him.

Romans 13:11 — "that the hour has come." ὅτι (that). ὅτι follows a verb of perception and introduces the content of that perception.

Romans 14:11 — "every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to God." ὅτι. ὅτι functions as hoti recitativum, equivalent to opening quotation marks introducing direct speech. It is not translated but signals that what follows is a verbatim oracle from God.

Romans 14:14 — "that nothing is unclean in itself." ὅτι (that). Following verbs of cognizance, ὅτι introduces the content of that cognizance, the specific doctrinal application the mature believer knows and appropriates with confidence. It functions as a subordinating conjunction meaning that.

Romans 14:23 — "because the eating is not from faith." ὅτι (because). ὅτι functions causally here, not as a simple declarative connector. It introduces the reason the weak believer stands in a state of condemnation: he does not act by means of doctrine.

Romans 15:29 — "I know that when I come to you." ὅτι (that). What Paul knows with certainty is the content introduced by the conjunction hoti (ὅτι), which after verbs of perception and knowledge introduces the content of what is known: Now I know that — followed by the substance of his confidence.

Disjunctive ἤ — "Or"

Romans 4:9 — "Is this blessing then only for the circumcised, or also for the uncircumcised?" ἤ poses the genuine alternative the argument will go on to resolve.

Romans 6:16 — "either of sin, which leads to death, or of obedience, which leads to righteousness." ἤ structures the two mutually exclusive options.

Romans 9:21 — "Has the potter no right over the clay." ἤ (Or). In Greek rhetorical convention the particle ἤ introduces a question structured to elicit a predetermined positive response, reinforced here by the negative οὐ within the question (corrected translation: Or does not the potter possess authority over the clay).

Romans 10:7 — "or 'Who will descend into the abyss?'" ἤ (or). Verse 7 opens with the disjunctive particle ē, or, functioning as an interrogative particle. It introduces a question parallel to that of verse 6, followed immediately by tis, who.

Romans 11:2 — "Or do you not know what the Scripture says about Elijah." ἤ (or). Verse 2b opens with the disjunctive particle ἤ. It opens the clause with rhetorical force, implying that the preceding statement should already preclude the need for the question that follows.

Romans 11:34 — "or who has been his counselor?" ἤ (or). The second question is introduced by the disjunctive ἤ, used in an interrogative sentence to introduce and add a further rhetorical question; rendered or. It appears twice in Romans 11:34–35, introducing the second and third rhetorical questions of the doxology.

Romans 14:10 — "Or you, why do you despise your brother?" ἢ (or, from ἤ). The second clause opens with the disjunctive particle ἤ, which separates opposites, here the weak and the strong believer; it is correctly translated or.

καθώς / καθάπερ καί — "Just As," "Even As"

Romans 4:6 — "just as David also speaks of the blessing." καθάπερ introduces the supporting scriptural parallel.

Romans 1:28 — "And since they did not see fit to acknowledge God." καθώς (paired with καί: καὶ καθώς) functions as a causal conjunction, making the verse a logical consequence of the entire sequence of verses 18–27: and since all of this — since they rejected after testing — therefore the third judicial "delivery" follows.

Romans 5:12 — "Therefore, just as sin came into the world through one man..." ὥσπερ introduces the extended Adam-Christ analogy that structures the remainder of the chapter.

Romans 9:13 (Malachi 1:2–3) — "As it is written." καθάπερ (just as). The verse opens with the comparative conjunction kathaper, just as or even as, introducing an analogy drawn from the Old Testament canon, the quotation from Malachi 1:2–3.

Romans 9:29 (Isaiah 1:9) — "And as Isaiah predicted." καί; καθώς (and so; just as). Paul introduces the Isaiah quotation with καί used not as a simple additive and but as a result-marker, and so or then, indicating that what follows is a conclusion from the preceding argument. καθώς, just as, marks the quotation as analogical: not merely historical background but an exact structural parallel; the principle that operated in Isaiah's day operates with equal force in Paul's day and in the Times of the Gentiles.

Romans 10:15 (Isaiah 52:7) — "As it is written." καθάπερ (just as). The quotation formula opens with kathaper, just as, even as. It introduces Old Testament documentation for a point already established by rhetorical argument: Paul has shown logically that missionaries must be sent and now grounds that conclusion in the permanent witness of the Hebrew Scriptures.

Romans 11:8 — "just as it is written." καθάπερ (just as). καθάπερ is an unusually long Attic comparative conjunction; after a series of short, elliptical Attic sentences, its length signals a shift of register as Paul slows the argument to introduce comparative documentation. It implies exact equivalence, stronger than ὡς.

Romans 11:26 — "as it is written." καθώς (just as it stands written). καθώς (just as, even as) introduces a comparative clause anchored in Scripture and signals an Old Testament quotation. γέγραπται is the perfect of γράφω; the perfect tense emphasizes existing results: the Old Testament canon was completed and its authority continues undiminished into Paul's present. The passive voice of this verb across Scripture encodes the mechanics of verbal plenary inspiration.

Romans 12:4 — "For as in one body." καθάπερ (just as, exactly as). The compound comparative kathaper (kata + haper) means just as or exactly as. The force of two conjunctions, gar plus kathaper, signals the gravity of the analogy between the human body with its many differentiated members and the body of Christ with its many differentiated believers.

Romans 15:7 — "as Christ has welcomed you." καθὼς καί (even as). The adverb of comparison kathōs (καθώς) introduces the standard: just as — or with the ascensive conjunction kai (καί) that follows, even as. The comparison is with Christ's reception of every believer at the moment of salvation.

Romans 15:9 — "As it is written." καθώς (just as, even as). The adverb is kathōs (καθώς), meaning just as or even as. It introduces a formal comparison with the written Word of God.

ἀλλά — Strong Adversative "But"

Marks a sharp contrast, stronger than the mild adversative δέ.

Romans 2:13 — "For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law who will be justified." The ἀλλά here is confirmatory rather than adversative: following a negative clause, it intensifies rather than contrasts — "in fact, not" — carrying the negation forward with even greater force: not only is the first assumption false, the second, seemingly stronger one is equally false.

Romans 3:27 — "Then what becomes of our boasting? It is excluded. By what kind of law? Of works? No, but by the law of faith." The contrast turns on οὐχί... ἀλλά, decisively excluding the law of works and asserting the law of faith in its place.

Romans 4:16 — "That is why it depends on faith, in order that the promise may rest on grace." The surrounding argument's contrast between law and grace is regularly marked by ἀλλά at the sharpest turns.

Romans 5:3 — "we rejoice in our sufferings" — the sharp turn from the expected (suffering as purely negative) to the actual apostolic response is of the kind ἀλλά typically marks.

Romans 6:14 — "since you are not under law but under grace." ἀλλά marks the sharp, categorical contrast between the two governing systems.

Romans 7:19 — "For I do not do the good I want, but the evil I do not want is what I keep on doing." ἀλλά marks the stark contrast Paul draws between intention and practice.

Romans 8:9 — "You, however, are not in the flesh but in the Spirit." ἀλλά marks the categorical contrast (see also the Proleptic Word Order entry, section XIV, on the emphatic σύ that precedes it).

Romans 8:32 — "he did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all." ἀλλά marks the contrast between what God did not do and what he did do.

Romans 8:37 — "No, in all these things we are more than conquerors." ἀλλά opens the verse with the sharpest possible contrast to the preceding catalogue of hardships.

Romans 9:7 (Genesis 21:12) — "but 'Through Isaac shall your offspring be named.'" ἀλλά (but). The second half of the verse is introduced by the adversative alla, which sets up a sharp contrast between Isaac and all the other children of Abraham, between the entirety of Abraham's physical descendants and the single line of election running through Isaac. The clause quotes Genesis 21:12.

Romans 9:8 — "but the children of the promise are counted as offspring." ἀλλά (but). alla is not the mild adversative de but the strong contrastive conjunction: what follows stands in categorical opposition to what preceded. It sets the racial Jew, who never advances beyond X-radical, against the regenerate Jew who moves into Y and Z-radical; children of the flesh and children of the promise are mutually exclusive categories, not different descriptions of the same group.

Romans 9:16 — "but on God, who has mercy." ἀλλά (but). alla sets up a strong contrast between the two false sources of blessing and the one true source, a contrast not merely of degree but of kind, entirely displacing human effort as a cause and substituting the sovereign mercy of God operating through the justice of God.

Romans 9:32 — "but as if it were based on works." ἀλλά (but). ἀλλά introduces a sharp contrast: not by faith, but, an emphatic opposition between what Israel should have done (pursued by faith) and what they actually did (pursued as by works). It is one of the strongest contrastive particles in Greek.

Romans 10:2 — "but not according to knowledge." ἀλλά. The strong adversative alla introduces a sharp contrast between the presence of zeal and the absence of epignosis, establishing the central paradox of Israel's religious condition.

Romans 10:8 — "But what does it say?" ἀλλά. Verse 8 opens with alla, contrasting the negative principles (salvation is not unattainable, not unavailable) with the positive reality now stated: salvation is attainable, available, and as near as the individual's own soul and body.

Romans 11:4 — "But what is God's reply to him?" ἀλλά (but). The strong adversative ἀλλά sets the human viewpoint of Elijah (arrogance, self-pity, preoccupation with disaster) against the divine viewpoint that follows. The contrast is corrective, not merely informational: the answer of God presents the facts as they actually are.

Romans 12:3 — "but to think with sober judgment." ἀλλά (but). The strong adversative alla sets up the positive counterpart to the prohibition, contrasting what must cease with what must replace it. The corrective command is a precise description of a cognitive habit grounded in doctrine, not vague encouragement toward humility.

Romans 12:20 — "To the contrary." ἀλλά (nevertheless). Verse 20 opens not with an inferential conjunction but with the adversative alla. When whole clauses are contrasted to signal a transition to a new element, alla carries the force of nevertheless: a transition to a more sophisticated application of the honor code requiring maximum doctrine.

Romans 13:3 — "but to bad." ἀλλά (but, on the contrary). Strong adversative ἀλλά sets up a direct antithesis between the two datives of 13:3, good function versus evil function, and signals that governing authority stands in an opposite relationship to each category.

Romans 13:5 — "but also for the sake of conscience." ἀλλά (but also). ἀλλά, combined with καί, is the preferential conjunction introducing the second and higher ground of subordination, conscience, presented as the preferred and more positive basis for submission to governing authority.

Romans 13:14 — "But put on the Lord Jesus Christ." ἀλλά (but). Strong adversative ἀλλά sets the negative catalogue of verse 13 against the single comprehensive positive command that follows. The prohibitions are answered not by a new list of virtues but by one commanding act: put on the Lord Jesus Christ.

Romans 14:13 — "but rather." ἀλλά (but rather). The adversative ἀλλά introduces a sharp contrast between the occupational hazard of the weak believer (judging) and that of the strong believer (placing obstacles). Neither group is exempt; the justice of God addresses both sides, making doctrine itself the issue for all.

Romans 14:17 — "but of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit." ἀλλά (but, on the contrary). ἀλλά is the strong adversative. It marks a shift not merely of topic but of register, from the incidental to the essential: from the non-essentials about which the believer must remain flexible to the essentials about which no flexibility is permissible. It is a categorical contrast, not a mild qualification.

Romans 15:21 — "but as it is written." ἀλλά (not only this, but also). The verse opens with the adversative-ascensive conjunction alla (ἀλλά), which here carries an ascensive force: not only this, but also.

δέ — Mild Adversative or Simple Connective "But/And"

Weaker than ἀλλά; often merely continuative rather than sharply adversative. Occasionally used for emphatic, almost intensive effect when combined with a proleptic pronoun (see section XIV).

Romans 2:2 — "We know that the judgment of God rightly falls." δέ, at the head of this verse, is adversative, establishing a contrast between the presumptive judgment of the self-righteous person in verse 1 and the perfect judicial verdict of God in verse 2.

Romans 2:17 — "But if you call yourself a Jew." δέ functions adversatively, contrasting the self-righteous Gentile of verses 1–16 with the self-righteous Jew of verses 17–29.

Romans 2:19 — "and if you are sure that you yourself are a guide to the blind, a light to those who are in darkness." δέ functions additively here rather than adversatively — better rendered "moreover" — indicating a close, progressive relationship between the self-descriptions of verses 17–18 and the further claims of verse 19.

Romans 4:5 — "and to the one who does not work but believes." δέ provides the mild connective contrast between the two categories of person.

Romans 5:8 — "but God shows his love for us." δέ connects this verse's demonstration back to the human analogy of verse 7, with a contrast of degree rather than outright opposition.

Romans 8:9 — "You, however, are not in the flesh" — the same δέ discussed above under ἀλλά functions here in its emphatic-intensive capacity (paired with the proleptic σύ) rather than as a plain adversative; Greek allows δέ this heightened, "in fact/indeed" force in certain emphatic constructions.

Romans 8:26 — "Likewise the Spirit helps us in our weakness." δέ, here mildly connective, ties the Spirit's help to the wider context of hope and suffering just discussed.

Romans 9:6 — "But it is not as though." δέ (however). The verse opens with the post-positive conjunctive particle de, translated but (corrected translation: However), which signals contrast with what has immediately preceded.

Romans 9:22 — "What if God." δέ (moreover, furthermore). The post-positive δέ, which never stands first in its clause, functions transitionally, not adversatively, connecting what follows to the preceding argument. Because of the aposiopesis and the chiasmus structure it is best rendered before the conditional: moreover if or furthermore if, as is the case, signalling that Paul is extending and climaxing what has already been established rather than introducing a new thought.

Romans 9:27 (Isaiah 10:22) — "And Isaiah cries out concerning Israel." δέ (in fact, indeed). The attribution to Isaiah is followed by the post-positive δέ in its intensive rather than adversative sense, best rendered in fact or indeed. It signals that the citation is not merely supplementary or transitional but strong confirmatory evidence for the argument of verses 22–26.

Romans 9:30 — "that is, a righteousness that is by faith." δέ (that is, in fact). The verse concludes with an appositional explanatory phrase introduced by δέ in its intensive use, meaning that is or in fact, marking an explanation rather than a contrast; what follows defines the character of the righteousness attained.

Romans 9:31 — "but that Israel who pursued a law that would lead to righteousness." δέ (but). Verse 31 opens with δέ used as a mild adversative, establishing a contrast between the Old Testament Gentiles who believed in Christ and the racial Jews who rejected Him: verse 30, the Gentiles attained righteousness they did not pursue; verse 31, Israel pursued righteousness and did not attain it. The adversative δέ marks the logical hinge between the two outcomes.

Romans 10:6 — "But the righteousness based on faith says." δέ (but). Verse 6 opens with the post-positive particle de, correctly but. This single particle establishes the governing contrast of the paragraph: the emphasis of verse 5 (doing the law, works righteousness, Leviticus 18:5) set against the emphasis of verse 6 forward (faith righteousness, the righteousness of God imputed at the moment of faith in Christ).

Romans 10:10 — "and with the mouth one confesses." δέ. The second clause opens with the connective and transitional de, indicating continuation with result connotations. The clause is not a parallel condition to the first but a sequential consequence of it: cause precedes effect, faith precedes confession.

Romans 10:14 — "And how are they to believe in him." πῶς (furthermore). The second question opens with the same pōs, maintaining the formal structure of the deliberative series, joined to de used not adversatively but transitionally: best furthermore rather than but or now. It signals a rational and logical advance within the sequence, not a contrast.

Romans 10:20 (Isaiah 65:1) — "Then Isaiah is so bold as to say." δέ (next). The post-positive particle de introduces the new witness and is translated next, carrying the sense of transition to the following testimony.

Romans 10:21 (Isaiah 65:2) — "But of Israel he says." δέ (but). De is used in an adversative sense, drawing a sharp contrast between Gentile believers receiving Christ and Jewish unbelievers rejecting him: the structural contrast of the inversion.

Romans 11:6 — "But if it is by grace." δέ (now). δέ opening verse 6 carries logical, not merely connective, force and is rendered now, signaling an immediate and urgent application. The KJV rendering and misses the exegetical weight: Paul is pivoting to the governing principle of all that has come before.

Romans 11:7 — "but the rest were hardened." δέ (but). In verse 7 δέ functions contrastively, setting Israel, which pursued salvation through self-righteousness and law-keeping, against the elected to privilege who trusted in Christ, and then setting the elect against the rest. It frames the verse as a study in contrast.

Romans 11:13 — "Now I am speaking to you Gentiles." δέ (now). Verse 13 opens with the postpositive conjunctive particle δέ, which in context signals the insertion of an explanation or parenthesis. In English the parenthetical function is conveyed by punctuation rather than by a separate connective word. The parenthesis extends through verse 14 and returns in verse 15 to the main argument.

Romans 13:1 — "and those that exist have been instituted by God." δέ (that is). δέ is used here not adversatively but as a transitional particle of explanation, best rendered that is. It introduces a clarifying restatement: authority has its sole origin in God, and the verse now specifies which authorities are in view.

Romans 13:2 — "and those who resist will incur judgment." δέ (in fact). In 13:2b δέ is not a simple connective but a transitional conjunction introducing an explanatory expansion of the preceding statement. It is best rendered in fact: what follows elaborates and intensifies the preceding clause.

Romans 13:3 — "Would you have no fear of the one who is in authority?" δέ (really, really now). The rhetorical question of 13:3b, a command in disguise, opens with the emphatic post-positive δέ carrying a tone of sarcasm, best rendered really or really now. Paul uses it not merely to intensify but to engage the reader's self-interest directly.

Romans 13:12 — "the day is at hand." δέ. δέ, though often adversative, functions here as a transitional particle introducing mild antithesis between night (phase two) and day (phase three).

Romans 14:3 — "and let not the one who abstains." δέ (furthermore). Instead of καί linking the two prohibitions, Paul uses the post-positive conjunctive particle δέ, which marks the superaddition of a clause, best rendered furthermore. The second command is not merely coordinate with the first but adds a distinct and equally serious concern.

Romans 14:23 — "But whoever has doubts." δέ (but). The post-positive δέ connects clauses where a contrast exists. Verse 22 addressed the mature believer, happy because he does not condemn himself; verse 23, introduced by δέ, turns to the weak believer, who lacks the doctrinal norms that produce either liberty or love in their proper application.

Romans 14:23 — "For whatever does not proceed from faith is sin." δέ (and). The second clause of Romans 14:23 is introduced by the post-positive conjunctive particle de (δέ), used here as a transitional particle without contrast — rendered simply as “and.”

Romans 15:1 — "We who are strong have an obligation to bear with the failings of the weak." δέ (now). The verse opens with the post-positive conjunction de (δέ), used here not contrastively but as a transitional particle. The correct rendering is now rather than but.

Romans 15:9 — "and in order that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy." δέ (and). Verse 9 opens with the postpositive conjunctive particle de (δέ), functioning as a transitional conjunction: and.

Romans 15:13 — "May the God of hope." δέ (now). The verse opens with the post-positive conjunctive particle de (δέ), used here as a transitional particle marking the shift from the catena of Old Testament citations to the benediction that concludes the doctrinal section. It carries a mild continuative force: 'now' or 'and so.'

Romans 15:23 — "But now." δέ (but). The verse opens with a post-positive conjunctive particle, the Greek δέ (de), used here in an adversative sense to mark a contrast with what preceded: Paul has been hindered from coming to Rome precisely because his missionary obligations in the east were unfinished.

Romans 15:25 — "At present, however, I am going to Jerusalem." δέ (but). The particle de (δέ) is a mild adversative conjunction establishing a contrast.

Romans 15:29 — "I know that when I come to you." δέ (now). Verse 29 opens with the post-positive conjunctive particle de (δέ), used here as a transitional conjunction introducing a new but related thought. It is correctly rendered now.

Romans 15:30 — "I appeal to you, brothers." δέ (now). The post-positive conjunctive particle de (δέ) marks a transitional conjunction rather than a sharp break.

Romans 15:33 — "Now the God of peace be with you all." δέ (now). The post-positive conjunctive particle de (δέ) functions here as a transition marker, not as an adversative ('but').

Romans 16:25 — "Now to him who is able to strengthen you." δέ (now). Verse 25 opens with the transitional use of the post-positive conjunctive particle de (δέ), translated now in the transitional sense rather than the adversative but.

Standalone Emphatic μέν

Used alone (without a following δέ in the same breath) to intensify or affirm a statement — "as a matter of fact," "indeed, in fact."

Romans 7:12 — "So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good." The μέν here (rendered "so" in most English translations, which under-represents its force) functions as a strong affirming particle: "as a matter of fact, the law is holy" — a firm, settled assertion closing off any doubt raised by the preceding verses.

Romans 10:1 — "my heart's desire and prayer to God for them." μέν (affirmative particle). After the vocative, Paul shifts into classical Attic Greek with the affirmative particle mén, an intentional stylistic elevation signaling the gravity of what follows. In Attic usage mén is preparatory: its clause will be set in antithesis to a following clause introduced by dé. Here the antithesis is implicit but clear: Paul desires the salvation of Israel; Israel through its own negative volition does not desire what he is presenting. The particle is a structural warning that a second, contrasting clause is coming.

ἵνα — Purpose Clauses

Introduces a subjunctive purpose clause, "in order that."

Romans 4:16 — "in order that the promise may rest on grace." ἵνα introduces the purpose of the arrangement.

Romans 5:21 — "so that, as sin reigned in death, grace also might reign." ἵνα introduces the purpose/result of the whole preceding contrast between Adam and Christ.

Romans 6:4 — "in order that... we too might walk in newness of life." ἵνα introduces the purpose of the baptism-into-death imagery.

Romans 6:6 — "so that the body of sin might be brought to nothing." ἵνα introduces the purpose of the co-crucifixion.

Romans 7:4 — "so that we may bear fruit for God." ἵνα introduces the purpose of the believer's death to the law through Christ's body.

Romans 8:4 — "in order that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us." ἵνα introduces the purpose clause discussed at length under the Culminative Aorist and Potential Subjunctive entries above.

Romans 8:17 — "provided we suffer with him in order that we may also be glorified with him." ἵνα introduces the purpose of the fellowship of suffering.

Romans 9:11 — "in order that God's purpose of election might continue." ἵνα (in order that). A final (purpose) clause follows, introduced by hina with a verb in the subjunctive mood, indicating future purpose; the subjunctive of menō is required by the hina purpose clause.

Romans 9:23 — "in order to make known the riches of his glory." ἵνα (in order that). Following καί is ἵνα with the subjunctive, introducing a final clause expressing the distinct aim or purpose of the action of the principal verb. In classical Attic usage it is rendered in order that; the Koine equivalent that is adequate but loses the precision of purpose. It governs the entire anacoluthon clause of verse 23, which states the purpose of God's patient endurance of vessels of wrath: the revelation of His glory on the vessels of mercy.

Romans 11:11 — "in order that they might fall." ἵνα (so as). ἵνα introduces a final clause expressing distinct purpose conceived as the objective of the main verb, followed by the aorist subjunctive of πίπτω: they did not stumble so as to fall into ruin. The subjunctive reinforces the negative answer demanded by μή.

Romans 11:19 — "so that I might be grafted in." ἵνα (in order that). ἵνα introduces a purpose clause: in order that I might be grafted in. The aorist passive subjunctive of ἐγκεντρίζω views the arrogant presumption in its entirety, regarding its existing results: the distortion of grace doctrine and the promotion of anti-Semitism. The purpose clause is grammatically real but theologically a distortion — the reasoning of interlocking systems of arrogance, not the actual design of God. The subjunctive also indicates that not all Gentile believers reach this conclusion.

Romans 11:25 — "Lest you be wise in your own sight." ἵνα μή (that not). ἵνα plus μή introduces a negative purpose clause. With the present subjunctive of εἰμί it forms the subjunctive of discontinuance, commanding the cessation of an action already in progress: that you stop being wise in your own estimation.

Romans 11:31 — "in order that by the mercy shown to you they also may now receive mercy." ἵνα (in order that). ἵνα plus the subjunctive introduces a final clause of purpose, aim, and goal. The aorist passive subjunctive of ἐλεέω (passive: to receive mercy) is culminative, viewing Jewish salvation in the church age in its entirety from the existing result in every generation: there will always be a remnant of Jewish believers, who receive mercy and do not generate it. Jewish unbelief in the church age is not the final divine intention.

Romans 11:32 — "that he may have mercy on all." ἵνα (in order that). The purpose clause ἵνα with the aorist active subjunctive of ἐλεέω governs the entire construction: the divine act of locking up the entire human race under disobedience is the judicial foundation for dispensing mercy to all. Mercy is grace in action; like grace, it originates not in the love of God but in the justice of God.

Romans 14:9 — "that he might be Lord both of the dead and of the living." ἵνα (in order that). ἵνα plus the subjunctive is the standard Greek idiom for purpose. The subjunctive with ἵνα does not signal potential: the Lordship of Christ is not conditional, and the subjunctive simply fulfills the grammatical requirement of the purpose construction.

Romans 15:4 — "that through endurance and through the encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope." ἵνα (in order that). The purpose clause is introduced by hina (ἵνα) with the subjunctive mood, forming a final clause denoting goal, objective, and purpose: in order that. This is a straightforward final clause rather than a sub-final (purpose-result blend). It affirms that God has a defined purpose for the believer's life as long as that life continues on earth.

Romans 15:6 — "that together you may with one voice glorify." ἵνα (in order that). Verse 6 opens with the Greek conjunction ἵνα (hina), which together with the subjunctive mood of the following verb introduces a purpose clause. Translated: in order that.

Romans 15:31 — "that I may be delivered from the unbelievers in Judea." ἵνα (that). Paul opens with a purpose clause introduced by the Greek conjunction hina (ἵνα), which signals a semifinal purpose clause. A semifinal purpose clause directs the action of the main verb toward a desired result — in this case, a result sought through prayer.

ὥστε — Inferential "So That," "Therefore"

Introduces a result or inferential clause, related to but distinct from purpose clauses with ἵνα.

Romans 7:4 — "Likewise, my brothers, you also have died to the law through the body of Christ, so that you may belong to another." ὥστε introduces the resulting state that flows from the believer's death to the law.

Romans 7:12 — "So the law is holy" — while the dominant particle here is the emphatic μέν discussed above, the inferential weight of the whole sentence functions in the same conclusion-drawing register as ὥστε elsewhere in Paul.

Romans 13:2 — "Therefore whoever resists the authorities resists what God has appointed." ὥστε (therefore). ὥστε introduces an independent clause with inferential force: therefore, in view of everything established in verse 1. The inference moves from the divine origin of all legitimate authority to the consequences of opposing it.

Romans 15:19 — "so that from Jerusalem and all the way around to Illyricum." ὥστε με (with the result that I). The result clause is introduced by hōste (ὥστε), which governs an accusative of general reference with the personal pronoun egō (ἐγώ): with the result that I.

καί — Connective, Ascensive, Adjunctive and Result Uses

Romans 9:4 — "the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the worship, and the promises." καί (and). The connective use of kai introduces each next item in Paul's list. The list structure, adoption, glory, covenants, law, worship, promises, is set up by the repeated kai, each conjunction adding another element of Israel's heritage.

Romans 9:23 — "in order to make known the riches of his glory." καί (and). Verse 23 opens with καί functioning not merely as a simple coordinating conjunction but as the structural connector that extends the aposiopesis from verse 22 into verse 23. It sustains the protasis of the first-class condition and signals to the reader fluent in classical Greek that the sentence remains deliberately open.

Romans 9:24 — "even us whom he has called." καί (even). Verse 24 opens with the ascensive use of καί, translated even, followed by the first-person plural accusative of ἐγώ: even us. The relative pronoun οὕς has its antecedent in vessels of mercy from verse 23: vessels of mercy, even us, whom He has elected.

Romans 15:3 — "For Christ did not please himself." καὶ γάρ (for even). The verse opens with the ascensive use of kai (καί) combined with the post-positive explanatory conjunction gar (γάρ), correctly rendered for even. The particle kai in its ascensive function intensifies the statement: not merely that Christ was thoughtful of others, but that even He — the unique God-man — operated under this principle. Gar introduces the basis on which the preceding exhortation rests.

Romans 15:6 — "the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ." καὶ πατέρα (even the Father). The conjunction καί (kai) here carries the ascensive force: even. The following accusative singular πατέρα (patera, Father) stands in apposition to theon: God, even the Father.

Romans 15:12 — "even he who arises to rule the Gentiles." καὶ ὁ ἀνιστάμενος (even he who rises). The ascensive use of kai (καί) is correctly translated 'even.' It introduces the articular present middle participle of anistēmi (ἀνίστημι), meaning to rise up — both in the sense of coming into historical existence and in the sense of literal bodily resurrection.

καί — Intensive Force (In Fact)

Romans 9:5 — "and from their race." καί (in fact). kai here carries the force of in fact, introducing the climactic item: in fact, from whom is the Christ.

Romans 14:6 — "while the one who abstains, abstains in honor of the Lord." καί (in fact). The clause about the immature believer opens with καί used not as a simple connective but as an intensive particle, in fact. It marks the transition from the mature believer’s thanksgiving to the immature believer’s parallel thanksgiving, with deliberate emphasis on the parallel structure.

Romans 16:17 — "avoid them." καὶ ἐκκλίνετε (in fact, keep turning away). The intensive conjunction kai (καί) introduces the imperative clause with added force: 'in fact.'

ἄρα οὖν — The Double Inferential

Romans 9:16 (Exodus 33:19) — "So then." ἄρα (so then). ara and oun both mean therefore; combined at the opening of a sentence they create an exceptionally emphatic double conclusion, rendered idiomatically so then rather than therefore therefore. The construction is rare in Paul; here it signals a double conclusion drawn simultaneously from Exodus 33:19 and from the preceding argument of Romans 9.

Romans 9:18 — "So then." ἄρα οὖν (consequently therefore). Each particle alone is inferential; together they signal a major conclusion, one of the strongest inferential constructions in Pauline Greek, rendered consequently therefore or so then. It announces that everything studied about the hardening of Pharaoh's heart in Exodus 9 and the preceding verses now converges in a single doctrinal statement.

ὅπως — Purpose Clauses

Romans 9:17 (Exodus 9:16) — "that I might show my power in you." ὅπως (in order that). The purpose clause opens with hopōs, introducing a final clause denoting aim or objective, that or in order that. Paired with the subjunctive, hopōs marks the construction as a divine purpose clause throughout; it is repeated with kai to introduce the second purpose, giving the two divine purposes behind Pharaoh's preservation: the demonstration of divine power and the worldwide proclamation of the divine person.

δέ — Intensive Force (In Fact)

Romans 9:18 — "and he hardens whomever he wills." δέ (in fact). The second clause opens with de, here neither transitional nor purely adversative but intensive, rendered in fact. The second clause is not a contrast qualifying the first but an equally absolute doctrinal statement standing alongside it.

Romans 15:14 — "I myself am satisfied about you." δέ (in fact). The intensive use of the post-positive conjunctive particle de (δέ) functions here as an emphatic marker, translated in fact.

Romans 15:15 — "But on some points I have written to you very boldly." δέ (in fact, nevertheless). Following the adverb, the post-positive conjunctive particle de (δέ) carries a light adversative or transitional force: in fact, nevertheless.

Romans 15:20 — "and thus I make it my ambition." δέ (in fact). The verse opens with the post-positive conjunctive particle δέ (de), used here in its intensive force. The translation 'yea' found in older English versions is archaic; the correct rendering is 'in fact.'

Romans 16:20 — "The God of peace will soon crush Satan." ὁ δὲ θεός (in fact, the God). The clause opens with the post-positive conjunctive particle δέ (de), used here in its intensive sense: in fact. The intensive δέ is not merely transitional; it draws a logical consequence from the preceding paragraph (verses 17–19).

μενοῦνγε — Triple-Compound Particle of Correction

Romans 9:20 — "But who are you, O man, to answer back to God?" μενοῦνγε (on the contrary). μενοῦνγε fuses three particles: μέν (correlative, on the one hand), οὖν (inferential conjunction drawing a conclusion from the preceding context) and γέ (an untranslatable intensive particle giving thrust and emphasis). This Pauline coinage serves a debating function: it signals that what has just been stated, the debater's questions of verse 19, represents erroneous thinking, and that the speaker is now correcting it. The best English rendering is on the contrary.

Romans 10:18 — "Indeed they have." μενοῦνγε (certainly, indeed). The emphatic affirmative answer is the compound particle menounge, formed from men, oun (the inferential particle), and ge (the emphatic particle), combined under a single accent: certainly they have, indeed they have, emphatically yes. It is one of the strongest affirmative constructions in Greek: the Gentiles have heard the gospel.

ἰδού — Demonstrative Particle of Attention

Romans 9:33 (Isaiah 28:16) — "Behold, I am laying in Zion." ἰδού (behold, take note, from ὁράω). ἰδού is a demonstrative particle, the aorist middle imperative of ὁράω used as an interjection, equivalent to the Hebrew hinneh. It demands perception and signals that what follows is of the highest importance, arresting attention before the announcement of the foundational stone laid in Zion.

οὕτως — Adverb of Manner Introducing a Quotation

Romans 10:6 (Deuteronomy 30:11–14) — "says." οὕτως (in this manner). The adverb of manner houtōs concludes Paul's introduction, in this manner, pointing forward to the content of what faith-righteousness communicates, Paul's quotation from and commentary on Deuteronomy 30:11–14.

ὡς — Characteristic Quality of a Category

Romans 10:15 (Isaiah 52:7) — "How beautiful are the feet." ὡς (how). The quotation opens with the relative adverb hōs, which in this interrogative construction introduces the characteristic quality of a category. The question does not ask for a description of physical appearance; it defines what is typical and distinctive about a class of person, here missionaries.

ἄρα — Illative Consequently

Romans 10:17 — "So faith comes from hearing." ἄρα (consequently). The verse opens with the illative particle ara, which draws an inference both from what has been argued and in anticipation of the conclusion to follow; correctly consequently. Verse 17 is the logical distillation of the chain in verses 14–16.

ἐπεί — Otherwise, the Logical Consequence

Romans 11:6 — "otherwise grace would no longer be grace." ἐπεί (otherwise). ἐπεί is a classical Attic conjunction introducing a logical consequence, used in an elliptical construction (associated with Xenophon) and uncommon in the Koine. Its appearance signals that Paul has shifted into the register of formal classical argument, with major premise, minor premise, and conclusion: if grace were mixed with works, grace would cease to function as grace.

Romans 11:22 — "Otherwise you too will be cut off." ἐπεί (otherwise). The apodosis of failure is introduced by the classical use of ἐπεί — not the Koine causal since but the classical alternative through ellipsis: if it were otherwise … otherwise. σύ emphasizes the individual Gentile believer, and the adjunctive καί adds also: Gentile believers are no less subject to divine discipline than Jewish unbelievers were to divine severity.

καί — Adjunctive Use (Also)

Romans 11:9 (Psalm 69:22–23) — "And David says." καί (also). καί opening verse 9 is adjunctive, also: David is the next in a sequence of Old Testament witnesses, alongside Elijah, Moses, and Isaiah, not merely a connective and.

Romans 12:2 — "Do not be conformed to this world." καί (also). The conjunction kai is used in the adjunctive sense, joining the prohibition of verse 2 to the command of verse 1; the corrected translation renders it also.

Romans 13:6 — "you also pay taxes." καί (also). The adjunctive καί functions adverbially, rendered also. It extends the implication of the previous verse into this new command and makes the connection explicit.

Romans 13:11 — "Besides this you know the time." καί (also). The adjunctive καί signals an addition: besides the believer's obligations to governing authorities (verses 1–7) and to fellow members of the royal family of God (verses 8–10), there is a personal obligation to self.

Romans 14:10 — "Or you, why do you despise your brother?" καί (also). The proleptic σύ addressed to the strong believer is combined with καί used as an adverbial adjunctive, or you also. The construction emphasizes that the strong believer is not exempt from blame: he too has an occupational hazard. The objective is maturity, not perfection.

Romans 15:14 — "able to instruct one another." καί (also). The adjunctive kai is translated also.
