Romans 10:2 — "not according to knowledge." ἐπίγνωσις (full, exact, operational knowledge). Epignosis must be distinguished from gnosis. Gnosis is doctrine in the left lobe, information that can be recited and recalled but is not yet operational. Epignosis is doctrine transferred to the right lobe, into the frame of reference, memory center, vocabulary and categorical storage, and the norms and standards of the conscience; only epignosis is applicable under pressure and productive for spiritual growth. The transfer operates through the faith-rest technique and the Grace Apparatus for Perception (GAP); where doctrine is resisted, it remains gnosis and never functions in the spiritual life.

ὑποτάσσω — Military Term, Placed in Rank Under Authority

Romans 10:3 — "they did not submit." ὑποτάσσω (to be subordinate, to submit to authority). Hupotassō is a military compound, hupo (under) + tassō (to arrange, to assign a position), meaning to be subordinate, to be placed in rank under an authority. It denotes the discipline of occupying one's assigned place within a command structure; applied here to submitting to the authority of God's imputed righteousness, which Israel refused.

Romans 13:1 — "Let every person be subject to the governing authorities." ὑποτάσσω (to subordinate oneself). ὑποτάσσω is a military compound of hypo (under) and tassō (to arrange in order). It means to subordinate oneself to authority and carries the force of ordered, voluntary alignment within a command structure.

ἄβυσσος — The Abyss as the Realm of the Dead

Romans 10:7 (Amos 9:2; Deuteronomy 30:13) — "into the abyss." ἄβυσσος (the abyss, the deep). Eis plus the accusative of abyssos. The term (alpha-privative + byssos, depth) denotes the realm of the dead, Sheol or Hades, and stands in deliberate contrast to the heaven of verse 6, the mirror image of ascent. In Revelation it is associated with fallen angels, but here it means descent into the underworld. It is Paul's Greek rendering of Sheol from Amos 9:2, substituted for Moses' sea analogy because Christ's soul ascended from Sheol, not from the sea, in the resurrection.

ῥῆμα vs. λόγος — The Proclaimed Word

Romans 10:8 (Deuteronomy 30:14) — "the word of faith." ῥῆμα (message, word). Rhēma, from rheō (to speak), denotes that which is said: a message, word, utterance. Here it is the message of salvation, the announcement of imputed righteousness through faith in Christ, the content of Deuteronomy 30:14 as Paul applies it. It is distinguished from logos in that rhēma often emphasizes the spoken or proclaimed word rather than the written or conceptual word.

ὁμολογέω — Legal Acknowledgment, Not Emotional Display

Romans 10:10 — "with the mouth one confesses." ὁμολογέω (to acknowledge, admit, concede). Homologeō is compounded from homos (the same) and legō (to say), but etymology does not determine meaning; usage does. It was the standard legal term for introducing testimony before a judge, a candid, factual statement under oath: to name, cite, acknowledge, admit, concede. It carries no emotional connotation and no implication of public demonstration; it is a statement made to God, the same verb that underlies the rebound technique of 1 John 1:9.

πλουτέω — To Be Rich and To Be Generous

Romans 10:12 — "bestowing his riches on all who call on him." πλουτέω (to be rich, to be generous). The predicate is the present active participle of plouteō. The verb means both to be rich and to be generous, two related but distinguishable domains, since wealth and generosity are not synonymous. In this context the generosity connotation is primary, grounded in Christ's inexhaustible divine resources. The participle is ascriptive, describing a permanent quality of Christ toward believers: the active, ongoing dispensation of the grace assets of salvation and logistical grace to all who call, without racial limit.

κηρύσσω / κῆρυξ — The Herald

Romans 10:15 — "And how are they to preach." κηρύσσω (to proclaim as a herald). Kēryssō derives from kēryx, a herald. In the Greco-Roman world the herald was a figure of high social standing, a representative of royalty or the governing council, always someone with established authority. He embodied the authority of the one who sent him and bore good news: when a king was about to visit a city, the herald announced the arrival, and the visit brought blessing. The word characterizes the gospel communicator as proclaiming a message not his own, with authority derived from another.

ὡραῖος — The Beauty of Timeliness

Romans 10:15 (Isaiah 52:7) — "How beautiful are the feet." ὡραῖος (timely, seasonable). The nominative plural adjective hōraios does not denote physical beauty or symmetry. It derives from hōra, the right time, the fitting season: the beauty of the missionary's feet is the beauty of timeliness, the right person arriving at the right moment with the right message for people whose positive volition has prepared them to receive it.

εὐαγγελίζω — From Victory Announcement to Technical Gospel Term

Romans 10:15 (Isaiah 52:7) — "those who preach the good news." εὐαγγελίζω (to proclaim the good news). Euaggelizō (eu, good + angellō, to announce) in classical Greek meant to announce the good news of military victory, the word associated with Pheidippides running from Marathon to Athens. In Koine Greek it is the technical term for the announcement of the work of Christ on the cross.

ὑπακούω — Hearing Under Authority

Romans 10:16 — "they have not all obeyed the gospel." ὑπακούω (to hear under authority, to obey). Hupakouō is compounded from hupo (under, in subordination to) and akouō (to hear): attentive, subordinate hearing, listening under authority, used in academic contexts for reception of instruction under a recognized teacher. It denotes the proper response to the gospel: to hear it accurately, perceive its content, and accept it. With the negative, the hearing occurred but the acceptance did not follow; disobedience to the gospel is an act of the will against clearly perceived information. It is a synonym for faith.

Romans 16:19 — "For your obedience is known to all." ἡ … ὑμῶν ὑπακοή (your obedience). The nominative singular noun hypakoē (ὑπακοή) means a report or obedience. The noun is built on akoē (ἀκοή, hearing, report) prefixed by hypo (ὑπό, under). Obedience is literally responsiveness under legitimate authority — the structural foundation of the royal family honor code.

ἀκοή — What Is Heard, the Message

Romans 10:16 (Isaiah 53:1) — "what he has heard from us." ἀκοῇ (report, message, from ἀκοή). The dative indirect object akoē derives from the same root as akouō (to hear) and means what is heard, the report or message. With the first-person plural possessive genitive it reads our report or our message, the apostolic proclamation continuous with the prophetic proclamation of the whole Old Testament canon.

γῆ vs. οἰκουμένη — Planet Earth vs. the Inhabited Earth

Romans 10:18 (Psalm 19:4) — "to the ends of the world." οἰκουμένη (inhabited earth). The first line uses gē, planet earth as a physical body (eis plus the accusative of pas and gē, God consciousness, universal). The second uses eis plus the accusative of peras, ends or limits, with the descriptive genitive of oikoumenē, the inhabited earth, that portion where people actually live. Gospel hearing reaches the ends of the inhabited earth: wherever people live, no geographical, linguistic, or cultural barrier can prevent gospel information for a soul positive at God consciousness.

γινώσκω vs. eidō — Experiential vs. Intuitive Knowledge

Romans 10:19 — "did Israel not understand?" γινώσκω (to know by experience). Ginōskō, to know by experience, is distinguished from eidō (to know intuitively or propositionally): ginōskō emphasizes experiential, participatory knowledge, here knowledge acquired through the ritual system of the Mosaic Law.

παροργίζω — Attic Vocabulary Preserved from the Septuagint

Romans 10:19 (Deuteronomy 32:21) — "with a foolish nation I will make you angry." παροργίζω (to provoke to anger). The second verb, future active indicative of parorgizō, to make angry, to provoke to anger, is Attic Greek, not Koine: Paul preserves the exact vocabulary of the Septuagint rendering of Deuteronomy 32:21. It announces the second dimension of inversion judgment: Jewish anger at the blessing of a nation without Israel's scriptural heritage.

ἀποτολμάω — Maximum Moral Courage

Romans 10:20 (Isaiah 65:1) — "Isaiah is so bold as to say." ἀποτολμάω (to be so bold as to). Apotolmaō compounds apo (intensifying) with tolmaō (to be brave, to dare): maximum courage, not reckless bravado or emotion-driven impulse, but cold, clear moral courage exercised with full awareness of consequences. The idiom apotolmaō kai legō, from the tradition of Demosthenes, is correctly is so bold as to say; within it the present active indicative of legō functions as an infinitive. It foregrounds Isaiah's courage in testifying, as a Jew, to Gentile salvation.

ὑπολείπω vs. καταλείπω — A Deliberate Paronomasia

Romans 11:4 (1 Kings 19:18) — "I have kept for myself seven thousand men." καταλείπω (to leave behind, to reserve). Elijah complained with ὑπολείπω, to be left under, the only one remaining beneath the general collapse. The divine reply uses καταλείπω, to leave behind or reserve, with the reflexive ἐμαυτῷ, to reserve to oneself. The wordplay is intentional: Elijah has gone under, while the seven thousand are still in their place of honor, refuting the arrogance of Elijah and affirming the standing of the pivot.

παγίς vs. θήρα — Snare vs. Trap

Romans 11:9 (Psalm 69:22) — "a snare and a trap." θήρα (trap). Paul amplifies the Psalm by adding θήρα as a second term. The snare (παγίς) is the responsibility itself, the possession of the gospel, the ritual, and the prophetic Word; the trap is the consequence of failing to respond to it. Ritual without reality is a trap: the Levitical system embraced as religion while Christ the antitype is rejected.

ἐκκλάω / κλάδος — A Deliberate Paronomasia

Romans 11:17 — "some of the branches were broken off." ἐκκλάω (to break off). The aorist passive indicative of ἐκκλάω (ek, out of + klaō, to break) is a deliberate paronomasia with κλάδος: the branches (kladoi) are broken off (ekklaō). The passive voice indicates that unbelieving Jews receive the action; they are broken off because they are not in union with the root — they have rejected Christ as Savior.

οἰκτιρμός vs. ἔλεος — Rational, Not Emotional, Mercy

Romans 12:1 — "by the mercies of God." οἰκτιρμός (mercies; grace blessings). Eleos can carry emotional connotations, compassion as a felt response. Oiktirmos denotes mercy or compassion on a rational basis, without emotional coloring, arising from rational evaluation rather than emotional impulse. Paul’s deliberate choice of oiktirmos rather than eleos establishes from the outset that God’s approach to the believer is rational, not emotional, and the honor code of the royal family of God operates on the same rational basis. In the plural it refers to the grace blessings imputed at maturity adjustment to the justice of God.

αἰών vs. κόσμος — Age, Not World

Romans 12:2 — "Do not be conformed to this world." αἰών (this age). The dative singular of aiōn, a segment of time, an age, with the demonstrative houtos. The object of the verb is not kosmos (world as a spatial or moral system) but aiōn. Age is the correct rendering because Satan’s policy of human good and evil takes a different form in every period; the command is age-specific, and the believer must resist the form that policy takes in his own day.

ὑπερφρονέω / φρονέω / σωφρονέω — A Paronomasia on the Root φρον-

Romans 12:3 — "not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think, but to think with sober judgment." ὑπερφρονέω (to overthink; stop thinking of self in terms of arrogance). Huperphroneō compounds huper (over, above, beyond) with the verb to think: to overthink oneself, to think above what is warranted, which is the definition of arrogance as a thought pattern; egoism is its functional expression. Without the prefix, phroneō denotes appropriate, warranted thinking; sōphroneō prefixes sōs (safe, sound): to be sane, rational without illusion. The paranomasia of Romans 12:3 sets huperphroneō against sōphroneō on the common root.

διώκω — To Pursue (12:13) and To Persecute (12:14)

Romans 12:14 — "those who persecute you." τοὺς διώκοντας (those who persecute, from διώκω). The present active participle of diōkō. In Romans 12:13 the same verb appeared in the positive command to pursue hospitality; here it carries the negative sense, to pursue in a hostile manner, to persecute, to press hard against.

ὑπερέχω — Governing, Not Merely Higher

Romans 13:1 — "the governing authorities." ὑπερέχω (governing). The present active participle of ὑπερέχω is used as an adjective modifying ἐξουσία. It does not mean simply higher but governing: it denotes duly constituted authority under divine institution number four (human government).

ἀντιτάσσω vs. ἀνθίστημι — Organized Opposition vs. Completed Application

Romans 13:2 — "Therefore whoever resists the authorities." ἀντιτάσσω (to form a battle line against). The articular present active participle of ἀντιτάσσω is a military term: to form a battle line against the opposition. It connotes organized, deliberate resistance, the product of a soul that has ordered its thinking in opposition to delegated authority.

Romans 13:2 — "resists what God has appointed." ἀνθίστημι (to oppose, to stand against). ἀνθίστημι (anti + histēmi) is slightly distinct from ἀντιτάσσω: ἀντιτάσσω denotes the organized thinking in opposition, while ἀνθίστημι denotes the completed application, the outward expression and result of that inward disposition.

φόβος — Fear for the Criminal, Respect for the Law-Abiding

Romans 13:3 — "For rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad." φόβος (fear; respect). φόβος, the predicate nominative of 13:3, carries a deliberate double meaning: fear for the criminal who opposes authority, and respect for the law-abiding citizen who operates within it. Both responses come from the same institutional structure; the difference lies entirely in the individual's orientation toward establishment.

διάκονος — Servant Executing a Commission for a Third Party

Romans 13:4 — "for he is God's servant for your good." διάκονος (minister, servant, deputy). The predicate nominative διάκονος denotes one who renders service to another as the representative of a third party: he carries out a commission. In classical usage it referred to a waiter at table, who does not own the establishment but serves the guests on behalf of the owner. Authority is never self-originating; it is always derived. The same word used of deacons and gospel ministers is applied here, deliberately and without qualification, to the civil magistrate.

Romans 15:8 — "Christ became a servant to the circumcised." διάκονον (minister, servant). The accusative singular direct object is diakonos (διάκονος). In its original usage the word referred to waiting on a table as a servant; from this the extended meaning of servant, one obligated to serve, minister. The word underlies the English transliteration deacon.

Romans 16:1 — "a servant of the church at Cenchreae." διάκονον (minister, helper). The word means minister, deputy, helper, agent. It denotes active, functional ministry, not merely a social title.

φορέω vs. φέρω — Bearing by Right of Office

Romans 13:4 — "for he does not bear the sword in vain." φορέω (to wear, to bear). φορέω means to bear or carry habitually, especially by right of authority. It is distinguished from the simpler φέρω by its connotation of bearing something as a mark of office or privilege: the government wears the sword by divine right and divine commission.

ἔκδικος — One Who Acts Out of Justice

Romans 13:4 — "an avenger who carries out God's wrath on the wrongdoer." ἔκδικος (punisher, avenger, executor of justice). ἔκδικος derives from ek (out of, from) and δίκη (justice, right, penalty): one who acts out of justice and brings justice to bear through punitive authority. It establishes that punitive action is the exclusive prerogative of those who hold legitimate authority within a defined sphere; unauthorized punishment (gossip, maligning, vigilante retaliation) usurps a function that belongs to authority alone.

κακός vs. πονηρός — Functional Evil vs. Intrinsic Wickedness

Romans 13:4 — "on the wrongdoer." κακός (evil, wrongdoing). κακός (with the generic article, the evil already defined in context) denotes evil in its active, functional dimension: wrongdoing that violates the rights and well-being of others and that civil authority exists to restrain and punish. It is distinguished from πονηρός, which emphasizes the intrinsic wickedness of a nature or character.

φόρος vs. τέλος — Direct Taxes vs. Indirect Taxes

Romans 13:6 — "you also pay taxes." φόρος (tribute, tax). φόρος denotes tribute or tax, specifically the direct tax paid by subject peoples to a ruling government, as distinct from customs duties or tolls. The accusative plural indicates that all applicable taxes are in view.

Romans 13:7 — "taxes to whom taxes are owed." φόρος (direct taxes). The first category is φόρος, repeated in the syntax to whom phoros, phoros. It refers to direct taxes imposed by the national government (income, property, sales tax, or equivalent levies). The repetition of the noun is a Semitic idiom for emphasis and immediacy.

Romans 13:7 — "revenue to whom revenue is owed." τέλος (indirect taxes). τέλος, which elsewhere means end or completion, here designates indirect taxes: customs duties, import fees, excise taxes. The distinction between φόρος and τέλος reflects the Roman tax system, in which direct tribute to Rome and local indirect customs duties were administered separately.

φόβος vs. τιμή — Respect for the Office, Honor for the Person

Romans 13:7 — "respect to whom respect is owed." φόβος (respect). φόβος can mean fear or respect depending on context. For the law-abiding citizen it means respect for the office of authority and for the institution of law and law enforcement; for the criminal it keeps its sense of fear of punishment. Assuming believers are law-abiding, the rendering here is respect, owed to the office irrespective of the personal character of the officeholder.

Romans 13:7 — "honor to whom honor is owed." τιμή (honor). τιμή is the highest of the four categories. Where φόβος goes to the office, τιμή goes to the person who holds the office, when that person merits it. Respect is always owed; honor is the additional recognition of personal excellence in office.

ἀλλήλων vs. ἕτερος — One Another of the Same Kind vs. Another of a Different Kind

Romans 13:8 — "except to love each other." ἀλλήλων (one another of the same kind). The direct object of ἀγαπᾶν is the reciprocal pronoun ἀλλήλων, one another of the same kind. It establishes a mutual, same-category relationship: believer to believer within the royal family of God.

Romans 13:8 — "for the one who loves another has fulfilled the law." ἕτερος (another of a different kind). ἕτερος, used as a substantive, means another of a different kind: another believer with a different personality and different opinions. Paul's choice of ἕτερος rather than ἄλλος (another of the same kind) underscores that impersonal love specifically targets the believer who is most unlike the one exercising it.

Romans 15:14 — "instruct one another." ἀλλήλους (each other of the same kind). When a plural subject is represented as mutually affecting one another through an interchange of actions, the reciprocal pronoun is used. The full infinitival phrase reads: being able also to have a corrective influence on each other.

Romans 16:16 — "Greet one another with a holy kiss." Ἀσπάσασθε ἀλλήλους (greet each other). Verse 16 opens with another aorist active imperative of aspazomai (ἀσπάζομαι), followed by the accusative plural of the reciprocal pronoun allēlōn (ἀλλήλων): 'Greet each other.' The reciprocal pronoun represents a plural subject engaged in an interchange of action with the verb.

μοιχεύω vs. πορνεία — Adultery as Both Sin and Crime

Romans 13:9 — "You shall not commit adultery." πορνεία (fornication). πορνεία is illicit sexual activity in its various forms; it is a sin. Adultery (μοιχεύω) is a subset of fornication with an additional dimension: it is also a crime, because it involves theft of a married woman who is her husband's legally recognized property. That double character is why adultery appears in this list of criminal prohibitions while fornication does not.

φονεύω — To Murder, Not Merely to Kill

Romans 13:9 (Exodus 20:13) — "You shall not murder." φονεύω (to murder). φονεύω does not mean to kill; it means specifically to murder, to take human life unlawfully and with malice aforethought. The sixth commandment is therefore thou shalt not murder, not thou shalt not kill. Killing in battle and through due process of law are authorized by Scripture (Genesis 9:6; Numbers 35:30–31; 1 Chronicles 5:22).

κλέπτω vs. μοιχεύω — Inanimate vs. Animate Property

Romans 13:9 (Exodus 20:15) — "You shall not steal." κλέπτω (to steal). κλέπτω (future active indicative with οὐ) addresses inanimate property: land, buildings, furnishings, clothing, tools, money, anything that can be owned. This distinguishes it from the adultery commandment, which addressed animate property, a man's wife.

ἐπιθυμέω — The Lust Pattern, Not Casual Desire

Romans 13:9 (Exodus 20:17) — "You shall not covet." ἐπιθυμέω (you shall not lust, you shall not covet). ἐπιθυμέω (future active indicative with οὐ) is not the language of casual desire but of the consuming lust pattern of the old sin nature, the craving to possess what belongs to another. Unique among the commandments cited, it targets the mental attitude that precedes and generates overt criminal acts.

ἀνακεφαλαιόω — To Bring Under One Head

Romans 13:9 — "are summed up in this word." ἀνακεφαλαιόω (to sum up, to epitomize). ἀνακεφαλαιόω is a compound of ana (up, again) and κεφαλή (head): to bring several things together under one head, to reduce to a single heading, to summarize, to epitomize. The five negative commandments are not abolished but gathered into the single positive principle of impersonal love.

εὐσχημόνως — Honorably, Befitting Royal Rank

Romans 13:13 — "Let us walk properly." εὐσχημόνως (honorably). εὐσχημόνως is from eu (well, nobly) and schema (bearing, form, outward manner): conduct that befits one's rank and station. The English renderings properly and honestly are inadequate; this is not establishment honesty available to any person of integrity but the honor belonging exclusively to the royal family of God, executable only in the filling of the Holy Spirit and in proportion to maximum doctrine in the soul.

πρόνοια — Forethought, Advance Provision

Romans 13:14 — "and make no provision for the flesh." πρόνοια (provision). πρόνοια is from pro (before) and nous (mind, thought): foresight, forethought, and by extension advance provision. Making provision for the old sin nature means directing one's mental energy (planning, attention, time) toward satisfying its appetites rather than toward the advance to maturity.

ἐξουθενέω — To Regard as Nothing

Romans 14:3 — "despise the one who abstains." ἐξουθενέω (to despise, to treat with contempt). ἐξουθενέω is a compound: ἐξ (out of) + the word for nothing. It means to regard as nothing, to reject with contemptuous disdain; it carries the specific force of contemptuous rejection, the strong believer’s occupational hazard toward the weak.

οἰκέτης vs. δοῦλος — House Slave vs. Field Slave

Romans 14:4 — "the servant of another." οἰκέτης (house slave, domestic servant). The object is οἰκέτης, modified by ἀλλότριος (belonging to another). οἰκέτης denotes specifically a house slave, as distinct from the field hand (δοῦλος), and the choice is exegetically significant. To criticize another person’s house slave directly was a recognized breach of etiquette in the Roman imperial world; every believer is a domestic slave of Christ, and no believer has standing to judge another believer’s slave.

ζάω (zō egō) — The Divine Oath Grounded in the Eternal Life of God

Romans 14:11 (Isaiah 45:23) — "As I live." ζῶ ἐγώ (I keep on living, from ζάω). Where the Hebrew of Isaiah 45:23 reads by myself I have sworn, Paul uses the Greek phrase meaning I keep on living. The two are not literal surface equivalents, yet Paul treats them as conveying the same theological content: the oath is grounded in God's own inherent perfections, and His eternal, self-existent life is the ultimate guarantee behind every divine oath. What they share is the divine essence, specifically the integrity of God (His righteousness and justice).

πρόσκομμα vs. σκάνδαλον — Obstacle and Trap

Romans 14:13 — "a stumbling block or hindrance." πρόσκομμα (an obstacle or a distraction). Two accusative singular direct objects follow. πρόσκομμα (from pros, toward, and koptō, to strike) is an obstacle, specifically to the spiritual growth of the weak believer. σκάνδαλον, originally the trigger of a trap, is a trap or distraction. Together they describe anything a strong believer might say or do that diverts the weak believer's attention from Bible doctrine and occupation with Christ.

βρῶσις, πόσις vs. βρῶμα — The Acts of Eating and Drinking vs. the Food Itself

Romans 14:17 — "eating." βρῶσις (eating). The first predicate nominative is βρῶσις, the act of eating food, distinguished from βρῶμα, the food itself. The active suffix in βρῶσις emphasizes the act of consuming. The kingdom of God is not constituted by or measured by the act of eating.

Romans 14:17 — "drinking." πόσις (drinking). The second predicate nominative, linked by καί, is πόσις, drinking, referring specifically to the drinking of alcoholic beverages. Neither the consumption of food nor of beverage defines, sustains or evaluates the spiritual life of the royal family; the single exception is drunkenness, which is a sin.

ἐπαναμιμνῄσκω — To Remind Again and Again

Romans 15:15 — "by way of reminder." ἐπαναμιμνῄσκων (reminding again and again). The participial phrase translated 'as putting you in mind' employs the present active participle of the triple compound verb epanamimnēskō (ἐπαναμιμνῄσκω). The compound means: to remind again and again.

σημεῖον vs. τέρας — Signs to Israel, Wonders Among Gentiles

Romans 15:19 — "by the power of signs and wonders." σημείων καὶ τεράτων (signs and wonders). While both terms refer to supernaturally produced events, each carries a different emphasis. Sēmeion established Paul's apostolic identity to Jewish hearers. Signs were directed toward Israel as the confirmation of apostolic authority.

φιλοτιμέομαι — To Make It a Point of Honor

Romans 15:20 — "I make it my ambition." φιλοτιμούμενον (considering it a point of honor). The governing verb is the present middle participle of φιλοτιμέομαι (philotimeomai), a compound of φίλος (philos, love) and τιμή (timē, honor). The compound verb means to love honor, to aspire to what is honorable, to make a point of honor. Correctly translated: I consider it a point of honor.

συναγωνίζομαι — To Join in the Team Effort

Romans 15:30 — "to strive together with me in your prayers." συναγωνίσασθαί (to contend together). The aorist middle infinitive synagōnizomai (συναγωνίζομαι) is a compound verb: syn (σύν, alongside, together with) plus agōnizomai (ἀγωνίζομαι, to carry on a conflict, to compete in athletic games, to fight in combat). The compound means to join in the team effort, to contend together. The military and athletic connotations are both in view.

συναναπαύομαι — To Find Rest Together With

Romans 15:32 — "and be refreshed in your company." συναναπαύσωμαι (I may find rest with). The final clause of verse 32 employs the aorist middle subjunctive of the compound verb synanapauomai (συναναπαύομαι), formed from syn (with) + ana (up) + pauomai (to rest, to cease). The compound denotes mutual rest and refreshment in company with another.

ὑποτίθημι + τράχηλος — To Put One's Neck on the Line

Romans 16:4 — "who risked their necks for my life." τὸν ἑαυτῶν τράχηλον ὑπέθηκαν (they risked their own necks). The main verb is an aorist active indicative of ὑποτίθημι (hypotithēmi), a compound of ὑπό (hypo, 'under') and τίθημι (tithēmi, 'to place'). From this literal sense the verb acquired its idiomatic meaning: to risk one's life, to put one's neck on the line.

κοπιάω — To Labor to the Point of Exhaustion

Romans 16:6 — "who has worked hard for you." ἐκοπίασεν (she labored to exhaustion). The verb is the aorist active indicative of kopiaō (κοπιάω), meaning to labor to the point of exhaustion, to work with intense and sustained effort. The cognate noun kopos (κόπος) is used elsewhere in the Pauline letters to describe apostolic labor and the work of doctrine communication.

συναιχμάλωτος — Taken at Spearpoint

Romans 16:7 — "my kinsmen and my fellow prisoners." συναιχμαλώτους μου (my fellow prisoners). The compound noun synaichmalōtos (συναιχμάλωτος) is composed of syn (together with) + aichmē (a spear) + halōtos (captured), literally 'taken at spearpoint,' i.e., a prisoner of war. By the first century it was used generally for any fellow prisoner.

ἐπίσημος — Prominent, Outstanding

Romans 16:7 — "They are well known to the apostles." ἐπίσημοι ἐν τοῖς ἀποστόλοις (prominent among the apostles). The adjective episēmos (ἐπίσημος) means prominent, outstanding, well-regarded. The dative plural en tois apostolois (ἐν τοῖς ἀποστόλοις) uses apostolos (ἀπόστολος) in its broader rather than its narrow sense.

δόκιμος — Tested and Approved

Romans 16:10 — "Greet Apelles, who is approved in Christ." δόκιμον ἐν Χριστῷ (tested and approved in Christ). The adjective dokimos (δόκιμος) carries the sense of approved, tried and true, genuine, reliable, esteemed. The corrected translation: tested and approved. The prepositional phrase en Christō (ἐν Χριστῷ) — in Christ — locates the sphere in which this testing and approval occurs.

συγγενής — Fellow Countryman

Romans 16:11 — "Greet my kinsman Herodion." τὸν συγγενῆ μου (my fellow countryman). The appositional accusative singular from the noun syngenes (συγγενής) identifies him as Paul's fellow countryman — one of the same race and nation. In Romans 9:3 the same term refers to fellow countrymen in the ethnic sense.

παρακαλέω — To Call to One's Side

Romans 16:17 — "I appeal to you, brothers." Παρακαλῶ (I urge). The main verb is the present active indicative of parakaleō (παρακαλέω), from para (παρά, alongside) + kaleō (καλέω, to call). The compound verb means to call someone to one's side — and therefore to appeal, to exhort, to encourage, or to rebuke.

διχοστασία — Taking Two Stances

Romans 16:17 — "those who cause divisions." τὰς διχοστασίας (dissensions). The first object is dichostasias (διχοστασίας), accusative plural of dichostasia (διχοστασία), from dicha (in two) + stasis (στάσις, a standing). The compound means to take two stances — to cause a split, to produce dissension.

σκάνδαλον — The Trigger Stick of a Trap

Romans 16:17 — "create obstacles." τὰ σκάνδαλα (enticements, traps). The second object is skandala (σκάνδαλα), accusative plural of skandalon (σκάνδαλον). The term denotes the trigger stick of a trap — the mechanism by which bait is set so that contact with it springs the trap.

κοιλία — The Hollow Cavity, a Metaphor for Emotion

Romans 16:18 — "but their own appetites." τῇ ἑαυτῶν κοιλίᾳ (their own emotion). What they do serve is expressed by the dative singular of koilia (κοιλία), a noun meaning cavity, hollow space. In classical and Koine Greek it is used for the womb and the stomach — both empty chambers that receive and respond to content. Here it designates the emotion of the soul: the capacity that is empty of thought, waiting to respond to stimuli.

χρηστολογία and εὐλογία — Smooth Speech and Flattery

Romans 16:18 — "and by smooth talk and flattery." διὰ τῆς χρηστολογίας καὶ εὐλογίας (by smooth speech and flattering speech). The adjective chrēstos (χρηστός) means good or pleasant — not the proper name Christ. Combined with logos (λόγος) for speech, the compound means pleasant speech, bland speech, smooth and gentle non-irritating speech that masks a fraudulent purpose. The ablative of means with dia signals that this smooth speech is the instrument by which the deception is accomplished — means accompanied by source. The adverb eu (εὖ) means well or good; logia means communication. Together: good communication, or in this context, flattering speech.

ἀκέραιος — Unharmed, Not Ravaged

Romans 16:19 — "innocent as to what is evil." ἀκεραίους δὲ εἰς τὸ κακόν (unharmed with reference to the evil). The second half of verse 19 presents a compound adjective that is frequently mistranslated. The compound therefore means not destroyed, not corrupted — that which remains in its original state of integrity. Its semantic range is closer to unharmed or unravaged — the state of something that has not been damaged by an outside corrosive force. The definite article with κακός is generic — referring to the category of evil as a whole. The full prepositional phrase εἰς τὸ κακόν therefore means 'with reference to the evil.'

οἰκονόμος — Steward, City Treasurer

Romans 16:23 — "Erastus, the city treasurer." ὁ οἰκονόμος τῆς πόλεως (the city controller). Paul identifies Erastus by the appositional nominative oikonomos (οἰκονόμος), a compound of oikos (household) and nomos (law, management). The term denotes a steward or manager of an estate. In its technical civic sense, used here with the descriptive genitive singular of polis (πόλις, city), it designates the city controller or treasurer — the official responsible for municipal finances.

στηρίζω — To Stabilize, to Make Firm

Romans 16:25 — "Now to him who is able to strengthen you." ὑμᾶς στηρίξαι (to sustain you). The aorist active infinitive of stērizō (στηρίζω) follows. From these classical precedents, the Koine adopts the meaning: to stabilize, to make firm, to establish. Corrected translation of the infinitive phrase: to sustain you, to support you.

εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων — Forever and Ever

Romans 16:27 — "be glory forevermore." εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων (to the ages of the ages). The temporal phrase eis tous aiōnas tōn aiōnōn (εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων) — 'to the ages of the ages' — is the standard idiom for 'forever and ever.' The first aiōn in the accusative plural carries the sense of 'forever'; the second in the genitive plural intensifies it: 'and ever.'

XX.Infinitives

Romans 1:15 — "so I am eager to preach the gospel to you also who are in Rome." εὐαγγελίσασθαι (aorist middle infinitive of εὐαγγελίζομαι) is an infinitive of intended result: the aorist gathers the totality of Paul's doctrinal communication into one entirety, while the infinitive marks the fulfillment of a deliberate objective.

Romans 2:19 — "and if you are sure that you yourself are a guide to the blind." εἶναι (present active infinitive of εἰμί) functions within an accusative-plus-infinitive construction; its progressive present force denotes a persistent, continuing state — the legalist claims to be, and continues to be, a guide and a light.

Romans 2:21 — "you then who teach others, do you not teach yourself?" The articular present active infinitive of κηρύσσω ("to proclaim, to herald" — from κῆρυξ, the royal herald who delivered a king's proclamation to an assembled crowd) denotes the Judaizer's ongoing, one-directional public proclamation.

Infinitive of Actual Result

States a result that actually, in fact, occurred.

Romans 4:1 — "What then shall we say was gained by Abraham, our forefather according to the flesh, has found?" εὑρηκέναι (the perfect infinitive of εὑρίσκω) presents Abraham's finding as an actual, historical result, not a merely conceivable or intended one (see also the Intensive Perfect entry, section II).

Romans 11:23 — "to graft them in again." ἐγκεντρίσαι (to graft in, from ἐγκεντρίζω). The aorist active infinitive ἐγκεντρίσαι, with the accusative αὐτούς (the Jewish unbelievers) as object, functions as an infinitive of actual result. The constative aorist contemplates the entire action — the moment of belief and the resulting grafting in — as a unified whole.

Romans 15:14 — "able to instruct one another." νουθετεῖν (to have a corrective influence on). The infinitive of actual result is taken from the compound verb noutheteō (νουθετέω), formed from nous (νοῦς, mind) and tithēmi (τίθημι, to place). Literally: to put into the mind or to place in thought. The verb connotes effect on the intellect and emphasizes the one qualified to exercise influence over the intellect.

εἰς τό + Infinitive — Purpose Clauses

A fixed construction using the preposition εἰς with the articular infinitive, expressing purpose.

Romans 4:11 — "that he might be the father of all who believe without being circumcised, so that righteousness would be counted to them as well." εἰς τὸ εἶναι and the following purpose infinitive together express the design of God's arrangement with Abraham.

Romans 4:16 — "in order that the promise may rest on grace and be guaranteed to all his offspring." A comparable εἰς τό-type purpose construction underlies this clause.

Romans 4:18 — "In hope he believed against hope, that he should become the father of many nations." εἰς τὸ γενέσθαι expresses the purpose/intended result of the promise given to Abraham.

Romans 11:11 — "so as to make Israel jealous." παραζηλόω (in order that they might be stimulated to emulation). The closing purpose clause is εἰς with the articular aorist active infinitive of παραζηλόω (παρά, alongside, plus ζηλόω, to be zealous, to emulate), with an accusative of general reference from αὐτός as subject of the infinitive. The divine purpose is that the faith of Gentile believers would provoke individual Jews to emulate that faith and believe in the Lord Jesus Christ.

Romans 12:2 — "that by testing you may discern." δοκιμάζω (that you may prove). The purpose of transformation is introduced by eis to dokimazein, eis plus the present active infinitive of dokimazō, to test for the purpose of approval. The present infinitive is perfective in force, emphasizing the continuation and results of existing conditions; the will of God is not passively received but actively discerned through doctrine-saturated thinking applied to the circumstances of life.

Romans 12:3 — "but to think with sober judgment." εἰς τὸ σωφρονεῖν (for the purpose of being rational without illusion, from σωφρονέω). The infinitive of purpose eis to sōphronein blends purpose and result. The standard rendering think soberly is misleading, suggesting mere restraint or gravity; the Greek means specifically to be rational without illusion, about oneself and about others.

Romans 15:8 — "in order to confirm the promises given to the patriarchs." εἰς τὸ βεβαιῶσαι (for the purpose of establishing). The purpose of Christ's ministry to Israel is stated by a prepositional phrase: εἰς (eis) plus the articular aorist active infinitive of βεβαιόω (bebaioō), meaning 'to confirm, to make firm, to establish.' The accusative of the definite article with εἰς introduces a purpose clause expressing the action toward which the main verb is directed: Christ has become a minister to the Jews for the purpose of establishing something.

Romans 15:13 — "so that by the power of the Holy Spirit you may abound in hope." εἰς τὸ περισσεύειν (that you may excel). The verse concludes with a purpose clause introduced by εἰς (eis) plus the accusative of the definite article, signaling an articular infinitive. The infinitive is περισσεύω (perisseuō), meaning to abound, to overflow, to be extremely rich in, to excel in, to be prominent in. The corrected translation: 'that you may excel in the hope.'

Romans 15:16 — "to be a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles." εἰς τὸ εἶναί (that I should be). The construction eis to (εἰς τό) followed by an infinitive introduces a purpose clause. Its function is to express the aim of the action denoted by the main verb of verse 15. The translation is: that I should be.

Infinitive of Intended Result

States a result that is aimed at or intended, though not yet (or not necessarily) accomplished.

Romans 4:24 — "It will be counted to us who believe in him who raised from the dead Jesus our Lord." The infinitival construction underlying "who raised" (τὸν ἐγείραντα, more precisely a substantival participle functioning with infinitive-like purpose-force in the flow of the sentence) points to the intended result of resurrection faith extending forward to future believers.

Romans 9:21 — "to make out of the same lump one vessel." ποιέω (to make, to manufacture). The infinitive is the aorist active infinitive of ποιέω. The constative aorist encompasses the entire creative act as a single event; the active voice designates God as the one who performs it. The infinitive functions as an infinitive of intended result: the creative act is purposive, directed toward a deliberate objective, the production of beings capable of genuine moral self-determination.

Romans 10:3 — "seeking to establish their own." ἵστημι (to establish). The complementary infinitive is the aorist active infinitive of histemi, to establish, to confirm. The aorist is constative, viewing the action as a single extended whole. It is the infinitive of intended result, combining purpose and result: the objective is to establish, and they succeed in establishing, within their own framework, a self-constructed righteousness.

Romans 11:25 — "I do not want you to be unaware of this mystery, brothers." ἀγνοέω (to be ignorant). The infinitive of ἀγνοέω (alpha-privative + to know; the root of English agnostic) follows. The descriptive present describes what is currently occurring among Church Age believers. The infinitive of intended result blends purpose and result, emphasizing the importance of the content that follows: For I do not desire you, brethren, to be ignorant of this mystery.

Romans 13:3 — "Would you have no fear." φοβέω (not to fear). The infinitive expresses intended result blended with purpose: not to fear is both the goal and the outcome of the action commanded in the imperative that follows (keep on doing the good).

Romans 13:5 — "one must be in subjection." ὑποτάσσω (to be subordinate). The infinitive of ὑποτάσσω expresses intended result: the purpose and the result of subordination are the same, namely freedom, privacy, and property.

Romans 13:8 — "except to love each other." ἀγαπάω (to love). The infinitive of ἀγαπάω is an infinitive of intended result, blending purpose and result, and functions here as an imperative infinitive: a command.

Romans 13:11 — "for you to wake from sleep." ἐγείρω (to wake up). The aorist passive infinitive of ἐγείρω functions as an infinitive of intended result, blending purpose and outcome.

Romans 15:1 — "have an obligation to bear with the failings of the weak." βαστάζω (are obligated to keep on bearing). The infinitive functions as an infinitive of purpose — here a sub-final purpose clause — indicating both purpose and intended result. The finite verb preceding it carries the force of obligation: opheilomen (ὀφείλομεν), we are obligated. Together they yield: are obligated to keep on bearing.

Romans 15:5 — "to live in such harmony with one another." φρονεῖν (to be thinking). The infinitive is an infinitive of intended result, blending purpose and result into a single concept.

Romans 15:24 — "to be helped on my journey there by you." προπεμφθῆναι (to be assisted on the journey). The main verb of this clause is the aorist passive infinitive of propempō (προπέμπω), meaning to escort, to assist with money, clothing, food, and companions for the journey. The infinitive expresses intended result: a blending of purpose and result in which the objective is deliberately pursued. Corrected translation: and by you be assisted to that place.

Romans 15:27 — "to be of service to them in material blessings." λειτουργῆσαι (to minister). The infinitive of intended result is the aorist active infinitive of leitourgeō (λειτουργέω), to perform a service, to discharge a public or cultic responsibility. Here it carries the force of an honor-code obligation: to minister to them in material things. The result infinitive blends purpose and outcome: the objective of the honor code is fulfilled in the act of giving.

Romans 16:19 — "but I want you to be wise as to what is good." θέλω … ὑμᾶς σοφοὺς εἶναι (I keep wanting you to be wise). The verb is the present active indicative of thelō (θέλω), expressing a wish or deliberate purpose. The progressive present indicates persistent desire: but I keep wanting you to be. The infinitive of eimi (εἶναι) follows in the perfective present, denoting the continuation of existing results — in this case, the results of sustained doctrinal intake. This is the infinitive of intended result, blending purpose and outcome.

Infinitive of Conceived Result

States a result that is merely conceived or imagined as a possibility, without asserting it as either intended or actual.

Romans 5:7 — "For one will scarcely die for a righteous person — though perhaps for a good person one would dare even to die." The infinitive ἀποθανεῖν ("to die") here names a conceived, hypothetical result Paul is exploring for the sake of illustration, not an intended or actual result of any specific narrated event.

Romans 9:3 — "that I myself were accursed." εἶναι (to be, from εἰμί). The infinitive einai functions as an infinitive of conceived result: the consequence assumed as following from the verb of wishing.

Romans 10:6 — "to bring Christ down." καταγαγεῖν (to bring down). The aorist active infinitive katagagein, to bring down, is constative, contemplating the action in its entirety; the active voice places the action on the rationalizing Jewish unbeliever. The infinitive expresses conceived result, a consequence assumed to follow from the nature of the rationalization itself: to bring Christ down from heaven, as if the first advent had not occurred.

Romans 10:7 — "to bring Christ up from the dead." ἀνάγω (to bring up). Paul draws the implication with the demonstrative plus eimi (this implies) and the aorist active infinitive of anagō, to bring up. The aorist is constative; the active voice places the action on the rationalizing unbeliever; the infinitive expresses conceived result assumed as a consequence of the rationalization.

Romans 14:14 — "for anyone who thinks it unclean." εἶναι (to be, from εἰμί). The present active infinitive εἶναι expresses the content of what the weak believer presumes. The present is a descriptive present for what is now going on among this category of believers, and the active voice shows that the weak believer himself makes the assessment. It is the infinitive of conceived result from a false assumption: the result he expects follows from premises that are themselves erroneous.

Romans 15:18 — "I will not venture to speak of anything." λαλεῖν (to speak). The present active infinitive λαλεῖν (lalein), from λαλέω (laleō), to speak or to communicate, introduces the content of what Paul refuses to presume upon. The descriptive present indicates what is currently the pattern of his experience. The infinitive expresses a conceived result, a consequence of having doctrine in the soul: because doctrine is resident, arrogance is absent.

Articular Infinitive as a Purpose Clause

The infinitive with the definite article, functioning to express purpose.

Romans 6:12 — "Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, to make you obey its passions." εἰς τὸ ὑπακούειν (articular infinitive with εἰς) expresses the purpose for which sin seeks to reign: specifically, to produce obedience to its own lusts.

Articular Infinitive as a Substantive Noun

The infinitive with the article functioning as the subject or object of a clause, essentially as a verbal noun.

Romans 7:18 — "For I know that nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh. For I have the desire to do what is right, but not the ability to carry it out." τὸ θέλειν ("the wishing/desiring," an articular infinitive) functions as a substantive, naming "the act of desiring" itself as a noun-like entity present in Paul — contrasted with τὸ κατεργάζεσθαι ("the accomplishing"), likewise substantival, which he finds absent.

Romans 14:21 — "not to eat meat." τὸ μὴ φαγεῖν (not-eating, from ἐσθίω). The subject of the clause is the articular aorist active infinitive of ἐσθίω negated by μή. The articular infinitive, an Attic idiom, converts the verbal idea into a substantive while preserving verbal force; the nominative neuter article makes it the subject of the implied verb to be, balanced against the predicate καλός: not-eating is honorable.

Infinitive of Intended Resolve

States a settled resolve or determination — the will fixed on a course of action, whether or not that resolve is realized.

Romans 7:21 — "So I find it to be a law that when I want to do right, evil lies close at hand." τὸ ποιεῖν ("the doing," an articular infinitive) names Paul's fixed resolve to do what is honorable — the resolve itself, as a settled disposition, standing independent of whether it is successfully carried out (which, per the surrounding argument, it consistently is not, apart from the intervention described in Romans 8).

Infinitive of Purpose

Romans 9:22 — "to make known his power." γνωρίζω (to make known, to reveal, to declare). A connective καί joins a second aorist active infinitive of purpose, γνωρίζω, with the accusative of δυνατός as object: and to reveal His omnipotence. God's endurance of Pharaoh's sustained defiance was not passive tolerance but an active demonstration both of His judgment of evil and of His power to accomplish His purposes through and in spite of that evil.

Romans 15:24 — "I hope to see you in passing." θεάσασθαι (to see in perspective). The infinitive of purpose following elpizō is the aorist middle infinitive of theaomai (θεάομαι), which means not simply to behold a person visually, but to see in perspective — to have capacity for seeing. Corrected translation: for I expect to see you.

τοῦ μή + Infinitive — Genitive Articular Infinitive of Negative Purpose

Romans 11:8 (Deuteronomy 29:4) — "eyes that would not see and ears that would not hear." βλέπω (eyes for the purpose of not seeing). τοῦ with the present active infinitive of βλέπω, negated by μή, is a genitive articular infinitive of negative purpose: eyes for the purpose of not seeing. The parallel τοῦ with ἀκούω and μή gives ears for the purpose of not hearing. Eyes and ears represent the two primary systems of perception through which doctrine enters the soul, and the big blot out closes both.

Romans 11:10 (Psalm 69:23) — "so that they cannot see." βλέπω (for the purpose of not seeing). The genitive article with the present active infinitive of βλέπω and the negative μή forms a negative purpose clause: let their eyes be darkened for the purpose of not seeing. The active voice indicates that the Jewish reversionists produce the action; the darkening is a consequence they bring upon themselves.

The Imperatival Infinitive

Romans 12:1 — "to present your bodies." παρίστημι (place under orders). Aorist active infinitive of paristēmi used as an imperatival infinitive, a classical Greek construction in which the infinitive carries imperative force. The command is the deliberate placement of the body under the command of God.

Romans 12:15 — "Rejoice with those who rejoice." χαίρω (keep on rejoicing). The present active infinitive of chairō functions as an imperative, as in Classical and Attic Greek (as early as Homer), to which Paul frequently reverts for a direct command. Paul uses the infinitive deliberately: the imperative chairete was a common greeting equivalent to hello, so the infinitive signals unambiguously a doctrinal imperative, not a salutation. The progressive present: keep on rejoicing.

Romans 12:15 — "weep with those who weep." κλαίω (keep on weeping). The present active infinitive of klaiō, to give outward expression to grief, loss, or suffering, again functions as an imperative, with meta plus the genitive plural participle: weep with those who are weeping. The weeping is not self-pity but the genuine expression of suffering.

Romans 16:17 — "to watch out for those who cause divisions." σκοπεῖν (keep watching). The present active infinitive of skopeō (σκοπέω) follows: to look at, to fix one's eyes upon, to scrutinize critically, to be alert. The infinitive here functions as an imperative.

Imperatival Infinitive

Romans 14:13 — "decide never to put a stumbling block or hindrance in the way of a brother." τίθημι (not to place). The articular present active infinitive of τίθημι, negated by μή, functions as an imperatival infinitive specifying the content of the strong believer's determination. The action negated is the placing of either πρόσκομμα or σκάνδαλον before the weaker brother.

ἐν τῷ + Infinitive — By Means Of

Romans 15:13 — "in believing." ἐν τῷ πιστεύειν (by means of believing). The instrumental phrase is en tō pisteuein (ἐν τῷ πιστεύειν). The preposition en with the instrumental case means 'by means of.' The definite article tō before the present active infinitive of pisteuō (πιστεύω) — 'to believe' — is significant: the article before an infinitive draws attention to the action as known and specific. This is not believing in the simple sense of initial faith in Christ.

τοῦ + Infinitive — From Doing

Romans 15:22 — "hindered from coming to you." τοῦ ἐλθεῖν (from coming). The articular aorist active infinitive of erchomai, ἔρχομαι, with the definite article used as a preposition of source, gives the construction “from coming.” The aorist infinitive gathers up the multiple intended journeys to Rome into a single entirety.

XXI.Selected Vocabulary in Doctrinal Context

τίς / οὖν / περισσός / Ἰουδαίου — The Opening Question of Romans 3

Romans 3:1 — "Then what advantage has the Jew? Or what is the value of circumcision?" τίς is the interrogative pronoun, nominative neuter, functioning as the subject of the clause. οὖν is the inferential particle drawing the question as a conclusion from chapter 2's demonstration of impartial justice. περισσός (rendered "advantage," more precisely "preeminence") is a predicate adjective used substantively, covering what exceeds the ordinary measure. Ἰουδαίου is a descriptive genitive covering both the racial and the national identity of Israel.

ὠφέλεια — Concrete Benefit or Profit

Romans 3:1 — "what is the value of circumcision?" ὠφέλεια (from ὠφελέω, "to help, to benefit") names concrete, accruing advantage or gain — distinct from the more abstract περισσός of the verse's first clause.

ἀσέβεια, ἀδικία — Recurring Across the Argument

See section XIX above for the full treatment at Romans 1:18; the same pairing recurs structurally across the letter as Paul's technical vocabulary for salvation maladjustment.

Romans 9:14 — "Is there injustice on God's part?" ἀδικία (injustice, unrighteousness). adikia, privative alpha plus dikē, carries precise legal force: legal injustice, partiality, prejudice, susceptibility to bribery, and the substitution of personal bias for fact in rendering judgment. Paul anticipates that readers will interpret the anthropopathism I hate Esau as evidence of bias in the divine decree, as though God condemned Esau on grounds other than Esau's own volitional rejection of the Savior; the charge is categorically denied by mē genoito.

Romans 11:26 — "he will banish ungodliness from Jacob." ἀσέβεια (godlessness; the godless ones). In Romans 11:26 the abstract noun ἀσέβεια is used collectively for the godless ones — the unbelieving Jews removed from Jacob at the baptism of fire. Its root meaning is minus God, minus salvation: those who have not made the salvation adjustment to the justice of God.

ἀνθρωποπάθεια — Anthropopathism as a Recurring Interpretive Key

Romans 1:18; 2:4; 9:13 — Divine anger, kindness, and hatred are each, in their turn, anthropopathisms: human characteristics ascribed to God as accommodations to human understanding, not literal descriptions of divine emotional experience. χρηστότης ("kindness"), ἀνοχή ("forbearance"), and μακροθυμία ("patience") at Romans 2:4 form a triad of such anthropopathisms describing the comprehensive fullness of what God's justice has arranged for the sinner who will adjust to it.

Romans 9:13 (Malachi 1:2–3) — "Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated." ἄνθρωπος + πάθος (anthropopathism, from ἀνθρωποπάθεια). The term is derived from anthrōpos, man, and pathos, a function of the soul with outward manifestation: a human-soul-function ascribed to God for communicative purposes only, a characteristic He does not actually possess, used to explain divine policy in terms of human frame of reference. Divine love and divine hatred in Romans 9:13 are such language of accommodation; anthropopathisms describe divine policy, not divine psychology.

Romans 9:22 — "desiring to show his wrath." ὀργή (indignation). The accusative singular ὀργή is an anthropopathism, attributing a human emotional state to God to convey a divine policy in humanly intelligible terms. Anger is a sin; God does not sin. The term does not describe a divine emotional reaction but the function of divine integrity against sin and negative volition: the righteousness of God rejects evil and the justice of God condemns it. Corrected translation: His indignation, understood as His judicial condemnation of evil.

Romans 10:19 (Deuteronomy 32:21) — "I will make you jealous." παραζηλόω (to provoke to jealousy). Parazēloō, para (intensifying) + zēloō (to be jealous), conveys very strong jealousy, and the Lord uses it of himself. Jealousy is a human, indeed sinful, characteristic; ascribed to God it is an anthropopathism, used to communicate divine disapprobation of Israel's idolatry within man's frame of reference.

μετάνοια — Change of Mind, Not Emotional Remorse

Romans 2:4 — "not knowing that God's kindness is meant to lead you to repentance." μετάνοια denotes a change of mind — specifically, in the evangelistic sense, the change of mind toward Christ that constitutes positive volition at gospel hearing, not sorrow or emotional contrition as an end in itself.

σκληρότης — The Scar Tissue of the Soul

Romans 2:5 — "But because of your hard and impenitent heart." σκληρότης ("hardness") names the scarring that accumulates in the soul through sustained negative volition — a doctrinal category, not merely a description of stubbornness.

καρδία — The Right Lobe of the Soul

Romans 2:5, 29 — "your hard and impenitent heart"; "circumcision is a matter of the heart." καρδία in Paul's technical usage designates the right lobe of the soul — the seat of doctrine storage, thinking, and the capacity for faith — not the physical organ nor a purely emotional center.

Romans 9:2 — "in my heart." καρδία (right lobe). The locative singular kardia specifies the location of the pain. In Pauline anthropology kardia designates the right lobe of the soul, the integrating center where doctrine is stored as epignosis and where all genuine human experience registers. The pain is primarily intellectual, originating in Paul's comprehensive doctrinal knowledge.

Romans 10:1 — "my heart's desire." καρδία (right lobe of the soul). Eudokia is joined by the possessive genitive of kardia, preceded by the possessive adjective emos, my. In New Testament usage kardia is not the physical organ or emotional feeling but the right lobe of the soul: the mentality, the thinking faculty, the final resting place of doctrine, and the source from which thought is projected into decision and action. Paul's motivation is therefore an intellectual and volitional reality grounded in Bible doctrine resident in the right lobe.

Romans 10:6 — "in your heart." ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ σου (in your right lobe). En plus the locative of kardia. Kardia never denotes the physiological organ in the New Testament; it designates the right lobe of the soul: frame of reference, memory center, vocabulary and categorical storage, and the norms and standards of the conscience. The possessive genitive sou, your, emphasizes that believing, like rationalizing, is irreducibly personal. The right lobe is the source of both faith and rationalization, and the choice between them is an act of volition.

Romans 10:8 — "in your heart." καρδία (right lobe). En plus the locative of kardia. Kardia is never the physiological pump but the right lobe of the soul, where thought is processed, evaluated, and stored; as the physical heart circulates blood, the right lobe circulates thought throughout the soul. Faith originates in the right lobe and the mouth expresses what the right lobe has processed. There is no distinction between head belief and heart belief in the New Testament.

Romans 10:9 — "believe in your heart." ἐν τῇ καρδία (in the right lobe). En tē kardia locates faith in the right lobe of the soul. The genitive personal pronoun sou makes it individual and non-transferable: faith is a personal, private, non-meritorious act of perception directed toward Christ.

δόξα, τιμή, ἀφθαρσία — Three Results of Salvation Adjustment

Romans 2:7 — "to those who by patience in well-doing seek for glory and honor and immortality." δόξα ("glory"), τιμή ("honor," something of intrinsic worth, tracing from Homeric material wealth to Attic abstract integrity), and ἀφθαρσία ("incorruptibility," the technical term for the future resurrection body) together name the guaranteed, irrevocable results of salvation adjustment, established at the moment of faith and resting on the integrity of the God who provides them.

θλῖψις, στενοχωρία — Personal and National Distress

Romans 2:9 — "There will be tribulation and distress for every human being who does evil." θλῖψις names pressure at the personal level; στενοχωρία (στενός, "narrow" + χώρα, "space") names a constricted environment — the national and historical level of temporal judgment, the collapse of a civilization's room to maneuver under the cycles of divine discipline.

Ἕλλην vs. ἔθνος — Culture Versus Bare Ethnicity

Romans 2:9–10 — Paul's choice of Ἕλλην ("Greek," a person shaped by Hellenistic culture — philosophy, rhetoric, art) rather than the more generic ἔθνος ("nation, Gentile") establishes the cultural dimension of the impartiality principle: no level of cultural achievement, any more than racial privilege, constitutes standing before the justice of God.

Romans 10:12 — "between Jew and Greek." Ἕλλην (Greek; all Gentiles). Hellēn denotes the Greek, but Paul uses it as a synecdoche for the entire Gentile world. From the Jewish perspective Gentiles were either the Greek, who had achieved some recognizable civilization, or the barbarian, who had not; Paul introduces no third term, and Hellēn stands for all non-Jews. Whatever distinction might be drawn, none constitutes a qualification for or against salvation.

ὁδηγός τυφλῶν, φῶς — Ironic Self-Description

Romans 2:19 — "and if you are sure that you yourself are a guide to the blind, a light to those who are in darkness." ὁδηγός ("guide," from ὁδός + ἡγέομαι) and φῶς ("light," echoing Isaiah 49:6's description of the Servant of Jehovah) are both deployed ironically: the self-righteous legalist claims titles that belong properly to Christ and to a nation adjusted to God's justice, while himself remaining blind.

δικαιοσύνη θεοῦ — The Recurring Central Phrase

Romans 1:17; 3:5, 21, 22 — δικαιοσύνη θεοῦ is the organizing phrase of the entire epistle: God's perfect righteousness and justice in unified operation. The anarthrous construction at 3:5 emphasizes the quality of God's integrity rather than merely identifying it, and — the source material notes — also signals the debater's own ignorance of what that integrity actually is.

Romans 10:3 — "being ignorant of the righteousness of God." δικαιοσύνη θεοῦ (the righteousness of God). The accusative direct object dikaiosyne is one half of divine integrity, God's absolute righteousness, with the possessive genitive of theos. This is the righteousness God imputes to the believing sinner at the moment of faith in Christ, a judicial gift from the justice of God, not a quality achieved by human effort. It is God's own property, perfect, and cannot be improved upon, supplemented, or augmented by any subsequent human performance.

δικαιόω — Vindication, Not Only Justification

Romans 3:4 — "Let God be true though every one were a liar... that you may be justified in your words." δικαιόω, ranging in meaning from "to regard as right" to "to acquit" to "to vindicate," here refers to the vindication of divine integrity through the doctrines of Scripture, distinct from its more familiar soteriological sense of the judicial declaration of righteousness at salvation (as at 3:24, 26).

διαστολή — No Distinction

Romans 3:22 — "for there is no distinction." διαστολή states that Jew and Gentile alike stand in identical condemnation under spiritual death, with no inherent advantage before the justice of God — the structural hinge of the entire argument from 1:18 through 3:20.

Romans 10:12 — "there is no distinction between Jew and Greek." διαστολή (distinction). Diastolē (dia, between + stellō, to set apart) denotes a qualitative distinction, a dividing line, a categorical difference. Paul already used it in Romans 3:22; the repetition is deliberate. What was established at the level of universal guilt (Romans 3) is restated at the level of universal access to salvation grace (Romans 10): the same justice that leveled the human race in condemnation levels it in the offer of mercy.

ἁμαρτάνω — To Sin, to Miss the Mark

Romans 3:23 — "for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God." ἁμαρτάνω, in the constative/gnomic aorist ἥμαρτον (see Aorist Tense entries), gathers all sin of the entire human race into one axiomatic statement, stated as a fact so fixed as to require no further argument.

λογίζομαι — Rigorous Inference, Not Casual Reflection

Romans 3:28 — "For we hold that one is justified by faith apart from works of the law." λογίζομαι, present middle indicative, denotes in classical usage an act of thought according to strict logical rules — here, "we conclude then," marking a self-evident logical outcome from the doctrine of divine integrity combined with propitiation.

νόμος πίστεως vs. νόμος ἔργων — Two Contrasted Principles

Romans 3:27 — νόμος πίστεως ("the law/principle of faith") is the fixed, invariable divine principle that a right relationship with God's integrity is received through non-meritorious faith in Christ alone, apart from any human work — contrasted directly with νόμος ἔργων ("the law/principle of works").

ἔθνος (genitive plural) — God of the Gentiles Too

Romans 3:29 — "Or is God the God of Jews only? Is he not the God of Gentiles also?" The objective genitive plural ἐθνῶν affirms that God is the God of the Gentile nations as fully as of Israel — the same integrity governs both.

λογίζομαι — "To Reckon, To Credit, To Consider"

The technical accounting/legal term underlying the entire doctrine of imputation across Romans 4–6.

Romans 4:3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 11, 22, 23, 24 — the verb recurs throughout the Abraham argument in its technical sense of crediting something to someone's account, the central vocabulary item of the imputation doctrine developed across the whole chapter.

Romans 6:11 — "consider [λογίζεσθε] yourselves dead to sin and alive to God" — the same verb, shifted from a purely judicial/forensic sense (imputation of righteousness) to a volitional, applicatory sense (the believer's own reckoning of a settled fact about himself).

Romans 9:8 — "are counted as offspring." λογίζομαι (to impute, reckon, calculate). logizomai, to impute, to reckon, to calculate, is the technical term for imputation in Pauline soteriology. In Romans 9:8 the children of the promise are imputed for seed.

στοιχέω — "To Walk in Line With, To Walk by a Rule or Standard"

Originally a military term for walking in formation, rank by rank; used metaphorically of consistent conduct according to a fixed standard.

Romans 4:12 — "who also walk in the footsteps of the faith that our father Abraham had" — the underlying verb behind "walk" here carries the sense of consistent, disciplined conformity to a pattern, not casual or occasional resemblance (see the Perfective Present entry, section III).

δικαιόω + τὸν ἀσεβῆ — "Justifies the Ungodly," a Doctrinally Startling Combination

The verb δικαιόω ("to justify, to declare righteous") combined with the object τὸν ἀσεβῆ ("the ungodly one") forms one of the most doctrinally loaded phrases in the chapter, since ordinary legal usage would never permit "justifying" (declaring righteous) one who is, in fact, guilty.

Romans 4:5 — "believes in him who justifies the ungodly" — the phrase is deliberately startling by the standard of ordinary judicial language: God's justification is not a declaration that the ungodly person is, in fact, innocent (which would be a legal fiction) but an act founded on imputed righteousness received by faith — a distinct category from ordinary human courtroom justification.

σφραγίς — "Seal," a Legal/Authenticating Mark

A term denoting an official seal, used to authenticate a document or certify ownership/completion.

Romans 4:11 — "he received the sign of circumcision as a seal [σφραγῖδα] of the righteousness that he had by faith while he was still uncircumcised." Circumcision functions here as a legal-authenticating mark certifying a righteousness Abraham already possessed by faith — the seal does not produce the righteousness, it certifies a prior, already-existing fact.

ζωοποιέω — "To Make Alive, To Give Life"

A compound of ζωή ("life") plus ποιέω ("to make, to do").

Romans 4:17 — "who gives life [ζωοποιοῦντος] to the dead" — describing God's characteristic action in Abraham and Sarah's case (restoring reproductive capacity to bodies as good as dead) and, by extension, his characteristic power generally.

Romans 8:11 — "he... will also give life [ζωοποιήσει] to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you" — the same verb, now applied to the future bodily resurrection of the believer.

νέκρωσις — "Deadness," the State/Condition of Being as Good as Dead

Romans 4:19 — the underlying description of Sarah's womb and Abraham's own body draws on this term-family: the condition in view is total, comprehensive incapacity, not partial weakness.

ἐνδυναμόω — "To Empower, To Strengthen"

A compound of ἐν ("in") plus δύναμις ("power"): to infuse with power from within.

Romans 4:20 — "he grew strong [ἐνεδυναμώθη] in his faith as he gave glory to God" (see the Combinative Aorist entry, section I) — the verb specifically denotes power supplied from an internal, resident source (doctrine converted to capacity), not merely an increase in resolve.

πληροφορέω — "To Fully Persuade, To Bring to Full Conviction"

A compound of πλήρης ("full") plus φορέω (an intensive form of φέρω, "to carry, to bear"): to be fully carried along to a settled conviction.

Romans 4:21 — "fully convinced [πληροφορηθείς] that God was able to do what he had promised" — see also the discussion of this term's distinction from πληρόω under section XIX.

Romans 14:5 — "Each one should be fully convinced." πληροφορέω (to be completely filled, to be fully persuaded). πληροφορέω is a compound of πληρόω (full, complete) + φορέω (to bear, to carry), meaning to be completely filled, fully persuaded, entirely convinced. In the passive voice the believer receives the action: he is filled by the doctrine that has been inculcated into him.

εἰρήνη — "Peace," Technical Sense of Prosperity/Well-Being

Beyond the ordinary sense of absence of conflict, εἰρήνη in Paul frequently carries the fuller Hebraic sense of shalom: total well-being, prosperity, right relationship.

Romans 5:1 — "we have [or, let us have] peace with God" — the term names the restored, prosperous relational condition between God and the believer established at justification, not merely a cessation of hostility.

Romans 14:17 — "peace." εἰρήνη (prosperity, well-being). The rendering peace imports the modern sense of the absence of conflict, which is not Paul's meaning. εἰρήνη is the exact equivalent of the Latin pax of the first-century Roman world, denoting the condition of well-being, order and prosperity that follows the cessation of hostilities. In 14:17 it is the prosperity imputed at maturity.

Romans 14:19 — "peace." εἰρήνη (prosperity). In 14:19 εἰρήνη means prosperity, not peace in the narrow sense. The generic article comprehends spiritual maturity as a unified category, encompassing the six categories of blessing imputed by divine justice to the righteousness of God in the mature believer.

Romans 15:13 — "joy and peace in believing." εἰρήνης (prosperity). The second object is introduced by the connective καί with the objective genitive singular of εἰρήνη (eirēnē). The standard translation 'peace' is secondary and in this context misleading. The corrected translation reads: 'with all happiness and prosperity.'

Romans 16:20 — "The God of peace will soon crush Satan." ὁ θεὸς τῆς εἰρήνης (the God of prosperity). The standard English rendering 'God of peace' translates the descriptive genitive singular of the noun εἰρήνη (eirēnē). In Classical and Koine Greek εἰρήνη carries a semantic range considerably broader than the English word 'peace.' The corrected translation therefore reads: the God of prosperity.

προσαγωγή — "Access, Introduction"

A term denoting formal introduction into the presence of a superior — court-language, describing being formally ushered into royal presence.

Romans 5:2 — "through whom we have also obtained access [προσαγωγήν] by faith into this grace in which we stand." The term's court-introduction background reinforces the formal, granted (not self-achieved) nature of the believer's standing before God.

θλῖψις — "Tribulation, Pressure, Affliction"

Literally denotes pressure or crushing, often used of external circumstantial pressure or persecution.

Romans 5:3 — "we rejoice in our sufferings [θλίψεσιν]" — external, circumstantial pressure specifically, the category of undeserved suffering under discussion throughout this stretch of the argument.

Romans 12:12 — "be patient in tribulation." θλῖψις (with reference to the pressure of undeserved suffering). The second command is introduced by a dative of reference singular from thlipsis, pressure, tribulation, here the category of undeserved suffering imputed as blessing from the justice of God to the mature believer.

ὑπομονή — "Endurance, Steadfastness Under Pressure"

A compound of ὑπό ("under") plus μονή (from μένω, "to remain, to abide"): literally, "remaining under" — the capacity to stay in place under sustained pressure rather than collapsing or fleeing.

Romans 5:3–4 — "suffering produces endurance [ὑπομονήν]" — the term names the specific capacity produced by properly processed θλῖψις: not mere passive tolerance, but active, sustained remaining-under.

δοκιμή — "Proven Character, Tested Approval"

A term denoting the quality that results from having been tested and having passed the test — approved character.

Romans 5:4 — "and endurance produces character [δοκιμήν]" — the tested, approved quality of soul that results when ὑπομονή is sustained to its completion.

ἐλπίς — "Hope," Technical Sense of Confident Expectation

Not a wishful uncertainty (the ordinary English sense of "hope") but a confident, doctrinally-grounded expectation of a certain future.

Romans 5:4–5 — "and character produces hope [ἐλπίδα], and hope does not put us to shame" — the term names the confident forward-orientation that results from the completed suffering-endurance-character sequence, and which cannot disappoint precisely because it rests on the settled character of God, not on uncertain circumstances.

Romans 12:12 — "Rejoice in hope." ἐλπίς (confident anticipation). Elpis means confident anticipation, not uncertainty. In classical Attic it could denote either good or bad expectation; in Koine and throughout the Pauline corpus it denotes only confident assurance of a good outcome, grounded in doctrine, not sentiment. Once the anticipated reality arrives, hope is replaced by fact.

Romans 15:4 — "we might have hope." ἐλπίς (hope, confident expectation). The accusative singular direct object elpida (ἐλπίδα, from elpis / ἐλπίς) is the culminating word of the verse and the governing concept for the extended doctrinal section that follows. In biblical usage, hope does not connote wishful thinking, uncertainty, or ignorance. Hope is absolute confidence — a settled, informed assurance with respect to future things.

ἀσθενής — "Weak, Without Strength"

Romans 5:6 — "while we were still weak [ἀσθενεῖς]" — describing the total incapacity of the human race, apart from Christ, to remedy its own condition.

ἀσεβής — "Ungodly, Impious"

Romans 5:6 — "Christ died for the ungodly [ἀσεβῶν]" — the same term discussed at Romans 4:5 above, here identifying the object of Christ's substitutionary death: not the righteous, but those in active opposition to or neglect of God.

ἁμαρτωλός — "Sinner," One Characterized by Sin

Romans 5:8 — "while we were still sinners [ἁμαρτωλοί], Christ died for us" — the noun form, naming the human race by its defining characteristic at the time Christ's death occurred.

ἐχθρός — "Enemy"

Romans 5:10 — "For if while we were enemies [ἐχθροί] we were reconciled to God" — describing the state of active hostility between the unregenerate human race and God prior to reconciliation.

Romans 11:28 — "they are enemies for your sake." ἐχθρός (enemy). ἐχθρός, nominative plural, is predicate: they are enemies. This does not mean God has personal hostility toward unbelieving Jews; it is an anthropopathism — a divine policy expressed in human relational terms. All unbelievers stand in spiritual death and so in enmity with God; the passage focuses on Jewish unbelievers because of the dispensational context. Compare Romans 5:8, 10.

Romans 12:20 — "if your enemy is hungry." ἐχθρός (the one hostile to you). The nominative echthros is an adjective meaning hated or hostile, used as a substantive: not so much a formal personal enemy as someone hostile, driven by arrogance, jealousy, implacability, or vindictiveness. With the dative of possession from su, the one hostile to you, particularizing the enmity as personally directed.

καταλλάσσω — "To Reconcile," Technical Term for Restoring Broken Relationship

Romans 5:10 (twice) — "we were reconciled [κατηλλάγημεν] to God by the death of his Son... having been reconciled [καταλλαγέντες], shall we be saved" — the verb names the specific act of removing the barrier of enmity and restoring right relationship, distinct from justification (which addresses the legal verdict) though accomplished by the same saving work.

αἷμα — "Blood," Metonym for Sacrificial Death

Romans 5:9 — "we have now been justified by his blood [αἵματι]" — "blood" functions here as a metonym for the entirety of Christ's sacrificial, substitutionary death, not a reference to the physical liquid in isolation.

τύπος — "Type, Pattern, Prefigurement"

A term denoting a prefiguring pattern that anticipates and corresponds to a later, greater reality.
