Romans 5:14 — "who was a type [τύπος] of the one who was to come" — Adam functions as a τύπος of Christ: a historical pattern whose very structure (one man's act determining the destiny of the many he represents) anticipates and corresponds to the greater reality accomplished in Christ.

ὁμοίωμα — "Likeness" (see also section XIX's fuller entry at Romans 8:3)

Romans 5:14 — "even over those whose sinning was not like [in the] likeness [ὁμοιώματι] of the transgression of Adam" — the term here distinguishes personal sins (committed between Adam and Moses) from Adam's specific, unique transgression against a direct, explicit command — the death that reigned over that intervening period did not depend on personal sins bearing an identical structure to Adam's original violation.

βαπτίζω — "To Baptize," Technical Term for the Spirit's Placing Work

Romans 6:3 (twice) — "all of us who have been baptized [ἐβαπτίσθημεν] into Christ Jesus were baptized [ἐβαπτίσθημεν] into his death" — the term here refers exclusively to the baptism of the Holy Spirit (the placing of the believer into union with Christ at the moment of salvation), not to water baptism, which functions elsewhere in the New Testament purely as a public picture/testimony of this prior spiritual reality.

ἀγνοέω vs. γινώσκω — "To Be Ignorant Of" vs. "To Know"

Simple antonyms, but Paul's deliberate choice between them structures his rhetorical questions.

Romans 6:3 — "Do you not know [ἀγνοεῖτε, "are you ignorant"]...?" — the negative form of the question assumes the Roman believers ought already to possess this knowledge, making their hypothetical ignorance rhetorically pointed.

Romans 7:1 — "Do you not know, brothers... that the law is binding on a person only as long as he lives?" — same rhetorical pattern, same verb, opening the marriage-analogy argument of chapter 7.

παρίστημι — "To Present, To Place At Someone's Disposal"

A term with a range of technical uses: presenting a sacrifice, presenting oneself for service, placing something or someone at another's disposal for use.

Romans 6:13, 16, 19 (see the Constative Aorist and Pictorial Present entries, sections I and III) — the verb recurs as the central vocabulary item of the "presenting" imagery running through the second half of chapter 6: the believer is repeatedly commanded to place himself, and his bodily members, at the disposal of either the sin nature or God, as an act of daily volitional surrender rather than a one-time gesture.

Romans 12:1 — "to present your bodies as a living sacrifice." παρίστημι (to deploy; to place under orders). Compound of para + histēmi (to place, to stand); primary classical sense, to place beside. In military usage it means to deploy, to set troops or cavalry in position under orders (Xenophon of cavalry on both wings before an engagement). The governing transitive sense is to be at the disposal of, to be under orders to. It is not passive yielding but active, deliberate placement of the body under the command of God.

ἅγιος / δίκαιος / ἀγαθός — The Triad Describing the Law (and, by Extension, God's Own Character)

Three adjectives applied together to the Mosaic law, each naming a distinct facet of its perfection.

Romans 7:12 — "So the law is holy [ἅγιος], and the commandment is holy [ἁγία] and righteous [δικαία] and good [ἀγαθή]." ἅγιος names the law's set-apart, consecrated character; δίκαιος names its perfect conformity to justice; ἀγαθός names its beneficial, good intent and effect — together, a comprehensive threefold defense of the law's own character against any suggestion (explicitly rejected at v.7 and v.13 by μὴ γένοιτο) that the law itself is somehow implicated in producing sin or death.

καρπός — "Fruit," Metaphor for the Result of a Governing Relationship

Romans 6:21–22 and Romans 7:4–5 both use καρπός/καρποφορέω metaphorically: the "fruit" produced by a life is determined by which husband/master governs it — shame and death as the fruit of the old marriage to the sin nature, sanctification and the fruit borne "for God" as the fruit of the new marriage established through Christ's body.

νόμος — Three Distinguishable Usages, Especially Concentrated in Romans 8:2

The single noun νόμος ("law") carries at least three distinguishable senses across the passage as a whole, and Paul deliberately exploits the ambiguity within a single verse at Romans 8:2.

The Mosaic Law proper, the historical body of legislation given through Moses — the dominant sense throughout Romans 7 (e.g., 7:1, 7, 12, 14).

A governing "principle" or "law" in the sense of a fixed, operative rule or force, not a body of legislation at all — this sense governs both occurrences of νόμος within Romans 8:2 itself: "the law [principle] of the Spirit of life" and "the law [principle] of sin and death."

A "law" discovered by observation, describing a recurring pattern of experience — Romans 7:21, "So I find it to be a law that when I want to do right, evil lies close at hand," uses νόμος in this observational, almost scientific sense: a regularity Paul has discovered empirically in his own experience, not a reference to the Mosaic legislation at all.

Romans 10:4 — "the end of the law." νόμος (law (the Mosaic law)). Nomos, used here without the article, refers to the Mosaic law, the system Israel had been attempting to employ for salvation, in its three codices: the Decalogue (Codex 1), the Levitical ordinances (Codex 2), and the laws of divine establishment (Codex 3). Paul elsewhere uses nomos for other portions of Scripture and occasionally for the entire Old Testament canon.

ἀδιάλειπτος / ὀδύνη — Constant, Unrelenting Pain

Romans 9:2 — "unceasing anguish." ἀδιάλειπτος (unceasing, constant, without interruption). adialeiptos is a compound of alpha privative plus dialeipō, to leave off, to intermit, modifying odunē, pain: pain that does not relent or cycle through remission but is the constant background register of Paul's soul-life. It does not imply that the pain has displaced happiness or occupation with Christ, but that it coexists with all other dimensions of his soul-life.

Ἰσραηλίτης — Israelite, Race and Client Nation

Romans 9:4 — "They are Israelites." Ἰσραηλίτης (Israelite). The predicate nominative plural Israēlitēs designates the descendants of Jacob as both a race and a covenant client nation. Its technical usage spans from the Exodus to the death of Saul; the broader usage in Romans 9:4 encompasses the entire Jewish people across all thirteen tribes. The name Israel means Prince of God.

δόξα — The Shekinah Glory

Romans 9:4 (1 Samuel 4:21–22) — "the glory." δόξα (Shekinah glory). The predicate nominative singular doxa in the context of Israel's covenant heritage refers specifically to the Shekinah glory, the personal presence of God the Son between the cherubim, not military, political or human glory of any kind. doxa is the term that translates the Hebrew kabod in the Septuagint. The Shekinah glory that departed the tabernacle returned in the incarnation of the Son of God.

διαθήκη — Covenant, a Sovereign Unilateral Disposition

Romans 9:4 — "the covenants." διαθήκη (covenant, disposition, arrangement). diathēkē, predicate nominative plural, denotes a disposition or arrangement made by one party upon another, not a bilateral contract but a sovereign declaration. In Romans 9:4 it refers collectively to the unconditional covenants God made with Israel, Abrahamic, Palestinian, Davidic and New Covenant to Israel, excluding the Mosaic Law, which is conditional. The diathēkē is binding not on the human recipient but on the divine Promiser. diatheke translates the Hebrew berith, and the New Testament is properly the New Covenant.

λατρεία — Worship in Its Full Cultic and Doctrinal Sense

Romans 9:4 — "the worship." λατρεία (worship). The predicate nominative singular latreia denotes the worship of God as expressed through the Levitical priesthood, the sacrificial offerings, the articles of furniture in the tabernacle and temple, and the system of holy days. The English rendering service is less precise; the word means worship in its full cultic and doctrinal sense, a typological presentation of the plan of God.

ἐπαγγελία — The Plural Promises

Romans 9:4 — "and the promises." ἐπαγγελία (the promises). The predicate nominative plural epangeliai is significant: it encompasses the full range of divine commitments to Israel, Messianic, temporal and eschatological. Their guarantee rests not on the merit of the recipient but on the integrity of God; this is why God's word has not failed (Romans 9:6), the promises being fulfilled in the spiritual seed of Abraham, constituted by faith, not by physical descent.

Romans 9:8 — "but the children of the promise." τέκνα τῆς ἐπαγγελίας (children of the promise, from ἐπαγγελία). tekna tēs epangelias uses the possessive genitive of epangelia. Epangelia refers to the contents of the Abrahamic, Palestinian, Davidic and New Covenants to Israel, an unconditional guarantee proceeding from the integrity of God, not a conditional offer. The children of the promise are heirs by virtue of their spiritual relationship to Abraham: they have believed in the Lord Jesus Christ as Abraham believed and received the same imputation of divine righteousness and eternal life.

Romans 15:8 — "the promises given to the patriarchs." ἐπαγγελίας (promises). The accusative plural direct object is ἐπαγγελίας (epangelias), 'promises.' In this context the term refers specifically to the unconditional covenants made to Israel: the Abrahamic covenant, the Palestinian covenant, the Davidic covenant, and the New Covenant to Israel.

ἀμήν — The Seal That Signals GAP

Romans 9:5 — "Amen." ἀμήν (so be it). amēn, transliterated from the Hebrew, is the liturgical seal of affirmation. In Paul's usage here it signals the function of the Grace Apparatus for Perception (GAP): converting doctrine received in the left lobe as gnosis into epignosis resident in the right lobe, the only category of resident doctrine capable of producing spiritual growth, momentum, motivation and capacity for life.

Ἰσραήλ — Two Referents in One Verse

Romans 9:6 — "For not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel." Ἰσραήλ (Israel). The indeclinable proper noun Israēl appears twice in Romans 9:6 with two distinct referents. The first (ex Israēl) is racial Israel, physical descent from Abraham, Isaac and Jacob; the second is true Israel, the regenerate Jew, the spiritual seed of Abraham, possessing imputed righteousness and eternal life through faith in the Lord Jesus Christ.

σάρξ — Physical Descent, Not the Old Sin Nature

Romans 9:8 — "it is not the children of the flesh." τὰ τέκνα τῆς σαρκός (the descendants of the flesh, from σάρξ). ta tekna tēs sarkos joins the plural of teknon, a child as heir, with the possessive genitive of sarx. Sarx here refers to the physical body and by extension to physical descent, the genetic lineage from Abraham, Isaac and Jacob; in this context it carries no moral connotation and simply denotes the physical as distinct from the spiritual. The descendants of the flesh are the racial Jews, whose relationship to the covenant is constituted solely by physical heritage.

Romans 11:14 — "my fellow Jews." σάρκα (my flesh, from σάρξ). Paul uses the possessive genitive of ἐγώ with σάρκα, the accusative of σάρξ. Here sarx does not carry the technical sense of the old sin nature but refers to the physical body — those who share Paul's genetic heritage. My flesh denotes the racial Jew who possesses the genes of the patriarchs but, as an unbeliever, does not possess the God of the patriarchs.

κοίτη — The Merely Natural Conception

Romans 9:10 — "when Rebekah had conceived children." κοίτην (became pregnant, from κοίτη). The accusative singular koitēn, direct object of the participle, literally denotes sexual intercourse; it is translated in context became pregnant. The term underscores the physical, natural character of the conception, the point being that what is merely natural cannot produce spiritual standing.

ἐκλογή — Election to Privilege, Never Applied to Unbelievers

Romans 9:11 — "God's purpose of election." ἐκλογή (election). eklogē, from eklegō, to choose out, is in Paul's usage the printout from the divine decrees that relates the believer to the plan of God in a specific dispensation. It always refers to those who are saved and is never applied to unbelievers; it is distinct from eklektos, the elect person, and the compound suneklektos, fellow-elect.

Romans 11:5 — "chosen by grace." ἐκλογή (election, selection to privilege). ἐκλογή, from ἐκλέγω, denotes selection from within a larger group for a specific assignment; in Romans 11:5 the selection is entirely non-meritorious, originating in divine grace. It is election to privilege, not election to salvation as such: it always concerns privilege, position, and function, never coerced belief. In the dispensation of Israel it related the believing Jew to his function in the client nation; in the Church Age it relates the royal family member to the Gentile client nation.

Romans 11:7 — "The elect obtained it." ἐκλογή (the election, the elected to privilege). ἐκλογή is a technical Pauline term for those selected to privilege, the privilege of being within the advancing plan of God. In the Old Testament context it is the born-again remnant of Israel; in the Church Age all believers constitute an elected-to-privilege body, the royal family of God.

τίς — Masculine Interrogative Focusing on a Personal Agent

Romans 9:19 — "For who can resist his will?" τίς (who?). The interrogative pronoun τίς is nominative masculine singular. In contrast to the neuter form used in the first question, the masculine focuses the inquiry on a specific human agent, a person capable of volition, rather than an impersonal force or thing.

τί — The Interrogative of Impudence

Romans 9:20 — "Why have you made me like this?" τί (Why? For what reason?). The embedded question begins with τί, nominative neuter singular of the interrogative pronoun, used adverbially. This is the interrogative of impudence: a question that presumes the right to demand an accounting from the Creator.

φύραμα — The Mixed Lump

Romans 9:21 — "out of the same lump." ἐκ τοῦ αὐτοῦ φυράματος (from the same lump, from φύραμα). φύραμα is derived from φυράω, to mix or mingle, specifically the mixing of clay with water to produce a workable medium; the noun designates the prepared, blended mass of clay ready for the potter's use. From the same lump establishes the common origin and equal ontological status of all members of the human race before God.

πλοῦτος τῆς δόξης — The Riches of His Glory

Romans 9:23 — "the riches of his glory." πλοῦτος; δόξα (the riches of His glory). The object of γνωρίζω is the accusative singular of πλοῦτος, a collective noun meaning wealth or riches, with δόξα in the possessive genitive and αὐτός as a third-person personal pronoun: the riches of His glory. δόξα here denotes the divine attributes, the fullness of what God is, not merely a luminous manifestation. The phrase means the wealth that derives from and reflects who God is, dispensed to the believer through the justice of God (the sixth and seventh imputations specifically).

Κύριος Σαβαώθ — The Lord of the Armies

Romans 9:29 (Isaiah 1:9) — "If the Lord of hosts." Σαβαώθ (Lord of the armies). Κύριος governs the indeclinable title Σαβαώθ. Greek translators transliterated rather than declined Semitic proper nouns and divine titles, so Σαβαώθ appears without a genitive ending though the construction is genitive in sense: the Lord of the armies, corresponding to the Hebrew YHWH Tsĕbaʾoth, the God of Israel as commander of the divine armies and controller of history. It is a Christological title identifying Jesus Christ as Jehovah of the armies, the Shekinah glory of Israel.

εὐδοκία — Motivation, Not a Mere Wish

Romans 10:1 — "my heart's desire." εὐδοκία (motivation, purpose, intention). The nominative singular subject eudokia stands with the definite article. Traditional interpretation, reflected in the King James heart's desire, took it as a wish directed toward a purpose; the papyrological evidence establishes a stronger sense: pleasure, purpose, intention, and thus motivation. The generic use of the article isolates Paul's motivation as singular, distinct from all other motivations. With the genitive of kardia the phrase is the motivation of my right lobe, a purposeful, doctrinally rooted volitional orientation rather than an emotional wish.

ἀδελφοί — Vocative Address to the Believing Community

Romans 10:1 — "Brothers." ἀδελφοί (brethren). The chapter opens with the vocative plural adelphoi, brethren. Throughout the Pauline Epistles adelphoi in the vocative refers primarily to fellow believers, members of the royal family of God united through the baptism of the Holy Spirit into union with Christ. Paul also uses the term for racial kinsmen (as in Romans 9), but here he speaks to those who possess divine righteousness and can therefore comprehend his concern for those who do not.

ἐπίγνωσις — Israel's Failure Was a Failure of Epignosis

Romans 10:3 — "being ignorant of the righteousness of God." ἐπίγνωσις (full, exact knowledge). Israel's ignorance of the righteousness of God is a failure of epignosis, not of mere information exposure. Self-righteousness and epignosis are mutually exclusive: the one operates from arrogance, the other from the Spirit-enabled reception of divine truth.

τέλος — Termination of the Law with Reference to Righteousness

Romans 10:4 — "Christ is the end of the law." τέλος (termination). Telos has a semantic range of termination or cessation, objective or goal, completion of a state, and the final or supreme stage. In Romans 10:4 contextual and grammatical evidence, confirmed by Romans 3:20, 28 and Galatians 2:16, supports termination or cessation: Christ ends the law as a mechanism for obtaining righteousness before God. Elsewhere the author adds the sense of designed conclusion and fulfillment: everything the law, especially Codex two, pointed toward is accomplished in Christ, so that law-keeping for salvation after the cross is both futile and a contradiction of the law's own purpose.

τοῦτ᾽ ἔστιν — This Implies

Romans 10:6 — "(that is, to bring Christ down)." τοῦτ’ ἔστιν (this implies). The near demonstrative touto (this, rather than the distant ekeino) with the present of eimi, literally that is or this is, is an idiom meaning this implies or this means. It introduces the logical consequence of the preceding rationalization rather than a simple identification. The same idiom recurs in verses 7 and 8.

πίστις — Four Principal Senses

Romans 10:8 — "the word of faith." πίστις (faith). In the phrase rhēma pisteōs, pistis carries four New Testament senses: faithfulness or reliability; the active exercise of trust in an object; the content of what is believed, doctrine; and a characteristic quality of fidelity. It is non-meritorious by nature: the merit resides in the object of faith, not in the act.

Κύριος — The Septuagint Rendering of the Tetragrammaton

Romans 10:9 — "that Jesus is Lord." Κύριος (Lord). For the Jewish audience, Kyrios in the Septuagint renders the tetragrammaton (Yahweh, pronounced Adonai). To confess Jesus as Lord is to assert that Jesus of Nazareth is the God of Israel, the covenant God who gave Moses the Law on Sinai. This is the Omega glory of Christ (his first-advent work); unbelieving Israel acknowledged the Alpha glory, the God of Israel in eternal existence, but suppressed the Omega glory, refusing to connect the God of Israel with the historical Jesus.

Romans 11:3 (1 Kings 19:10, 14) — "Lord, they have killed your prophets." Κύριος (Lord, from κύριος). In the citation of 1 Kings 19, Paul uses Κύριος where the Hebrew original uses the Tetragrammaton. Though the word can be a social honorific in secular Koine, its use as the LXX rendering of YHWH establishes that in New Testament theological usage it carries the full weight of the divine name, denoting full deity.

ἐπικαλέω — Calling Upon the Lord as a Synonym for Faith

Romans 10:12 (Joel 2:32) — "all who call on him." ἐπικαλέω (to call upon). Epikaleō (epi, upon + kaleō, to call) is frequently used for prayer, calling upon God for help, but its usage in this context, confirmed by verse 13 where it functions as a direct synonym for faith in Christ, determines its meaning here: the voluntary, non-meritorious act of believing in the Lord Jesus Christ. Calling upon the Lord is the vocalized expression of faith, correlating with confession with the mouth in verse 9.

πούς — The Feet as the Whole Act of Going

Romans 10:15 (Isaiah 52:7) — "the feet of those who preach the good news." πούς (foot). The plural of pous denotes the feet not as objects of aesthetic interest but as the means by which the missionary travels, a synecdoche for the entire act of going: departure from a client nation, transit, and arrival in a foreign country. The detail reinforces the missionary, rather than local, scope of the passage.

ἀγαθός — Absolute, Intrinsic Good

Romans 10:15 (Isaiah 52:7) — "those who preach the good news." ἀγαθά (intrinsically good things). Agatha, plural of agathos, denotes intrinsic good, good that belongs to something by its very nature, equivalent to the Hebrew tov of Isaiah 52:7. In context it refers not only to the gospel of salvation but to the entire plan of God: salvation adjustment, rebound, and maturity adjustment to the justice of God. Corrected translation: How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim good news about intrinsic good things.

Romans 13:3 — "Then do what is good." ἀγαθός (the good). ἀγαθός with the generic article is the same adjective as in Romans 8:28 and four times in Romans 12. Its meaning is consistent: absolute, intrinsic good, good in and of itself in any age of history and under any condition of culture or technology. In this passage it encompasses both the perception of Bible doctrine and the believer's conformity to divine establishment principles; it is distinguished from καλός (outward excellence).

τίς — Salvation as an Individual Transaction

Romans 10:16 (Isaiah 53:1) — "Lord, who has believed what he has heard from us?" τίς (who?). In the citation the vocative Kurie is the Greek equivalent of Adonai, addressing God the Father. The interrogative pronoun tís, who?, refers to the individual, reinforcing that salvation is an individual transaction of volition, not a collective or national act; the nation's collective blackout is the aggregate of individual decisions over successive generations.

φθόγγος — The Voice of Nature

Romans 10:18 (Psalm 19:4) — "Their voice has gone out to all the earth." φθόγγος (sound, voice). The subject of the first line is phthongos, a poetic and onomatopoetic term meaning sound or voice, specifically the voice of nature. With the genitive plural of autos, their voice, the referent is the created order, the heavens and firmament, communicating the existence of God through rational inference. The first line corresponds to God consciousness; the second (their words, rhēma) to gospel hearing.

θυσιαστήριον — The Altar and Its Typological Content

Romans 11:3 — "they have demolished your altars." θυσιαστήριον (altar of burnt offering). The direct object θυσιαστήριον is the altar of burnt offering, the central locus of the sacrificial system that portrayed the person and substitutionary work of Christ. Its destruction was an assault on the typological content of the Mosaic covenant and on the doctrine of propitiation.

κἀγώ μόνος — In Fact, I Alone

Romans 11:3 — "and I alone am left." κἀγώ (in fact, I, from ἐγώ). κἀγώ is the crasis of καί and ἐγώ and is not a simple coordinating conjunction; the contraction carries the intensive force of the pronoun. With the adjective μόνος it yields in fact, I alone, an expression of pronounced self-isolation that foregrounds the self-focus of Elijah, which most English renderings miss.

χρηματισμός — The Divine Answer

Romans 11:4 — "But what is God's reply to him?" χρηματισμός (the divine answer, the divine response). The subject of verse 4 is χρηματισμός, a technical term for an oracular or authoritative divine pronouncement: a formal, definitive response from God to the one making inquiry, here the reply to Elijah at Horeb.

ὅστις / οἵτινες — The Qualitative Relative Pronoun

Romans 11:4 (1 Kings 19:18) — "who have not bowed the knee to Baal." οἵτινες (who are of such a character that, from ὅστις). The clause is introduced by the qualitative relative pronoun οἵτινες, nominative masculine plural. Unlike the simple relative ὅς, it denotes character, not mere identity: the seven thousand are of such a character, spiritually mature, that they have not bowed a knee to Baal.

Romans 16:4 — "who risked their necks for my life." οἵτινες (who are of such a category as). The verse opens with a nominative masculine plural form of the indefinite-categorical relative pronoun ὅστις (hostis). Unlike the simple relative pronoun ὅς (hos), hostis designates a category of persons defined by their essential character. The force of the pronoun is: 'who are of such a category as.'

λεῖμμα — The Remnant, the Pivot

Romans 11:5 — "there is a remnant." λεῖμμα (a remnant, a pivot). λεῖμμα, the subject of verse 5, is drawn from the semantic field of καταλείπω in verse 4: that which has been left behind in the honorable sense. It is functionally equivalent to the pivot, the body of spiritually mature believers within a client nation whose adjustment to the justice of God sustains divine blessing on the nation.

πωρόω / πώρωσις — Callus, Scar Tissue of the Soul

Romans 11:7 — "but the rest were hardened." πωρόω (to harden, to cover with scar tissue, to petrify). πωρόω does not mean to blind but to cover with scar tissue, to petrify, to harden; the root πῶρος is a hard callus or calcified deposit. In the spiritual domain it is scar tissue of the soul: the accumulated barrier, laid down layer by layer by persistent negative volition, that renders the right lobe incapable of perceiving doctrinal truth, the blackout of the soul.

Romans 11:25 — "a partial hardening has come upon Israel." πώρωσις (hardening, callousness). The noun πώρωσις, from πωρόω, rendered hardening or blindness in most translations of Romans 11:25, describes the callousing of the cardiac faculty, the right lobe of the soul, through sustained negative volition toward truth. The result is scar tissue of the soul, a barrier that progressively prevents accurate perception of divine reality.

κατάνυξις — Insensibility, Not Absence of Intelligence

Romans 11:8 (Isaiah 29:10) — "a spirit of stupor." κατάνυξις (stupor, insensibility, deep sleep). κατάνυξις, from κατανύσσω (to prick sharply, to stupefy), is drawn from the LXX of Isaiah 29:10 and denotes a supernatural stupor descending on those who have sustained negative volition toward the Word. It is not absence of intelligence but intelligence rendered non-functional for spiritual perception. Where the piercing of conviction should produce repentance (Acts 2:37), persistent rejection produces insensibility; insensibility captures both the cause and the result better than stupor.

τράπεζα — The Spiritual Heritage of Israel

Romans 11:9 (Psalm 69:22) — "Let their table become a snare." τράπεζα (table). τράπεζα with the genitive plural of αὐτός gives their table; Greek expresses the possessive by the genitive pronoun rather than the Hebrew suffix, approximating the Hebrew structure. The table is the spiritual heritage of Israel as a client nation: the Mosaic Law, the Levitical offerings, the revealed gospel in ritual form, and the prophetic canon.

σκάνδαλον — Stumbling Block for the Accountable

Romans 11:9 (Psalm 69:22) — "a stumbling block." σκάνδαλον (stumbling block). As in 1 Corinthians 1:23, where Christ crucified is σκάνδαλον to Jews and foolishness to Greeks, the distinction is deliberate. For Gentiles without client-nation responsibility the cross was simply irrational; for Jews, the client nation from the Exodus to AD 70, it was an obstacle they tripped over because of their own accountability. The one with greater responsibility suffers more acutely from failing to meet it.

ἀνταπόδομα — Retribution Proportional to Responsibility

Romans 11:9 (Psalm 69:22) — "a retribution for them." ἀνταπόδομα (retribution, just recompense). ἀνταπόδομα derives from ἀντί (against, in return) and ἀποδίδωμι (to give back, to render what is due). It denotes just punishment rendered in return, retribution proportional to the failure of responsibility: the justice of God administering the cycles of discipline to Israel and to any client nation that rejects its spiritual heritage.

ἥττημα — Failure, Loss of Client Nation Status

Romans 11:12 — "if their failure means riches for the Gentiles." ἥττημα (failure, defeat). ἥττημα means failure or defeat, not merely diminishing as the KJV renders it. It denotes the loss of client nation status: the failure of Israel as the divinely appointed missionary and evangelistic nation.

πλήρωμα — Fullness, Full Measure

Romans 11:12 — "their full inclusion." πλήρωμα (fullness). πλήρωμα with the possessive genitive of αὐτός, their fullness, connotes restoration to completeness and the resumption of full function: the eschatological restoration of Israel as a client nation at the second advent and through the Millennium. The cognate πληρόω elsewhere in Paul connotes divine blessing reaching its intended completeness; the πλήρωμα of Israel will be the fullest expression of that pattern in history.

Romans 11:25 — "until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in." πλήρωμα (fullness, full measure). πλήρωμα denotes that which fills the full content of a container — a basket, a ship, a group — connoting totality, entirety, or the full measure. With the genitive plural of ἔθνος (equivalent to Hebrew gōy) it yields the full measure of the Gentiles: the church age from Pentecost to the rapture, distinguished from the Times of the Gentiles (Luke 21:24).

Romans 15:29 — "in the fullness of the blessing of Christ." ἐν πληρώματι (in full measure). The phrase is formed by en plus the locative of plērōma (πλήρωμα), meaning fullness, completeness, full measure. This term does not merely indicate quantity but quality of content: the totality of advanced doctrine which Paul alone possessed and was uniquely qualified to communicate.

διακονία — Ministry and the Gift of Service

Romans 11:13 — "I magnify my ministry." διακονία (ministry, service). The direct object is the accusative singular of διακονία, best rendered ministry. The term carries several distinct ranges: (1) civil authority serving under divine establishment; (2) Christ's first-advent service to Israel (Romans 15:8, where He is called a διάκονος of the circumcision); (3) every believer's general ministry as royal family; (4) the administrative function of the local church deacon; (5) the pastor-teacher's ministry of doctrinal communication. In Romans 11:13 it refers to Paul's full apostolic ministry.

Romans 12:7 — "if service, in our serving." διακονία (service). Eite with the accusative singular of diakonia, the noun from which deacon derives. In this context it does not denote the office of deacon but the spiritual gift of service, aid, support, and charitable assistance, the most common of the Church Age gifts.

Romans 15:31 — "my service for Jerusalem may be acceptable to the saints." διακονία (ministry). The nominative singular subject is diakonia (διακονία), a noun covering both the teaching of doctrine and administrative service — the English word 'deacon' derives from this root. The corrected translation: and that my ministry to Jerusalem might become acceptable to the saints.

τις vs. τίς — Indefinite and Interrogative Distinguished by Accent

Romans 11:14 — "and thus save some of them." τις (some of them). The accusative plural (τινάς) of the indefinite pronoun τις — distinguished from the interrogative pronoun by the absence of an acute accent — designates a specific category, the racial Jew, without specifying number. It reflects realistic expectation: not all will respond, but some will in every generation.

ἀποβολή — Rejection: The Fifth Cycle of Discipline

Romans 11:15 — "For if their rejection means." ἀποβολή (rejection, casting away). The nominative subject ἀποβολή, with the possessive genitive of autos (their rejection), refers to the administration of the fifth cycle of discipline to Israel, which destroyed Israel's client-nation status in AD 70. This act halted the dispensation of Israel and inserted the dispensation of the royal family of God — the Church Age.

ἅγιος in Romans 11:16 — Integrity of Relationship with the Plan of God

Romans 11:16 — "If the dough offered as firstfruits is holy." ἁγία (holy). The predicate adjective ἁγία does not denote ritual purity primarily but integrity — specifically, integrity of relationship with the plan of God. The first fruits are holy because Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob stood in a grace-oriented relationship with the justice of God through faith in Christ and advance to maturity; the holiness of the lump derives from and must conform to that standard.

φοβέω — Fear and Respect

Romans 11:20 — "but fear." φοβοῦ (keep having respect, from φοβέω). The adversative ἀλλά introduces the antithesis, with the present middle imperative φοβοῦ. The verb carries two nearly antithetical ranges: fear — the dread that characterizes metal-attitude failure — and respect — the honor-based orientation toward legitimate authority that characterizes biblical humility. In Romans 11:20 both are operative: fear of divine discipline for the one who remains in arrogance, and respect for the one who exits it.

χρηστότης / ἀποτομία — Integrity and Severity of God

Romans 11:22 — "the kindness and the severity of God." ἀποτομία (severity). ἀποτομία derives from apo (away from) and tomē (a cut), from temnō (to cut): to cut away from, severity in the sense of a decisive, final severance. Both nouns are governed by the genitive θεοῦ. χρηστότης is the positive, blessing side of the justice of God; ἀποτομία the punitive side of the same justice. Both flow from one source, the integrity of God; neither is capricious.

κἀκεῖνοι — Crasis Signalling a Reversal

Romans 11:23 — "And even they." κἀκεῖνοι (and those also). The verse opens with crasis (κρᾶσις), the merging of adjacent words through elision and contraction of vowels, a feature of Koine as the vernacular of everyday speech. κἀκεῖνοι fuses καί and ἐκεῖνοι (those ones), referring to the Jewish unbelievers described as broken-off branches. The rhetorical function of the crasis is to signal a reversal of expectation: after the severity of the condemnation, a note of hope.

πάλιν — Return to Spiritual Heritage, Not Re-Salvation

Romans 11:23 — "to graft them in again." πάλιν (again, back). The adverb πάλιν denotes a return. It does not imply that a Jew is saved again — salvation is not reversible — but that the believing Jew returns to his spiritual heritage, now with the added dimension of membership in the royal family of God.

μυστήριον — Classical Term for Doctrine Known to Initiates

Romans 11:25 — "I do not want you to be unaware of this mystery." μυστήριον (mystery). μυστήριον is a classical Greek term, not distinctive to Koine, from μύστης, used in Greek fraternal associations (mystery schools) for doctrine known only to initiates. In New Testament usage it is a technical designation for Church Age doctrine withheld from Old Testament revelation. In Romans 11:25 the mystery is not that Israel would eventually be saved but the precise mechanism: Israel's hardening is partial and temporary, calibrated to the ingathering of the Gentiles. Ignorance of it produces arrogance.

Romans 16:25 — "according to the revelation of the mystery." μυστηρίου (of the mystery). In classical and Hellenistic Greek, μυστήριον denoted secrets known only to those initiated into a particular fraternity — most famously the mystery cults associated with Dionysus. The noun derives from the ancient noun μύστης (mystēs), designating a person being initiated into fraternal doctrine under an oath of confidentiality. Μύστης is in turn derived from the verb μυέω (myeō) — to initiate, to instruct in the doctrines belonging to the fraternity, and to pledge the initiate to silence before outsiders.

πᾶς Ἰσραήλ — All Israel

Romans 11:26 — "And in this way all Israel will be saved." πᾶς Ἰσραήλ (all Israel, from Ἰσραήλ). In Romans 11:26 the adjective πᾶς with the indeclinable proper noun Ἰσραήλ designates not the entire ethnic Jewish people but the complete body of regenerate Jews, those who believe in Christ, who pass through the Tribulation and are delivered at the second advent. The ground is Romans 9:6b, οὐ γὰρ πάντες οἱ ἐξ Ἰσραήλ, οὗτοι Ἰσραήλ; the phrase has nothing to do with universal ethnic salvation.

Ἰακώβ vs. Ἰσραήλ — National Totality and Spiritual Dimension

Romans 11:26 — "from Jacob." Ἰακώβ (Jacob). ἀπό plus Ἰακώβ designates the nation in its racial totality. Jacob (chisler, supplanter) was renamed Israel (Prince of God). When the text wishes to present the Jews in their national and racial dimension, Jacob is the designation employed; Israel designates the spiritual dimension.

διαθήκη — Contract, Not Testament

Romans 11:27 (Jeremiah 31:33–34) — "and this will be my covenant with them." διαθήκη (contract). The predicate nominative διαθήκη, conventionally covenant, is more precisely contract: the new covenant to Israel first given in Jeremiah 31:33–34. It refers not to a testamentary will, which requires the death of the testator, but to a binding contractual disposition made by one party in favor of another. Since God and the resurrected Christ cannot die, the titles Old and New Testament should properly be Old and New Covenant or Contract. Hebrew equivalent: berith.

ἁμαρτία in Romans 11:27 — Punishment for Sin (Hebrew chata'th)

Romans 11:27 (Jeremiah 31) — "when I take away their sins." ἁμαρτία (punishment for sin). The accusative plural ἁμαρτία is conventionally sin, but this is a quotation from the Hebrew of Jeremiah 31, where the underlying chata'th with its suffix means punishment for sin or for idolatry — here the fifth cycle of discipline administered to Israel in AD 70. The referent is the removal of the historical, collective punishment, terminated at the second advent.

ἀγαπητός — Technical Term for Covenant Standing

Romans 11:28 — "they are beloved for the sake of their forefathers." ἀγαπητός (beloved). The predicate nominative plural ἀγαπητός (beloved, dear, accepted) requires the verb to be supplied: they are beloved. The referent is the Jewish believers of the dispensation of Israel. The term is technical in Pauline usage for the church age believer as one accepted in Christ through positional truth; here it is applied to Jewish believers of the prior dispensation in terms of their covenant standing.

ἀμεταμέλητος — Irrevocable

Romans 11:29 — "are irrevocable." ἀμεταμέλητος (irrevocable). The first and last words of the verse are γάρ and ἀμεταμέλητος, a compound adjective (alpha-privative + μεταμέλω, to feel regret, to repent of a decision) in the neuter plural nominative as predicate: that which cannot be regretted, beyond reconsideration — irrevocable. In the neuter plural it predicates irrevocability of both subjects: the grace benefits and the election.

χαρίσματα (Plural) vs. κλῆσις (Singular)

Romans 11:29 — "the gifts and the calling of God." χαρίσματα (grace benefits). χαρίσματα is neuter plural while κλῆσις is singular — not accidental. A charisma (charis + the -ma suffix of result) is that which results from grace: a grace benefit, the entire range of what God bestows through the grace pipeline, not spiritual gifts in the narrow charismatic sense; these differ by dispensation (plural). κλῆσις functions technically for election to privilege, singular because it does not vary across dispensations: always obtained through faith in Jesus Christ — one gospel in all dispensations.

συγκλείω — To Shut Up Together

Romans 11:32 — "God has consigned all to disobedience." συγκλείω (to lock up together). συγκλείω, aorist active indicative, is built from σύν (together) + κλείω (to shut): to close up together, to hem in. It does not mean merely to categorize or conclude logically; it means to enclose within a bounded space from which there is no independent escape. Military in origin (soldiers in close ranks within an encirclement), later of prisoners and of fish caught in a net (Luke 5:6).

τοὺς πάντας — The Entire Human Race

Romans 11:32 — "consigned all to disobedience, that he may have mercy on all." τοὺς πάντας (the entire human race). The accusative plural article τούς used generically with πᾶς forms the idiom τοὺς πάντας, literally the all ones — a Pauline idiom for the entire human race without ethnic, moral, or historical qualification. The article particularizes the group while pas expresses totality. It appears twice in the verse, governing both the condemnation and the mercy clauses.

βάθος — Depth as Inexhaustibility

Romans 11:33 — "Oh, the depth of the riches." βάθος (all the inexhaustibility). βάθος belongs to the classical and literary register rather than common Koine. In the ancient world depth was the standard image for inexhaustibility — the mariner's unfathomable sea. bathos does not connote inferiority here but that which exceeds all human measurement; the best rendering is all the inexhaustibility.

σοφία vs. γνῶσις — Omniscience and Foreknowledge

Romans 11:33 — "wisdom and knowledge of God." γνῶσις (foreknowledge). σοφία encompasses self-knowledge and omniscience and programs the computer of divine decrees; γνῶσις in this verse is foreknowledge, which is not omniscience but the printout of the divine decrees. Nothing can be foreknown until it is first decreed. Foreknowledge acknowledges what is certain because omniscience has first decreed it; it makes nothing certain by external compulsion.

ἀνεξερεύνητος — Below the Line of Visual Penetration

Romans 11:33 — "How unsearchable are his judgments." ἀνεξερεύνητα (inscrutable, unfathomable). The nominative neuter plural ἀνεξερεύνητα combines the alpha-privative with a verb meaning to search out thoroughly. The classical form denoted something lying below the line of visual penetration in deep water, where sunlight can no longer illuminate the sea floor; it then extended to any reality exceeding human cognitive reach. What is anexereunētos lies beyond bathos: the decrees of God extend infinitely beyond the horizon of human cognitive reach.

ὁδοί / ἀνεξιχνίαστος — Untrackable Policies of God

Romans 11:33 — "how inscrutable his ways!" ἀνεξιχνίαστος (untrackable). ὁδοί (roads, highways) here means God's attributes and the policies that flow from them. The predicate adjective ἀνεξιχνίαστος, not to be tracked out, untrackable, occurs only here and in Ephesians 3:8 (the untrackable wealth of Christ). The image is a trail leaving no recoverable trace: God's operational policies cannot be reconstructed by unaided human reason; Bible doctrine is the sole instrument of penetration.

νοῦς — The Mind, Left Lobe of the Soul

Romans 11:34 (Isaiah 40:13) — "the mind of the Lord." νοῦς (mind). The accusative νοῦς is the mind as the faculty for thought — the left lobe of the soul in its general technical sense. It corresponds to Hebrew ruach in Isaiah 40:13, there the breath, spirit, and thinking of the Lord, applied to the humanity of the Lord Jesus Christ. The possessive genitive Κύριος renders the Tetragrammaton.

παρακαλέω — The Commanding Officer’s Call to One’s Side

Romans 12:1 — "I appeal to you." παρακαλέω (I urge). Present active indicative, first person singular, a compound of para (beside) + kaleō (to call): to call someone to one’s side. In its classical military use (Xenophon, Polybius) it is the address of a commanding officer to his troops before an advance, explaining the objective and authorizing the advance. Paul uses it with apostolic authority, directing the royal family of God toward the high ground of maturity adjustment to the justice of God.

Romans 12:8 — "the one who exhorts." παρακαλέω (if counseling). The articular present active participle of parakaleō, to call to one’s side for comfort or encouragement, designates a distinct spiritual gift, more precisely translated counseling than exhortation: the ministry of comfort and encouragement to individuals and small groups, distinct from the exhortation that belongs to the pastor-teacher.

σῶμα — The Body as the Point of Contest

Romans 12:1 — "to present your bodies." σώματα (bodies, from σῶμα). Accusative plural direct object. The specification of the body rather than the soul or the spirit is deliberate: the body of the Church Age believer is simultaneously the temple of the Holy Spirit and the residence of the old sin nature, two mutually antagonistic indwellers, and so the body is the point of contest for the control of the soul. This grounds the command in rebound and the filling of the Spirit.

μέτρον — A Standard, Not a Quantity

Romans 12:3 — "the measure of faith." μέτρον (a standard of thinking). The accusative singular of metron, conventionally rendered measure, carries the more precise sense of a standard, a criterion. It is not a quantity distributed in varying amounts to different believers but a single objective criterion, Bible doctrine, by which all are to operate.

πρᾶξις — Function, Not Office

Romans 12:4 — "the members do not all have the same function." πρᾶξις (function). The accusative singular of praxis means function, activity. The verse does not describe positional hierarchy among believers but the diversity of operational roles within the body, a diversity governed by spiritual gifts.

διάφορα — Different in Category and in Expression

Romans 12:6 — "Having gifts that differ." διάφορα (differing, various). Diaphora carries two simultaneous implications: believers possess different spiritual gifts, and even within a common gift category there are variations. No two pastor-teachers have identical gifts; the gift is common in category but individualized in expression.

ἀνυπόκριτος — Without the Actor’s Mask

Romans 12:9 — "Let love be genuine." ἀνυπόκριτος (non-hypocritical). The compound predicate adjective joins the alpha privative an- to hypokritos, actor, hypocrite: non-hypocritical, without pretense, without the facade of performed affection concealing an interior of jealousy, bitterness, vindictiveness, or implacability.

προσκαρτερέω — To Persist Face to Face

Romans 12:12 — "be constant in prayer." προσκαρτερέω (persist). A present active participle used imperativally from the compound proskartereō, pros (face to face, toward) + kartereō (to endure, to be strong): to persist, to continue steadfastly, to devote oneself constantly. Its object is the dative singular of proseuchē, prayer: persist in prayer.

Romans 13:6 — "attending to this very thing." προσκαρτερέω (to persist in, to devote oneself to). προσκαρτερέω is a compound of pros (toward) and kartereō (to be strong, to endure). It denotes sustained, full-time devotion to a task, often in the face of monotony or lack of appreciation: civil servants who make a career out of public service.

φιλοξενία — Love of the Stranger

Romans 12:13 — "seek to show hospitality." φιλοξενία (hospitality). The accusative singular direct object philoxenia compounds philos (friend, loving) and xenos (stranger, foreigner): the active, generous reception of others, stranger or fellow believer, into one’s home and life.

εὐλογέω — Meaning Set by the Subject

Romans 12:14 — "Bless those who persecute you." εὐλογέω (keep speaking well of). Present active imperative of eulogeō (eu + legō), whose semantic range depends on the subject. With God as subject it means to bless; with a believer as subject and God as object, to praise; with a believer as subject in the context of persecution, as here, simply to speak well of, to refrain from retaliation in speech. It is not invoking divine favor upon persecutors.

φρόνιμος — Self-Validating Pseudo-Wisdom

Romans 12:16 — "Never be wise in your own sight." φρόνιμος (wise (in a negative sense: conceited)). The predicate nominative plural phronimos, from the same root as phroneō, here denotes one who has a thought that entrances him, a pseudo-wisdom in which possession of an opinion becomes self-validating: intellectual vanity masquerading as discernment, the conflation of personal opinion with doctrinal truth.

ἐξουσία — Delegated Authority

Romans 13:1 — "For there is no authority except from God." ἐξουσία (authority, delegated authority). ἐξουσία (here the predicate nominative singular) carries the sense of rightful, recognized, officially granted power: authority that comes from a source above the one exercising it. The statement is absolute: no ἐξουσία of any kind, in any sphere, at any level, does not derive from God.

ἄρχων — Holder of Delegated Governmental Power

Romans 13:3 — "For rulers are not a terror." ἄρχων (governing authority, official of state). In Greek civic usage ἄρχων designated one of the rulers of Athens, and the term became generalized to mean any holder of delegated governmental power. The articular nominative plural is generic, denoting the class of individuals entrusted with enforcing freedom, privacy, and property within the national entity.

ἔπαινος — Legitimate Recognition, Not Flattery

Romans 13:3 — "and you will receive his approval." ἔπαινος (legitimate praise, approval, recognition). ἔπαινος is legitimate recognition, not flattery or fawning commendation. It is the recognition that accrues to the citizen who operates within the structure of legitimate authority and fulfills the duties that establishment requires.

μάχαιρα — The Sword of Capital Punishment

Romans 13:4 — "for he does not bear the sword in vain." μάχαιραν (the sword, from μάχαιρα). μάχαιρα is the symbol of capital punishment and of the judicial authority to execute. In the Roman world the sword was the instrument of official execution for citizens (decapitation), as distinguished from crucifixion for non-citizens; here it stands for the whole apparatus of punitive jurisprudence: apprehension, trial, verdict, and sentence.

εἰκῇ — Not for Nothing

Romans 13:4 — "for he does not bear the sword in vain." εἰκῇ (without cause, to no purpose, for nothing). εἰκῇ means without cause, to no purpose, for nothing; the clause reads he does not wear the sword for nothing. Capital punishment is not ornamental: it puts teeth in the law and is the final deterrent of jurisprudence.

ἀνάγκη — Structural Necessity

Romans 13:5 — "Therefore one must be in subjection." ἀνάγκη (it is necessary). ἀνάγκη is a noun of necessity or compulsion, best translated it is necessary. Its force is not moral suasion or prudential advice but structural necessity, arising from the nature of freedom itself: freedom cannot exist without authority, and authority must precede freedom.

τελέω — To Discharge an Obligation in Full

Romans 13:6 — "you also pay taxes." τελέω (to pay in full). The root meaning of τελέω is to finish or complete, but here it means to carry out, to put into full operation, and so to pay: to discharge an obligation in full.

λειτουργός — Public Servant

Romans 13:6 — "for the authorities are ministers of God." λειτουργός (public servant). λειτουργός comes from the vocabulary of public administration: one who performs a public service, an official whose function serves the community. It had no inherent religious connotation in classical usage. Paul uses it to show that the civil servant, from head of state to sanitation worker, functions within the structure God has ordained for human society; the genitive of God speaks of institutional legitimacy, not personal righteousness.

Romans 15:16 — "to be a minister of Christ Jesus." λειτουργόν (minister). The accusative singular noun leitourgos (λειτουργός) carries several related meanings: (1) a servant; (2) a government official — the term reflects the principle of divine establishment, under which government officials are servants, not masters; (3) a Levitical priest functioning at the altar, as the word is used in Hebrews 8:2; and (4) a communicator of Bible doctrine — in Paul's era designated apostle, in the present church age designated pastor-teacher.

αὐτός — Intensive Pronoun

Romans 13:6 — "attending to this very thing." αὐτός (this same thing). The phrase to this same thing uses the intensive pronoun αὐτός to emphasize the identity of the function: public service is a legitimate vocation in its own right, not merely incidental labor.

λόγος — Governing Principle, Not Saying

Romans 13:9 — "are summed up in this word." λόγος (principle). ἐν with the locative of οὗτος and λόγος yields not in this saying but in this principle. λόγος here carries doctrinal weight: a governing principle, not merely a quoted saying.

πλησίον — The One Near You

Romans 13:9 — "You shall love your neighbor as yourself." πλησίον (the one near you). The word rendered neighbor is not a noun but an adverb of place, πλησίον, near, in the vicinity of. The article τόν before it particularizes the reference: not an abstract category of person but a specific individual, the one near you, whoever is in your periphery.

κακός — Crime and Human Good

Romans 13:10 — "Love does no wrong to a neighbor." κακός (evil). κακός in Pauline usage covers two domains. In association with sin it denotes crime, the overt violation of another's life, freedom, or property. In association with human good, the well-intentioned activity of the old sin nature under the energy of the flesh, it denotes the most insidious evil, because human good erodes freedom under the guise of benevolence.

πλήρωμα νόμου — Fulfillment of Codex 1

Romans 13:10 — "therefore love is the fulfilling of the law." πλήρωμα νόμου (fulfillment of the law). In πλήρωμα νόμου the law in view is Codex 1 of the Mosaic Torah, the criminal code defining freedom through the prohibitions of the Decalogue. Impersonal love fulfills Codex 1 by eliminating at the mental attitude level the sins from which criminal conduct originates.

ὥρα — The Appointed Moment

Romans 13:11 — "that the hour has come." ὥρα (hour, appointed moment). ὥρα is used both for a unit of clock time and, as here, for a critical or appointed moment. With ἤδη the predicate nominative construction, it is already the hour, carries the force of a solemn announcement.

σωτηρία — Deliverance, Here the Rapture

Romans 13:11 — "For salvation is nearer to us now than when we first believed." σωτηρία (deliverance). σωτηρία is usually rendered salvation, but its range includes deliverance in the broader sense. With the rapture of the church as the eschatological horizon, the referent here is the rapture itself, the ultimate deliverance of the royal family from this present age.

νύξ / ἡμέρα — Phase Two and Phase Three

Romans 13:12 — "The night is far gone." νύξ (night). νύξ, with the generic article, is a metaphor for the duration of the Church Age, phase two of the plan of God: the believer's life on earth between salvation and physical death or the resurrection of the Church. Night here does not carry a primarily moral connotation; it stands in contrast to day, phase three, eternity.

Romans 13:12 — "the day is at hand." ἡμέρα (day). ἡμέρα represents physical death or the Rapture of the Church, whichever ends the believer's current phase of existence first; it is the doorway to phase three.

ὅπλα — Hoplite Armor

Romans 13:12 — "and put on the armor of light." ὅπλα (armor, from ὅπλον). ὅπλα originally meant the equipment of a Greek heavy infantryman and by Paul's time was applied to Roman military armor in all its components. The pieces are not listed here; that is reserved for Ephesians 6:10–17. The armor of light is maximum doctrine resident in the soul.

κῶμος / μέθη, κοίτη / ἀσέλγεια, ἔρις / ζῆλος — The Three Couplets of Romans 13:13

Romans 13:13 — "not in carousing." κῶμος (rioting). κῶμος was originally a procession in honor of Dionysus and by extension a disorderly assembly in which constituted authority has been set aside. It represents the rejection of externally constituted authority in any sphere.

Romans 13:13 — "drunkenness." μέθη (drunkenness). μέθη is intoxication resulting from the failure of personal volition to regulate intake. It represents the rejection of one's own authority over oneself, the abdication of volitional self-discipline.

Romans 13:13 — "not in sexual immorality." κοίτη (fornication). κοίτη in this context is illicit sexual intercourse in all its forms, both normal fornication (one man, one woman outside marriage) and abnormal sexual degeneracy.

Romans 13:13 — "sensuality." ἀσέλγεια (licentiousness, wantonness). ἀσέλγεια is the ungoverned mental orientation that lusts after illicit sexual experience: the inner disposition of licentiousness rather than a specific overt act, the failure of volitional self-discipline at the level of thought.

Romans 13:13 — "not in quarreling." ἔρις (strife). ἔρις is discord and contention arising from mental attitude sins: the overt result of uncontrolled arrogance, jealousy, and vindictiveness expressing itself in relational conflict.

Romans 13:13 — "and jealousy." ζῆλος (jealousy). ζῆλος, in its negative sense, is jealousy as a mental attitude sin and the internal cause of strife (ἔρις). It orients toward its object with destructive intent (maligning, gossiping, judging, grudge-bearing) rather than with the impersonal love the honor code demands.

Κύριον Ἰησοῦν Χριστόν — Putting On a Person

Romans 13:14 — "But put on the Lord Jesus Christ." Κύριον (the Lord Jesus Christ, from κύριος). The three accusative singular direct objects, Κύριον, Ἰησοῦν, Χριστόν, together identify the full person and office of the Savior. The command is not to put on a system of doctrine in the abstract but a person; maturity adjustment to the justice of God is inseparable from occupation with Christ. This phase-two command is not to be confused with the baptism of the Holy Spirit, which is phase one, non-volitional, and unrepeatable.

ἐπιθυμίαι (Plural) — The Full Range of the Flesh's Distractions

Romans 13:14 — "to gratify its desires." ἐπιθυμία (lusts). εἰς ἐπιθυμίας, with reference to its lusts, uses the plural of ἐπιθυμία (strong desire, craving, lust). The plural is significant: it covers the full range of distractions the old sin nature can generate, not only overtly sinful appetites but socially approved pursuits, such as a crusade to reform society or a consuming business ambition, that divert the believer from daily intake of doctrine.

πίστις — Doctrine, That Which Is Believed

Romans 14:1 — "weak in faith." πίστις (faith; faithfulness; doctrine (body of belief)). πίστις carries three related connotations: (1) faith, non-meritorious trust or confidence in the active sense; (2) faithfulness, as an attribute of reliability; (3) doctrine, that which is believed, the body of belief in the passive sense. The third connotation governs in Romans 14:1, as it does throughout Hebrews 11, so the weak believer is weak in the doctrine.

λάχανον — Vegetables, Not Herbs

Romans 14:2 — "eats only vegetables." λάχανον (vegetables). The direct object is the accusative plural of λάχανον, derived from λαχαίνω, to dig in a garden; hence, what is dug out of the garden: vegetables. The rendering herbs in older versions is a mistranslation. The word designates the ascetic restriction to a meatless diet.

τίς — The Interrogative of Indignant Challenge

Romans 14:4 — "Who are you to pass judgment." τίς (who are you?). The nominative interrogative pronoun τίς follows σύ. In context it is an idiom of indignant challenge, equivalent to Who do you think you are?; it is not a request for biographical information but a challenge to the weak believer’s assumed authority to judge another believer.

στήκω — To Stand Firm, a Military Word

Romans 14:4 — "he stands or falls." στήκω (to stand firm, to be stabilized). στήκω, a favorite of Paul’s, is a Hellenistic present-tense form derived from the perfect of ἵστημι, which accounts for its stative, stabilized meaning. It is a military word denoting stabilized defense or steady disciplined advance (compare 1 Corinthians 16:13, Philippians 4:1, Galatians 5:1). Paired with πίπτω: the believer stands firm or becomes a casualty before his own Lord.

κύριος — The Preferred Reading over θεός in Romans 14:4

Romans 14:4 — "for the Lord is able to make him stand." κύριος (Lord, master). The subject of the final clause in the better manuscripts is not θεός (Textus Receptus) but κύριος, supported by the Alexandrian witnesses, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus and the papyri; hence for the Lord, not for God. The article is generic, identifying the Lord Jesus Christ as master of the household slave, the controlling image of the verse.

κρίνω — Judging Days Is Judging People

Romans 14:5 — "esteems one day as better than another." κρίνω (to judge, to reach a decision, to consider). The choice of κρίνω is precise and intentional. The weak believer does not merely observe a holy day for himself; he judges days, and in judging days he judges people who do not share his calendar. When his calendar becomes the standard for measuring others, κρίνω has exceeded its legitimate domain and become an instrument of arrogant legalism.

ἕκαστος — Each One, the Privacy of the Priesthood

Romans 14:5 — "Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind." ἕκαστος (each one). The subject of the command is the nominative singular adjective ἕκαστος, used substantivally and carrying the full weight of individual identity before God. It emphasizes personal privacy, personal responsibility and each believer’s right to occupy his own position in the plan of God without another’s standards being imposed on him; it establishes the individual character of the priesthood of the believer.

ἀποθνῄσκω — Death as Departure

Romans 14:8 — "if we die, we die to the Lord." ἀποθνῄσκω (to die, to depart from life). ἀποθνῄσκω is a compound of ἀπό (from, away from) + θνήσκω (to die). The compound emphasizes the departure involved in death: death as separation from the body and from temporal existence.

τί — Neuter Interrogative, Why

Romans 14:10 — "Why do you pass judgment on your brother?" τί (why, from τίς). The neuter gender of the interrogative shifts the translation from who to why: the question is not one of identity but of motivation and cause.

βῆμα τοῦ θεοῦ — The Tribunal of God

Romans 14:10 — "the judgment seat of God." βῆμα (judgment seat, tribunal). βῆμα is an elevated judicial seat or tribunal. The possessive genitive here is from θεός, not Χριστός as in 2 Corinthians 5:10. The use of θεός emphasizes that the one presiding at the tribunal, the Lord Jesus Christ, is God, with full divine cognizance of all facts (John 5:22); every believer will receive a completely fair evaluation.

πᾶς — Universality Without Exception

Romans 14:11 — "every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to God." πᾶν γόνυ (every knee, from πᾶς). The subject of the oath is πᾶν γόνυ, nominative neuter singular. πᾶς as a nominative modifier asserts universality with no exceptions among those in view, here the entire royal family of God. It is used twice in the verse, with γόνυ (every knee) and γλῶσσα (every tongue), so that no member of the royal family of God is excluded from the big genuflex.

ἕκαστος — Individual Accountability at the Judgment Seat of Christ

Romans 14:12 — "each of us." ἕκαστος (each one). The subject is the nominative singular adjective ἕκαστος used as a substantive. The word is deliberate and emphatic: accountability at the judgment seat of Christ is intensely personal, and no corporate identity absorbs or distributes it. The genitive plural ἡμῶν identifies the subject specifically as the royal family of God, Church Age believers.

λόγος — An Account Rendered to the Living Logos

Romans 14:12 — "will give an account." λόγον (an account, from λόγος). The accusative direct object λόγον means a rendering of accounts, a statement of definite content. With δίδωμι it forms an eschatological paronomasia: each believer gives a logos to the living Logos, the Lord Jesus Christ (John 1:1). The word chosen for account is the same root as the title of the eternal Son of God.

ἀλλήλων — Reciprocity in the Royal Family of God

Romans 14:13 — "pass judgment on one another." ἀλλήλων (each other). The direct object is the accusative plural of the reciprocal pronoun ἀλλήλων. Reciprocity in the modus vivendi of the royal family of God is the controlling principle: what is prohibited toward one class is prohibited toward all.

Romans 14:19 — "mutual upbuilding." εἰς ἀλλήλους (to each other, from ἀλλήλων). The verse closes with εἰς ἀλλήλους, to each other. The reciprocal pronoun confirms that the blessing generated by the mature believer's advance is not directed inward but flows outward to the community of the royal family of God, the mechanism by which blessing by association reaches every believer in his periphery.

οὐδείς — Absolute Scope Within the Non-Essentials

Romans 14:14 — "nothing is unclean in itself." οὐδείς (nothing). The predicate nominative neuter οὐδείς governs the entire clause. The scope of the declaration is absolute within its context: no food, no beverage, no day (none of the non-essentials under discussion) is in and of itself categorically unclean.

κοινός — Common, and Ceremonially Unclean

Romans 14:14 — "nothing is unclean in itself." κοινός (unclean). κοινός carries two semantic fields: (1) common, shared, that which comes into contact with something else; and (2) ceremonially impure or unclean. In the Septuagint it translates the Hebrew vocabulary for ceremonial impurity under the Mosaic Law. Paul uses it to address both the Jewish weak believer bound by the levitical food code and the Gentile weak believer bound by ascetic taboos, with the same doctrinal principle.

ἐκεῖνος — The Remote Demonstrative Marking the Weak Believer

Romans 14:14 — "it is unclean for anyone who thinks it unclean." ἐκεῖνος (to that one). The clause concludes with the dative singular of the remote demonstrative ἐκεῖνος, which resumes and refers back to the weak believer just identified. It is translated to that one, not merely to him, emphasizing the precise category under discussion; the remoteness of the demonstrative reinforces the distinction between the strong believer and the weak believer (the exception).

Romans 14:15 — "the one for whom Christ died." ἐκεῖνος (him, the weak believer). The accusative direct object is the remote demonstrative ἐκεῖνος, used as a third-person pronoun for the weak believer. The remote demonstrative carries distance and distinction: the other person, whose conscience is full of legalism, hypocrisy and rigidity with respect to non-essentials.

περιπατέω — Technical Term for the Pattern of Daily Conduct

Romans 14:15 — "you are no longer walking in love." περιπατέω (you walk). The verb is the present active indicative of περιπατέω, used throughout Paul's epistles as a technical term for the pattern of the believer's daily life and conduct.

ἀγάπη — Impersonal Love as the Commanded Standard

Romans 14:15 — "walking in love." ἀγάπη (love). In the royal family honor code ἀγάπη denotes impersonal love: a relaxed mental attitude toward all believers based on the subject's doctrinal integrity, not on the character or behavior of the object. It is distinguished from personal love (erōs, philia, storgē), which is selective and object-focused. Every New Testament command to love the brethren or the neighbor uses ἀγαπάω, a command to impersonal love, never to universal personal love.

βλασφημέω — Blasphemy Toward God, Slander Toward Men

Romans 14:16 — "be spoken of as evil." βλασφημέω (to slander). Used in relation to God, βλασφημέω denotes blasphemy. Used in relation to men it means to defame, to injure the reputation, to slander: to spread false reports, utter falsehoods, circulate known sins, impugn by innuendo or maligning.

ἀγαθός — Good of Intrinsic Value

Romans 14:16 — "what you regard as good." ἀγαθός (the good). The subject of the passive verb is the nominative neuter singular of ἀγαθός used as a substantive. It is good of intrinsic value: the advance to spiritual maturity under the privacy of the priesthood and the function of the royal family honor code. It is not moral behavior or philanthropic activity but the specific result of the plan of God through the mature believer, maturity adjustment to the justice of God. The same word appears in Romans 8:28, a promise belonging to the mature believer.

δικαιοσύνη — Divine Righteousness and Imputed Righteousness

Romans 14:17 — "righteousness." δικαιοσύνη (righteousness imputed at salvation). δικαιοσύνη is the first predicate nominative. In Romans it carries two interlocking senses: the perfect righteousness belonging to God's own nature, and that same righteousness imputed judicially to the believer at salvation. Both are operative in 14:17; the imputed righteousness is the platform on which all subsequent divine blessing rests.

χαρά — Divine Happiness (plus H), Not Emotion

Romans 14:17 — "joy." χαρά (happiness). χαρά denotes a happiness surpassing anything achievable through human resources, a sharing in the very happiness of God, technically designated plus H. It is not an emotion generated by favorable circumstances but a steady-state condition maintained by an interior resource.

Romans 15:13 — "fill you with all joy." χαρᾶς (happiness). Chara is conventionally rendered joy, but this translation has become theologically misleading because of its association with emotional expression. The word denotes a thought-category, not an emotional state. It is better rendered happiness.

Romans 15:32 — "I may come to you with joy." ἐν χαρᾷ (in happiness). The phrase 'in happiness' renders the prepositional phrase en chara (ἐν χαρᾷ) — not the sharing of momentary emotional pleasure, but the sharing of the happiness of God, the inner stabilizer resident in the mature believer.

Χριστός — Appointed, Not Merely Anointed

Romans 14:18 — "Whoever thus serves Christ is acceptable to God and approved by men." Χριστῷ (the Christ, from Χριστός). The participle governs the dative indirect object Χριστῷ. The generic use of the definite article with Χριστός emphasizes the uniqueness of the second person of the Trinity as the God-man in hypostatic union. Χριστός carries the force not merely of anointed but of appointed: the one appointed as Savior of the world.

δόκιμος — Approved After Testing, Respected

Romans 14:18 — "Whoever thus serves Christ is acceptable to God and approved by men." δόκιμος (respected). The second predicate nominative, introduced by καί, is δόκιμος: approved after examination and testing, here carrying the sense of respected, held in regard. Being respected by man is the function of the royal ambassadorship, by which the believer represents God before humanity.

διώκω — Military Term for Exploiting a Breakthrough

Romans 14:19 — "let us pursue." διώκω (we run after). διώκω originally had two ranges: to impel, to set in motion, to drive; and to pursue, chase, persecute and expel. It became a standard military term for exploiting a breakthrough, the momentum of pursuit after the enemy line has been broken, and that military connotation is active in Paul's usage here.

καταλύω — Demolition of a Building

Romans 14:20 — "destroy the work of God." καταλύω (to demolish). καταλύω means to destroy, demolish, tear down, nullify, abrogate, specifically the demolition of a building. The compound (kata, down, and lyō, to loose, dissolve) reveals its force. In 14:20 it describes the destruction of the edification complex being built in the weak believer's soul.

καθαρός — Ceremonially Pure

Romans 14:20 — "Everything is indeed clean." καθαρός (clean). πάντα (all things, every category of food) takes as predicate nominative the neuter plural of καθαρός, ceremonially pure, clean. The statement is absolute: all foods are clean. To the Gentile believer this means edible without restriction; to the Jewish believer, no longer bound by Mosaic dietary law in the Church Age.

καλός — Honorable, Freighted with the Honor Code

Romans 14:21 — "It is good." καλός (it is honorable). Verse 21 opens with the predicate nominative neuter singular of καλός: honorable, noble, admirable, a term freighted with the full weight of the royal family honor code. It refers to the conduct of the royal family under the honor code in relation to weaker members of the body.

κρέας — Meat, Not Food in General

Romans 14:21 — "not to eat meat." κρέας (meat). The accusative plural direct object κρέας means meat, not food in general. The taboo in view is the vegetarian scruple of the weak believer.

οἶνος — Fermented Wine

Romans 14:21 — "drink wine." οἶνος (wine). οἶνος is the standard Greek term for fermented grape wine, used in John 2:1–11, 1 Timothy 5:23 and Romans 14:21, and always referring to alcoholic wine in context. As with eating, the aorist infinitive of πίνω indicates a specific occasion, not a policy of permanent abstinence.

προσκόπτω — To Strike Against, the Blind Man's Stumble

Romans 14:21 — "causes your brother to stumble." προσκόπτω (to stumble). προσκόπτω (pros, against, and koptō, to strike) means literally to strike or dash against something, the image of a blind person stumbling over an unseen obstacle. It is an apt analogy for the weak believer, blind in the soul because he lacks doctrine. The active voice assigns the stumbling to the weak believer himself.

μακάριος — Happy Is, the Shared Happiness of God

Romans 14:22 — "Blessed is the one." μακάριος (happy is). The subject is μακάριος, predicate nominative masculine singular. The word usually appears in the plural, conventionally translated blessed; in the singular it emphasizes the state of a specific category of person, happy is. It is not happiness contingent on circumstances but the shared happiness of God imputed to the mature believer who has cracked the maturity barrier.

εἰμί — The Explanatory Copula, Equivalence Not Identity

Romans 14:23 — "For whatever does not proceed from faith is sin." εἰμί (is tantamount to). The explanatory use of the copula eimi (εἰμί) then follows, indicating equivalence rather than identity: “is tantamount to” or “is equivalent to.” The predicate nominative is hamartia (ἁμαρτία), personal sin. The grammar is decisive here. The explanatory copula signals equivalence, not identity.

ἕκαστος — Distributive, Not Collective

Romans 15:2 — "Let each of us please his neighbor." ἕκαστος (each one). The verse opens with the adjective ἕκαστος (hekastos), nominative masculine singular, functioning here as a substantive: each one. The term is not collective but distributive. God does not address the congregation as an undifferentiated mass; He addresses each soul as an individual.

οἰκοδομή — The Construction of a Building

Romans 15:2 — "to build him up." οἰκοδομή (edification, construction). The term derives from the Greek noun οἰκοδομή (oikodomē), itself a compound of οἶκος (oikos, a house or building) and the classical verb δέμω (demō, to build, to erect, to construct). The compound therefore means to construct a building. In the New Testament it is applied metaphorically to the construction of spiritual maturity in the soul and human spirit of the believer.

ὁμοθυμαδόν — With One Motivation

Romans 15:6 — "that together you may with one voice glorify." ὁμοθυμαδόν (with one motivation). The next word is the adverb ὁμοθυμαδόν (homothymadon), a compound of the adverb ὁμο- (homo-, meaning together or in the same place) and θυμός (thymos, the mind or soul under strong passion — anger, rage, or simply intense motivation). The compound adverb conveys the inner unity of a group engaged in similar action. Corrected translation: with one motivation.

στόμα — The Mouth as the Message Spoken

Romans 15:6 — "with one voice." ἐν ἑνὶ στόματι (by one message). The prepositional phrase that follows is ἐν (en) plus the instrumental singular of στόμα (stoma, mouth). In Romans 15:6 the phrase therefore does not mean 'with one physical mouth' but by one message.

ἀγαθωσύνη — The Quality of Intrinsic Good

Romans 15:14 — "full of goodness." ἀγαθωσύνης (goodness). The possessive genitive singular from the substantive agathōsynē (ἀγαθωσύνη) is a Koine coinage. The suffix indicates the quality possessed by one who is agathos (ἀγαθός) — good of intrinsic value. The intrinsic good within the believer is Bible doctrine.

τολμηρότερον — More Boldly, More Alertly

Romans 15:15 — "I have written to you very boldly." τολμηρότερον (more boldly, more alertly). In adverbial form the comparative yields: more boldly, more alertly, with greater audacity.

ἱερουργέω — To Perform Sacred Rites

Romans 15:16 — "in the priestly service of the gospel of God." ἱερουργοῦντα (performing sacred rites). The compound means to perform sacred rites — specifically the ritual functions of a priest at the altar.

καύχησις — The Esprit de Corps of the Royal Family

Romans 15:17 — "I have reason to be proud." καύχησιν (esprit de corps). The direct object is the accusative singular of kauchēsis (καύχησις), a noun consistently rendered 'boasting' in most English translations, including the King James Version. Kauchēsis here denotes the esprit de corps of the royal family: the inner confidence, momentum, and collective identity that flows from knowing what is essential and what is not, from being inflexible about doctrine and completely flexible in its application. It is not arrogance; it is aristocracy in function.

νυνί — Now, a Decisive Transition

Romans 15:23 — "But now." νυνί (now). The adverb of time νυνί (nyni) — now — marks a decisive transition in Paul's situation.

ἐπιποθία — A Very Strong Longing

Romans 15:23 — "since I have longed for many years to come to you." ἐπιποθίαν (a very strong longing). The accusative singular direct object is ἐπιποθία (epipothia), a compound noun conveying a very strong longing or desire. The descriptive present tense portrays what is actively present in Paul's soul at the moment of writing.

εὐδοκέω — To Decide With Pleasure

Romans 15:26 — "have been pleased to make some contribution." εὐδόκησαν (have decided with pleasure). The main verb is the aorist active indicative of eudokeō (εὐδοκέω), from eu (εὖ, well, good) + dokeō (δοκέω, to think, to assume). The compound means to think well of something, to be pleased, to take delight in, and therefore to decide for. Used with an infinitive, as here, it expresses a choice arising from proper motivation — a pleasurable decision. The corrected translation: have decided with pleasure.

ὀφειλέτης — Under Honor Obligation

Romans 15:27 — "and indeed they owe it to them." ὀφειλέται (debtors, those who are obligated). The predicate noun opheiletai (ὀφειλέται), nominative plural of opheiletēs (ὀφειλέτης), means 'debtors' or 'those who are obligated.' The obligation in view is not a legal debt but an honor code obligation — a moral indebtedness arising from the receipt of spiritual blessings through the Jewish channel.

σαρκικός — Material Things, Not a Moral Category

Romans 15:27 — "in material blessings." ἐν τοῖς σαρκικοῖς (in the material things). The prepositional phrase concluding the verse is en tois sarkikois (ἐν τοῖς σαρκικοῖς), in the material things.
