The adjective sarkikos (σαρκικός) here functions not as a moral category but as a category of material or physical provision — money, goods, practical support — as distinct from spiritual or doctrinal things. The contrast is not between sin and holiness but between two spheres of value: the spiritual and the material.

προστάτις — Patroness

Romans 16:2 — "for she has been a patron of many and of myself as well." προστάτις (patroness). The predicate nominative is prostatis (προστάτις), meaning patroness, one who provides great assistance, one who stands before another in advocacy and support. In the ancient world, a patron was a person of means who recognized talent in another who lacked resources and provided the material support necessary for that person's work to continue.

XXII.The Definite Article

The Generic Article

Romans 9:5 — "is the Christ." ὁ Χριστός (the Christ). After the ablative of source construction, from whom, with the verb again implied by ellipsis, comes the predicate nominative ho Christos. The generic article before Christos underscores the uniqueness of his person: not merely a christ but the singular Anointed One of Israel's entire prophetic anticipation.

Romans 9:6 — "the word of God." ὁ λόγος (the Word of God, from λόγος). The noun subject ho logos takes the possessive genitive tou theou. The definite article carries a generic force, denoting the absolute uniqueness of the canon of Scripture. Logos means more than word; it encompasses the thought that words convey, the ordered communication of meaning.

Romans 9:17 — "For the Scripture says." γραφή (the Scripture). The nominative singular graphē, writings, is used with the generic definite article to designate the Old Testament canon as a sacred and authoritative body of literature, the Scripture; the article sets it apart as the Word of God in a categorical sense.

Romans 9:20 — "what is molded." πλάσμα (what is molded, from πλάσσω). The subject πλάσμα, nominative neuter singular, denotes what is formed or molded, the product of the potter. It is an articular noun functioning as a generic singular: it refers to the category of molded objects as such, not to a specific vessel, a sense preserved by what is molded.

Romans 9:27 (Isaiah 10:22) — "the number of the sons of Israel." ἀριθμός (number). The subject of the protasis is ἀριθμός (number, root of English arithmetic). The article accompanying it is a generic article, comprehending racial Israel as a single whole: the totality of physical descendants of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob considered as one category.

Romans 9:30 — "that is, a righteousness that is by faith." τήν. The article τήν appears in the accusative in its generic use, comprehending divine righteousness as a unique category set entirely apart from all forms of creature righteousness: it marks δικαιοσύνην as a class unto itself.

Romans 10:6 — "the righteousness based on faith." δικαιοσύνη. The generic use of the definite article with dikaiosynē categorizes and classifies God's righteousness as absolutely unique, the only righteousness by which man can be justified before God.

Romans 10:9 — "God raised him from the dead." ὁ θεός. Hoti introduces the content of faith. The subject ho Theos carries a generic use of the article indicating both God the Father and God the Holy Spirit, both active in the resurrection of Christ (the Father: Colossians 2:12, 1 Thessalonians 1:10, 1 Peter 1:21; the Spirit: Acts 2:24, Romans 1:4, Romans 8:11, 1 Peter 3:18).

Romans 10:11 — "For the Scripture says." γραφή. The subject graphē has the generic use of the article, signaling that it is unique, a category unto itself: not a single passage in isolation but the Old Testament canon as the living, abiding word of God.

Romans 11:6 — "grace would no longer be grace." χάρις (grace). χάρις appears twice in verse 6, both times with the generic article. The generic article sets grace apart as a special category, grace as a system and the operative policy of the integrity of God, rather than a specific act of grace; a category that admits no compromise.

Romans 11:7 — "The elect obtained it." ἐκλογή (the election, the elected to privilege). The nominative singular ἡ ἐκλογή carries the generic article, marking the elect as a distinct and privileged category: believers in Israel who in every generation have trusted in the Lord Jesus Christ and possess imputed divine righteousness. ἐκλογή here is not abstract predestination but election to privilege.

Romans 11:7 — "but the rest were hardened." λοιποί (the rest, the others, from λοιπός). The nominative plural οἱ λοιποί, with the generic article, designates a special category: racial Jews who, despite physical descent from the patriarchs and the spiritual heritage of the Mosaic economy, remained unbelievers. Physical birth confers no standing before the justice of God; new birth is required.

Romans 11:8 — "God gave them." ὁ θεός (the God, from θεός). The subject ὁ θεός carries the article generically, marking the subject as fully definite and theologically specific: the God of Israel, the Lord Jesus Christ. Its use frames what follows as an act of divine initiative, in judicial consequence rather than grace.

Romans 11:11 — "salvation has come to the Gentiles." ἡ σωτηρία (the salvation, this salvation, from σωτηρία). The article with σωτηρία functions as a categorizing marker: this specific salvation, the salvation belonging to the Levitical-prophetic heritage of Israel (Codex Two of the Mosaic Law: offerings, priesthood, holy days, prophets), which now passes into the custody of Gentile client nations.

Romans 12:9 — "Abhor what is evil." πονηρός (the evil). The generic definite article with ponēros presents evil as a complete and separate category, distinct from all other categories of existence: the policy of Satan as ruler of this world and the function of the old sin nature. The doctrine resident in the soul generates the standard by which evil is recognized.

Romans 12:9 — "hold fast to what is good." ἀγαθός (the good). The object is the dative singular of agathos, good of intrinsic value; the generic definite article defines the good as a complete and separate category: adhere to the good. In Romans 12 it carries three referents: Bible doctrine of intrinsic value, the royal family honor code, and the equation of imputation.

Romans 12:21 — "Do not be overcome by evil." κακός (evil). The definite article before kakos is generic: it designates evil as a category, not a specific instance, and is not translated.

Romans 13:5 — "not only to avoid God's wrath." διὰ τὴν ὀργήν (because of the wrath). In διὰ τὴν ὀργήν the article is generic: the wrath, meaning wrath as a category, the punishment and wrath delegated from God to those in civil authority. This is the first and most common principle of subjection: fear of punishment.

Romans 13:10 — "Love does no wrong to a neighbor." ἀγάπη (love). The subject ἀγάπη has the generic article, which specifies a particular category of love: not personal love in any of its three forms but the impersonal love required by the royal family honor code, which gives privacy to others, tolerates non-essential differences, and keeps a relaxed mental attitude.

Romans 14:3 — "for God has welcomed him." ὁ θεός (the God, from θεός). The subject ὁ θεός has the generic use of the definite article, which comprehends a category as a single whole and distinguishes it from all other categories. The translation the God is therefore precise: the God, as opposed to all other claimants to divine authority.

Romans 15:1 — "We who are strong." ἡμεῖς οἱ δυνατοί (we, the strong). The nominative plural personal pronoun hēmeis (ἡμεῖς), we, is the subject. Standing in apposition to it is the nominative masculine plural adjective dunatos (δυνατός), meaning powerful, capable, strong. The combined construction, hēmeis hoi dunatoi, is rendered we, the strong. The definite article is generic: it identifies a category, the mature believer who has maximum doctrine resident in the soul.

Romans 15:3 — "For Christ did not please himself." ὁ Χριστός (the Christ). The subject is the nominative singular ho Christos (ὁ Χριστός), 'the Christ.' The definite article here is generic, employed to emphasize the absolute uniqueness of the Lord Jesus Christ. No better illustration of the generic article exists in the New Testament than its use with Christos.

Romans 16:10 — "Greet those who belong to the family of Aristobulus." τοὺς ἐκ τῶν Ἀριστοβούλου (those of the household of Aristobulus). The accusative plural direct object is drawn from the definite article used in its generic function, comprehending a class as a simple whole and distinguishing it from any other class. The prepositional phrase is formed from ἐκ (ek) plus the possessive genitive of the proper noun Aristobulus (Ἀριστόβουλος, Aristoboulos): the slaves of Aristobulus.

The Article as Demonstrative Pronoun

Romans 9:13 (Malachi 1:2–3) — "Jacob I loved." Ἰακώβ (that Jacob). The clause opens with an accusative singular definite article before the indeclinable proper noun Iakōb, marking Jacob as the direct object with God as implied subject. The article functions as a demonstrative pronoun, that Jacob, calling special attention to the person and investing the statement with pointed particularity.

Romans 9:25 (Hosea 2:23) — "Those who were not my people." τόν (those). The accusative singular definite article τόν functions as a demonstrative pronoun, those, and combines with a relative clause to identify the referent as Gentiles: those who are not my people. The possessive genitive of ἐγώ (my) indicates divine possession: God claims as his people those who have believed in Christ, effective from the moment of faith.

Romans 10:17 — "So faith comes from hearing." πίστις (that faith). The subject pistis has the definite article used as a demonstrative pronoun to single out a particular dynamic concept: that faith, the specific faith that is the non-meritorious means of salvation adjustment to the justice of God. It encompasses faith in Christ at salvation, the faith-rest technique, and reverse concentration. The second clause likewise uses the article demonstratively with akoē: that message.

Romans 10:20 (Isaiah 65:1) — "by those who did not seek me." τοῖς (by those). Paul uses the plural article tois as a demonstrative pronoun, by those, rather than a simple pronoun. Articles functioning as demonstratives carry a sharpness of reference, identifying a specific category with rhetorical precision; combined with the chiasmus they give the text a clipped, staccato urgency, pressing against the audience's resistance. In the second line the article as demonstrative again marks the Gentiles in whose interests Christ became manifest.

Romans 12:14 — "Bless those who persecute you." τοὺς διώκοντας (those who persecute). In tous diōkontas the definite article functions as a near-demonstrative: speak well of those, pointing to a specific category of people in the believer’s life who are actively pressing against him.

Romans 13:9 — "For the commandments." (this). The nominative neuter singular article functions as a demonstrative pronoun, this, pointing specifically to the portion of the Mosaic Law that pertains to criminal activity.

Romans 13:10 — "Love does no wrong to a neighbor." πλησίον (his neighbor). πλησίον, an adverb functioning as a substantive (near one, neighbor, those in one's periphery), is the indirect object, and the article with it functions as a personal pronoun: his neighbor.

Romans 13:14 — "for the flesh." σάρξ (your flesh). σάρξ here refers specifically to the old sin nature, and the definite article functions as a possessive pronoun: your flesh, your old sin nature. The verse does not command the elimination of the old sin nature (sinless perfection is not attainable in phase two) but the refusal to give it one's resources and attention.

Romans 14:1 — "the one who is weak." τόν (that one). The definite article with the participle of ἀσθενέω functions as a demonstrative pronoun, that one, so the phrase reads now that one who is weak. The article is in the accusative case as direct object of the command to receive.

Romans 15:3 — "The reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me." οἱ ὀνειδισμοί (the blasphemous insults). The nominative plural subject of the quotation is oneidismoi (ὀνειδισμοί), from the noun oneidismos (ὀνειδισμός), meaning insults, reproaches, abuses. The definite article functions as a demonstrative pronoun, pointing to a specific category of sin: blasphemy. The corrected translation is the blasphemous insults.

Romans 15:17 — "my work for God." τὰ πρὸς τὸν θεόν (in those things pertaining to God). The phrase 'in those things' translates a neuter plural definite article used as a demonstrative pronoun. The demonstrative function of the article sets this content apart for special emphasis: not just any things, but those specific doctrines.

Romans 15:31 — "delivered from the unbelievers in Judea." ἀπὸ τῶν ἀπειθούντων (from those who are disobedient). The preposition apo (ἀπό) governs the ablative plural of the definite article used as a demonstrative pronoun: 'from those.' The corrected translation of this phrase: that I may be delivered from those who are disobedient in Judea.

The Article of Previous Reference

Romans 9:22 — "What if God." ὁ θεός (the God). The subject ὁ θεός is nominative with the definite article signalling anaphoric reference: the same God who has been the subject of the discourse throughout the chapter. No new deity is being introduced; this is the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the Lord Jesus Christ as the God of Israel, who acted in sovereign freedom in the Exodus.

Romans 12:21 — "overcome evil with good." ἀγαθός (the good). The definite article before agathos carries previous-reference force, pointing back to Romans 8:28. The good in verse 21 is therefore not a general moral category but the specific content of God’s plan for the mature believer as articulated in the imputation structure of Romans 8.

Romans 15:6 — "glorify the God and Father." τὸν θεόν (the God). The accusative singular direct object is τὸν θεόν (ton theon). The definite article indicates previous reference — this is the God already under discussion.

The Article as Possessive Pronoun

Romans 10:1 — "prayer to God." δέησις. With deēsis stands the definite article functioning as a possessive pronoun, yielding my prayer.

Romans 10:3 — "their own." ἴδιος. With idios stand the understood noun dikaiosyne and the accusative definite article functioning as a possessive pronoun. Full translation: and by seeking to establish their own righteousness.

Romans 15:2 — "please his neighbor." τῷ πλησίον (his neighbor). The indirect object is πλησίον (plēsion), with the dative singular of the definite article functioning as a personal pronoun: his neighbor. Plēsion is originally an adverb meaning near or nearby, and when used as a noun it denotes whoever is in one's immediate social environment — the one in your periphery.

The Article as Relative Pronoun

Romans 10:5 — "the righteousness that is based on the law." τὴν δικαιοσύνην τήν. Dikaiosynē is bracketed by two definite articles, both accusative feminine singular. The first carries a back-reference to the human self-righteousness from keeping the law described in verses 3 and 4; the second functions as a relative pronoun: about the righteousness which is.

XXIII.Pronouns

ὅστις — The Indefinite Relative of Category

Romans 9:4 — "They are Israelites." ὅστις (who are of such a category as to be). Verse 4 opens with the nominative masculine plural of the indefinite relative pronoun hostis, which differs from the ordinary relative pronoun in that it designates a category rather than a specific individual: of such a kind as to be. It introduces the entire category of the Jewish people, believers and unbelievers alike, race and nation together.

Romans 16:6 — "who has worked hard for you." ἥτις (who is such a one as). The relative clause opens with the nominative feminine singular of the indefinite relative pronoun hostis (ἥτις). This is not the standard relative pronoun hos (ὅς). The indefinite relative pronoun carries a categorical force: it defines its subject not merely as an individual but as a representative of a distinct class of people.

Romans 16:12 — "who has worked hard in the Lord." ἥτις (who is such a one as). The relative clause describing Persis employs ἥτις (hētis), the indefinite relative pronoun, rather than the simple relative ἥ (hē). In Greek grammar, the indefinite relative pronoun does not express uncertainty but rather classifies its referent as belonging to a special category of unique individuals.

οὗτοι — The Demonstrative Identifying True Israel

Romans 9:6 — "belong to Israel." οὗτοι (these very ones, from οὗτος). The predicate is the demonstrative pronoun houtoi, these, these very ones, which emphasizes the true Israel: all born-again believers in Christ, the spiritual seed rather than the physical seed. It supplies the predicate nominative, requiring the implicit copula: are really Israel.

οὗτος + εἰμί — The Idiomatic Transition (This Means)

Romans 9:8 — "This means that." οὗτος (this means). The verse opens with a nominative neuter singular of the demonstrative houtos, referring to what immediately precedes, paired with a present active indicative of eimi. Together they form an idiomatic transition: literally that is, idiomatically this means. The construction signals that what follows is a doctrinal inference drawn from the argument of verses 6–7.

ὃς ἄν — The Indefinite Relative of a Definite Category

Romans 9:15 (Exodus 33:19) — "on whom I have mercy." ὃν ἄν (whomever). The relative pronoun hos with the indefinite particle an creates an indefinite relative pronoun, not vague or universalistic but specific in category. With eleeō the category is the believer who has cracked the maturity barrier through sustained positive volition toward doctrine; with oiktirō the contingency is salvation adjustment to the justice of God, faith in the Lord Jesus Christ.

Romans 16:2 — "in whatever she may need from you." ἐν ᾧ ἂν ὑμῶν χρῄζῃ (in whatever she may need from you). The scope of assistance is qualified by the prepositional construction en hō an chrēzē: the preposition en plus the relative pronoun hos plus the untranslatable particle an plus the present active subjunctive of chrēzō (χρῄζω), 'to have need of.' The particle an indicates uncertainty and contingency — Paul does not know what Phoebe's specific business in Rome is, and deliberately refrains from specifying it.

αὐτός — Attributive Use Meaning Same

Romans 9:17 (Exodus 9:16) — "For this very purpose." αὐτό (same, from αὐτός). The neuter singular accusative auto derives from the intensive pronoun autos in its attributive function, a relatively rare usage, where it carries the force of same rather than the ordinary third-person personal pronoun. Combined with the immediate demonstrative touto it reads: for this same purpose.

Romans 15:5 — "to live in such harmony with one another." τὸ αὐτὸ φρονεῖν (to be thinking the same things). The object of the verb is the present active infinitive of phroneō (φρονέω), with the accusative neuter singular of the intensive pronoun autos (αὐτός). The full phrase is to auto phronein — 'to be thinking the same things,' or more precisely, 'to be thinking the same category of things.'

The Emphatic Personal Pronoun

Romans 10:19 (Deuteronomy 32:21) — "I will make you jealous." ἐγώ (I). Paul quotes only the second half of Deuteronomy 32:21, God's reply. It begins with the emphatic personal pronoun egō, placed before the verb for special stress: the voice of the Lord Jesus Christ as the God of Israel speaking in the first person. The emphatic position underscores divine agency in the counter-provocation.

Romans 10:20 (Isaiah 65:1) — "those who did not seek me." ἐμέ (me). The accusative direct object is eme, the emphatic form of egō: me, the Lord Jesus Christ, the God of Israel, speaking through Isaiah's prophecy.

Romans 15:14 — "I myself am satisfied about you." καὶ αὐτὸς ἐγώ (even I myself). Paul reinforces his identity with the ascensive use of kai (καί) — translated even — combined with the repetition of the first-person singular personal pronoun egō (ἐγώ) and the predicate use of the intensive pronoun autos (αὐτός). In classical Greek, autos in the predicate position is translated self, emphasizing Paul's identity as an apostle. The prepositional phrase peri (περί) plus the genitive of the personal pronoun su (σύ) means concerning you.

ὅς — The Relative Pronoun Used as a Demonstrative

Romans 14:2 — "One person believes." ὅς (the one). There is no γάρ in the opening clause. Paul uses the nominative singular of the relative pronoun ὅς as a demonstrative pronoun designating a specific category of believer, a usage that reaches back to Sanskrit (yas) and is preserved in Homeric Greek. He is not speaking of a person who but pointing to a defined class: the mature believer as a type.

Romans 14:5 — "One person esteems one day." ὅς (this one / that one). The subject of each clause is the nominative singular of ὅς used in its demonstrative function. It refers not to a specific individual but to a category: this one, the weak believer, and in the second clause that one, the strong or mature believer.

αὐτός — Intensive Pronoun Serving as the Third-Person Pronoun

Romans 14:3 — "for God has welcomed him." αὐτόν (him, from αὐτός). The direct object is the intensive pronoun αὐτόν. Koine Greek has no third-person personal pronoun, and the intensive pronoun αὐτός fills that function. The referent is the mature or strong believer, not every believer indiscriminately.

ὅσος — As Many Things As

Romans 15:4 — "For whatever was written in former days." ὅσα (as many things as). The nominative neuter plural correlative particle hosa (ὅσα), from hosos (ὅσος), means as many things as, encompassing the entirety of the Old Testament corpus — every book, every verse, every word.

τις — The Indefinite Pronoun Delineating a Category

Romans 15:18 — "to speak of anything." τι (anything). The accusative neuter singular τι (ti), from the indefinite pronoun τις (tis), functions here not to express true indefiniteness but to delineate a category.

Romans 15:26 — "some contribution." κοινωνίαν τινά (a special offering). The accusative singular direct object combines the indefinite pronoun tis (τις) with the noun koinōnia (κοινωνία). In this context, tis is not indefinite but categorical — it marks a category of special significance, an emphatic use reflecting distinction and importance. Koinōnia ordinarily means fellowship or participation, but in a giving context it specifically denotes a contribution or offering — participation in a shared act of grace. The phrase therefore means a special offering or a distinguished contribution.

ἡμῶν vs. μου — Our Versus My

Romans 16:9 — "Greet Urbanus, our fellow worker in Christ, and my beloved Stachys." ἡμῶν … μου (our … my). The descriptive genitive plural of the personal pronoun ἐγώ (egō), rendered our, rather than my, indicates that Paul did not know Urbanus personally at the time of writing. The first-person plural signals knowledge by reputation rather than by direct acquaintance. Unlike Urbanus, whom Paul knew by reputation alone, Stachys was known personally.

τοιοῦτος — Of Such a Kind

Romans 16:18 — "For such persons." οἱ τοιοῦτοι (such believers). Next follows the lengthened demonstrative pronoun toioutos (τοιοῦτος), used here as a substantive adjective with the definite article. It designates a specific, identifiable category of believers — the weak reversionist type.

XXIV.Word Order and Rhetorical Devices

Foregrounding the Mother

Romans 9:10 — "when Rebekah had conceived children by one man, our forefather Isaac." Ῥεβέκκα (Rebecca). The nominative subject is the proper noun Rebekka. Paul names the mother, not the father, at the outset, a deliberate rhetorical strategy: by foregrounding Rebecca and deferring Isaac, he leads the reader toward the assumption that the mother will again be the issue, only to demonstrate that she is not.

Emphatic Fronting of the Object

Romans 9:13 (Malachi 1:2–3) — "but Esau I hated." Ἠσαῦ (but I hated that Esau). The postpositive de functions as an adversative, marking the contrast between the divine attitude toward Jacob and toward Esau. The direct object Esau is positioned first for emphasis, highlighting the person and the contrast: but I hated that Esau.

The Rhetorical Question Series (πῶς)

Romans 10:14 — "How then will they call on him in whom they have not believed?" πῶς (how). Pōs is used here not in its simple interrogative sense but as a rhetorical device of logical progression. Each pōs tightens the chain: the first question presupposes the second, and the second the third. The effect is a structured reductio exposing layer after layer of deficiency in the mission field, not to condemn the Gentiles who have not heard but to indict the failure of the client nation that should have sent the message. Pōs occurs four times across Romans 10:14–15.

The Debater's Formula ἀλλὰ λέγω

Romans 10:19 — "But I ask." ἀλλά (but I say). In Paul's debater's technique, alla plus legō, but I say, introduces a counter-question on behalf of a hypothetical advocate, which Paul then refutes with scriptural evidence. It appears twice in succession (verses 18 and 19), with the aoristic present of legō.

Chiasmus

Romans 10:20 (Isaiah 65:1) — "I have been found by those who did not seek me; I have shown myself to those who did not ask for me." χιασμός. Chiasmus, from the letter chi, arranges clauses in a crossing or inverted parallel structure for emphasis. Paul reverses the two lines of Isaiah 65:1, moving from chronological order (God-consciousness, then gospel-hearing) to logical-rhetorical order (gospel-hearing, then God-consciousness), forcing attention onto the fact of Gentile salvation: they were found; they received the gospel.

Gaps in Coverage — Stated Plainly

Romans 4:15 has no corresponding source chapter in the manuscript material. No entries exist for this verse.

Second-class conditions (contrary-to-fact) are illustrated at Romans 9:29 (Isaiah 1:9), the one verse in Romans 1–16 the source labels as second class. Fourth-class conditions (remote possibility) are named and defined in the source's four-class framework (laid out in connection with Romans 7:2), but no verse in Romans 1–16 is labeled as an instance.

This guide covers Romans 1:1–16:27, the whole epistle. Every citation carries its own quotation, Greek term, and explanation.
